INTRODUCTION. 

The supply of text books on corporation law is plentiful, and ranges in bulk from paper covered pamphlets of statutes through single volume manuals to multi-volume exhaustive editions.

This book will enable novitiates to acquire, without waste of time and effort, a working knowledge of the law of corporations of the state of New York. A reading of the proof sheets has convinced me that it supplies a great need and will be welcomed by instructors and students. 

Nor is it a book likely to be cast aside and forgotten by the graduate. It is terse, clear and accurate. 

Every working day and hour of the writer of this foreword has been occupied for more than twenty years with the subject of which this book treats. He has been favored by fortune with the privilege of sitting at the feet of wisdom and listening to the learned discussions of those distinguished members of the profession who constituted the Joint Legislative Committee and the committee composed of representatives of the bar associations, which drafted the revision of the New York corporation statutes begun in the year 1921 and completed in 1929.

Yet, notwithstanding the benefit derived from such constant drill, the examination of Professor Cady's work has been of pronounced value to him, not alone as a review and reminder of things once learned and then partially forgotten, but because the orderly and logical development of the subject, the apt citation, comparison and discussion of cases, and the discerning comment on the statutes, as they stand revised, throw upon the scene a clear and searching light which reveals in bold outline matter of substance otherwise difficult of discernment amongst the shadows. So I believe that whoever reads this book, be he student, instructor, practicing attorney or layman, will thereafter keep it on his book-shelf, within convenient reach.

The task of selecting and condensing from the tremendous mass of available material, the essence of the law of corporations as it is set forth in this book is one from which

IV INTRODUCTION 

a less industrious writer than Professor Cady might well recoil. The result which he has achieved could only have been accomplished by an author who combined with native talent, special training in the art of teaching and the technique of law book writing.

Not the least valuable feature of the book is its readableness. It holds one's interest, carries on along a straight and even course and lures the reader ever to turn another page, confident that he will find thereon some worthwhile recompense for his quest of knowledge. The book indicates the approach to practically every form of corporate problem. 

Professor Cady is to be congratulated upon the successful issue of a difficult and laborious undertaking. 

Ghank S. Sharp

Hon. Frank S. Sharp is Deputy Secretary of State of the State of 

New York in charge of the Corporation Division of the Department of State, and was of counsel to the Joint Legislative Committee, named in 1921, the work of which resulted in chap. 650 Laws of 1929, entitled “An Act to Amend the General Corporation law, generally."

12. Power to hold real property. § 1. 

Corporation Defined.

A corporation is a separate legal entity, created by association of its members in a public manner as permitted or compelled by a statute, vested by policy of law with rights, powers and privileges, and limited and controlled in its exercise thereof solely by principles of law. 

The corporation is brought into being for the benefit of its members. The legislature has no power to compel ordinary businesses to incorporate. Duckniet v. Harris, 209 N. Y. 17. Under the police power, the state may refuse to charter corporations to conduct businesses which are affected with a public interest, except under drastic conditions. Cady on Insurance, sec. 27; Ins. Law sec. 54. 

A statute directing the formation of a corporation for the insurance business, and containing provisions so drastic as to exclude from the business, by practical effect, other persons and corporations, for the benefit of a corporation directed to be incorporated by the statute, so as to constitute, in effect, a monopoly in the domain of private business, is unconstitutional under the 14th amendment to the U. S. Constitution; for "life, liberty and property" include also the right to earn a livelihood by any lawful calling,

and to pursue any livelihood or vocation. So, a statute of 

Massachusetts, supplementing a statute which required every owner of a motor vehicle to carry insurance to compensate others from accidents, and requiring all owners to contribute to the capital of a private or quasi public corporation to be formed to write such insurance, was, in the opinion of justices of the Massachusetts court, unconstitutional. In re Opinion of Justices, 171 N. E. 294 (Mass.).

The right to be a corporation is not a natural or civil right of persons, and unless the right is conferred by a statute or in some other way by a sovereign state, the relations and liabilities of those who intended to incorporate would be that of partnership. People v. Mackey, 255 Ill. 

144 at p. 156; Ernest v. Bartley, 1 Johns Cas. 319: Stevens v. Episcopal Ch. Hist. Co., 140 App. Div. 570, 125 N. Y.

Supp. 573. The policy of the state usually provides general laws under which all may incorporate, but where the objects of the corporation can not be attained under general laws a corporation may be created by special act. New 

York Constitution, Art. 8, sec. 1, see Appendix B. The courts can not interfere with the exercise of the legislative discretion conferred by the Constitution and exercised thereunder.

Some of the chief benefits of incorporating, from a member's standpoint are immunity from liability for the acts and debts of the corporation, except for the sum dedicated by him therefor; the privilege of conducting business in perpetuity, through the corporate officers under the corporate aegis, using the corporate name and seal; and the facility of business through aggregations of capital, contributed by many, and conducted by the best methods through the selection of a competent board of directors. For this the members abnegate the closer touch with the business, and the control of its policies and acts, which they would be able to exercise in a partnership. 

§ 2. Other Leading Definitions. 

Many have preferred to put the emphasis on the rights, powers, and privileges granted the corporation, instead of on the legal entity. Comyn defined a corporation as "a franchise created by the king" and "a body constituted by

policy with a capacity to take or to do." Comyn's Digest, p. 332. See Appendix D, infra. Chancellor Kent's definition is "a franchise possessed by one or more individuals, who subsist, as a body politic, under a special denomination, and are vested, by the policy of the law, with the capacity of perpetual succession, and of acting in several respects, however numerous the association may be, as a single individual." 2 Kent. Comm. p. 267. Strictly, however, the franchise is the right to exercise as a corporation the purposes granted-the corporation's area of authorized activity. Chief Justice Marshall's definition placed the emphasis on the juristic personality of the corporation, saying it is "that invisible, intangible, and artificial being, that mere legal entity. . . It is defined (in England) as a mere creature of the law." Kyd's definition, formulated in the first quarter of the 18th century, was "a collection of individuals united into one body under a special denomination, having perpetual succession under an artificial form, vested by the policy of law with the capacity of acting in several respects as an individual, particularly of taking and granting property, of contracting obligations, of suing and being sued, of enjoying privileges and immunities in common, and of exercising a variety of political rights more or less extensive according to the design of its creation, or any subsequent period of its existence." 1 Kyd on Corporations, sec. 13 (1713).

There being no physical entity to a corporation, the possession by the corporate entity of an "organic nature” is unthinkable. The term "legal entity" may be thought of as a "mere metaphorical recognition and designation of the legal, philosophical, political, and utilitarian considerations" which arise from the interplay of duties and liabilities peculiar to corporate organizations, to which the law gives effect. In re Brown's will, 252 N. Y. at p. 277; 

Farmers L. & T. Co. v. Pierson, 130 Misc. 110, 222 N. Y. 

Supp. 532. 

§ 3. Conflict of Laws. 

"A corporation created under the laws of a state is from its creation through the whole of its existence, a citizen of that state." Williams v. Village of Port Chester, 97 App.

Div. 84, 89 N. Y. Supp. 671, affirmed 183 N. Y. 550. It is a "person" within the meaning of laws regulating suits and actions, but it is the kind of a person who can not emigrate from the state. The laws of the state where the corporation is incorporated fix, limit and qualify the powers, franchises, capacities and liabilities both of the corporation and of its members, regardless of where the action is brought, and of course, must be proved as facts in actions in foreign states. In re Rochester H. & L. Co., 45 Hun, 126; Harrison v. Triplex Gold Mines Ltd., 33 Fed. (2d) 667; Sutherland v. Behn, Meyer & Co., 33 Fed. (2d) 643. 

§ 4. Usual Mode of Creating a Corporation. 

The statutes usually provide that a corporation is brought into being by the mere execution and filing of a certificate of incorporation by a stated minimum of persons, usually three, and as a perquisite for filing, the payment of certain fees to the state and county. Sec. 5 S. C. L. See Appendix

B. Filing gives a degree of publicity to the act of incorporating. In the discretion of the legislature, with the exercise of which the courts can not interfere, other steps may be required. U. S. Trust Co. v. Brady, 20 Barb. 119.

These are, usually, such as requiring the deposit of funds with the state for the security of those contracting with the corporation, the procuring of subscriptions to stock in advance of incorporating (Eastern Plankroad Co. v. 

Vaughan, 14 N. Y. 546), the filing of maps showing the proposed route of a transportation corporation (Lamming v. Galusha, 81 Hun 247, affirmed 151 N. Y. 648), or the payment in advance of stock subscribed for. Maxwell, Bank Comr. v. Thompson, 195 App. Div. 616, 186 N. Y. 

Supp. 208, appeal dismissed 231 N. Y. 542, affirmed 232 

N. Y. 619.

The rights, powers and privileges of a corporation are frequently more extensive than can be enjoyed by private persons. A corporation may have perpetual succession, G. C. L. sec. 14 subd. 1, and still take real property in fee for the same period. Nicoll v. N. Y. & E. R. R., 12 N. Y. 

121, Cases p. 163.

པ་ 

§ 5. The Legal Entity Regarded. 

The following statement in People v. Knapp, 206 N. Y. 

273, 29 N. E. 841, has been much criticised:-"A corporation . . . is a mere conception of the legislative mind. It exists only on paper through the command of the legislature that its mental conception shall be clothed with power." 

The words do not fit all cases. Where there is no fraud, the law treats a corporation both as respects the public and its members, not as a "mental conception" but as a substantial reality, and a separate entity. In re Mt. Sinai 

Hospital, 250 N. Y. 103, 164 N. E. 871. The corporation is by statute, a "person," Gen. Const. Law sec. 37; and masculine or neuter in gender. Ib. sec. 22. A corporation is not a "colored person," so as to come under restrictive covenants in a deed tho all its stockholders are of that designation. 

People's Pleasure Park Company v. Rohleder, 109 Va. 439: 

Cady's Cases on Pri. Corps. p. 17.

As respects the ownership and conveyance of property, the effect of corporate contracts, and the right to maintain actions to enforce rights or remedy corporate wrongs, courts of law, as distinguished from courts of equity, recognize the corporate entity only, and ignore the fact that members may have rights as against each other. The corporation may contract with its members as with strangers, may sue its members, and may be sued by them at law. 

Gerlen v. N. Y. Drug Co., Inc., 193 N. Y. Supp. 1. The corporation is an entity separate from its stockholders, even where one stockholder owns all, or nearly all, the stock -sometimes called "One-man" corporations. 

In the leading case of Button v. Hoffman, 51 Wis. 20, 20 N. W. 567 (1884), the plaintiff, an individual, was seeking to replevy a chattel. His proof showed that the chattel belonged to a corporation, all of whose shares of stock he owned by having purchased them in the market. The court held that this proof established that the corporation was the owner. Complaint dismissed. The leading case on this point in New York is Brock v. Poor, 216 N. Y. 387, where 

Mr. Justice Hiscock, writing for the court, said that "even complete ownership of capital stock does not operate to transfer the title to corporate property," and that “owner-

ship of capital stock is by no means identical with or equivalent to ownership of corporate property," and, quoting from Button v. Hoffman, said, "they have created a legal entity and that entity is alone responsible to persons dealing with it for the conduct of such business." In Saranac etc. Co. v. Arnold, 167 N. Y. 368, 374, it is said: "While the defendants owned substantially all the stock, they did not own the corporation itself. 

It was not their chattel but was a distinct legal entity, with the right to own property, and they could not appropriate its property to their own use." The property can not be taken to pay the debt of the principal stockholder. In re John Koke Co., 38 Fed. (2d) 232; Vanier v. 

Anti Saloon League etc., 238 N. Y. 463, 464. A mortgage that would be usurious if given by an individual may be valid if given by a one-man corporation; for the corporation is a single and complete creation, and, by statute in 

New York can not plead usury to avoid its obligations. 

Sec. 374 Gen. Business Law; see Salvin v. Myles Rty. Co., 227 N. Y. 51. The owner of a lease assigned it to a corporation formed to operate the premises. He owned practically all the capital stock, when an employee of a tenant on the premises was negligently injured through the fault of the corporation. It was held that, tho the corporation, as an entity, might be liable, the owner of the stock was not liable. Ellenkrieg v. Seibracht, 238 N. Y. 254, Cady's 

Cases p. 10. Maryland, Alabama, California, Texas, and some other states incline to disregard the corporate entity when dealing with one-man corporations. Swift v. Smith, 64 Md. 428, 5 Atl. 534; Bauernschmidt v. Bauernschmidt, 101 Md. 148, 60 Atl. 437; First Natl. Bank etc. v. Winchester, 119 Ala. 168, 24 So. 351; Wenoan Estate v. Hewlett, 193 Cal. 675, 227 Pac. 723; Gamer Paper Co. v. Tuscany, 264 S. W. 132 (Tex.).

Also courts have drawn a distinction between the stockholders and the artificial legal entity in the matter of the "residence" and "citizenship” of the corporation. For the purpose of fixing the county in which suits and actions are to be brought (excepting those concerning the title to real property and other cases covered by particular statutes),

the corporation is a resident of the county which is specified in the certificate of incorporation as the location of the principal place of business, altho the stockholders reside elsewhere, and the corporation has other offices at which a greater amount of business is done. Ajax Rubber Co., Inc. v. Devine Co., 126 Misc. 351; Cady's Cases p. 34; 

Western N. Y. Water Co. v. Buffalo, 242 N. Y. 202. It is a "citizen" of the state in which it is incorporated. In an action in the federal court, a corporation, incorporated in New York, was held to be a citizen of New York state, and thus capable of suing its stockholders in the federal courts, when practically all the stockholders resided in New Jersey. 

Doctor v. Harrington, 196 U. S. 574.

Those who have voluntarily and knowingly incorporated can not thereafter be heard to assert that as to themselves, though not to the world in general, the corporate form was a mere empty shell or cloak thrown around what was in fact a copartnership or joint venture. Thomashefsky v. 

Edelstein, 192 App. Div. 368, 182 N. Y. Supp. 707. The chief rights of the stockholder are: 

1. To vote for directors, if the class of stock which he holds is voting stock. 

2. To receive his proportionate share of dividends, whenever declared by the directors. This right is subject to be contracted away by him. 

3. To invest in new issues of stock. 

4. Such rights as the statutes may give him, as where the statutes require consents for certain corporate acts, or that certain information as to corporate finances, etc., be given on demand. 

5. At dissolution, after debts are paid, to receive his share of the assets in cash.

The distinction between the entity and the stockholders is further illustrated by the method established by law for the conduct of its affairs. The business of the corporation is conducted by the board of directors, or by the officers elected or agents appointed by the board of directors, and to the mere stockholders the corporation is an entity, separate and apart. The member is not liable on the contracts of the corporation, for there is no implied relation

of agency between himself and the corporation, and therefore he is not liable on the doctrine of undisclosed principal, nor are the contracts of the corporation joint contracts of the member and of the corporation. U. S. Shipping Board 

Emergency Fleet Corporation v. Tavas, 22 Fed. (2d) 398. 

In a corporation which deals in realty, no consents of the stockholders are required in order that the officers may sell the realty. Keating v. Coleman, 214 App. Div. 668, 213 N. 

Y. Supp. 213. Declarations and admissions of stockholders may not be received against the corporation; but the admissions of officers, in the scope of their authority are receivable. Pan Amer. Pet. Co. v. U. S., 9 Fed. (2d) 761. 

Richardson on Evidence, sec. 391. 

§ 6. The Legal Entity Disregarded. 

In a few exceptional instances to prevent slacking of justice against those hiding behind and pointing to the artificial legal entity as the culprit, the law has gone forth directly against those who, as officers, agents or stockholders of the corporation, committed the acts. The exceptions may be grouped under four heads: (a) Crime. 

Fraud on creditors and other frauds. (c) Illegalities.

Subsidiary corporations. U. S. v. Milwaukee R. T. Co., 142 Fed. 247, 255. These will be considered in order. (b) (d) (a) One who has committed a crime, cannot escape by attributing the act to the artificial legal entity. The treasurer and manager of a corporation whose laundry was a public nuisance was convicted. Peo. v. Cooper, 200 

App. Div. 413; likewise the principal stockholder of a corporation which ran a bucketshop. Peo. v. Crossman, 211 

App. Div. 673. Similarly, a corporation may be convicted of crimes committed by its agents and officers. See chapter entitled "Torts and Crimes," infra. (b) Fraud. If a debtor incorporates and turns over his property to a corporation, leaving his creditors unpaid, whether the entity will be disregarded turns upon the bona fides of those buying stock in, or otherwise dealing with, the corporation. Montgomery Webb Co. v. Dienelt, 133 

Pa. St. 585, 19 Atl. 428; Booth v. Bunce, 33 N. Y. 139; 

Keating v. Hammerstein, 125 Misc. 334, 209 N. Y. Supp.

769; Candee v. Smith & F. S. R. Co., 126 App. Div. 15, 110 N. Y. Supp. 355; In re O'Brien, 40 Fed. (2d) 554.

Fraud is a term of broad meaning and of wide application, to corporations. Ritz Realty Corporation v. Eypper & Beckman, Inc., 138 Atl. Rep. 900; Donovan v. Purtell, 216 Ill. 629, 75 N. E. 334; 12 Cornell Law Quarterly, 504-9; 

36 Yale Law Journal, 254.

The corporate agent of a one-man corporation, who, by means of an intriguing arrangement which he had made with the broker employed by the chief stockholder to negotiate the sale, received an illegal commission, was compelled to refund the commission to the chief stockholder, tho the latter had paid it voluntarily, and in voluntary ignorance of the identity of the recipient. Garrigues Co. v. Internat. Agric. Co., 159 App. Div. 877, 144 N. Y. Supp. 

982. But unless fraud of the kind that is legally cognizable is shown, the corporate veil can not be pierced. The mere fact that one man owns all the stock is not fraud, and his identity is swallowed up and absorbed by the corporation. 

Salvin v. Myles Rty. Co., 227 N. Y. 51. It is not fraud to create a corporation to own a lease and manage the property, the impelling motive for its creation being the escape from personal liability and the advantage of immunity. 

Ellenkrieg v. Siebrecht, 238 N. Y. 454; Werner v. Hearst, 177 N. Y. 63; Compare, In re Farmers L. & T. Co., 252 

N. Y. 316, 169 N. E. 612. (c) Illegality. Two leading cases where the entity was disregarded for illegality of acts are State v. Standard Oil 

Co., 49 Ohio State, 137, in which a judgment of ouster was rendered, and Peo. v. North River Sugar Ref. Co., 121 N.

Y. 582, where the corporation was drastically dissolved and a decree of corporate death entered. In both these cases monopolistic contracts were entered into by masses of stockholders which were not signed by the respective corporations. The court disregarded the entity in each case, and ridiculed the argument that the corporations were guiltless, not being bound by the tainted contracts, "while all that was human and could err had sinned." The term "illegality" covers a broad field and includes a great variety of cases where the corporate form was attempted to be used

to circumvent statutes. Where non-residents, in order to avoid a state statute which limited the insurance business to residents, incorporated in another state, the corporate form was disregarded by the court, and the license avoided on the ground of non-residence. State ex rel. 

Johnson & Higgins Co. v. Safford, 159 N. E. 829 (Ohio).

Had the business not been one affected with a public interest, but some ordinary and every day business enterprise, the opinion infers that the entity would not have been disregarded. (d) Subsidiaries. Where one corporation owns a controlling interest in the stock of another, and so commingles its affairs with its own as to make them practically one, the second corporation becoming a mere conduit of the will and a subsidiary of the first, the court may deal with the substance, and hold the first liable on the contracts and for the torts of the second. U. S. v. D. L. & W. R. R. Co., 238 

U. S. 516; Illinois Bell Telephone Co. v. Monihan, 38 Fed. (2d) 77. But mere identity of stockholders or mere interrelated dealings are not enough. Berkey v. 3d Ave. Ry. Co., 244 N. Y. 84. The dividing line is a wavering one. Interstate Tel. Co. v. B. & O. Tel. Co., 51 Fed. 49, affirmed 54 

Fed. 50; In re Waterbury Paper Co., 169 Fed. 252; N. Y.

Air Brake Co. v. Internat. Steam Pump Co., 64 Misc. 347, 

120 N. Y. Supp. 683. The keeping of separate books, assets, separate creditors, separate organizations, and conducting business in a separate corporate form, are matters to be considered. In re Waterbury Paper Co., 169 Fed. 252.

Where the same people incorporate in different states in the same corporate name each corporation is usually considered a separate and complete entity. 

§ 7. Tests of Corporate Existence. 

Corporate existence is a question of law, and those concerned can not complain that their actual intent was different from their legal intent. A statute which created a corporation expressly provided that it "should not be construed an act of incorporation" but it was held to be one. 

Liverpool Ins. Co. v. Mass., 10 Wall. (U. S.) 566. The leading New York case, Thomas v. Dakin, 22 Wend. 9, states as the principal indications of corporate existence, the

power (1) to have perpetual succession under a special name, and in an artificial form; (2) to take and grant property, contract obligations, sue and be sued in its corporate name, as an individual; and (3) to receive and enjoy in common grants of privileges and immunities. will now be considered. 

§ 8. Perpetual Succession. 

These

By this is meant continuity of existence of the corporation, irrespective of that of its members, during the period for which the corporation is formed or extended, and perpetually when no period is specified in the charter. 

G. C. L. sec. 14, subd. 1, App. B. If another person succeeds to the stock of a member through transfer, death, disability or otherwise, corporate life goes on unaffected “in like manner as the River Thames is still the same river though the parts which compose it are changing every instant." 

1 Bl. Comm. 468. The absence of power to transfer stock is a fact to be taken into consideration, but is not absolutely fatal to the existence of the corporation. In membership corporations of various kinds, clubs, hospitals, and endowed institutions in general, one may not become a member by buying out a member. Van Campen v. Olean Gen. Hospital, 210 App. Div. 204, 205 N. Y. Supp. 554; Warner v. 

Beers, 23 Wend. 103. 

§ 9. 

Artificial Form. 

By this is meant that the corporation is not governed by its members, but by a board of directors, who elect or appoint officers and agents, and whose powers are not derived from delegation by the members, but from the provisions of the charter, the by-laws, and the law. By the possession of original and not delegated powers, they are the agents and officers of the artificial legal entity. Drucklieb v. Harris, 209 N. Y. 211, 216, 102 N. E. 599, 601. 

§ 10. Corporate Name and Seal. 

The artificial legal entity must have a name for identification. "When a corporation is created a name must be given to it. . . . Such name is the very being of its constitution." 

1 Bl. Comm. 968. The charter may authorize the bringing of suits in the names of its officers. Thomas v. Dakin, 22

Wend. 9, and may authorize the use of more than one name. 

Senn v. Levy, 111 Ky. 318, 63 S. W. 776; Grt. Amer. Home 

Sav. Inst. v. Lee, 288 Mo. 679. By the weight of authority, the misnomer of a corporation may be explained by parol. 

Mail & Express Co., Inc. v. Parker Axles, Inc., 204 App. 

Div. 327, 198 N. Y. Supp. 20. In Harms Co. v. Leonhard- 

Michel Brewing Co., 228 N. Y. 265, 126 N. E. 705, the plaintiff was permitted to recover on a guaranty of a contract which purported to be made by the "Bond Development Company," which was a fictitious name used by the defendant as a trade name for part of its activities. 

At common law the corporation was unable to make a contract except in writing and under its seal; and it had implied power to choose a seal. 1 Bl. Com. 475. These requirements have long since been abandoned. Leinkauf v. Calman, 110 N. Y. 53. G. C. L. sec. 14 expressly empowers the corporation "To have a common seal, and to alter the same at pleasure." See sec. 59, infra. 

§ 11. Immunities. 

The stockholder of a corporation incorporated under the laws of New York undertakes to lose only what has been dedicated to the corporation-the amount subscribed for the stock and a primary liability, under some statutes, to laborers, servants and employees. Sec. 71 S. C. L. In banking corporations, he assumes a liability for the debts and liabilities of the corporation up to a further sum which will equal the original subscription for his stock, he having already paid for the stock once. N. Y. Const., Art. VIII, sec. 7, Appendix A. The element of immunity is not essential to corporate existence. There may be "full liability” corporations. Sec. 6 of the business corporations law. c. 691 L. 1892 now repealed. Const. of California, art. 

12, sec. 3, Civ. Code Cal. sec. 322. Thomas v. Matthiesen, 252 U. S. 221, 245. 

§ 12. Power to Hold Real Property. 

This power was implied at common law, provided the property was owned for the purposes of the corporation. 

It is expressly conferred by sec. 14 G. C. L. A conveyance to a national bank, which, by its charter, is prohibited from

owning real estate, is a valid conveyance, and does not make the title bad. Kerfoot v. Farmers Bank, 218 U. S. 281. 

See also sec. 60 and chap. VII infra.

§ 13. Kinds of Corporations. 

(a) Domestic and foreign. G. C. L. sec. 3, subd. 10, defines a domestic corporation, for the purpose of substantive law, as one "incorporated by or under the laws of the state or colony of New York," and states:-"Every corporation which is not a domestic corporation is a foreign corporation, except as provided by the civil practice act with respect to the construction of such act." This is a reference to sec. 7, C. P. A., subd. 7, which, for the purposes of the pleadings and other proceedings in an action, adds to the definition of domestic corporation, all corporations "located in the state and created by or under the laws of the United States." A corporation organized under federal law is, for purposes of procedure, a domestic corporation, if it does business in New York. Gould v. Tex. & Pac. R. Co., 176 App. Div. 818, 163 N. Y. Supp. 479. A corporation of one state which has obtained a license to do business in another state, is still, as to the latter, a foreign corporation. American Soap Co. v. Bogue, 150 N. E. .743. The distinction between domestic and foreign corporations is important for the reason set forth in sec. .14

2, supra, and also for the reason that Civil Practice Rule 93, of New York, requires the plaintiff in every action to which a corporation is a party plaintiff or defendant, to state in the complaint that it is a corporation, and whether domestic or foreign; and if foreign, further to allege the state, country, or government under whose laws the corporation was incorporated. If the defendant in his answer denies this allegation, the plaintiff need not prove it, nor will the defendant be permitted to introduce evidence in support of his denial, unless the defendant has inserted in his answer an affirmative allegation and the answer be verified. Second Natl. Bank v. Breitung, 201 App. Div. 

636, 197 N. Y. Supp. 375; Long Island Ry. Co. v. Jones, 151 App. Div. 407, 135 N. Y. Supp. 954. (b) "Municipal," "public benefit corporation," "public corporation," and "private corporation." A municipal corporation is a "territorial division of the state established by law with powers of local government," G. C. L. sec. 3, subd. 1. "A public benefit corporation," is a corporation organized to construct or operate a public improvement wholly or partly within the state, "the profits of which shall inure to the benefit of this or other states, or to the people thereof." Subd. 2, Ib. A "public" corporation is one instituted and controlled by the state, which alone is entitled to all the profits. U. S. v. Brown, 247 N. Y. 211, 216; Van 

Campen v. Olean Hospital, 210 App. Div. 204, 205 N. Y. 

Supp. 554; Russel v. Trustees of Purdue University, 168

N. E. 529. The distinguishing feature of private corporations is that they are formed for private and personal gain instead of public ends. (c) Stock and nonstock corporations. "A stock corporation is one having shares of stock and which is authorized by law to distribute dividends to the holders thereof." 

G. C. L. sec. 3, subd. 3. Membership corporations frequently issue certificates of membership resembling in appearance stock certificates and bearing the legend, "certificates of stock." The said statute provides that "A corporation which is not authorized by law to distribute dividends is not a stock corporation because of having issued certificates called certificates of stock, but which are in fact

merely certificates of membership." Ib. Sec. 2, art. 1 of the Membership Corporation Law defines a "membership corporation" as "a corporation not organized for pecuniary profit, incorporated under this chapter or under any law repealed by this chapter." Stationers & Publishers Board of Trade v. Flynn, 226 App. Div. 496, 235 N. Y. Supp. 58.

All corporations other than stock, municipal, or public benefit corporations are "nonstock" corporations. G. C. L. 

3. Subd. 4. (d) Moneyed, railroad, transportation, co-operative and business corporations. Subdivs. 5 to 9 of sec. 3, G. C. L., define these. A "moneyed" corporation is one formed under or subject to the banking or insurance laws. A "railroad" corporation is one formed under or subject to the railroad law. A "co-operative" corporation is one formed under or subject to the co-operative corporations law. A "business" corporation is one formed under or subject to article two of the stock corporation law other than a moneyed, railroad, transportation, or co-operative corporation. 

§ 14. New York's Scheme of Statutes Relating to Private 

Corporations.

Corporations have no powers except those conferred by statute, or contained in the certificate of incorporation pursuant to law. G. C. L. sec. 13. To ascertain the powers of a corporation, consider first, the general statute under which the corporation is formed. These are found under appropriate titles, such as, "banking law," "education law," etc. If the general act does not provide an answer, and it is a stock corporation, consider next the "stock corporation law;" and third, the “general corporation law." Peo. ex rel. W. U. Tel. Co. v. P. S. Comm., 230 N. Y. 95; Gause v. 

Boldt, 188 N. Y. 546. If it is a nonstock private corporation, consider first, the statute under which it is incorporated, such as the "benevolent orders law," "co-operative corporations law," etc. All private corporations are affected by the general corporation law. These statutes have sometimes been represented as a tree, the trunk of which, composed of the general corporation law, is rooted in the legislature, the Constitution, and the decisions. The stock corporation law, benevolent orders law, co-operative cor-

porations law, etc., are the limbs of the tree, and these in turn are divided into their appropriate branches. 

§ 15. Corporations distinguished From Associated Forms. 

Partnership 

1. Created and also terminated, by agreement. 

2. No continuing existence, dissolved by (a) Death or disability of a partner-consider effect of agreements to continue in spite of death. (b) Sale of a partner's interest, voluntary or involuntary. Exception, mining ptshp. 

Bissel v. Foss, 114 U. S. 252. 

3. Conveyance, by members. 

4. May increase its enterprises by simple agreement. 

5. Firm contracts bind members individually. 

6. Firm debts are the debts of the partners. 

7. On death of partner, his right in specific property vests in the survivors; of the last surviving partner, in his personal representatives. 

8. Are tenants in partnership of firm property. 

9. Suits and actions by and against the firm must be brought in the names of the partners. 

Union Wine Co. v. Green, 62 

Misc. 551, 115 N. Y. Supp. 921, 29 L. R. A. (N. S.) 283. 

10. The firm is the sum total of the individual members. 

11. No income tax is exacted at present on firm profits; but each partner may be taxed on his income.

Stock Corporation 

1. Created and terminated only by consent and sanction of the state expressed in a statute. 

2. Perpetual succession. 

3. Conveyance by the entity pursuant to by-laws or resolutions by the board of directors. 

4. Limited to charter powers. 

5. Stockholders not bound. 

6. Stockholders are not liable for debts, except by rare statutes. 

7. Shares of stock are always personalty, and on death of holder the shares go by will or by statute of distribution. Title to corporation's property is not affected. 75 N. Y. 211. 

8. All property is owned exclusively by the corporation. 

9. Can only sue or be sued in the corporate name. 

Rule 93,

Rules of Civil Practice. 

10. Artificial legal entity, separate and apart from the members. 

11. Pays a federal, but not a state, income tax.

12. Notice to notice to the firm. one partner is 

13. Admissions by partner usually may be shown against the firm. 

14. Partners owe to each other "the duty of finest loyalty the punctilio of an honor the most sensitive." 249 N. Y. at p. 

15. Except where a balance has been struck or the liability liquidated, a partner may not sue his firm on a transaction with it, except in the form of an action for an accounting. 

12. Notice to a stockholder is not notice to the corporation, unless he was authorized to act on behalf of corporation. 

13. Admissions made by a member concerning and while engaged in a transaction as authorized agent for the corporation, or while the member is testifying concerning a transaction of the corporation, may be used against the corporation. Sec. 340 C. P. 

A.; Pan-Amer. Pet. Co. v. U. S., 9 Fed. (2d) 761; Richardson on

Evidence Sec. 391. 

14. Stockholders deal with each other, or with the corporation, at arms length. 

15. Is ordinarily a stranger to the corporation, and may freely. sue it. 

Ross v. Willett, 76 Hun. 211, 27 N. Y. Supp. 785, defines a joint adventure as "a limited partnership, not limited in a statutory sense as to liability, but as to scope and duration, and, under our law, joint adventures and partnerships are governed by the same rules." Meinhard v. Salmon, 249 

N. Y. 458, 164 N. E. 545.

The general principles of partnership apply to the relation between the joint adventurers. They can not sue each other at law for anything relating to the concerns of the joint enterprise until after a settlement and balance struck and an express promise to pay, amounting to an account stated between them. Langford v. Delalle, 136 Misc. 62, 239 N. Y. Supp. 107. If an associate brings action for an accounting, all the associates must be made parties. Arnold v. Arnold, 90 N. Y. 580. § 16. Corporations distinguished from joint stock associations and business trusts.

A joint stock association differs from a corporation in

that there is no artificial legal entity. It is like a partnership in respect to the ultimate legal liability, in that its members are ultimately liable for its debts. In a corporation the rights and liabilities of the members merge in it, but in a joint stock association the rights and liabilities of the members continue. Fletcher, Enc. Corp. p. 271. It has, similar to a corporation, an artificial name, seal, perpetual succession, and government by officers. It can not be sued in the artificial name, but is permitted by statute to sue or be sued in the name of its president or treasurer in either actions or proceedings (in New York, the General Associations Law, chap. 20 of the consolidated laws, extracts from which are printed in App. F. infra).
