If a claimant elects to bring suit against the association first, the member is secondarily liable, but, as there is no artificial legal entity, the judgment in the first action is not res adjudicata as to the defendants in the second action so as to preclude defenses which were not pleaded in the first action. 

11. Has limited power to own real property. Title in names of officers. Secs. 6, 8, 16. 

12. Officers removed by action by attorney general, or by order of court. Secs. 9, 10. Also sec. 

136 G. C. L. 

13. Receiver may be appointed. 

Sec. 9. 

14. The stock is always personalty, even if the assets of the association are realty. Mtr. of 

Jones, 172 N. Y. 575. 

15. As between the members of the association, and the members and the officers, the articles of association bear the same relation as the charter does to a corporation. Bray v. Farwell, 81 

N. Y. 600. 

16. Has no entity distinct from its members. Mtr. of Willmer, 153 App. Div. 804, 138 N. Y. 

Supp. 641. not a citizen under the "privileges and immunities" clause of the U. S. Constitution. Doctor v. 

Harrington, 196 U. S. 579. 

8. All suits, actions and proceedings in the corporate name. 

Compare Thomas v. Dakin, 22 

Wend. 9; Cady's Cases on Pri. 

Corps. p. 6. 

9. No liability, except by exceptional statutes. 

10. No secondary liability of stockholders, except for claims of laborers, servants and em ployees. Sec. 71 S. C. L. Also stockholders of banking corporations to the face amount of their stock. Art. VII, sec. 7, N. Y. 

Const. App. A. infra. 

11. Title in corporate name, and unlimited power, "for the purposes of the corporation." 

12. Under statute only. 

13. Same, sec. 150 G. C. L. being sec. 307 renumbered. 

14. Shares of stock are always personalty, no matter what the character of the corporate property may be. Kent v. Quicksilver 

Mining Co., 78 N. Y. 179. 

15. The whole world when dealing with a corporation, is bound to know the powers and purposes contained in the charter. Jemison v. Cits. Sav. Bank, 122 N. Y. 135. 

16. Charter creates a legal entity distinct from members and from other corporations. In re 

Mt. Sinai Hospital, 250 N. Y. 

103, 164 N. E. 871.

17. Various kinds of joint stock associations are liable to an annual franchise tax. Sec. 182 et sec., Tax Law App. K. 

18. Pays a federal income tax. "The term corporation includes association, joint stock company, and insurance company." Sec. 

701, Revenue Act of 1930. Pays no state income tax. "The term corporation includes joint stock company or association and any business conducted by a trustee or trustees wherein interest or ownership is evidenced by certificate or other written instrument." Sec. 208 Tax law. 

17. Pay a franchise tax. 

18. Pays a federal income tax but no New York state income tax.

A further point requiring attention is the effect of Art. 

VIII, sec. 3 of the Constitution of New York, which is as follows: "The term corporation as used in this article shall be construed to include all associations and joint stock companies having any of the powers and privileges of corporations not possessed by individuals or partnerships. And all corporations shall have the right to sue and shall be subject to be sued in all courts in like cases as natural persons." The source of this section is the Constitution of 1846. It will be noted that Art. VIII is not of general application, for its application is expressly limited by the words, “as used in this article." Within the termini of Art. VIII, joint stock. 

associations doubtless fare the same as corporations, for "The power to sue or to be sued in the name of the president is one of the powers and privileges of corporations not possessed by individuals." Westcott v. Fargo, 61 N. Y. at p. 550. The power to sue or to be sued in the name of president is a corporate power, not possessed by a partnership, and is conferred, not by the constitution, but by the general associations law. The latter act was an outgrowth of chap. 245 of the laws of 1854. The statute and the constitution therefore, considered from their historical standpoint, were developed side by side. Neither supplants the other. 

Therefore as a matter of the history of legislation, the distinctions between corporations and joint stock associations have not been obliterated.

Furthermore the above words "as used in this section" do not wipe out the distinction. They are limited and refer to the various subdivisions of Art. VIII which contain only the following provisions: (1) Corporations, when to be created under general laws, and when by special act; (2) dues secured by individual liability and other means as prescribed by law; (3) the right of corporations and joint stock associations to sue and be sued in all courts; (4) liabilities of stockholders of savings banks (which sometimes used to be conducted by joint stock associations. Warner v. Beers, 23 Wend. 103) and of stockholders of banks; and (5) provisions relating to counties, cities and towns. None of these heads are adapted to extinguish the distinctions between joint stock associations and corporations. Matter of Empire 

City Bank, 18 N. Y. at p. 218 (1858).

A very real purpose of Art. VIII is to give sanction to the existence of joint stock associations. Early cases based on the so-called "Bubble Act," (6 Geo. 1, sec. 18) held joint stock associations illegal Rex v. Dodd, 5 East 516; Josephs v. Pebrer, 3 B. & C., 639 (1825). Still later, before chap. 14, Laws of 1854 (supra) was enacted, joint stock associations were held to be mere partnerships, having none of the immunities of corporations, and the officers were held to be partners, and, as such, possessed of no powers of office arising from the articles of association. Skinner v. Dayton, 19

Johns. 513. After the passage of the aforesaid joint stock companies act in New York in 1854, and in England in 1856 (19 and 20 Victoria, c. 47) disabilities were gradually removed, until Art. VIII, sec. 3 of the constitution removed the last disability in the way of a joint stock association bringing actions in the name of its president or treasurer. 

Briefly, the purpose was to confer the power to sue or be sued; and they did it by indirection. 

§ 17. Business Trusts. 

Commercial or business trusts are substitutes for business corporations. Burdick on Partnership (3d ed.) p. 43 et sec.

Thompson on Business Trusts etc., p. 28. The agreement of the parties and their acts thereunder determine whether a trust relationship, a partnership, or a joint adventure, has been created,. That which is usually termed a "syndicate"

is either a partnership, a joint stock association, or a joint adventure, and it is sometimes difficult to distinguish between them. The fact that certificates of stock have been issued is not alone the criterion. If a "business trust" has been created, the tests that apply to trusts in general may be applied: that is, there must be (1) a trustee (2) the property must be vested in him, (3) a beneficiary, (4) a lawful term. Godley's Outline of Equity, chap. III, Woolley's 

Outline of Laws of Trusts, sec. 1. If the trustees or managers act as principals and are free from the control of the certificate holders, a trust is created; but if they are subject to the control of the certificate holders, it is a partnership. 

Frost v. Thompson, 219 Mass. 360, 106 N. E. 1009, 1010. If the stockholders have reserved the right to remove and replace the trustees without legal cause or to amend the declaration of trust, the association is a partnership with all the liabilities thereof. Ib. If it is a true business trust, of which the managers are trustees, the managers, in New York, are personally liable as principals in their contracts with strangers. If the whole management, and the declaration and division of profits, rest in the sole discretion of the syndicate managers, to the exclusion of all agency features, the subscribers can not be held liable for debts or be made parties to actions arising from a trust transaction, for it is a trust relationship. Jones v. Gold, 209 N. Y. 410, 103 N. E. 720; Crehan v. Megargel, 234 N. Y. 67, 136 N. E. 296; Byrnes v. Chase National Bank, 225 App. Div. 102, 232 N. Y. Supp. 224, affd. 251 N. Y. 551.

Business trusts frequently operate under a fictitious name, issue certificates of interest similar to shares of stock, both common and preferred, and pursuant to provisions of the trust deed under which they are formed, may enjoy other advantages of a corporation except however, immunity from liability.

Business trusts are created under statute in Massachusetts and are sometimes called "Massachusetts Trusts"; but the term should be restricted to those formed within that state. The principles relating to Massachusetts trusts as worked out in the state of Massachusetts have not been fully adopted elsewhere: but the methods of formation and opera-

tion of "business trusts" in other states than Massachusetts are of the same general nature, and will be discussed in the following section. 

§ 18. 

Massachusetts Trusts.

The state of Massachusetts prohibited by statute the organization of corporations to own or deal in lands, ordinarily termed "holding companies." The legal minds of the 19th century proved quite as able to devise an ingenious, practical, and lawful way to obey the statute, as were those of the 13th century who had to struggle with the Statute of Mortmain of 1279 A. D. The aversion to the perpetual tenure of lands was met and satisfied by means of deeds of trust, entered into by virtue of contract, specifying a period of duration, which, in New York, must not exceed 21 years and 9 months after the death of the two measuring lives named in the contract. Sec. 42 R. P. L. and sec. 11 P. P. Law.

The trust usually is formed by means of a contract between the owner of land or other subject matter, and a trustee or trustees. The contract is incorporated into a trust deed which is recorded as a conveyance in the office of the Register of Deeds or other proper officer of the county in which the subject matter is situate. Usual provisions of the contract are:-1. The contract shall bind the beneficiaries, the trustee, and all persons who may succeed to the interest of the beneficiaries by buying shares of the interest of the beneficiaries, or by investing money in trust certificates, to be issued by the trustee. The certificates, when issued, are generally made to resemble certificates of stock of a corporation, and may be listed on stock exchanges, and be classified into common and preferred shares, or as to income, risk, and limitation of voting for successor trustees, and of transfer on the books of the trustees. 2. The trustees are given full power to manage, to appoint officers and agents, and transact all business within the purposes set forth in the deed. The certificate holders are specifically deprived of power to meddle in the business. 3. A fictitious name for the concern is specified, and a common seal. 4. A provision that dividends are to be declared from surplus in the sole discretion of the trustees, whose decision shall be

final; and who may also set aside a surplus without declaration of a dividend. 5. The duration. Upon its expiration, another additional period may be agreed upon. 6. A provision that neither trustees, nor stockholders shall be liable for more than the amount which they have invested in the stock, and that trustees may invest and deal in the stock as freely as other stockholders. 7. A provision that in every contract made by the trustees there shall be inserted a provision that the other contracting party, in event of loss, shall look solely to the property of the trust for satisfaction of his claim, and shall in no event have recourse to either the trustees or stockholders. This provision is held a valid release in Massachusetts. Rand v. Farquar, 226 Mass. 91.

Other states present a conflict of authority. In Texas they are treated as partnership associations, with partnership liabilities for debts incurred by the trustees in carrying on business. McCamey v. Hollister Oil Co., 241 S. W. 689 (Tex.), sec. 6061 Fletchers Enc. of corporations. The purchaser from a trustee as such, has notice of every matter appearing in his chain of title and of which he would have learned by due search and inquiry, including the trust disclosed by the recorded trust deed. Simmons Creek Coal Co. v. Doran, 142 U. S. 417, 26 R. C. L. 1280. See Sears "Trust 

Estates as Business Companies."

The expedient succeeded, and companies capitalized for many millions have been formed under it; for instance, the 

Mackey companies, which include a holding company controlling a cable line and the "Postal Telegraph System"; the Massachusetts Gas Companies; the Chicago Elevated 

Railroads; and the Amoskeag Manufacturing Company which succeeded a corporation created nearly a century before. The idea has permeated to states whose statutes were unfavorable to corporations, such as California. Pacific 

Guano & Fert. Co. v. Opolinsky, 135 Misc. 265, 237 N. Y. 

Supp. 682. It has proved popular in states, like Texas, where corporations of certain kinds, such as oil companies, are subject to drastic regulation by the state. Unlike corporations, Massachusetts trusts have a constitutional right to do business in any state without first obtaining a license. This is a right of its associates as indi-

viduals.

There is no legal entity apart from the associates, and Art. IV. sec. 2. of the U. S. Constitution provides that 

"the citizens of each state shall be entitled to all privileges and immunities of citizens in the several states." 

In Massachusetts, these trusts attained a statutory status, and the declaration of trust must be filed with the proper officers of every city or town in which the association does business, thus giving notice of the trust relationship to all persons. Malley v. Howard, 281 Fed. 363. The Massachusetts statute has no extraterritorial force. Bartley v. Andrews, 208 App. Div. 702, 202 N. Y. Supp. 227, 204 N. Y. 

Supp. 892. In Kansas the Massachusetts trusts have been held to be corporations under its state constitution and statutes. Harris v. U. S. Mexico Oil Co., 110 Kan. 532, 204

Pac. 754; and the associates are generally held, outside of 

Massachusetts, to be partners or adventurers, personally liable on contracts, unless expressly exempted, or unless the contracting parties had notice of the trust; and liable for the torts of the association. 23 Columbia Law Review 423.

When formed outside of Massachusetts, the trust is sometimes termed a "business trust," "common-law trust,' "voluntary association," and, except for the statute, does not differ materially from the business trust discussed in sec. 17 supra. 

The liabilities of a trustee under this form of trust, and those of a director of a corporation are not similar, for the former, has, as trustee, legal title to the property composing the corpus and income, and is fixed with the responsibilities and duties of a trustee in dealing with trust property as defined in treatises on the law of Trusts. Prima facie, the trustee is personally liable on all contracts made by him, for, unless he is bound personally, the contract would be unilateral and nobody would be bound. Several authorities hold that the other party may agree in advance to look only to the trust fund, and absolve the trustee. Taylor v. Davis, 110 U. S. 911, 41 L. R. A. 252. Where a promissory note read, "We as trustees but not individually promise to pay,' the trustees were held not to be personally liable on the note. Shoe & Leather Nat. Bank v. Dex, 123 Mass. 148, 25 Am. Rep. 49. There is no decision in New York that is 99

precisely in point. The trust property can not be reached here in an action at law. Bartley v. Andrews, supra. There is a dictum in New v. Nicholl, 73 N. Y. 127, to the effect that the trustee may, by express agreement, charge the trust estate with the contract, if authorized to do so by the trust deed; but a dictum in the opinion of WERNER, J., in Hibbs v. 

Brown, 190 N. Y. 167, Cady's Cases on Private Corporations page 46, suggested that an exemption clause in bonds issued by a joint stock association should be disregarded, as being contrary to public policy. Unlike corporations, the meetings of stockholders of a Massachusetts or a business trust may be held without the state of creation, the associates are not required to be residents of the state or citizens of the United States, and the minutes, articles of association, and records need not be in the English language. Owners of property, for instance, who desire to erect a hotel, may execute a trust deed to themselves as trustees, and proceed to sell stock without further formalities. Graham Hotel 

Corp. v. Leader, (Tex. Civ. App.), 241 S. W. 700. 

§ 19. Steps in Incorporating. 

The usual steps to be pursued when incorporating a business corporation under a general statute are: 1. Secure the name. 2. Prepare and execute the certificate of incorporation in the English language in triplicate original. 

3. File one original in the department of state, and file and record another original, (or a copy certified by the secretary of state) with the receipt of the secretary of state, showing the payment of the statutory fees and organization tax, in the office of the county clerk of the county which is designated in the certificate as the county in which the office of the corporation is to be located, who must also index it. 

G. C. L. sec. 8, S. C. L. sec. 5, App. B. The corporation is "formed" as soon as the certificate is filed in the department of state. S. C. L. sec. 5. The following steps follow in usual course: 4. Hold organization meeting of the subscribers named in the certificate of incorporation, S. C. L. 5, subd. 8, at which the certificate of incorporation is accepted, by-laws adopted, etc. 5. Hold first meeting of directors, at which the officers are elected, agents appointed, stock allotted to the subscribers, books of subscription opened, and

business begun. G. C. L., sec. 30 empowers the attorney general to bring action to dissolve a corporation, other than a railroad corporation, "which shall not organize or undertake its corporate duties within two years from the date of its incorporation." In re Yaddo, 216 App. Div. 1, 214 N. Y. Supp. 523.

If the corporation was formed under special act, a formal acceptance of the charter is required. In re Juilliard's Will, 207 App. Div. 478, 202 N. Y. Supp. 429. This is further illustrated by a case where the corporation was formed under a special Act which consolidated three insurance corporations and provided that the act should "not affect the legal rights of said corporations at meetings called for that purpose." It was held that a member who had not consented to the new charter had no relationship by contract or otherwise, with the new corporation. Gardner v. Ham. 

Ins. Co., 33 N. Y. 421. 6. Register the principal place of business with the taxing authorities if required by law; sec. 275 tax law. S. C. L., sec. 5.

The general method is varied in other kinds of corporations. The certificate of incorporation of a bank is drawn by the superintendent of banks, and the by-laws and other papers are essential factors to obtaining a charter. The certificate of incorporation of a membership corporation must have endorsed thereon or annexed thereto the approval of a justice of the supreme court of the district in which the office of the corporation is to be located. Memb. 

Corp. law, sec. 10. Special consents or approvals are sometimes required by law. If formed for the care of children or invalids, a hospital or the like, the approval of the state board of charities is required; for a school, of the commissioner of education; for a fire corporation, the consent of the authorities of each city, village, town or fire district in which it purposes to act; for a society for the prevention of cruelty to children or to animals, and for the incorporation of a Y. M. C. A. or a Y. W. C. A., a bar association, soldier's monument corporation, an existing unincorporated association, or for the reincorporation of membership corporations created by special law, certain auxilliary approvals or papers are required. Membership Corps. law,

secs. 10-13. App. J. S. C. L., sec. 6. In re Daughters of 

Israel Orphan Aid Society, Inc., 125 Misc. 217, 210 N. Y. 

Supp. 541.

The certificate of a religious corporation is filed with the clerk of the county where the principal office or place of worship is to be situated, and if none, then in the office of the secretary of state. Sec. 2, Religious Corporations law. 

The county clerk is thus constituted a quasi judicial officer to pass upon the certificate. Defects appearing in the face of the county clerks record are not necessarily fatal to the corporation, and the true facts may be shown by parol. St. 

Jacobs Lutheran Church v. Bly, 73 N. Y. 323. The unwrit ten practice in New York requires in addition to the statutory requirements a set of minutes by the board accepting the name of the corporation. 

§ 20. Name of Corporation. 

The corporation must have a name in which to contract, take and convey title, sue and be sued. "It is an element of the corporation's existence." Amer. Steel Foundries v. 

Robertson, 209 U. S. 372, 40 Sup. Ct. 160. At common law it was held that if no name was given it by its charter, it might adopt a name. Morawetz on Private Corporations, 2d ed., sec. 353. The misnomer of the corporation in a pleading, contract, grant, conveyance or will permits a resort to parol evidence to determine the identity of the corporation intended. Richardson on Evidence, 3d ed., sec. 

446; 2 Fletch. Cyc. Corps. sec. 742. A signature by executive officers, accompanied by the seal of the corporation is not a misnomer, for the seal of the corporation is prima facie, its signature by common law. United Surety Co. v. 

Meenan, 211 N. Y. 39. A contract signed by the officers alone, but lacking the seal or other signature of the corporation, may be shown by parol to be the contract of the corporation as undisclosed principal, except in the case of negotiable instruments and instruments under seal. Milliken v. Western Union, 110 N. Y. 403; Briggs v. Partridge, 64 N. Y. 357.

Within statutory limitations, adapted to prevent deception and unfair competition and to protect personal rights, the corporators may choose any name they see fit for the

corporation, provided it be written in English letters. 

G. C. L., secs. 8, 9. Longenecker v. Longenecker Bros., 140 

N. Y. Supp. 403. The following restrictive provisions are of this character, and apply equally to the name proposed in the certificate of a domestic corporation which is sought to be filed and recorded, and to the name of a foreign corporation applying to the secretary of state for a certificate of authority under G. C. L. 210 to do business in this state: (a) The name must not be identical with the name of an existing domestic corporation, or of a foreign corporation already licensed to do business in this state, or so nearly resemble it as to be calculated to deceive. G. C. L., sec. 9. (b) Except for religious, charitable, or benevolent corporations, or bar associations, the name must contain “such word or words, abbreviations, affix or prefix” as will clearly distinguish it from a natural person, association or a partnership. A foreign corporation may use with its corporate name in this state such affix or prefix without going through the process of changing its name. G. C. L. sec. 9. (c) Corporations that are not moneyed corporations (sec. 13 (d), supra), are not allowed to use a name indicative of a banking or insurance business. Terms, ordinarily associated with banks, prohibited by statute to ordinary corporations, are "trust, bank, banking, banker, bankers, acceptance, finance, savings, investment, loan"; terms suggesting insurance and specifically prohibited are "assurance, insurance, indemnity, guarantee, guaranty, title, casualty, surety, fidelity, bond, bonding, mortgage, or benefit." G. C. L., sec. 9. No corporation may use the word "co-operative" in its name unless formed under the cooperative corporations law. Ib. (d) The name of a living person may not be adopted without his consent. Secs. 50, 51, Civil Rights law. (e) The corporate name must not be prejudicially similar to the assumed name under which a person or persons may be conducting business pursuant to a certificate filed under sec. 440 penal law, cf. secs. 80-82 partnership law. App. B. (f) The corporate name must not be deceptively similar to an established trade name or trade mark. (g) A new corporation which, by merger or consolida-

tion takes the place of former corporations; or a new corporation formed by reincorporation of other corporations; may have the name of one of them. G. C. L., sec. 9. Where there has been a reorganization by the sale of the corporate property and franchises of a corporation pursuant to secs. 

96, 97, 98, S. C. L., the new corporation may have the same name as the old corporation. See S. C. L. 22.

The unwritten practice in obtaining a name is to propose several names in order of choice, to the department of state, corporation division with a request that the one available be mentioned. Upon receipt of a favorable reply, the name so mentioned is inserted in the certificate, which, with the required fees and tax, is mailed to the department for filing and recording. The secretary of state knows officially the signatures of all notaries public and commissioners of deeds in the state of New York, so that no county clerk's certificate as to their signatures to the acknowledgment of the certificate need be attached. But if the duplicate original certificate is to be filed in a county other than the one in which the signature of the notary or commissioner is recorded, a certificate of the county clerk certifying that the notary or commissioner is such, must be attached. If the acknowledgment is taken outside the state of New York, the county clerk's certificate must be attached to the original copy filed in New York in the department of state, as well as to all duplicate originals filed in the office of a county clerk. Executive law, sec. 105, subd. 2. 

§ 21. Names Identical or Prejudicially Similar to the Names of Other Corporations. 

"The public policy of this state is against permitting the use of misleading names by corporations." Benevolent &

Protective Order of Elks v. Improved Benevolent & Pro tective Order of Elks, 205 N. Y. 459. “It is fraud where the person, firm or corporation has established a trade and carries it on." Chapman v. L. E. Waterman Co., 176 App. 

Div. 697, 163 N. Y. Supp. 1059, appeal dismissed 221 N. Y. 

637, Cady's Cases on Private Corporations, at p. 75. A word changed here and there in the name is not enough difference if there is a deceptive similarity. Right Worshipful, etc. v. Johnson, 107 Misc. 249, 177 N. Y. Supp. 500.

AL

Under a statute similar to ours, it was held that the secretary of state has vested in him discretionary power of a ministerial nature to determine whether the forbidden resemblance exists, and the courts will not interfere with his discretion either to compel him to file, or to strike from his files, unless he has acted arbitrarily or capriciously. State ex rel Bellingham Pubs. Co. v. Hinkle, 120 Wash. 85, 206 

Pac. 942.

The statute, G. C. L. sec. 9, does not require the department of state to search outside of the lists of names of corporations on the files in its office. These include the names of domestic corporations and of such foreign corporations as have been granted a license to do business in this state only. It has no list of names of foreign corporations engaged in interstate commerce in this state, or of partnerships, unincorporated associations, or of the filed assumed names of natural persons. But it is not correct to say that the discretion of the department of state is limited by its files. It has been held that mandamus should not be granted to compel the secretary of state to approve a name which the court would later enjoin the corporation from using, at the suit of an aggrieved party on the ground of unfair competition. In Illinois, a corporation applied for a charter under the name "United States Express Company.'

A joint stock association, which operated in the State and elsewhere under that name, was granted an injunction restraining the granting of the charter. Peo. ex rel. U. S. 

Express Co. v. Rose, 219 Ill. 46, 76 N. E. 42. Similiter, a peremptory writ of mandamus was granted requiring the superintendent of insurance to accept and file the certificate of reincorporation of an expired company under its former name, although he had already recognized another proposed corporation as entitled to the name, it appearing that only a short time had elapsed and no known rights of strangers had intervened. Peo. ex rel. Brith Abraham v. Payn, 161 

N. Y. 229. It must appear however, that the plaintiff is not wrongly in the state. A domestic corporation was granted a charter in New York under the name "American Tartar 

Co." A foreign corporation of the identical name, which, without authorization to do business in this state, had manu-

factured the product in Brooklyn for a substantial period before, doing an intrastate business without right in violation of sec. 210 G. C. L., was denied an injunction to restrain the new corporation from using its name, which, it appeared, was also the plaintiff's trade-name and trademark. Legal rights are not identical with clean hands. 

American Tartar Co. v. American Tartar Co., 57 App. Div. 

411, 68 N. Y. Supp. 236.

By the terms of G. C. L. sec. 9, a foreign corporation which has complied with our law (G. C. L. sec. 210) is entitled to be protected by the state against infringement of its name by a proposed domestic corporation or by another foreign corporation applying later for authorization. The latter must change its name by a proceeding in the state of incorporation. The term "designation" in the statute is said to be used in the sense of additional words, not a part of the name given in the certificate of incorporation, but used in the sense of a trade or occupation, to distinguish the corporation from others, or the addition of a prefix, affix or words denoting the corporate character. 

Inglis v. Pontius, 102 Ohio St. 140, 131 N. E. 509.

The right of a corporation to the exclusive use of its name is not always observed, and if the statutory prohibition against prejudicially similar names has not been heeded, equity may enjoin the use of the prohibited name under the head of equitable jurisdiction against fraud. Intention of the offending party to deceive is not a necessary element. 

Germ. Amer. Button Co. v. Heymsfeld, Inc., 170 App. Div. 

416, 156 N. Y. Supp. 223. Chapman v. Waterman, supra.

In the injunction proceeding, the court will not change the infringing name, for its jurisdiction is not based on the fact that the state has failed to obey its own statute in naming its creature, but on fraud. Higgins v. Higgins Soap

Co., supra. A separate proceeding to change its name must be brought by the corporation that has been enjoined, if it desires to continue in business. In re Baumann Furniture 

Co., 163 N. Y. Supp. 360. G. C. L. sec. 40. The remedy of certiorari, brought with the object of having the offending charter struck from the files, is generally denied, for the reason that the rights of stockholders and of innocent

parties who may have dealt with the corporation can not be adjusted in that proceeding. Peo. ex rel. Columbia Chem. 

Co. v. O'Brien, 101 App. Div. 296, 91 N. Y. Supp. 649. If the imitation of the name is shown to have been intentional, monetary damages, if proved, may be awarded in addition to the injunction. Storey v. Excelsior Shook & Lumber 

Co., 128 App. Div. 505, 112 N. Y. Supp. 813.

The test of unlawful resemblance of names is whether they are so similar that a person using that care, caution and observation which the public uses would mistake one for another, assuming that the public uses the same reasonable intelligence and discrimination with regard to the identity of two corporations which they use when intending to deal with individuals having similar names. Buffalo 

Typewriter Exchange, Inc. v. McGarl, 240 N. Y. 113, 147 

N. E. 546. State v. McGrath, 92 Mo. 355, 5 S. W. 29. The principal factors of proof are:-1. Location and territory covered. 2. Character, scope and identity of business conducted. 3. Similarity of product. 4. How far the name is descriptive of the article produced, and of its quality. 

5. Other material circumstances surrounding the parties. 

Corning Glass Works v. Corning Cut Glass Co., 197 N. Y. 

173. Equitable relief is denied where the names are identical but the business is different. These are as distinct as two natural persons of the same name: thus, where one did fire insurance, and the other life and marine insurance. 

The Comr. Union Assur. Co. v. Smith, 2 N. Y. Supp. 296, 18 N. Y. St. Rep. 151. See Eastern Const. Co. v. Eastern 

Eng. Corp., 246 N. Y. 459. Where the territorial section of the city covered, and the nationality of the clientele, was such as to prevent competition, though the general scope of the business, that of artificial flowers, was practically the same, an injunction was denied. Brown v. Farda, 194 N. Y. 

Supp. 247. Where there was no competition, deception or damage, as where the defendant acted in good faith, and had made large expenditures, whereas the plaintiff, though incorporated prior to defendant, had never engaged in business, so that there was no deception of the public, or possibility of confusion, an injunction was denied. Hygeia 

Water Ice Co. v. N. Y. Hygeia Ice Co., 140 N. Y. 94; Par-

sons Trading Co. v. Hoffman, 107 Misc. 536, 177 N. Y. 

Supp. 713. Where the corporation is not organized for business purposes but for eleemosynary or charitable purposes, having nothing to sell and not engaged in soliciting contributions, the rules are relaxed, and injunction denied. 

Colonial Dames of America v. Colonial Dames of the State of New York, 173 N. Y. 586. New Thought Church v. 

Chaplin, 159 App. Div. 723, 144 N. Y. Supp. 1025. If the officers use the similarity of names for deceptive purposes, in subscriptions, sale of tickets, and the like, or there are assessments to be paid by members, the same rule is applied to eleemosynary corporations that is applied to those organized for gain, and the use of the deceptive name enjoined. B'klyn. Heb. Home & Hospital for the Aged v. 

Jewish Home for Aged and Infirm, 117 Misc. 347, 192 N. Y. 

Supp. 301; Natl. Circle Daus. of Isabella v. Natl. Order 

Daus. of Isabella, 270 Fed. 723; Order of Moose, 123 Atl. 

532, 131 Atl. 219. Masonic orders are protected by the express terms of the statute. G. C. L. sec. 9. 

§ 22. Distinctive Words in Name. 

The use of distinctive words, affix, prefix, or abbreviation in the name of a business corporation has been required in this state for all corporations formed since Chap. 638 laws of 1911. Prior to that date the word "company" might be used in the name of a corporation, a partnership, or an unincorporated association with the effect that actions were delayed, and the service of process frequently set aside by reason of the misdescription of the defendant. If a corporation which has existed from a date prior to 1911 desires to change its name, the new name must contain the distinctive corporative words. In re American Cigar 

Lighter Co., 77 Misc. 643, 138 N. Y. Supp. 455. 

In Peo. ex rel. United Verde Copper Co. v. Hugo, 181 

App. Div. 149, 168 N. Y. Supp. 80, a motion for a writ of mandamus, made by a Delaware corporation, to compel the secretary of state to grant it a license to do business in New York was denied, on the ground that its name was not of a corporate character. Its officers, stockholders and property were those of a West Virginia corporation of the

same name which had a license to do business here, all of whose stock was owned by its stockholders. 

There is considerable play in the choice of the distinctive word. Thus, if the proposed name were "Anonymous," it might be written "Corporation Anonymous," "The Anonymous Corporation," "The Corporation Anonymous,' "Anonymous Inc.," "Anonymous Corp.," "Anonymous, A 

Corporation," "Anonymous Incorporated," "Corp. Anonymous," "Inc. Anonymous," "Society Anonymous, Incorporated," etc. 

§ 23. 

Prohibited Names. 

The use of names of persons for purposes of trade without their consent (Civ. Rights law secs. 50, 51); of the words "university" or "college" by an institution not having degree conferring power or a permit from the regents of the university (education law sec. 56); or of a name indicating connection with the national guard or naval militia by a private corporation (military law sec. 241) is forbidden under appropriate penalties. A person has a right to transfer his name to a corporation in which he is interested, tho it may result that, upon severance of his relation, he may not use his own name in a competing business. World's Dispensary Medical Association v. Pierce, 203 N. Y. 419. N. J. Henry, one of the incorporators of 

N. J. Henry Manufacturing Co., Inc., a large and successful concern, sold his interest and later organized a competing corporation known as the Henry Screen Manufacturing Company, Inc. Both corporations made and sold fly screens. It was held that the latter concern, should be enjoined from using in the name the word "Henry," though not from placing on its letter heads and in its advertising the words "N. J. Henry President." 

N. J. Henry Mfg. Co., Inc. v. Henry Screen Mfg. Co., 204 

App. Div. 27, 197 N. Y. Supp. 445.

The civil rights law was passed to protect property rights in one's own name. The statute applies only to a name by which a person may be identified; and it has been held that injunction will not lie to restrain a corporation from using as part of its corporate name a name that is the same as the surname of a person, without his consent, provided there is

nothing to identify the individual. Pflaudler v. Pflaudler 

Co., 114 Misc. 477, 186 N. Y. Supp. 725. 

§ 24. Prohibited Words in Corporate Names. 

The policy of the state with reference to words expressly prohibited, (sec. 20, subd. c. supra) has been to regard the statute as remedial and to give it a liberal construction. Under the prohibition of the use of the word "benefit," the court refused to give its approval to the name "Howard 

Aid Society Incorporated." In re Incorporation of Howard 

Aid Society, 160 N. Y. Supp. 789; and to a "mutual aid" society, holding that the words "aid" or "mutual aid" could be applied only to corporations organized under the banking law. In re Antipoller Mut. Aid Society, 100 Misc. 589. In 

Matter of Barker, 135 App. Div. 16, 119 N. Y. Supp. 777, the motion for a writ of mandamus, made by a firm of real estate brokers, who desired to incorporate under the name "Lloyds New York, Incorporated" was denied. The opinion held that the word "Lloyds" was synonymous in the public mind with the prohibited word "insurance." 

§ 25. Assumed Name Authorized by Law. 

A corporation may enjoin simulation of its name by an individual and vice versa. Columbia University was granted an injunction against those who were doing business in New York city under the filed name of "Columbia

Educational Institute." Trustees of Columbia University v. Axenfeld, 241 N. Y. Supp. 4. Individuals who were doing business in one of their branches in New York City under the filed name of "American Watchman's Clock Company," selling and installing watchman's clocks, were granted an injunction against a corporation later incorporated in this state for the same business. Pettes v. American Watchman's Clock Co., 89 App. Div. 345, 85 N. Y. Supp. 900; see Kozy Theatre Co. v. Love, 191 Ky. 595, 231 S. W. 249.

Where two individuals assumed the respective names "Utica 

Floral Company" and "Utica Manufacturing Floral Company" and dealt in flowers in Utica, N. Y. but one dealt only with Italians living in the Italian section, in which his store was located, and the other dealt exclusively with other nationalities, an injunction was denied. Brown v.

Farda, 194 N. Y. Supp. 247. The provisions of sec. 440

Penal law relating to the filing of a certificate of doing business in an assumed name were inserted into the statute by chap. 446 Laws of 1915. The penal law is not retrospective, and those who acquired by user the right to an assumed business name before the statute took effect are exempt from its provisions. Fawcett v. Andrews, 203 App. Div. 

591, 197 N. Y. Supp. 208. 

§ 26. Trade-names and Trade-marks. 

It has been asserted, and denied, that a corporation name is a trade mark or entitled to protection like a trade-mark. 

In some cases the name may be found to consist of words not in common use and containing elements of a trade mark, the most important feature of which is that it will be protected as the monopolistic property of the person who first used it. 

Higgins Co. v. Higgins Soap Co. supra. Where the name is not of a nature adapted to come under the designation of trade-mark, the protection afforded by the courts is similar to that where a firm name is enfringed. See Pansy Waist 

Co., Inc. v. Pansy Dress Co., Inc., 196 N. Y. Supp. 825; 

White v. William G. White, 145 N. Y. Supp. 743; Ball v. 

Broadway Bazaar, 194 N. Y. 429; Nims on Unfair Competition and Trade Marks (3d Ed.) 221a. The owner of a trade mark may enjoin the use of the mark on articles which he does not himself sell. He has a right to use it to extend his business. As was said in the "Aunt Jemima" case, 247 Fed. 407, 410, L. R. A. 1918, C. 1039, "No one has a right to apply another's name to his own goods. If, for instance, one were to publish a book on banking under the name of a firm of bankers, it would be no answer to say that there was no competition between banking and publishing, or that the bankers had sustained no pecuniary damage, or that the book was a good book. The act would still be a trespass, for which the bankers would be entitled to at least nominal damages at law, and, that remedy being inadequate and the trespass being a continuing one, they would be entitled to relief in equity." 

§ 27. Who May Be Corporators. 

The certificate of incorporation must be subscribed and acknowledged by the corporators, by making, acknowledg-

ing, subscribing and filing the certificate of incorporation. 

They must be natural persons, of full age, and at least three in number; at least two thirds of them must be citizens of the United States, and at least one of this group a resident of the state of New York. Each must become a subscriber for at least one share of stock, by a subscription set forth in the certificate of incorporation. Each corporator's name and post office address must be set forth in the certificate. S. C. L., sec. 5, subd. 9, 10. For the formation of a stock corporation there exists no requirement that the names of the subscribers to the stock should be disclosed. The directors do not execute the certificate. 

Corporators are merely the legal means specified for starting the corporation. Somebody must take the first step. 

Corporators exist before stockholders; "When stockholders come in, corporators cease to be." It is not necessary that the corporators ever become stockholders. Chase v. Lord, 77 N. Y. 1.

S. C. L., secs. 68 and 96, apparently lend sanction to the proposition that a corporator is not disqualified to act as such by an agreement with a subscriber or some other person, by which the latter agrees to relieve him from his liability to take the share of stock set opposite his name, for it provides that one who at foreclosure, etc., has bought the property and franchises of a corporation, may "associate with him any number of persons" not less than the number required for corporators, with the same qualifications as corporators, who, by filing a certificate, may form a new, reorganized corporation. 

Where the certificate falsely recited that two thirds were residents, and failed to allege anything as to citizenship, but was nevertheless filed by the secretary of state, it was held that a corporation resulted, and that the stockholders were not partners for corporate debts. American Salt Co. v. Heidenheimer, 80 Tex. 344, 15 S. W. 1038. A corporation may not be a corporator, even by the use of dummies, but it may be a subscriber for stock. Schwab v. Potter 

Co., 194 N. Y. 109; U. S. Vinegar Co. v. Foehrenbach, 148

N. Y. 58. It has been generally held that the corporators must be persons capable of contracting. In re Globe Mut.

Ben. Assn., 135 N. Y. 280. The fact that one of the corporators is an infant was held in England not to render the incorporation invalid when the question was raised collaterally as distinguished from a proceeding by the state to annul the charter. In re Laxon & Co., 3 Ch. 555 (1892).

In order to avoid the expense of obtaining certified copies, the practice is that the corporators execute the certificate of incorporation in triplicate original. The three copies are later used as follows: one for filing in the office of the secretary of state; one, together with the receipt of the secretary of state, for filing in the office of the clerk of the county specified in the certificate pursuant to sec. 6, subd. 

5, S. C. L.; and the third, annexed to the corporate minutes, is the one accepted by resolution passed at the organization meeting. 

§ 28. Fees and Organization Tax. 

The organization tax, payable upon filing the certificate of incorporation in the office of the secretary of state, is one twentieth of one per cent upon the amount of the par value of all the shares with a par value which are authorized by the certificate of incorporation, and a tax of five cents per share on each share without par value similarly authorized. The minimum tax is $10. The corporation is not formed until this tax is paid. Sec. 180, tax law, App. B. 

This is paid to the secretary of state, and his receipt therefor must be filed in the county clerk's office as hereinafter specified. The fee of the secretary of state for filing the certificate of incorporation of any other corporation than a railroad company is $30, and for a railroad corporation $50 payable upon filing. Executive law, sec. 26, subd. 10.

The fees of the county clerk in any of the counties composing the City of New York are $3 for filing, and 25 cents a folio for recording the certificate, G. C. L., sec. 8 (2) and Civil Practice Act, sec. 1557a, subds. 29 and 31. In all other counties of the state except Westchester, the fee is 

25 cents for filing the certificate, and 15 cents a folio for recording it. Sec. 1554, subdivs. 6 and 9, C. P. A. In 

Westchester County, the fee for filing the certificate is $1, and the fee for recording it is 15 cents a folio. Ib.

Sec. 29. 30.

§ 29. Definitions and Elements. Illustrations. 

A corporation de jure ("of law") is a legal corporate body which has organized in substantial compliance with the material requirements of a valid statute. A corporation de facto ("from assumption") is one in which the charter has been secured, but "the proceedings for its organization are irregular or defective, when, by regularity of proceedings to incorporate, it might be one de jure." 

City of Guthrie v. Wylis, 6 Okla. 61, 55 Pac. 103; Kardo 

Co. v. Adams, 231 Fed. 950. The distinction is important.

A de facto corporation may be ousted and lose its charter in a direct proceeding by the state. It can not enforce subscriptions to its stock made in contemplation of incorporation. In some states it can not exercise the power of eminent domain. Title obtained through it is more likely to be questioned. And, in general, it is more difficult to prove that it is a corporation, than if it were a corporation de jure.

Assume that the associated body sues, claiming to be a corporation. The defendant's answer raises the issue. Rule 

93, C. P. R. At the trial it appears that there was a statute, but plaintiff did not take all the specified steps to incorporate under it. The facts being undisputed, whether a corporation was formed is a question of law for the court to 41

decide, and not a question of fact for the jury. There are several possibilities: (1) If not enough was done under the statute to incorporate, then the complaint should be dismissed, for plaintiff is a partnership or joint venture because the fatal defects in organization lead the court to hold that what was done was not enough to get the consent of the state to an exemption from personal liability. 

Perrine v. Levine, 68 Misc. 327, 123 N. Y. Supp. 1007; 

Schantz v. Oakman, 163 N. Y. 148, 57 N. E. 288; Stevens v. Episcopal Ch. Hist. Co., 140 App. Div. 570, 125 N. Y. 

Supp. 570. (2) If all material requirements of the statute have been substantially performed, plaintiff is a corporation de jure. Defendants attack fails. (3) If there is no corporation de jure, still the associates have assumed to act as a corporation although there are irregularities and omissions and an imperfect organization under the statute. It may be that, as a matter of public policy, since the state does not object to the continuance of the defective corporation, no volunteer ought to be permitted to take upon himself to question the validity of that in which the state acquiesces. If the court reaches this conclusion, it has decided that the composite unit is a corporation de facto. 

Courts are not inclined to reach this conclusion unless the following four elements are found:

I. A statute under which a corporation de jure of that kind could be formed, in force at the time of the attempted incorporation. 

II. A colorable attempt honestly to incorporate under the statute.

III. User in the name of the corporation of some of the powers which a de jure corporation would have possessed. 

IV. Good faith of the members of the assumed corporation who are asking that collateral attack be denied. See 

Tulare Irrigation Dist. v. Shepard, 180 U. S. 1, 46 L. ed. 

773, 22 Sup. Ct. 531.

If there is substantial compliance with all the mandatory statutory provisions, a corporation de jure results. Substantial compliance forbids the omission of any positive requirements, but does not require strict and accurate performance of provisions that are merely directory. Thus,

a corporation whose name violates a statute forbidding the secretary of state to file certificates of incorporation that contain names prejudicially similar to names of other corporations filed in his office, is a corporation de jure. Wash. 

Fire Co. v. Yates, 13 Del. Ch. 32, 115 Atl. 365. In Meyer v. Brunson, 104 S. C. 84, 88 S. E. 359, the court construed a 

South Carolina statute which provided that "irregularities" should not affect the creation of a corporation, saying, "we take it that the legislature meant that a failure of the corporators to comply regularly and exactly with all the provisions of the law about the formation of corporations should not vitiate the charter. We think that it did not mean that the corporators might ignore the substance of the law." But where the state brought action to deprive the corporation of its charter, and the corporation proved that, under a statute which required the certificate of incorporation to be subscribed and acknowledged by five or more persons, it had filed a certificate subscribed by five persons but acknowledged by only four of them, the state must prevail. The corporation by its own proof was one de facto, whereas, as against direct attack of the state in a quo warranto proceeding or ouster, the corporation, to succeed, must prove that it is a corporation de jure. Peo. v. 

Montecito Water Co., 97 Cal. 276, 32 Pac. 236, 33 Am. St.

Rep. 172. Its proof of corporate existence would have been sufficient against collateral attack even if made by the state.

The following were held to be corporations de facto, not subject to collateral attack if made by others than the state, in spite of the following imperfections:-Where copies of the certificates filed differed slightly from one another. 

Saunders v. Fenner, 62 N. H. 572. Failed to give all the facts. Lamming v. Galusha, 130 N. Y. Supp. 747, affd. 151 

N. Y. 648. Stated incorrectly some of the facts, such as the termini and length of the railroad. Buff. & P. R. Co. v. 

Hatch, 20 N. Y. 157. Omitted a declaration of bona fide intent to build the road. Buff. & R. Co. v. Cary, 26 N. Y. 75.

Some of the corporators were infants. In re Laxon & C., 3 Ch. (Eng.) 555, cf. In re Globe Mut. Ben. Assn., 135 

N. Y. 280. Corporators failed to subscribe, but signed be-

fore the attestation clause, and duly acknowledged the execution before the notary. Lyell Ave. Lumber Co. v. 

Lighthouse, 137 App. Div. 422, 121 N. Y., Supp. 802. Certificate omitted to state distinctly the principal place of business. Finnegan v. Noerenberg, 52 Minn. 239, 53 N. W. 1150. 

§ 30. Effect on Powers and Liabilities of Incorporating a De Facto Corporation. 

A de facto corporation may do every act of a de jure corporation within its charter, and its members and officers have the same privileges and duties. If the state proceeds against it, all its prior acts are valid. Coxe v. State, 144 

N. Y. 396, 409, 39 N. E. 400. Its duties and responsibilities for taxes and fees to the state are the same as de jure corporations. Amer. Cem. Co. v. U. S., 28 Fed. (2d) 918. 

§ 31. What Proof of Corporate Existence is Required. 

If a domestic corporation was incorporated under a general law of this state, nothing more in the way of proof of the charter is required than the production of the filed copy of the certificate of incorporation, G. C. L., sec. 12, or of a certified copy of the copy on file, Civ. Pract. Act, sec. 382, G. C. L., sec. 11. The court takes judicial notice of the general law. Richardson on Ev., sec. 19. If the domestic corporation was incorporated by special act of the legislature, the statute under which it was formed must be proved. Except when directly attacked by the state, proof of existence as a corporation de facto is sufficient, and this is proved by introducing the charter, or a certified copy, and proof of user under it. Acker Merrill & Condit v. 

Richards, 63 App. Div. 305, 71 N. Y. Supp. 929. To prove the incorporation of a foreign corporation, prove the foreign statute as a fact, and introduce into evidence an exemplified copy of the charter. G. C. L., sec. 12. When two or more corporations have merged or consolidated, our statute permits the use as evidence of a certificate of the state officer in whose office the certificate of merger or consolidation was filed. Ib. subd. 3. Whether a corporation exists, the facts being undisputed, is a question of law. Therefore, whether a jury is present or not it is held by the clear

weight of authority, that the question, "Is B. Silk Company a corporation?" is objectionable, on the ground that it calls for the witness' conclusion of law, which is a conclusion which only the Court can draw. Maagget v. Brawer Silk 

Co., 95 N. J. Law 72, 111 Atl. 656; Amer. Ins. Co. v. Mc- 

Clelland, 184 Ill. App. 381; Peo. v. Struble, 275 Ill. 162, 113 N. E. 938; Owen v. Shepard, 59 Fed. 746.

The rule is relaxed, in favor of the state, in a criminal prosecution of the corporation. Since the evidence is all in the hands of the defendant, and the question is merely incidental, reputation evidence may be used in such a case, to prove the fact of incorporation. State v. Rogeboom, 145 

Iowa 620, 124 N. W. 783, 29 L. R. A. (N. S.) 37; Peo. v. 

Chadwick, 2 Parker Cr. R. 163.

It will be kept in mind that a defendant not affirmatively alleging in a verified answer the contrary of the existence of the corporation alleged in the complaint, admits the allegation, and can not at the trial put in evidence the certificate of incorporation of the plaintiff to show that the corporation was not duly formed. Schmidt v. Nelke Art 

Lithog. Co., 17 Misc. 124, 39 N. Y. Supp. 358., C. P. R. 93.

In an action between a corporation and an individual, contracts made between the two, admitting by recital or otherwise the corporate charter, operate as an admission to prove the fact of incorporation. U. S. Vinegar Co. v. Schlegel, 143 N. Y. 537, 38 N. E. 729. 

§ 32. The Statute. 

Declared Unconstitutional.

Incorporation Under Statute Later 

If there was no statute under which a corporation with some of the powers assumed could be incorporated, there was no good faith assumption of corporate powers, and two elements of proof of a de facto corporation are thus lacking. There can be no corporation except by consent of the state. The statute is an offer, incorporation under it the acceptance. Dartmouth College case, 4 Wheat 518, Cady's Cases p. 321; Chenango Bridge Co. v. Paige, 83 

N. Y. 178, 190. A special act of the legislature of Indiana incorporated a railroad. There was no express acceptance by the railroad until an amendment to the state constitution took effect which provided that corporations, other

than banks, should not be created by special act. Some time after the amendment took effect, the corporation organized. In a direct proceeding by the state it was held that no corporation existed. State v. Dawson, 16 Ind. 40.

The question may be raised collaterally, for it is not a question of de facto existence, but of any existence at all. 

Davis v. Stevens, 104 Fed. 235.

If the statute under which the members incorporated is later declared unconstitutional, there are three views: (1) Some states, such as California, Georgia, Indiana,

Michigan and Wisconsin, hold that no corporation was formed, and that the alleged unit is subject to collateral attack. Burton v. Schildbach, 45 Mich. 504, 8 N. W. 497. (2) Others adopt the fairer doctrine that the corporation is a good de facto corporation, in cases where it becomes necessary so to hold in order to prevent unjust enrichment of those who have gotten possession of corporate assets. 

Some cases base the decision on the point that only the state should be permitted to disclaim the corporation which it created. Taylor v. Portsmouth & R. Co., 91 Me. 193, 39 

Atl. 560; Winget v. Quincy Bldg. &c. Assn., 128 Ill. 67, 21 

N. E. 12. In Coxe v. State, 144 N. Y. 396, a corporation was created by special act to build dykes, and reclaim the lands along the shores off Staten Island, etc., and to acquire title upon payment to the state of sums fixed by commissioners. It brought action to recover moneys so paid, on the ground that the statute was unconstitutional, and violative of both the constitutions of the U. S. and of the state. Granting a new trial, the court, in an opinion by O'Brien, J., in which all the judges concurred, said: "it is undisputed that it organized, assumed and exercised corporate powers under an act of the legislature, and thus it was a corporation de facto, if not de jure, and it required the judgment of a competent court or an express act of the legislature to terminate its existence." ... "If the company aliened or encumbered any of the lands for a consideration, that fact should be considered in diminution of the claim. . . . I am not prepared to say that it was impossible for the company if it continued to exist, to receive some benefit upon the faith of a colorable title."

(3) The stockholders and officers may be held estopped to assert the unconstitutionality of the statute. Morawetz, sec. 759; McCarthy v. Lavasche, 89 Ill. 270. (4) Some decisions hold that the one dealing with the corporation, is estopped. Sec. 36, infra.

If incorporation was had under an invalid statute when there was a valid one, it may be held that a corporation de facto resulted. The first element is satisfied by the existence of a valid statute. McTighe v. Macon Const. Co., 94 Ga. 

306, 21 S. E. 701, 32 L. R. A. 208, 47 Am. St. 153.

In New York, and in most states, the constitution prohibits the legislature from granting exclusive franchises or privileges. The prohibition is interpreted as applying only to an exclusive right which is created by the terms of the grant, so as to grant to one class privileges which on the same terms are withheld from others. Long Sault Development Co. v. Kennedy, 158 App. Div. 398, 143 N. Y. 

Supp. 454, affd. 212 N. Y. 1. Cady's Cas. on Pri. Corps. p. 46.

The United States Constitution confers no express power on Congress to create corporations. Eight out of 11 states in the original constitutional convention voted against conferring this power. Madison papers, Sept. 14, 1787; 4 Jef ferson's Mem. Corresp. § § 523, 526. Therefore, Congress has no implied power to incorporate except as a means or necessary instrumentality to accomplish the express powers. 

U. S. Const. Art. I, sec. 8. Amendment X. Under its in cidental powers congress has created corporations both public and private. Such is the Bank of the United States, (3 U. S. Stat. at Large, 266; McCulloch v. Maryland, 4 

Wheat. 316. Bank held not taxable by states. Osborn v. 

The Bank of U. S., 9 Wheat 61). Under its power to build post roads, Congress created many corporations to build and operate railroads, the first being the Pacific Railroad. 

California v. Pac. R. R. Co., 127 U. S. 39. During the 2d session of the 50th Congress, it incorporated the Maritime Canal of Nicaraugua, for an interoceanic canal through 

Nicaraugua and Costa Rica. During the World War, Con gress passed acts directing that corporations be incorporated in the District of Columbia and in various states;

for instance, the U. S. Shipping Board Emergency Fleet 

Corporation in the District of Columbia and the Spruce Production Corporation in the State of Washington, under powers conferred for war purposes. Clallam Co. v. U. S. 

263 U. S. 341, 44 S. Ct. 121, 68 L. ed. 328. U. S. ex rel. 

Skinner & Eddy Corp. v. McCarl, 275 U. S. 1. Although in form these were private corporations, empowered to sue and to be sued as such, it was held that the U. S. was the principal, the corporations mere agencies for public services, and that the United States could sue to recover overpayments made by them. U. S. Grain Corp. v. Phillips, 261 

U. S. 106, 67 L. Ed. 552, 43 Sup. Ct. 283; Sloan Shipping

Corp. v. U. S. Shipping Board Emergency Fleet Corp., 258 

U. S. 549, 66 L. ed. 762, 42 Sup. Ct. 386; Cox v. Lykes 

Bros., 237 N. Y. 376.

Congress has incorporated federal and land banks, Smith v. Kansas City Title & Trust Co., 255 U. S. 180; and cor porations to construct bridges between states. Luxton v. 

North River Bridge Co., 153 U. S. 525.

Congress has power to legislate in the territories, and "to exercise exclusive legislation in all cases whatsoever" in the District of Columbia, and has the same power to create corporations there as is possessed by the legislatures of states. U. S. Const., Art. I, sec. 8; Stoutenburg v. Hennick, 

129 U. S. 141, 32 L. ed. 737. Congress may authorize a territorial legislature elected by the citizens of the territory to create corporations, and a grant of general power to legislate is construed to carry the necessary authority. 

Williams v. Bank of Mich., 7 Wend. 539; Rogers v. Burlington, 3 Wall. 654, 662, 18 L. ed. 79. U. S. R. S., sec. 1889, prohibits territorial legislatures from granting “private charters or especial privileges" but provides that they may, by general incorporation acts, permit persons to associate themselves together as "bodies corporate" for a variety of purposes there specified.

The legislature, for the purpose of curing mere defective incorporation under general acts, or Congress, may ratify incorporation under invalid acts of territorial legislatures. 

The corporation thus becomes a corporation de jure, since all that was needed at any time was the consent of the

state, which may be given afterwards with the same force and effect as if antecedent. Colorado Springs Co. v. Amer. 

Pub. Co., 97 Fed. 843; Syracuse City Bank v. Davis, 16 

Barb. 188; Smith v. Haveras Relief Fund Soc., 44 Misc. 544, 90 N. Y. Supp. 168. The prohibition against the creation of corporations by special act permits expressly incorporation by special legislation, "where, in the judgment of the legislature, the objects can not be attained under" general laws; and if the corporation purported to incorporate where there was no authority of law, but only color of law, a subsequent statute ratifying what has been done cures all defects and validates all contracts, since the legislature is the sole judge of the necessity of the special act. N. Y. 

Const., Art. VIII, sec. 1; Smith v. Havens Relief Fund Soc., supra; State v. Squires, 26 Iowa 340. Contra, where the constitution merely prohibits the legislature from creating corporations by special act. Oroville & V. R. Co. v. Comrs., 37 Cal. 354.

Ratification by the state, by a curative act, defeats the attempts of creditors to enforce the personal liability of the corporators and members of a corporation illegally organized, on a contract entered into prior to ratification. The statute is held not to be unconstitutional as impairing contract obligations, for contracts should be construed in accordance with the intent of the contracting parties, and a statute which effectuates intent does not impair obligations or the vested rights of contracts. Shields v. Clifton 

Hill Law Co., 94 Tenn. 123, 28 S. W. 668, 26 L. R. A. 509. 

§ 33. Effect of Nonperformance of Conditions Precedent and Subsequent.

There is no corporate body in existence, not even de facto, unless there has been an attempt to perform the formal steps prescribed for incorporation. Card v. Moore, 173

N. Y. 598. As to the formal steps, there is no distinction between mandatory and directory provisions. Brown v. Webb, 60 Ore. 526, 120 Pac. 387. The certificate must be prepared, executed after some fashion, filed in the office of the secretary of state. Perrine v. Levine, 68 Misc. 327, 123 N. Y.

Supp. 1007. The fees must be paid, and the charter accepted. 

If the formal steps which the legislature has made condi-

tions precedent to formation have not been colorably attempted, there is no legal capacity to transact business as a corporation. Eaton v. Aspinwall, 19 N. Y. 119; Peo. v. Troy 

House Co., 44 Barb. 634; Haviland v. Chase, 39 Barb. 283;

Epis. Ch. Hist. Co. v. Stevens, 140 App. Div. 570, 125 N. Y. 

Supp. 573; Munter v. Ideal Peerless Laundry, 229 App. Div. 

56, 241 N. Y. Supp. 411. Sometimes statutes prescribe that subscriptions to stock are required as a condition precedent to a grant of the charter. A failure of compliance would prevent the creation of the corporation. Lake Ontario A. & N. Y. R. Co. v. Mason, 16 N. Y. 451. A provision that unless the railroad were commenced and completed within a term specified it should "forfeit the right acquired by it" is a condition subsequent, the breach of which does not ex proprio vigore put an end to corporate life, nor subject it to collateral attack. Matter of Brooklyn 

Elevated R. R., 125 N. Y. 434; Peo. v. Western & D. R. Co., 128 N. Y. 240, 28 N. E. 635. A requirement that the corporation should not begin business until 10 per cent was paid in was held a condition subsequent, and the stockholders not liable. Eaton v. Aspinall, 19 N. Y. 119.

The condition subsequent may be so drawn as to be self executing, so that upon failure to perform the condition, no procedure will be necessary by the state to terminate corporate life. G. C. L., sec. 30, once read that if the corporation should not "organize or commence transacting its business or the discharge of its corporate duties within two years from the date of its incorporation, its corporate powers shall cease;" and it was held that the statute was self executing so that no action or judicial proceeding was needed to declare or complete the loss of its corporate powers. Peo. v. Stillwell, 157 App. Div. 839, 142 N. Y. Supp. 881. The statute was amended in 1927 to provide that if there was no organization or user within two years from the date of its incorporation it might be dissolved, thus bringing the section within the prevailing rule that breaches of conditions subsequent do not defeat the de facto status of the corporation, but may change a corporation de jure into one de facto.

§ 34. Effect of Inclusion of Powers not Authorized by the 

Statute.

The mere fact that the charter purports to comprehend powers for which there is no statutory authority does not prevent the corporation from being one de facto if other valid powers are included, for here there is color of law for its formation, and, unless indivisible, the unlawful provisions may be regarded as surplusage. Thus where a 

California statute did not permit the issuance of stock of differing par values, the formation of a corporation under a certificate embodying such a stock scheme was held to make a de facto corporation. Westlake Park Inv. Co. v. 

Jordan, 198 Cal. 609, 246 Pac. 847; Holmes Electric Protective Co. v. Armstrong, 97 Misc. 184, 162 N. Y. Supp. 

779. Where the certificate expressed a duration in excess of the maximum period, the corporation terminates at the expiration of the statutory period. Peo. v. Cheeseman, 7 

Colo. 376, 3 Pac. 716.

If the certificate of incorporation discloses that the purpose was wholly illegal or immoral, no corporation results, and its organization may be attacked collaterally. Chicora 

Co. v. Crews, 6 S. Car. 243 (to rebel against the U. S. 

Government). Lewarne v. Meyer, 38 Fed. 91 (to run a lottery). Peo. ex rel. Floersheim v. Purdy, 221 N. Y. 481 (to practice law). 

§ 35. Expired Corporations as De Facto. 

If the charter fixes the date of expiration, as if it specifies that the corporation shall continue "until" a certain date, the weight of authority is that corporate life ceases the day before the date specified, no adjudication being necessary to terminate it. Peo. v. Walker, 17 N. Y. 502; Sturges v. 

Vanderbilt, 73 N. Y. 384. In re Friedman, 177 App. Div. 

755, 164 N. Y. Supp. 892. Under the principle of succession, in the absence of term-fixation by either charter or statute, mere cessation of business, however long, will not terminate the corporation so long as any stockholder or officers remain. Petrogradsky M. K. Bank v. Natl. City 

Bank, 253 N. Y. 23, 170 N. E. 479. Where, however, there is a statute under which the directors might decide to continue the term of existence, by a mere application therefor,

without thereby creating a new corporation, and, instead of applying for winding up the business, they simply continue to transact business as a going corporation, it is, for the additional term, a corporation de facto. Wilson v. 

Brown, 107 Misc. 167, 175 N. Y. Supp. 688; Central Savings Bank v. Walker, 66 N. Y. 424. 

§ 36. Estoppel to Question Validity of Incorporation. 

One who deals with a de jure or a de facto corporation in its corporate capacity is estopped from disputing its corporate existence. But where the corporation was not so far organized as to be even a de facto corporation, no one dealing with it is estopped, and it is subject to collateral attack. Clark v. Amer. Cannel Coal Co., 165 Ind. 213, 73 

N. E. 213.

The principles of estoppel apply to a particular transaction. 

See the authorities on equity. Godley's Outline of Equity, chap. XI. The decisions are roughly classifiable as follows: 

1. The corporation, its members and those who have participated in organizing or managing the assumed corporation are estopped to deny corporate existence as against creditors, members, the state, or against anyone who asserts or claims against the unit as a corporation. Those estopped by thus holding out cannot set up as a defense that it is not a corporation, and the claimant cannot be put to proof on the point. Buffalo & A. R. Co. v. Cary, 26 N. Y. 

75; Dorris v. Sweeney, 60 N. Y. 463; Phoenix Warehousing 

Co. v. Badger, 67 N. Y. 294. 

2. As against a corporation de facto one who has contracted with it in its corporate capacity, is estopped when sued on a claim arising in some way under the contract, from disputing its corporate existence. A bank, sued by its depositor to recover the deposit, is estopped from claiming that the charter of the depositor had been annulled by a decree made at a date prior to the deposit. Joint Stock Co. v. National City Bank, 240 N. Y. 368, 148 N. E. 552. The execution of a written contract which contains a statement or recital that the now plaintiff is a corporation, constitutes an admission, available as evidence, to prove prima facie the fact of incorporation by estoppel. U. S. Vinegar Co. v. Schlegel, 143 N. Y. 537, 38 N. E. 729.

3. One who contracts or deals with an association as a corporation is not estopped to sue the members or officers individually; and the latter are entitled to immunity only if the association is proven to be at least a corporation de facto. The elements of estoppel are lacking. By entrapping strangers into contract with a pretended corporation-with a principal who has no existence-no immunity is gained. Estoppel is based, primarily, on the fraud of the plaintiff, by which the one who claims the estoppel was misled. Harrill v. Davis, 168 Fed. 187, 22 L. R. A. (N.S.) 

1153; Welland Canal Co. v. Hathaway, 8 Wend. 480.

On this point there is considerable conflict. Some writers contend that as the associates never intended or agreed to be held personally liable, the court can not make a different contract for the parties, and so hold them liable as partners or joint adventurers. Morawetz, Private Corporations (3rd ed.) pp. 113, 122. 

§ 37. What Amounts to User. 

Mere organization and election of officers and authorizing them to do business is not enough to satisfy the requirements of user. Emory v. De Peyster, 77 App. Div. 65, 78 

N. Y. Supp. 1056. To constitute user, some of the corporate powers and franchises granted in the charter must be exercised. When the certificate filed in the secretary of state's office authorized the corporation to "manufacture, use and sell" hay presses, but it did not include the power to "purchase and sell," the purchase of hay presses was not user.

A subscriber to stock might legally withdraw his subscription before the contract for purchase was performed. De 

Witt v. Hastings, 69 N. Y. 518.

The carrying on of business in a corporate name when the statute under which the corporation incorporated was unconstitutional, does not constitute user. Chenango Bridge 

Co. v. Paige, 83 N. Y. 178, 190. 

§ 38. Good Faith. 

Not only must there be a bona fide attempt to form a corporation, but if, instead, the corporation was conceived in fraud, the statements in the certificates being false and intended to defraud creditors, it may be held that no de

facto corporation resulted. Eastern Products Corporations v. Tennessee Coal, Iron & R. Co., 151 Tenn. 239, 269 

S. W. 4; Christian & Craft Grocery Co. v. Fruitdale Lumber Co., 121 Ala. 340, 25 So. 566; 21 Harv. Law Rev. 323-5.

In some states it has been held bad faith and a fraudulent evasion of the statute for its citizens to incorporate in another state for the purpose of evading stringent laws of their own state. Hill v. Beach, 12 N. J. Eq. 31; Empire 

Mills v. Alston Groc. Co. (Tex.), 15 S. W. 200. New York holds such corporations valid. Lancaster v. Amsterdam 

Imp. Co., 140 N. Y. 576; Cady's Cases p. 586. 

§ 39. Effect of Incorporating De Facto on Subscriptions to Stock.

One who subscribes for stock before the corporation is formed or who enters into a contract for the benefit of the proposed corporation can only be held if a corporation de jure is formed. This is an implied term of the contract. 

De Witt v. Hastings, 69 N. Y. 518; Dorris v. Sweeney, 60 N. Y. 463; Dutchess & R. Co. v. Mabbett, 58 N. Y. 397; 

Cayuga Lake R. R. Co. v. Kyle, 64 N. Y. 185; Phoenix 

Warehousing Co. v. Badger, 67 N. Y. 518. Those who subscribe for the stock of a de facto corporation after it is formed are bound. Buffalo R. R. Co. v. Cary, 26 N. Y. 75; 

U. S. Vinegar Co. v. Schlegel, 143 N. Y. 537, 38 N. E. 729.
