§ 40. 

Promoter Defined. Distinguished from Corporator.

All persons who act before incorporation or reorganization to bring together the persons who invest in the enterprise are promoters. Downey v. Finucane, 205 N. Y. 251.

Promotion consists in exertions to form and to "float" the corporation. Armstrong v. Sun Printing and Pubs. Assn., 137 App. Div. 828, 122 N. Y. Supp. 521. Those who obtained subscriptions to finance the production of a moving picture, representing that the subscribers were buying stock in a corporation to be formed, and that the stock would be issued to them as soon as the film was completed, were promoters. 

Detwiler v. Clune, 77 Cal. App. 562, 247 Pac. 264. Persons with whom a promoter makes a contract for services in connection with forming the proposed corporation also become promoters. Van Zandt v. St. Louis Wholesale Grocers Co., 196 Mo. App. 640, 190 S. W. 1050. The term is said to have originated in the methods by which joint stock companies were formed in England. St. Louis & Co. v. Tiernan, 37

Kan. 606, 15 Pac. 544. It is a term of business, not of art, or law, and it does not imply that the promoters are afterwards brought into the corporation as officers, directors or stockholders, for they may promote the corporation and later deal with it as strangers. Hutchinson v. Simpson, 92 

App. Div. 382, 87 N. Y. Supp. 369. Partners who reorganize their business on a corporate basis are promoters. 

Dickerman v. Northern Trust Co., 176 U. S. 203, 44 L. Ed. 55

423; Bigelow v. Old Dominion Copper Mining & Smelting 

Co., 74 N. J. Eq. 456, Cady's Cas. p. 140.

Promoters are distinguished from corporators in that corporators first become such when the work of promoters bears fruit in the actual work of incorporating. Corporations may authorize promoters to act for the corporation after it is incorporated in the capacity of agents, but only up to the election of officers. Corporators exist before stockholders, and do not exist with them. "When stockholders come in, corporators cease to be." Chase v. Lord, 77 N. Y. 1.

The corporators act for the corporation from the time of the granting of the charter to the time of organizing and issuing stock, but promoters can not bind the corporation.

Corporators, like promoters, may delegate their powers to one of them, or may act all together. Harrison v. Vermont 

Mang. Co., 1 Misc. 402, 20 N. Y. Supp. 894. The admissions of a corporator, like those of every other member of the corporation made within his authority are competent evidence against the corporation in an action in which the corporation is a party; Couro v. Port Henry I. Co. 12 Barb. 27, Sec. 340 C. P. A. Promoters have no power to bind the corporation by their admissions. Sec. 43 infra. McCallum v. Purssell Mfg. Co., 1 N. Y. Supp. 428. 

§ 41. Relation and Liabilities of Promoters Inter Se. 

By contract with each other, promoters usually agree to divide stock or profits to be derived from promotion. Apart from agreement, they do not share losses. Co-promoters are not, as it was once held, necessarily and ipso facto partners. Shantz v. Oakman, 163 N. Y. 148; Holmes v. 

Higgins, 1 B. & C. 74; Jones v. Gould, 209 N. Y. 419; Mines etc. Co. v. Close, 186 App. Div. 23, 174 N. Y. Supp. 80.

Whether the relationship between the promoters is partnership, joint adventure, or employer and employe depends upon the terms of the contract between them, either oral, written, or spelled out from their acts. Boice v. Jones, 106 

App. Div. 547, 94 N. Y. Supp. 896. The mere fact that one originates and proposes an idea, which is later successfully promoted by others, does not constitute him a co-promoter. 

Flaherty v. Murray, 60 App. Div. 92, 69 N. Y. Supp. 675.

Some elements of partnership are frequently present. For

PROMOTERS 

57 instance, promoters are liable to 3d persons on their contracts and representations. Sec. 42, infra. But in the absence of an agreement to pay, one promoter is not liable to another for services, losses or expenditures. Baily v. 

Burgess, 48 N. J. Eq. 411, 22 Atl. 733; Miller v. Baker, 161 

Iowa 136, 140 N. W. 407. Nor is he entitled to contribution. 

Belding v. Vaughan, 108 Ark. 69, 157 S. W. 400. If one sues the other for an accounting of profits received, the same legal rules apply to the promoters inter se as would be applied to joint adventures or as to a partnership. Spier v. Hyde, 92 App. Div. 467, 87 N. Y. Supp. 285 (for facts see 

78 App. Div. 151, 79 N. Y. Supp. 699). Joint adventurers owe the duty of the utmost good faith to each other and are accountable for secret profits. Modlin v. Licht, 224 App. 

Div. 614, 231 N. Y. Supp. 265.

Promoters are bound in good faith to endeavor to carry out the promotion in accordance with the contract between them; but if they once abandon the scheme, any of them may proceed to carry out a similar scheme with the same parties without being liable to his associates for profits or otherwise. Where the essential part of the scheme, to wit, that the proposition should be one that would enlist J. P. 

Morgan & Co. as trustee and treasurer for the pooling of assets, failed, and thereupon some of the promoters excluded the plaintiff and proceeded with the plan and eventually incorporated, it was held that the original contract between them had been terminated by abandonment, although it was without any express time limit, and that the plaintiff was not entitled to a share of the profits. Parks v. 

Gates, 84 App. Div. 534, 82 N. Y. Supp. 1070. If the contract between the promoters mentions no time for performance, a reasonable time is implied, to be fixed by the jury. 

Moore v. Maddock, 224 App. Div. 401, 231 N. Y. Supp. 291.

When promoters breach their contracts with each other the proof of damages frequently presents difficulties. If they contracted to divide the stock of a corporation to be formed by means of investments by others, and the contract was breached by one of them before the corporation was formed, it might be impossible to prove damages cognizable by law. The contract would not be binding on the corpora-

tion when formed. Hunter Smokeless Powder Co. v. 

Hunter, 100 App. Div. 191, 91 N. Y. Supp. 620. But one promoter may have damages against the others for breach of their agreements, if the damages are not too speculative. 

Where they agreed to form a corporation to take over the ship they were constructing, and one of them, instead, sold the ship at a profit, the other was allowed his share of the profits proportionate to his contribution. Dyckman v. 

Valiente, 42 N. Y. 549. Damages may be liquidated, as where one pledged his stock as security for his performance of an agreement to form a corporation to take over a going concern. Later upon his withdrawal, a recovery of the stock pledged was denied. Electric Fireproofing Co. v. 

Smith, 113 App. Div. 615, 99 N. Y. Supp. 37; Jewell v. 

McIntyre, 62 App. Div. 396, 70 N. Y. Supp. 826, affd. 172 

N. Y. 638. If one of the promoters drops out and accomplishes the result aimed at by the original agreement between them through other means than those contemplated by the agreement, the one excluded without his consent may compel specific performance of the agreement to turn over stock. Babbit v. Gibbs, 150 N. Y. 281. But where the damages are anticipative only, as where the agreement between the promoters provided that stock of a corporation that was never formed, and whose success was problematic, should be divided, the damages of those injured by the withdrawal of one of the promoters should be limited to their expenditures, for the other damages are too doubtful, speculative and uncertain of proof. Curran v. Smith, 149 

Fed. 945; Kirschmann v. Lediard, 61 Barb. 673. In the absence of negative covenants one promoter can not enjoin the others from organizing a different corporation, in violation of the agreement. Perrin v. Smith, 135 App. Div. 127, 119 N. Y. Supp. 990.

Promoters' contracts inter se frequently bind them to use their influence to secure the allotment of a controlling interest in votes by issuing stock to themselves, either for their services as promoters or to be taken and paid for, and that they will combine to secure the observance of a specified policy by the corporation. Such agreements are valid, unless they embody an interest adverse to the corporate inter-

PROMOTERS 

59 est. Mildenberg v. James, 31 Misc. 607, 66 N. Y. Supp. 77, affd. 175 N. Y. 494. An agreement that each should receive half the capital stock, that one group should have the management of the business, and should guarantee an annual dividend of 7% for 7 years, was held valid. Lorillard v. 

Clyde, 86 N. Y. 384. An agreement that stock should not be allotted to anyone who would not agree in advance that the other should be employed as general manager at one third its gross receipts was held void as against public policy. Flaherty v. Cary, 62 App. Div. 116, 70 N. Y. Supp. 

951, affd. 174 N. Y. 550, 67 N. E. 1082. Agreements not to sell stock without first offering it to the other are valid as between the promoters. Burden v. Burden, 159 N. Y. 

287, 54 N. E. 17. The acceptance of a substitute agreement from the corporation when formed, will bar a promoter from enforcing a former agreement, inconsistent with it, against his co-promoters. Mildenberg v. James, supra. A director has no right to sell his influence in the company and a stockholder has no right to sell his vote. An agreement between promoters to elect one of them to the board of directors is void as against public policy. Stockholders have the right to combine, and to control the acts of the corporation in any lawful path; but the policy proposed to be achieved, is not a valid consideration for the agreement to vote. Kountze v. Flannagan, 64 Hun 635, 19 N. Y. Supp. 

33. S. C. L., sec. 47; Rosenthal v. Light, 185 App. Div. 702, 173 N. Y. Supp. 743, affd. 227 N. Y. 587. 

§ 42. Promoter's Liabilities to 3d Persons. 

The promoter who makes a contract in behalf of a corporation to be formed is personally liable, since he purports to act for a principal who does not exist. He may exempt himself by a provision that the other party shall look to the corporation only. Munson v. Syracuse G. & C. R. Co., 108 N. Y. 58, 8 N. E. 355. The claim against the promoter may be lost by an election to look to the corporation. 

Lane & Co. v. United Oil Cloth Co., 103 App. Div. 378, 92 

N. Y. Supp. 1061. Subsequent adoption of the contract by the corporation when formed will not release the promoter, unless the promisee expressly so agrees. Thistle v. Jones, 45 Misc. 215, 92 N. Y. Supp. 113. If one promoter at the

instance of all enters into the contract, all the promoters become liable on it. Ijams v. Andrews, 151 Fed. 725; 

Downey v. Finucane, 205 N. Y. 251; Cady's Cas. on Priv. 

Corps. 241. 

§ 43. 

Good Faith.

The promoter is not like a broker that the principle of caveat emptor should apply, for he does not sell, but induces people to invest. He does not deal at arms length, for he occupies a position of unfair advantage, and is a fiduciary, held to the responsibility of an agent of the corporation, Hutchinson v. Simpson, 92 App. Div. 382, 87 

N. Y. Supp. 369. His contracts are those denominated uberrimae fidei and his duty to make full and complete disclosure protects the original, but usually not subsequent stockholders, the corporation, and creditors with whom he contracts. Ritchie v. Strange Oil & Ref. Co., 279 Fed. 49.

As was said by the court in McManus v. Durant, 168 App. 

Div. 643, 154 N. Y. Supp. 580, quoting Sir George Jessel in Dunn v. English, L. R. 18 Eq. 535, "It is not sufficient for a person in a fiduciary capacity to say, 'I gave you sufficient information to put you upon inquiry'."

The fiduciary relationship is unlimited by definition. 

Many of the cases are classifiable under the following heads: 

1. The owners of property incorporate and issue stock and, perhaps, bonds also, to themselves in excess of its value. The promoters and the company here do not constitute conflicting interests and no wrong has been done. 

Seymour v. Spring Forest Cem. Assn., 144 N. Y. 333, 39 

N. E. 365; Cady's Cas. on Priv. Corps. p. 550. 

2. The promoters mentioned under the first head, later sell the stock and bonds without disclosure. If there was no misrepresentation sufficient to support a deceit action in favor of the purchaser personally, there can be no recovery; for caveat emptor applies as to the purchasers; and, as to the corporation, no injury has been done it. Parsons v. 

Hayes, 14 Abb. N. C. 419; Barr v. N. Y. & R. R. Co., 125 

N. Y. 263, 26 N. E. 145; Drake v. N. Y. Suburban Water 

Co., 26 App. Div. 499, 50 N. Y. Supp. 826; Ball v. Breed et al., 294 Fed. 227, Cady's Cas. on Priv. Corps. p. 118; 

Blum v. Whitney, 185 N. Y. 232, 75 N. E. 1159.

PROMOTERS 

61 

3. The promoters, without risking their own money or property, promote the corporation and invite the public to subscribe the funds necessary to float the enterprise. Here it is the duty of the promoters to make full disclosure of all the material facts. It is the duty of the promoters to work for the benefit of the corporation and of the investors, without any contrivance to benefit themselves or others at the expense of the corporation or the investors, except as fully disclosed and agreed to by corporation and stock purchasers. 

Erlanger v. New Sombrero Phosphate Co., L. R., 3 App. 

Cas. 1218. 

§ 44. Secret Profits. 

Promoters are under the same disabilities as agents in respect to enjoying secret profits, and are held accountable therefor both to the corporation, subscribers and stockholders. Hutchinson v. Simpson, 92 App. Div. 382, 87 N. Y.

Supp. 369. Secret profits are simply those that are not disclosed to the parties in interest and their consent obtained. 

A secret agreement between the directors of a corporation and the promoters, by which the promoters are to receive a dividend out of the profits before any dividend is paid to the stockholders, is an agreement for a secret profit, and invalid. Dillon v. Commercial Cable Co., 87 Hun 444, 34 

N. Y. Supp. 370.

It is unnecessary to show any wrongful intent on the part of the promoter. The honesty of the transaction is no defense, for the law will not permit the promoter to take a position inconsistent with his duty to investors. Munson v. 

S. G. & C. R. Co., 103 N. Y. 74, 8 N. E. 358. In order that the promoter may be safe from the corporation and stock purchasers in his secret profits it is said that he must pursue one of four courses: 

1. Provide an independent board of officers in no sense under his control, and secure its consent. This, in legal effect, is full disclosure to the corporation. 

2. Make full disclosure to each original subscriber for stock. See Appendix G. 

3. Procure a ratification of the contract by the stock holders, say at the organization meeting, after full disclosure.

4. The promoters themselves be the real subscribers for the entire share capital, and then sell the shares to outside parties. Allenhurst Park Estates, Inc. v. Smith, 138 Atl. 

(N. J.) 709. The burden of proof is on the promoter. 

Victor Oil Co. v. Drum, 184 Cal. 226, 193 Pac. 243; Colton 

Imp. Co. v. Richter, 26 Misc. 26, 55 N. Y. Supp. 486; Dillon v. Com'r Cable Co., 84 Hun 444, 34 N. Y. Supp. 370.

Devices frequently used to cover secret profits are:- 

1. Sales by the promoter to the corporation of property bought for that purpose without disclosing the profit. He is then liable to the corporation and to the original subscribers for damages. 

2. Promoter buys an option on the property and sells it to the corporation at an advance. The stockholders or corporation may compel an accounting. Getty v. Devlin, 70 

N. Y. 504. 

3. Sale to the corporation through a controlled board.

The corporation may rescind. Barr v. N. Y. L. E. & W. R. 

Co., 125 N. Y. 263, 26 N. E. 145. 

4. An arrangement whereby the promoters get stock at a less consideration than the subscribers. The corporation may recover the value of the shares distributed, or the subscribers may recover their personal damages, or, if the stock held by the promoters has not been sold and delivered to innocent purchasers for value, the stock representing the secret profit may be cancelled. Brewster v. Hatch, 122 

N. Y. 349; Yerser v. U. S. Board & Paper Co., 107 Fed. 340. 

5. A mortgage or other lien on the property executed to a nominee of the promoter with the usual estoppel statements, and with or without a bond issue. 

The foreclosure of the mortgage may be resisted, the mortgage and bonds cancelled, excepting those which have passed through the hands of a holder in due course. If the holder of negotiable bonds is a holder in due course, of which fact he has the burden of proof, the bonds are enforceable, and the promoter alone is liable to those injured. 

Midwood Park Co. v. Baker, 128 N. Y. Supp. 954, 144 App. 

Div. 949, affd. 203 N. Y. 545, Cady's Cas. p. 122. If the subscription agreement discloses the existence and amount of the mortgage there was no secret profit. Home Trust

PROMOTERS 

63 

Co. v. Bauchens, 151 App. Div. 416, 135 N. Y. Supp. 881; 

Cady's Cases on Pri. Corps. p. 127. 

6. The promoter makes the transfer at a profit on terms known to all the stockholders of that issue, with the plan of reaping a harvest from later investors without disclosing the prior stock watering. There are conflicting decisions on this procedure. In Old Dominion Copper Mining Co. v. 

Lewisohn, 210 U. S. 206, 216, 52 L. ed. 1025, Cady's Cas. on Pri. Corps. p. 128, the Supreme Court placed its approval on the transaction, tho the promoter's profits, and the loss to subsequent investors, were very large; and held that if full disclosure was made to all members at the time of the transaction, the corporation, having come under the control of later investors, could not complain. Massachusetts held the promoters liable, because of the control exercised over the board by the promoters. Old Dominion 

Copper Mining Smelting Co. v. Bigelow, 209 Mass. 159, 89 N. E. 193; Cady's Cases p. 134; and so did New Jersey, Ib. p. 140. See Continental Sec. Co. v. Belmont, 206 N. Y. 7.

In Piggly Wiggly, Del., Inc. v. Bartlett, 129 Atl. (N. J.) 413 where the promoters later sold the stock as treasury stock, with the implied representation to purchasers that the proceeds would go into the corporation, it was held that the corporation could not recover from the promoters their profits. In Mason v. Carrothers, 105 Me. 392, 74 Atl. 1030, it was held that subsequent purchasers of the stock might maintain a stockholders representative suit to cancel the stock issued to the promoters as a mere device to cheat subsequent investors. In Piggly Wiggly supra the stock was issued in consideration of the transfer of a license; and in the Mason v. Carrothers case supra for the assignment of a patent right. 

7. The promoter with the approval of all the members, turns in the property at a profit, taking his pay in stock, part of which he turns back to the corporation as treasury stock to sell to later investors. Most courts hold that under these circumstances the promoters owe no duty to the subsequent purchaser of stock. Neither the promoters, the directors nor the corporation are liable. The effect is to bring in stockholders on an unequal basis of investment, but in the

absence of proof of an actual fraudulent intent, it is doubted whether there is any cause of action. Re British Seamless 

Paper Box Co., L. R. 17 Ch. Div. 467. 

§ 45. Fraud and Misrepresentation. The Prospectus. 

The promoter is liable for all damages that may ensue to any one through reliance on material misrepresentations of fact made by him mediately or immediately, or contained in the prospectus, in the preparation or circulation of which the promoter had some part. Laska v. Harris, 215 N. Y. 

554. The burden of proof of the elements of fraud is on the plaintiff. Pryor v. Foster, 138 N. Y. 178. Morgan v. Skiddy, 62 N. Y. 319, Easterday's Cases on Torts, page 640. The burden of proving good faith is on the promoter. Walsh v. 

Walsh, 285 Missouri 181, 220 S. W. 236. See Ginen v. 

Powell, 145 A. D. 559, 129 N. Y. Supp. 869. In order to hold one promoter for the breach of duty, misrepresentation, or concealment knowingly made by another, either in the prospectus or while they were engaged in the promotion, the relationship of the promoters must be shown by the plaintiff to have been that of co-adventurers or at least that of participation in or authorization of the prospectus. 

Reno v. Bull, 226 N. Y. 546; Walker v. Anglo-American 

Trust Co., 73 Hun 334, 25 N. Y. Supp. 432, Brewster v. 

Hatch, 122 N. Y. 349, 25 N. E. 505.

The English rule is that only the original allottee of stock may sue for misrepresentations or concealments amounting to fraud. This rule is based on two grounds: 

1. that the representation was made only to induce the original subscription and was not made to subsequent purchasers of stock; 2. that a purchaser from a subscriber has no interest in the application of the purchase money which he paid for his shares, and therefore, is not injured, but the original subscriber has such an interest. Derry v. Peek, 14 

Ap. Cases 337; Peck v. Gurney, L. R., 6 H. L. 377; Scott v.

Dickson, L. J. Ex. 62. The English rule was quoted with approval in Walker v. Anglo-American Trust Co., 73 Hun 

334, 25 N. Y. Supp. 432, where, however, only the rights of original purchasers were involved.

If the misrepresentation was made with intent that another should act upon it, the person who made it is an-

PROMOTERS 

65 swerable for what he intended to accomplish. Ottinger v. 

Bennett, 144 App. Div. 529, 129 N. Y. Supp. 819, rev. 203

N. Y. 554 on dissenting opinion. So, where the prospectus invited subscriptions for bonds alone, one who subscribed for stock in reliance thereon was granted recovery. Greene v. Merc. Trust Co., 60 Misc. 189, 111 N. Y. Supp. 802, aff'd 

128 App. Div. 914, 112 N. Y. Supp. 1131. Any person acting upon representations made to the public at large may sue. Brackett v. Griswold, 112 N. Y. 454 at p. 467. False statements in stock certificates address themselves to whoever may purchase them. Sykes v. Pure Food Cider Co., 157 Iowa 601, 138 N. W. 544.

The corporation, according to the rule universally held, is not responsible for fraudulent representations made by the promoter to induce the subscription before incorporation, or the promoter at that time is without authority to represent the corporation or its officers. The corporation, however, may be held to have ratified the promoter's act if it takes advantage of the subscription with knowledge of the false representations. N. Y. Exch. Co. v. De Wolf, 31 

N. Y. 273. But if the company accepts the subscription without knowledge of the fraud, the subscriber cannot, ordinarily, rescind or sue the corporation for damages. His only action is against the promoter. The situation is entirely different where stock is sold by false representations made by the officers or the agent after it is formed. The corporation then cannot retain the benefits and repudiate the fraud. Churchill v. St. George Development Co., 174 

App. Div. 1, 160 N. Y. Supp. 357; Talmage v. Sanitary 

Security Co., 31 App. Div. 498, 52 N. Y. Supp. 139. McDermott v. Harrison, 56 Hun 640, 9 N. Y. Supp. 139.

If debts have been created by the corporation, the creditors may be presumed to have relied upon the subscription, and the subscriber is estopped by his laches involved in his delay, from withdrawing his subscription. Kent v. Quicksilver Mining Co., 78 N. Y. 159; Cady's Cases on Private 

Corporations, p. 447.

Representations regarding the future are ordinarily held not to be fraudulent. Titus v. Poole, 73 Hun 383, 26 N. Y. 

Supp. 451, aff'd 145 N. Y. 414. A representation that stock

is nonassessable may be either a prediction, or a misrepresentation of fact. A misrepresentation of the laws of a foreign state, relied on, was held a misrepresentation of fact, since, on the sale of shares of stock of a foreign corporation in New York, it is not presumed that the purchaser knows the law of the foreign state. Van Slochem v. Villard, 207 N. Y. 587, 101 N. E. 467. If the prospectus refers to other documents the subscriber, by the weight of authority, must examine the documents and cannot rely on the general statement in the prospectus which is contrary to the documents. Webster v. Upton, 91 U. S. 65, Hallowes v. Ferney, L. R., 3 Ch. 467.

Whether silence constitutes fraud depends upon whether the silence results from the suppression of facts or from concealment. Mere suppression where there is a duty to disclose renders the promoter liable to the stockholder. 

McManus v. Durant, 168 App. Div. 643, 154 N. Y. Supp. 

580. But as concerns the prospectus, it seems that a slightly different test is applied, and entire silence regarding certain phases of the proposition wholly isolated and unrelated to the phases discussed is held not to render the promoter liable to the subscriber. But if they undertake to speak regarding a condition of the company, the property, or the business, they owe the duty to speak the whole truth, in substance at least; and, as of course, it is assumed that they said what they meant, and meant what they said. A combination of express declarations, which are true, coupled with a skillful omission of details, may readily amount to concealment. The effect of the statements is to be measured by "the ordinary understanding of the ordinary mind," regardless of "by what trick or device or ambiguous language" it is conveyed. Thus, a true statement that the land is 3 miles from the railroad terminal is rendered fraudulent by the concealment of the fact that an unbridged river intervenes; that fortunes are made out of farming 10 acre tracts near at hand, though true, is rendered false by failure to state that the corporation's land is wild, and requires extensive drainage; that a pier is already built, by concealing that it is largely impracticable, and that only insignificant boats approach at unscheduled intervals. Churchill v. St.

PROMOTERS 

67 

George Dev. Co., 174 App. Div. 1, 160 N. Y. Supp. 357.

Conversely, it may be doubted whether duty required any disclosure as to terminal, farming, and pier, and whether complete silence would have given a cause of action. 

Concealment, however, renders the promoter liable. "A declaration that dividends have been paid imports that they have been earned." Ottinger v. Bennett, 144 App. Div. 525, 129 N. Y. Supp. 819 at p. 824, rev. on dissenting opinion below, 203 N. Y. 554.

The statement that the corporation "had purchased" the land is not satisfied by the fact that one of the promoters had paid down $25,000 on the purchase price of one and a half millions, and intended to turn it in for stock of the corporation to a large amount. Rives v. Bartlett, 156 App. Div. 

532, 141 N. Y. Supp. 56, rev. on other grounds, 215 N. Y. 

33. It would be fraudulent for a syndicate member to state, in order to induce subscriptions to purchase stock, that he was "putting in cash the same as" one of the subscribers, and that "any man in joining puts in a dollar against the other man's dollar," when the whole truth was that he already owned the majority of the stock to be purchased, which he later turned over for the money subscribed. Heckscher v. Edenborn, 203 N. Y. 210, at pp. 221-222. Without reference to their own moral guilt or innocence, a fraudulent intent on the part of those mediately or immediately circulating the prospectus "may be inferred from the falsity of the statements therein contained." Downey v. Finucane, 205 N. Y. 251, 98 N. E. 391, 40 L. R. A.

The interpretation of the prospectus is generally the crux. 

Plaintiff is bound to prove intentional fraud as distinguished from mere breach of duty, such as carelessness or misjudgment. Bell v. James, 198 N. Y. 513, 92 N. E. 1078, affirming 128 App. Div. 241, 112 N. Y. Supp. 750; Canadian

Agency v. Assets Realization Co., 165 App. Div. 96, 150 

N. Y. Supp. 758. The use of ambidextrous language cannot shield the promoter if the effect produced upon the ordinary mind would be false. Von Au v. Magenheimer, 196 N. Y. 

510, affirming 126 App. Div. 257, 110 N. Y. Supp. 

629. To illustrate:-A statement that a corporation had acquired and owned the other company is interpreted

strictly and is not satisfied by the fact that it owned a majority of its stock which it had purchased with borrowed money. Mack v. Latta, 83 App. Div. 242, 82 N. Y. Supp. 

130, rev'd on other grounds, 178 N. Y. 525; that the cost was so much means that the amount stated was paid for it. 

Lehmen-Charley v. Bartlett, 135 App. Div. 674, 120 N. Y. 

Supp. 501, affd. 202 N. Y. 524; Rives v. Bartlett, 156 App. 

Div. 552, 141 N. Y. Supp. 561, rev. on other grounds, 215

N. Y. 33. A statement that the profits of a corporation would be larger than those of the co-partnership which it had succeeded, and that it would be to the advantage of plaintiff, who was then an employee of the firm, to subscribe for stock and become a salaried employee, may be false where the plaintiff has proof to show that the one making them had reason to believe at the time he made them that performance was impossible, Ritzwoller v. Lurie, 225 N. Y. 

464; that it was listed on the stock exchange, Sarantides v. 

Williams, 180 N. Y. Supp. 741; that all the stock has been subscribed for, and that well known persons had subscribed, when in fact, their stock had been given to them, Talmadge v. Sanitary Security Co., 31 App. Div. 498, 52 N. Y. Supp. 

139. But a statement that the railroad has enough subscriptions to construct the road is a matter of opinion. Goodrich v. Reynolds & Co., 31 Ill. 490, 83 Am. Dec. 240. Declaring and paying dividends that have not been earned to induce deeper investment, is fraud. Keeler v. Seaman, 47 Misc. 

292, 95 N. Y. Supp. 920.

For a classification of statements made in the prospectus which are strictly construed as to language and effect, and those in which the promoter is not liable where the statement is relatively true, the student is referred to treatises on the promotion of companies. 

§ 46. Blue Sky Laws. 

The foregoing principles proved insufficient to protect the investor from deceitful practices pursued contrary to the rules of common honesty but in accord with the principles of law above referred to. For the protection of the public most states have passed statutes commonly called "Blue Sky Laws." The purpose at which they are aimed is to protect investors against "speculative schemes which

PROMOTERS 

69 have no more basis than so many feet of blue sky." The 

Kansas legislature led off in 1911. The statute in New York is called the Martin Act, ch. 649 laws of 1921 as amended, contained in the General Business Law, sec. 352 at seq., and is also contained in the Penal Law, secs. 421, 421a.

The Blue Sky laws in New York empower the attorney general to conduct an investigation whenever it appears to him that "negotiable documents of title" are about to be sold or promoted by what is defined in the statute as “fraudulent practices," and provides for the appointment of a receiver in a proper case. The statute defines "commodity" as "any negotiable document of title," or "something dealt with on any exchange for future delivery.' 

Sec. 352. Security is defined as "stocks, bonds, notes, evidences of interest or indebtedness or other securities." Sec. 

352. Dealer is defined as "every person, partnership, corporation, trust, or association, except a domestic municipal corporation who trades in securities by selling or obtaining them for sale to the public or who deals in futures or margins." § 359e. Fraudulent practice is defined as any fraudulent scheme, artifice, fictitious or pretended sale of commodities, or any course of business relating to the sale of business or commodities which is: 1. fraudulent, or 2. in violation of law, or 3. which has operated or may operate as a fraud upon the purchaser, or 4. false pretenses, representation, or promises by any dealer offering securities, or made to obtain money by false pretenses, § 352.

The remedies provided by the statute are as follows: the attorney-general may require a. a statement under oath in any form prepared by him giving all the facts and circumstances concerning the subject matter which the attorney-general believes to be to the public interest to investigate. Sec. 352. b. "any books, and papers to be produced for his inspection" c. compel the attendance and examination of witnesses under oath before him, or a magistrate, a court of record or a judge or justice thereof, before bringing proceedings. Failure to obey is a misdemeanor. It is further provided that the power of subpoena shall not abate or terminate by reason of any action or proceeding hereinafter mentioned, which will have been

begun by the attorney-general; d. enjoin foreign corporations, not licensed under 210 G. C. L., from continuing the "fraudulent practices" above defined; e. move for the appointment of a receiver in the action. The failure to appear and be examined or to produce books and papers, or to furnish the statement aforesaid, constitutes prima facie evidence that the sale or offering for sale, or advertisement of the securities is "fraudulent practice" and may in the discretion of the court be treated as a sufficient basis for a preliminary injunction against the continuance of the offering.

The statute further empowers the court at any stage of the proceedings to appoint a receiver and to grant a preliminary injunction and further to appoint a referee who will have power to punish for contempt. Sec. 456, B. S. L.

As to a witness who claims that the testimony required of him might tend to incriminate him or to subject him to a penalty or forfeiture, it is provided, that if directed by the court, the referee, magistrate, or officer conducting the inquiry to testify or produce the books, papers, or documents, the witness will not thereafter be prosecuted or subjected to any penalty or forfeiture for or on account of any transaction, matter, or thing concerning which he shall testify; and it is further provided that "no testimony so given or produced shall be received against him upon any criminal action, suit or proceeding, investigation, or inquiry." The immunity does not apply to a corporation or the officers as such. Sec. 359, B. S. L.

The sale by the issuer or underwriter of a security is exempted from the definition of "trading in securities."

The statute further requires every dealer to file a "state notice" before selling or offering for sale to the public any securities issued or to be issued, giving the name and business or post office address of the dealer, the name of the security or securities offered with the name, post office address, state and country of organization of the corporation, association, or similar association issuing the securities. 359e, sub. 2 and 3 B. S. L. 

Securities, issued or guaranteed by the United States, or its possessions, states, or political divisions thereof, the

PROMOTERS 

71 dominion of Canada, or by any foreign government with which the United States has diplomatic relations, and certain banks, public service corporations, any security, other than common stock, outstanding for a period of not less than five years upon which no default exists, negotiable instruments maturing in not more than twelve months from the date of issue, bonds and mortgages, securities fully listed upon any New York exchange on January 1, 1925, or subsequent thereto, and published by the exchange in the state paper, sale or sales by pledgee or mortgagee, and negotiable documents of title, and foreign currency orders and calls or options therefor are specially exempted by sec. 359f, B. S. L.

In Oregon it was held that the Blue Sky Law included such schemes as the sale of "units of interest" in an electrical invention to extract gold from the waters of Mono 

Lake, California. State v. Whiteaker, 118 Ore. 656, 247 

Pac. 1077.

The statute, it is said, is intended to prevent the offering for sale or the sale of stocks, bonds, or other commodities by means of fraudulent schemes, and the question is whether the defendant has, by fraudulent means or deceitful practices sold or intended to sell the commodities. 

People v. Smith Co., Inc., 136 Misc. 449, 240 N. Y. Supp. 807.

In the latter case a receiver was appointed for two foreign corporations, the Fairfax Corp., and the F. H. Smith Co., Inc. The facts were that in 1926 a first mortgage of $1,200,000 as security for a bond issue on an apartment house known as Cleveland Hall in Buffalo, was offered for sale by the F. H. Smith Co., Inc. Subsequently, the Fairfax

Corp. decided to change Cleveland Hall into an apartment hotel and to issue a first and refunding mortgage of $1,550,000 collateral to bonds of that amount to the F. H.

Smith Co., Inc. which was to return $350,000 thereof to the 

Fairfax Corp. The attorney-general demanded the books of the F. H. Smith Co., which, not being forthcoming, a temporary injunction was granted. On the final hearing, it appeared that appraisals printed in the prospectus or advertisement had been skilfully manipulated, and that the probable value

of the real estate was considerably less than the face of the bonds offered to the public. The court noted that the usual loan made in good times did not exceed 65% of the value of the property and held that the advertisement came under the definition of "fraudulent practices" as used in the Martin Act. The court said that these words included what is called "equitable fraud" and misrepresentation and concealment of material facts without intent to defraud. 

In Kerst v. Nelson, 213 N. W. 904, it was held that the sale of a tract of land, with an agreement on the part of the seller to cultivate grapes thereon and to market the crop for ½ the profits, the seller to make up any deficit, the buyers not to default in the payment of installments, the management to remain in the seller for 5 years and the sale being in small lots of land, incapable of independent successful operation, came under the blue sky law. In Reilly v. Clyne, 234 Pac. 35 (Ariz.) the blue sky law was held to comprehend not only corporations, but also joint stock companies and other associations exercising any of the powers of a corporation and including a Massachusetts trust. The subscription to the stock in this case was by means of promissory notes. It was held that a subscriber might rescind his subscription on the ground that the corporation was not complying with the Blue Sky Laws, under the rule that "where a statute imposes a penalty for an act" a contract founded on the act is void although the statute does not declare it such or prohibit such a contract expressly. 25 R. C. L. 979, sec. 228, 40 A. L. R. 1012. § 47.

Adoption of Promoters Contracts. 

The rule universally adopted is that the corporation is not liable on the contracts of promoters, however worded, unless it has done something to adopt, either expressly or impliedly, such of their contracts as the corporation itself is authorized to make by its charter. Kirkup v. Anaconda 

Amusement Co., 59 Mont. 469, 197 Pac. 1005, 17 A. L. R. 

441; Martin v. Remington-Martin Co., 95 App. Div. 18, 88 

N. Y. Supp. 378; Munson v. Syracuse R. Co. 103 N. Y. 58,

Cady's Cases on Pri. Corps. p. 153; Thistle v. Jones, 123 

App. Div. 40, 107 N. Y. Supp. 840.

Adoption may be by act of the directors or by a resolution

PROMOTERS 

73 of all the members at a meeting at which all the directors are present, and all concur, with full knowledge of all the facts. Kirkup case, supra.

By the weight of authority, the corporation, after it is formed, may make itself liable by knowingly receiving the benefits of promoter's contracts. Morgan v. Bon Bon Co., 222 N. Y. 22, Cady's Cases on Pri. Corps. p. 147; Shaffer v. 

Mohawk Brewing Corp'n, 221 N. Y. 697; Bommer v. Amer. 

Spiral Spring Butt Hinge M'fg. Co., 81 N. Y. 468.

Parol evidence may not be received to show that a resolution of the board was intended to adopt promoters contracts where the language of the resolution itself does not indicate such intent, and declarations of board members made outside of a board meeting may not be received to explain the intent of the resolution. Gardner v. Bronx Nat. Bank, 158 App. Div. 288, 142 N. Y. Supp. 713, aff'd 216 N. Y. 683 (mem.).

The decision whether to regard the liability of the corporation as resting on ratification, adoption, novation, or a continuing offer, is complicated by the fact that the corporation usually adopts the contracts of promoters by a resolution at the organization meeting of members, (See App. G.) usually comprising in number those who participated in the making of the contract. The better rule is to regard the contract as a continuing offer made to the corporation, which, by its adoption after it comes into being, is turned into a binding contract, from which neither party may withdraw. Morgan v. Bon Bon Co., supra. The doctrine of implied adoption is in reality an application of the doctrine of estoppel. United Germ. Silv. Co. v. Bronson, 92 Conn. 266, 102 Atl. 647.

The Massachusetts and the later English rule is that the corporation's adoption of a contract made in its behalf before it existed is a mere offer, which must be accepted by the offeree in order to turn it into a contract. 

Lothrop, 191 Mass. 357, 77 N. E. 842. 

Pennell v.

Adoption may be by act of officers of the corporation within their authority. Where the promoter who made the contract became president of the corporation, it was held that his ratification bound the corporation. Oakes v. Cat-

taraugus Water Co., 143 N. Y. 430; Mesinger v. Mesinger 

Bicycle Saddle Co., 44 App. Div. 26, 60 N. Y. Supp. 431.

In some states it has been held that the promoters necessary expenses for obtaining the charter, securing subscriptions to the stock, and otherwise in perfecting the organization of the company, if performed with the expectation of being paid, are valid debts of the company by the fact of its acceptance of benefits after organization. Kentucky,

New Hampshire and Vermont are states asserting this rule. 

The reason assigned is that without such a rule the formation of a company would be well nigh impossible. The weight of authority is that unless the obligation to pay is imposed by a charter provision or by adoption by the corporation, it is not liable although it receives the benefit. An interesting case several times before the courts arose in connection with the enterprise that resulted in the construction of the Equitable Building in New York City. A promoter employed the plaintiffs intestate to use his acquaintance with the officers of the Equitable Life Assurance Society to learn how to prepare an entertainable proposition, for which the plaintiff was to receive $100,000 in money and $100,000 of common stock of the eventual corporation. The services were performed, and a proposition resulted, which was finally accepted by the corporation later formed to develop it. Meanwhile, the promoter turned the whole promotion scheme over to a second promoter, who agreed with the first promoter that the plaintiff's cash commission should be paid out of the first moneys available from the sale of preferred stock and bonds, and from the stock issued. After the projected corporation had been formed and the second promoter had become a director in it, it contracted to pay to the second promoter his "expenses ....incurred." Plaintiff, being unrecompensed, died, and his representatives sued the corporation. It was held that there was no express contract of the corporation that would amount to an adoption of the contract with plaintiff, and no implied adoption arising from the undoubted acceptance of the benefits, for all these were performed before incorporation, at the request of the promoter. Gardner v. Equitable Office Building Corporation, 273 Fed. 441, 17 A. L. R.

PROMOTERS 

75 

431. cf. Wentworth v. Northern Producing Co., Inc., 172 N. Y. Supp. 342. But where knowledge of the agreement is imputable to the corporation at the date of acceptance of benefits, there is an adoption. Bommer v. Spring & Co., 81 N. Y. 468. There is a radical difference, also in the rule of benefits cum onere, between a promise made on behalf of a corporation to be formed in the future and to be performed by the corporation itself after formation, and a contract made with the promoter to cause the corporation to assume the contract. If the benefit and the onus are both stated in the contract itself, the corporation can not accept the benefit without accepting the onus. Ib. 

Adoption must be with full knowledge and the agreement may be set aside by the corporation on discovering the fraud therein. Finch v. Canadaway Fert. Co., 152 App. Div. 391, 136 N. Y. Supp. 914; 208 N. Y. 607, 102 N. E. 1102.

A contract made with the promoters alone, and not appearing to have been made in contemplation of a benefit to be reaped by the corporation, cannot be ratified; for the corporation cannot thrust itself upon the contracting party any more than any other stranger. Little Rock & Ft. S. R. 

Co. v. Perry, 37 Ark. 164.

A promoters contract that is ultra vires cannot be adopted by the corporation. But if the contract appears to be a reasonable means of carrying out the powers authorized, it may be adopted. Thistle v. Jones, 45 Misc. 215, 92 N. Y. 

Supp. 113, rev. on other grounds, 123 App. Div. 40, 107 

N. Y. Supp. 840; Avendon v. Gem Dress House, 232 N. Y. 

505; Burden v. Burden, 159 N. Y. 287.

Payment by a corporation on account of bills for services rendered on a promoters contract for the corporation is prima facie proof of adoption. Galdieri & Co. v. Arthur 

Waist Co., 98 Misc. 612, 163 N. Y. Supp. 154. 

§ 48. Preliminary Expenses of Promoter. 

These fall into two classes: promotion and organization. 

The former generally include preliminary investigation, with possible expenditures for engineering, accounting, marketing, legal advice, preliminary legal searches, the preparation of surveys, estimates of cost, income and expenses; procuring options and assembling parties of the

requisite managerial and technical ability so that there may be a clear proposition to advance to investors, backed up by trustworthy papers; and brokers commissions and the like. 

They may run into large sums. Long Sault Dev. Co. v. 

Kennedy, 212 N. Y. 1; Cady's Cases on Pri. Corps. p. 47.

Organization expenses include legal fees for incorporating the company and the expense of preliminary meetings. 

The weight of authority is that the corporation has the option to refuse to act, although the repudiation of the benefits might prevent the corporation from coming into being. If the advantages of the proposition are enough to convince the corporation, then, by accepting the benefit, it is held subject to the attached conditions. Where promoters obtained stock subscriptions under a contract by which they were to be secured by real estate mortgages, the bank can not take the benefit of the subscriptions without accepting a condition in the contract, that the bank would clear off prior liens. Burrows v. Smith, 10 N. Y. 550. To bind the corporation it will be essential that it had previous knowledge or notice of the existence of the claim and of the material facts on which it was founded. Low v. Conn. & P. 

River R. Co., 45 N. H. 370.

If the minutes of the board do not purport to adopt the promoters contract, parol evidence may not be received to show that a resolution was intended to be an adoption. An "organization committee," promoting the organization of a bank, made a report to the bank when formed, containing recommendations concerning the compensation of the promoter. The board of directors passed a resolution commending the report and acting on certain of the recommendations. It was held that parol evidence could not be introduced to show that the intention of the board was that the resolution should be considered as approving the promoter's claim for compensation. Gardner v. Bronx Nat. 

Bank, 158 App. Div. 288, 142 N. Y. Supp. 713, aff'd, 216 

N. Y. 683, (mem.). 

Where the expenditure of the promoter is incurred for matters remote from the work immediately necessary for the organization and the corporation received no direct and tangible benefit, the corporation cannot be held except by

PROMOTERS 

77 charter provisions. 

Williams v. McNally, 270 Pac. 411 (Wyo.); Weber v. Clymax Molybdenum Co., 127 Misc. 470, 216 N. Y. Supp. 481.

Stock cannot validly be issued in consideration of services rendered before incorporation, unless tangible benefit accrues after incorporation. S. C. L. 69 provides: "No corporation shall issue either shares of stock or bonds except for money, labor done, or property actually received for the use and lawful purposes of such corporation." The "labor done" refers to labor rendered the corporation. Otherwise, the entire capital stock might be issued without visible assets in the corporation. Herbert v. Duryea, 34 App. Div. 

478, 54 N. Y. Supp. 311, aff'd 164 N. Y. 596; Lamphere v. 

Lang, 157 App. Div. 306, 141 N. Y. Supp. 967, rev. on other grounds, 213 N. Y. 585, 108 N. E. 82; American Macaroni 

Corp. v. Saumer, 174 N. Y. Supp. 183. It is proper for the corporation to assume the expenses of a reorganization committee in a case where the situation is such as would have authorized the directors to direct that a study be made of the situation. Yoakam v. Providence Biltmore Hotel 

Co., 34 F. (2d) 533. 

§ 49. Actions Against Promoters. 

Promoters are jointly and severally liable for secret profits, or for fraud and deceit. Old Dominion etc. v. Bigelow, 188 Mass. 315, 74 N. E. 653; Bigelow v. Old. Dom. etc. Co., 74 N. J. Eq. 457, 71 Atl. 153; Walker v. Anglo-Amer. Mtg. & Tr. Co., 72 Hun 334, 25 N. Y. Supp. 432; Richardson's 

Outline of Contracts, secs. 351, 352. Several remedies are open to those injured by secret profits:- 

1. The corporation may restore or offer to restore what it has received from the promoter, and sue to set the transaction aside and to recover what it has parted with. Munson v. Syracuse G. & C. R. Co., 103 N. Y. 58. 

2. It may compel an accounting for the secret profits made. Hutchinson v. Simpson, 92 App. Div. 382, 87 N. Y. 

Supp. 369; Colton Imp. Co. v. Richter, 26 Misc. 26, 55 N. Y. 

Supp. 486. Recission is not a proper preliminary to the action for accounting. Wills v. Nehalem Coal Co., 52 Ore. 70, 96 Pac. 528. 

3. It may sue in assumpsit to recover the secret profits;

but if it is unable to restore what it has received, this action is not maintainable. Simmons v. Vulcan Oil & Mining Co., 100 Am. Dec. 628 (Pa.); Head v. Tattersall, L. R. 7 Exch. 

7; Ball v. Breed, etc. 294 Fed. 227. 

4. It may bring an action for damages. Getty v. Devlin, 70 N. Y. 504, 54 N. Y. 403. 

5. If the corporation issues stock to the promoter for his secret profits, it may cancel the stock on learning that fact. If the stock has been negotiated by the promoter to a purchaser for value in good faith without notice, the promoter may be held for an accounting of the profits of the sale, on the ground that they are secret profits. Travis v. Travis, 104 N. Y. Supp. 1021, 140 App. Div. 191. P. P. L. 

169. Camden Land Co. v. Lewis, 63 Atl. 523 (Me.); Yeiser v. U. S. Board & Paper Co., 107 Fed. 340, 52 L. R. A. 724.

The stockholder has no direct cause of action against the promoter for secret profits, for the injury is in the first instance to the corporation. But if the corporation refuses to sue, or is in the control of the wrong-doers, the stockholder is permitted to bring a representative action for the benefit of the corporation, which must be joined as a party defendant with the wrong-doers. Brewster v. Hatch, 122 

N. Y. 349.

The subscriber who has been brought into the proposition by means of the promoters fraudulent misrepresentations or concealments has three lines of relief open to him: 1. To retain what he has received and sue for damages for the fraud. 2. Bring action to rescind the subscription, tendering back anything he has received under the contract. 

3. Bring action based on a prior recission, having previously tendered back any stock received, and recover all amounts paid. Hecksher v. Edenborn, 203 N. Y. 210.

The corporation may bring action to compel the promoter to account for secret profits, and in that action a mandatory injunction may be entered compelling the payment over. 

Getty v. Devlin, 74 N. Y. 504; 54 N. Y. 403.

Where the separate rights of shareholders have been infringed, they must sue individually. But wherever the company's rights have been violated, it may sue; and, if the injury is to the corporation only, the stockholder can

PROMOTERS 

79 not sue unless either the corporation has been dissolved or unless he brings a stockholders representative suit on behalf of the corporation and excuses the failure of the corporation to bring it by showing the domination of the present board by the promoter. The stock investors may maintain an action for accounting for secret profits, as where the promoter, through an option, received a portion of the purchase price paid by the corporation for its property. Hebgen v. Keffler, 97 Wis. 313, 72 N. W. 745. New Sombrero 

Phosphate Co. v. Erlanger, L. R. 5 Ch. Div. 73, aff'd, 3 App. Cas. 1018. In the case last mentioned, the promoter purchased a lease of an island containing guano deposits, took title in the name of his nominee, and sold the lease at considerable profit to a corporation which he promoted, the directors of which were selected by the promoter, and who purchased the lease, in ignorance of the interest of the promoter, and relying on his statement of the value, with money obtained by the subscription to stock. In the 

New Sombrero case there was, then, no fraud on the stockholders individually. The fraud in fact was perpetrated only after they had taken their shares, and paid for them. 

The injury was, therefore, to the shareholders in their collective capacity only, and therefore the cause of action belonged to the corporation.

The primary rule of damages is that the purchaser may recover the difference between what he paid for the stock or bonds, and their actual intrinsic value, if less, on the day of sale. Reno v. Bull, supra. Where there is no market, sales may be shown at an earlier or later date; and the book value and subsequent history of the company may be considered on the question of value in a case where there have been no sales. Van Au v. Magenheimer, 110 N. Y. 

Supp. 629, at p. 638, 126 App. Div. 257, aff'd, 196 N. Y. 

510, 89 N. E. 1114. The subsequent history aforesaid may be relevant, for, in the language of Mr. Justice Holmes in Whitney v. Price, 172 Mass. 240, 51 N. E. 1084, "subsequent events may be likened to the coming out of a latent defect existing in a horse at the time of a fraudulent sale.” 

§ 50. 

Underwriting. 

An underwriting contract is a contract to offer for sale

the shares or bonds of a corporation and to take and pay for the whole issue or the number mentioned in the agreement unless sold to others. 1 Fletcher, Enc. of Corp., sec. 

444. Underwriting is frequently done by bankers or by a syndicate of bankers or brokers. The underwriters endeavor to interest their depositors and allies in the enterprise. The contract of underwriting may be so drawn that the underwriters are (1) guarantors of the subscription to the issue either wholly or in part, and liable for damages only; (2) conditional subscribers bound to take what was unsold to the public, Burke v. Smith, 16 Wall. (U. S.) 390, 21 L. ed. 361; (3) subscribers. A positive agreement to take the shares and pay for them under definite specified terms produces this effect. Positry Corp. of A. v. Flowers, 36 F. (2d) 617 cf. 32 F. (2d) 202; Yonkers Gazette Co. v. 

Taylor, 30 App. Div. 334, 51 N. Y. Supp. 969; Sanders v. 

Barnaby, 166 App. Div. 274, 151 N. Y. Supp. 580; or, (4) makers of an agreement to subscribe. Avon Springs Sanitarium Co. v. Weed, 119 App. Div. 560, 104 N. Y. Supp. 58; 

Cady's Cases on Pri. Corps. p. 358. A complete underwriting agreement where the corporation is not yet formed ordinarily involves two instruments: the first, between the underwriters, and the second, between the underwriters and the syndicate manager. When the flotation is of the stock or bonds of an existing corporation, three documents are usually required; the first, among the underwriters; the second, between the corporation and the underwriters, providing for the latter's compensation, expenses, and powers, such as that of acting as fiscal agent and transfer agent; and the third, between the existing stockholders, the corporation and the underwriters, covering the changes to be made in the board or by-laws, etc. for the adequate protection and representation on the board of the new interests which are to be brought in, and for what period of time the new interests shall be in whole or in partial control, and binding the old stockholders to vote for these changes at a stockholders meeting to be held after the new subscription.

Sometimes a voting trust for not more than ten years is added, sec. 50, S. C. L., and guarantees of dividends, etc.

Underwriting agreements frequently embody provisions for

PROMOTERS 

81 an increase of stock, the inspection of books, records, plants, and contracts, and the virtual control and reorganization under new officers, in accordance with the wishes of the new interests. Underwriting contracts are said to have originated in France. See Cleveland's "Promotion and

Capitalization of Railroads." The practice became common in England and the United States about 1875.

§ 51. Express Powers. Specified in the Certificate of 

Incorporation or Conferred by Statute.

The specification of powers in the certificate of incorporation embodies the objects of the corporation, and the means of attaining them, on which shareholders, subscribers, and all other contracting parties are deemed to rely. The powers of the board of directors and of the officers flow from the documents composing the certificate of incorpora- 82

tion and its amendments, which are, in effect, the constitution of the corporation.

The charter confers franchises and immunities, and is the measure of the powers granted. The "franchise" is the right to exist as a corporation. 7 R. C. L. sec. 66. Strictly speaking, the franchise of a corporation consists of the rights, powers, and privileges given by the act of the legislature incorporating it, or the certificate of incorporation creating it pursuant to statutory authority. Municipal grants and consents, sometimes referred to in judicial writings as franchises, are, in fact, conditions precedent to operation. Peo. v. Consol. Gas. Co., 115 N. Y. Supp. 393 

130 App. Div. 626. See also, Holmes Elec. Prot. Co. v. 

Williams, 228 N. Y. 407.

Powers are the rights possessed by all citizens to carry on business which are granted the corporation by being set forth expressly or by necessary implication in its charter. 

7 R. C. L. sec. 66. The general rule is that the enumeration of these powers implies the exclusion of all others. Doubtless, the state, by general language in the certificate of incorporation, might grant any power not infringing the prohibitions laid upon it by the state and federal constitutions; and might even grant such a power of sovereignty as the right of eminent domain, if only the particular property to be taken over was to be devoted to a public use. 

Matter of Niagara F. & W. Ry. Co., 108 N. Y. 375. Matter of Tuthill, 163 N. Y. 133. Matter of Deansville Cem. Assoc., 66 N. Y. 569. It has always been the policy of New York state to require the application for a charter to state expressly the powers, with the effect that all concerned were advised of the businesses to be transacted. The danger inherent in a general grant of powers was emphasized by an experience with banking charters. Peo. v. Manhattan Co., 9 Wend. 351.

The English rule gives corporations all the powers of individuals unless expressly restricted by charter. Ashbury

Railway Carriage & Iron Co. v. Riche, L. R. 9 Exch. 224. 

The tendency of the modern decisions in America is to assimilate the rights, duties, and liabilities of the corporation to those of an individual, but limited to the line of

business expressly defined by charter, and such powers as reasonably may be implied for the purpose of carrying out the express powers. Thomas v. West Jersey R. Co., 101 

U. S. 71, 25 L. Ed. 950. The "charter" comprises the certificate of incorporation and the statutes applicable to the corporation. Mtr. of Timmis, 200 N. Y. 177, Cady's Cas. p. 255. The powers expressly conferred are executed by the officers acting under the board of directors. Wattley v. National Drug Stores Corp., 204 N. Y. Supp. 254, 122 

Misc. 533. A 3 million dollar corporation, whose express powers were to manufacture and sell gold and silverware, was held without power to buy, sell, and deal in goods of a cheaper grade than those manufactured by it. Peo. ex rel. 

Tiffany & Co. v. Campbell, 144 N. Y. 166. 

§ 51a. Amendment of Purposes. 

If the certificate fails to state the true object, an amended certificate may be filed. G. C. L. sec. 10. The amendment under this section is for three narrow purposes only: 1. To eliminate any informality. 2. To strike out any matter not authorized by law to be stated in the certificate. 3. To correct a defective proof or acknowledgment. The statute, being curative, is remedial. The amendment makes the corporation de jure for all purposes. (Cf. p. 49, supra.)

It is not the intent of G. C. L. 10 to provide for the correction of the certificate where the filed certificate is faulty in terminology or phraseology. An application made under G. C. L. 10 to classify directors and to change preferred stock dividends on the ground that the certificate did not truly set forth the objects and purposes, was denied. 

In re Horace Keane Aerplanes, Inc., 194 App. Div. 873, 185 

N. Y. Supp. 163 (1st department). The amendment of

G. C. L. 10 by c. 650, laws of 1929 has probably rendered obsolete the decision in Millspaugh v. Cassidy, 191 App. Div. 

221, 181 N. Y. Supp. 276 (2d department), in which the court reformed the certificate so as to deny to preferred stockholders the right to vote. Amendments that are not authorized by G. C. L. 10 may be made in compliance with 

S. C. L. 35, 36.

All other amendatory certificates must be made by filing an amendatory certificate under secs. 35 and 36 S. C. L. 

& 52. General Rules for the Construction of Powers 

Specifically Granted.

Powers conferred on the corporation, whether by the general acts or special acts, must be construed according to the rules for construction of statutes in general. Some of the principles most frequently cited are as follows: 

1. Decisions handed down prior to the enactment of affirmative statutes are not superseded by the statute. Affirmative statutes are to be construed in accordance with the common law decisions. Negative statutes are construed strictly so as not to change any more of the common law than is strictly requisite. Potters-Dwarris on Statutes, sec. 70. 

2. A declaratory statute, also called cumulative, is one that declares the common law and is to be considered in the light of decisions. Geisler v. De Graaf, 166 N. Y. 339. 3. Remedial statutes modify the common law and are to be construed liberally in accordance with the intent. Penal statutes, being those in derogation of rights or creating penalties, are construed strictly. Loucks v. Standard Oil 

Co., 224 N. Y. 99. Osborne v. International Ry. Co., 226

N. Y. 421. An act conferring on a corporation certain privileges and restraining the rights of the citizen is penal, and must be strictly construed. Sprague v. Birdsall, 2 Cow. 419. (4) Statutes in derogation of the common law must be strictly construed, and the common law no further abrogated than the clear import of the language of the statute absolutely requires. In re Carnegie Trust Co., 206 N. Y. 390. 

5. Non compliance with mandatory provisions of statutes render things done void. Acts under provisions of a directory statute are valid, tho the statutory method of doing the thing was not strictly followed. Wiles v. Peck, 26 N. Y. 42. 

6. General words in a statute must yield to the necessary particular application specified therein. Peo. ex rel. Urban 

Water Co. v. Connelly, 149 N. Y. Supp. 693, 164 App. Div. 

163. Where general words in a statute follow specific words denoting special things, the general words are, as a rule, limited to specifications of the same general nature as those specified, called the principle of ejusdem generis. For in-

stance, a bootblack stand in a booth or apartment, is not included in the phrase "places of public accommodation or amusement" in a statute that enumerates, as the subjects to which it is to apply, "inns, restaurants, hotels, eating houses, bath houses, barber shops, theatres, music halls, public conveyances on land and water, and all other places of public accommodation or amusement" for the indefinite words can bring within the purview of the statute only such things as are in the same category with the clear terms. 

Burks v. Bosso, 180 N. Y. 341. The principle is subordi nate, however, to the rule that statutes should be construed in the light of the intent of the legislators. People v. Dr. 

Kelly Med. Co., 146 N. Y. Supp. 398, 160 App. Div. 644. 

O'Connor v. City of New York, 165 N. Y. Supp. 625, 178

App. Div. 550. 7. The maxim, expressio unius est exclusio alterius, applies to the construction of statutes. Express enumeration of powers excludes all powers not enumerated. 

Where a statute details the manner in which certain acts may be done, all other methods are impliedly excluded. 

People v. Gorman, 231 N. Y. Supp. 85, 133 Misc. 161. This rule of construction, however, must yield to the use of clear legislative intent. Conroy v. Sewell, 126 Misc. 418, 213 N. Y.

Supp. 602. The general rule is that the certificate of incorporation is to be fairly and liberally construed. Thus, general corporation acts have usually been given a sufficiently broad interpretation to meet progressive inventions in the enterprises mentioned in the charter. Holmes Elec. 

Prot. Co. v. Williams, 228 N. Y. at p. 420, opinion of

CRANE, J. In the said case, it was held that a company incorporated under the "Telegraph Act" of 1848, to maintain an electric telegraph, prior to the general use of telephones, and which had purchased in 1883, the Holmes Burglar Alarm overhead wires of telegraph systems, had power to operate an electric signal service by which a burglar registered his burglarious entry in the company's offices, and that the city of New York could not compel the removal of its wires from the usual conduits, as the city had assumed to do, assigning as a reason that the powers granted did not include the use of later scientific developments. 

The following are to be strictly construed against the

corporation, nothing passing by implication:-1.

All ex clusive privileges. Art. 1 of the N. Y. S. Const. provides: 

"The legislature is prohibited from passing private or local bills granting to any private corporation, association, or individual any exclusive privilege, immunity or franchise whatever, or from granting to any person, association, firm, or corporation, an exemption from taxation on real or personal property." The word, "exclusive," in the constitution relates to monopolies. It does not prevent the legislature from incorporating a company to dam a river, build a bridge, or run a ferry, altho it is intended that the charter be exclusive since no other bridge, ferry or dam can be constructed at the same place. Long Sault Dev. Co. v. 

Canada, 212 N. Y. 1, Cady's Cases on Pri. Corp. p. 46. 

2. All powers granted in derogation of public right, or of the rights or franchises of other corporations. Auburn & 

Cato P. R. Co. v. Douglas, 9 N. Y. 444 at p. 451. 3. All provisions whereby the state restricts its own sphere of action, or appears to grant rights in derogation of general laws, are to be construed strictly. Tying v. Com'r. Warehouse Co., 58 N. Y. 208 at p. 314. 

§ 53. Illegal Powers Specifically Conferred. 

If illegal powers are specifically conferred, they are to be regarded as surplusage, unless they are the only powers, in which case, the state may institute quo warranto proceedings and oust the association from the exercise of corporate powers. State v. Critchett, 37 Minn. 13, 32 N. W. 

787. State v. Debenture Guarantee & Loan Co., 26 So. 600. 

If the purpose is illegal, as, for instance, in violation of some principle of morality or public policy or a statutory prohibition, the corporation will not be recognized by the courts, nor will it be permitted to sue as a corporation. 

Thus, a corporation formed to rebel against the United 

States, St. Louis & etc. Assoc. v. Hennessy, 11 Mo. App. 555, or a corporation to run a lottery, Boyd v. Alabama, 91 U. S. 

645, will be granted no recognition. Motive is immaterial if the stated purpose of the corporation is legal. Peo. v. 

Manhattan Co., supra.

§ 54. Effect of Non-user. 

In the absence of statutes, the courts, both of law and equity, refused to compel corporations to put into force their purposes except where there was clear language in the charter considering that their powers were granted for their own individual benefit. Atty. Gen. v. Oxford & Ry. 

Co., 2 W. R. 330. Mayor of Liverpool v. Chorley & Co., 2 De 

G. M. & G. 852, 860. The public obligation of local government boards and other municipal corporations to attempt to attain their objects might be thought to comprise a duty enforceable by the courts, but the courts have been loathe to interfere unless substantial injury to the public would result. Our statute, G. C. L. sec. 30 was discussed in sec. 19, supra. The word, "organization," as used in the statute, is defined as the election of officers, providing for the subscription and payment of the capital stock, the adoption of bylaws and such steps as are necessary to endow the legal entity with the capacity to transact the business for which it was incorporated. Walton v. Oliver, 49 Kan. 107, 33 Am. State Rep. 355. Commonwealth of Pa. v. McGlinn 

Distilling Co., 265 Penn. St. 346, 350.

Corporations may decline to use some of their special powers or to completely carry on the whole of the enterprises authorized by the charter, and encourage one part of the business and discourage or abandon another, according to the contingencies of the trade. There is a general authority to use the capital to the best advantage. Powers so neglected are not lost. Skinner v. Smith, 134 N. Y. 240. 

Matter of Timmis, 200 N. Y. 177. Cady's Cases on Pri. 

Corp. p. 253. Buffalo & Jamestown RR. Co. v. Gifford, 87 

N. Y. 294. Cady's Cases on Pri. Corp. p. 363 at p. 365.

A total suspension of the ordinary and lawful business for one year is a ground for action to dissolve the corporation. G. C. L. sec. 71 (3). Hollender v. Roch. Food Prod. 

Corp., 242 N. Y. 490. Cady's Cases on Pri. Corp. at p. 337. 

§ 55. Limitations in the Certificate. 

G. C. L. sec. 13 (2) authorizes the insertion in the certificate of certain limitations on powers and rights, but not such as to exempt the corporation, its stockholders, directors, or members from the performance of any obligation

or duty imposed by law. The statute specifies limitations upon : (1) The regulation of its business, (2) The conduct of its affairs, (3) The powers of the corporation, (4) The rights of its stockholders, (5) The powers of its directors.

Under these might be comprised many things, such as provisions for the discharge of debts and liabilities out of certain property, and limiting the powers of officers and directors accordingly; fixing the dividend policy of the corporation; defining a quorum at stockholders and at directors meetings; and giving the corporation power to buy in a member's stock, or, conversely, requiring the stockholder to offer it to the corporation first, and fixing a method for computing the value by the omission or inclusion of values assigned to good will.

The limitation must not violate a duty or obligation imposed by law, and must limit, not increase, the powers of the corporation, directors or stockholders. Peo. ex rel. 

Barney v. Whalen, 189 N. Y. 560. Cady's Cases on Pri.

Corp. p. 52. A similar provision in the by-laws would be invalid. Ripin v. U. S. W. L. Co., 205 N. Y. 442. Cady's

Cases on Pri. Corp. p. 513. The design, so far as stockholder's rights are concerned, seems to have been to increase the power of the minority so as to protect against the oppression and abuse of power by the majority, tho, of course, the majority when acting in accordance with the letter of the statute must act in the utmost good faith. Kavanaugh v. Kavanaugh Knitting Co., 226 N. Y. 185. 

A limitation that required unanimous vote to change the number of directors was held valid. Ripin v. U. S. Woven 

Label Co., supra, while one that required unanimous consent to change the directors was held void because of the statute which requires that "directors....shall be chosen ....by a plurality of the votes at such election." S. C. L. 

sec. 55. Boulevard Theatre & Realty Co. v. Graf, 195 App. 

Div. 518, 186 N. Y. Supp. 430, aff'd 231 N. Y. 615. Cady's 

Cases on Pri. Corp. p. 511. A contract between the stockholders by which they agree to retain certain directors and

officers is valid. Harris v. Magrill, 226 N. Y. Supp. 621, 131 Misc. 380.

A contract between stockholders to accomplish the election of dummy or nominal directors was held illegal for the reason that directors may not be deprived of the statutory powers to control the affairs of the corporation; and, by parity of reason, the result could not be attained by a provision in the charter. Manson v. Curtis, 223 N. Y. 313.

Provisions to perpetuate directors in their office are usually held to be contrary to public policy and void. Matter of 

Keogh, 183 N. Y. Supp. 408, 192 App. Div. 624. 

§ 56. Common Law Implied Powers that Have Become Express Powers. 

Blackstone mentions as the implied powers: 

1. To have perpetual succession. 2. To sue and be sued in its corporate name. 3. To purchase lands and other property. 4. To have a seal. 5. To make by-laws (including those for the expulsion of members). Blackstone's classification of implied powers has been made the subject of statute and are now found in sec. 14 G. C. L. In Blackstone's day it was not necessary to express the aforesaid implied powers, nor is it necessary today, although, since they are in the statute, they are thereby, ipso facto, express powers, since the charter consists of the certificate of incorporation, its amendments, and all the statutes applicable to the corporation. The import of the statute is:-Every corporation has power, although not specified in the law under which it was incorporated: 1. To have succession for the term specified in its charter, and if no such period of time be mentioned, to have perpetual succession. 2. To have a common seal. 3. To acquire, for corporate purposes, property by grant, gift, purchase, devise, or bequest, and to hold and dispose of the same subject to such limitations as may be prescribed by law. 4. To appoint all necessary officers and agents and to fix their compensation. 

5. To make by-laws not inconsistent with law for the transaction of all its business. Municipal corporations are excepted from subdivisions four and five. 

§ 57. Power to Make By-laws. 

By-laws are those fixed and known rules established by

the corporation, for the benefit of it and of its members, in accordance with which their internal government is carried on and its internal affairs regulated. For instance, one would expect to find in a savings bank's by-laws a provision placing the power to invoke the 60 day withdrawal clause; and in the by-laws of every corporation a definite allocation of powers to definite officers, to impress the corporate seal on contracts, to sign checks, and to withdraw cash from the bank checking account. The preparation of the original set of by-laws is usually intrusted to the attorney. 

G. C. L. 14, sub. 5 specifically authorizes by-laws, not inconsistent with law, "for the management of its business, the regulation of its affairs, the transfer of its stock, and the calling of meetings of its members," and also "to fix the amount of stock" (in a stock corporation) "or the number of members" (non stock corporation), "to constitute a quorum, unless otherwise provided by law." Furthermore, it provides that "by-laws duly adopted at a meeting of the members of the corporation shall control the action of its directors." G. C. L. 27 gives the directors power to make necessary by-laws subject to other by-laws adopted by the members of the corporation, and requires that by-laws adopted by the board to regulate elections of directors (by the stockholders) or officers (by the board) shall be published at least once in each of two successive weeks in a newspaper in the county where the election is to be held, the last publication to be at least 30 days before such election. G. C. L. 27 also authorizes a by-law to fix a quorum at directors meetings at not less than one-third the entire board. The act of a majority of a quorum binds the corporation, unless more are present, in which case, the act of a majority of those present will be the act of the board. 

G. C. L. 26 makes an exception to the rule that a by-law must not be inconsistent with law by stating: "Except as otherwise provided by law or the by-laws, special meetings of the members of a corporation may be called in the same manner as the annual meeting." S. C. L. 55 authorizes bylaws to fix the number of shares requisite to constitute a quorum at meetings to elect directors, but provides that the number specified shall be one "not exceeding a majority.”

In the absence of statute, by-law, or a charter provision of like tenor, those present, not less than two members,-would constitute a quorum. S. C. L. 55 also authorizes a by-law, if "adopted at a stockholders meeting," to provide that directors need not be stockholders-similar to the English practice whereby the credit attached to a great name is garnered by the corporation. Other statutory provisions relating to by-laws will be noticed under other heads and grouped in the index, infra.

The principal rules to be observed in drawing by-laws is that the by-laws 1. must not be inconsistent with statute, or charter, or to the common law of the state of incorporation; 2. must not be ultra vires, in the sense of being in excess of the powers and purposes set forth in the charter; 

3. must not be retrospective, in the sense of depriving a member of vested rights; 4. must not purport to impair the rights of members who became such before the by-law was passed, unless they specifically consent; 5. must be general; 6. must be reasonable and not oppressive. To illustrate: 

1. A by-law forbidding a change in the number of directors except by vote of 90% of the stockholders was passed, whereas S. C.
