L. 35 (c) requires only the votes of the holders of record of 2/3 the outstanding shares. The said by-law, prescribing differently from the statute, was inconsistent with it,-tho`not contrary to it-and was, therefore, held void. Katz v. H. & H. M'fg. Co., 95 N. Y. Supp. 663, 109 App. Div. 49, aff'd 183 N. Y. 578; Stein v. Marks, 89 

N. Y. Supp. 921, 41 Misc. 140. See also, Kent v. Quicksilver 

Mining Co., 78 N. Y. 159, Matthews v. Associated Press of 

State of New York, 136 N. Y. 333, 32 N. E. 981, cf. St. 

John of Vizzini v. Cavallo, 224 N. Y. Supp. 683, 134 Misc. 

152. In Raub v. Gerken, 111 N. Y. Supp. 319, 127 App.

Div. 42, the by-law infracted the common law as set forth in the decisions. The by-law there under consideration, passed by the directors to provide for the removal of members of the board, contravened the common law rule that, since the members have a right to designate by their votes what directors shall represent them, the members alone may provide by by-law for the removal of these elected; and even a stockholders' by law might be regarded as in-

consistent with a statute giving the power of removal to some one else. Compare G. C. L. 136 and 60 (4). The by-law must not be in restraint of trade. Matthews v. 

Assoc. Press, 136 N. Y. 333, 32 N. E. 98; or in other respects violate the statute, tho apparently authorized by the charter. Seneca Co. Bank v. Lamb, 26 Barb. 595. A bylaw that requires the unanimous consent of the board to the sale of the property and franchises of the corporation, otherwise than in the usual course of business, is not inconsistent with S. C. L. 20. Levin v. Mayer, 149 N. Y.

Supp. 112, 86 Misc. 116. The by-law must not contravene the charter so as to make a new charter. Drake v. Hudson 

Riv. R. Co., 7 Barb. 508. A by-law, ineffective when passed because the statute required a certificate to be filed in order to effectuate it, was held validated by the subsequent filing of the certificate. George v. Holstein-Friesian Assoc., 238 

N. Y. 513. In re George, 199 N. Y. Supp. 557, 205 App. 

Div. 234. 

2. By-laws can neither extend nor diminish the powers as set forth in the certificate of incorporation, but they may be explanatory of those powers, and, by setting forth the purposes in detail, may provide, with the general statement contained in the certificate, a complete system for administering corporate affairs. To determine the right of exemption from taxation of a stone quarry belonging to a corporation organized exclusively and used exclusively for the mental and moral improvement of men and women, the court looked into the certificate, which was silent as to the quarry, but provided that it was organized under the Membership Corp. Law; and into the by-laws which provided for the use of property for "retreats" and stated in part that "No retreat...shall be used for any purpose other than for the moral and mental improvement of men and women," etc., with other protective clauses in effect providing a complete and exclusive system, and struck the assessment of the quarry from the tax roll. Corp. of Yaddo v. Saratoga, 216 App. Div. 1, 214 N. Y. Supp. 523. See In re L. I. R. 

Co., 19 Wend. 37. Nat'l League of C. M. of U. S. v. Horning, 129 N. Y. Supp. 437, 72 Misc. 181. 

3. By-laws must be general, and not unreasonable and

oppressive. It has been held that a by-law prohibiting the transfer by a stockholder without the consent of all the stockholders is contrary to public policy and void. Hassel v. Pohle, 214 App. Div. 654, 212 N. Y. Supp. 561, Cady's

Cases on Pri. Corp. p. 391. Bank of Attica v. Manufacturers' & Traders' Bank, 20 N. Y. 501. Farmers' & Merchants' Bank of Lineville v. Wasson, 48 Iowa 336, 30 Am.

Rep. 398. But to those who assent, the by-law has the force of a contract. Barrett v. King, 181 Mass. 476, 63 N. E. 934.

By-laws of a trade union benefit insurance corporation that a reinstated member should not participate until six months after the arrears are paid up are not unreasonable. Hart v. 

Adams Cylinder & Web Press, 69 App. Div. 578, 75 N. Y. 

Supp. 110. A corporation cannot provide by a by-law for the sale or forfeiture of shares because of non-payment of assessments, In re Long Island R. Co., 19 Wend. 37, 32

Am. Dec. 429; or impose or increase the liability of stockholders for corporate debts, Mitcham v. Citizens' Bank of 

Bullochville, 34 Ga. App. 707, 131 S. E. 181; Rousch v. 

Longdale Independent Tel. Co., 78 W. Va. 136, 88 S. E. 623; or confer upon stockholders the right to return their shares to the corporation at a fixed value or limit their liability to creditors as fixed by law. Wells v. Black, 117 Cal. 157, 48 Pac. 1090. A by-law authorizing the issue of preferred stock, if preferences are not authorized in the charter, is prejudicial to the common stock owner and he may enjoin the corporation. Kent v. Quicksilver Mining Co., 78 N. Y. 159. 

The following restrictions in by-laws have been held valid: No stockholder shall vote more than one-quarter of the total stock. Such provision cannot be avoided by the distribution of stock immediately preceding election. Mack v. Debardeleben Coal Co., 90 Ala. 396, 20 So. 150. Non residents shall not vote. State v. Hunton, 28 Vt. 594. 

Dunlay v. Ave. M Garage & R. Co., Inc., 253 N. Y. 274, 170 

N. E. 917.

The same body that has power to make by-laws, may also repeal and amend them but the amendments must observe the same general rules as apply to the adoption of by-laws in general. The amendment of the by-laws of a fraternal

beneficiary insurance corporation to increase rates which members must pay or to scale down death benefits is void in so far as it tends to impair vested rights of contract. 

Rockwell v. K. T. & M. M. A. A., 119 N. Y. Supp. 515, 134

App. Div. 736. In Whalen v. Hudson Hotel Co., 183 App. 

Div. 316, 170 N. Y. Supp. 855, a clause in articles of incorporation providing that in the absence of actual fraud, no action taken by a majority of the directors should be invalid, because some or all of the directors were interested therein, was held invalid. A by-law requiring that directors may be elected by a vote other than as prescribed by S. C. L. 60 (by a plurality of votes cast) is inconsistent with statute and void. Reiss v. Levy, 161 N. Y. Supp. 1048, 175 App. Div. 938. 

4. The by-laws, whether known or not known to the member at the time when he became such, create vested rights in him, of which he can not be deprived except with his consent or in accordance with statute, charter or bylaws. Kent v. Quicksilver Min. Co., 78 N. Y. 159. Cady's

Cases on Pri. Corp. p. 447. Cowles v. Cowles Realty Co., 201 

App. Div. 460, 194 N. Y. Supp. 546; Cady's Cases on Pri. 

Corp. at p. 393. Ripin v. U. S. Woven Label Co., 205 N. Y. 

442, 447; Cady's Cases on Pri. Corp. at p. 392. In Bechtold v. Stillwagon, 195 N. Y. Supp. 66, 119 Misc. 177, a by-law providing for the election of a treasurer and other officers by the stockholders was held to be invalid because inconsistent with S. C. L. 60 which declares that the directors of a stock corporation may appoint or elect a treasurer and other officers. Todd v. Keator, 177 App. Div. 112. 

§ 57a. Construction and Effect of By-laws. 

"A by-law of a corporation has the force of a statute and is as binding upon the company and its members as any public law of the state." Timolat v. Held Co., 17 Misc. 556, 40 N. Y. Supp. 692. Members who are not acquainted with the by-law are chargeable with notice. State ex rel. Webber v. Shaw, 103 Ohio St. 660, 134 N. E. 643. Further, if a person becomes a stockholder after the passage of a valid by-law, he, too, impliedly consents to it and is chargeable with notice thereof. Matthews v. Associated Press of State of N. Y., 136 N. Y. 333, 32 N. E. 981. Strangers are not

affected by a by-law respecting the powers of an executive committee or an agent, but may rely on the apparent authority. Rathbun v. Snow, 123 N. Y. 343, 349, 25 N. E. 379. 

§ 58. Succession. 

This, by the common law, was an absolute essential of the corporation. Even the crown, it was held, could not of its prerogative, create corporations having a limited duration. Various notable corporations, such as the East India 

Company, the Bank of England, and the South Sea Company, were created by Special act for limited periods. The statute, G. C. L. 14 (1), is affirmative of the common law insofar as it confers perpetual succession where no limitation is stated in the certificate. cf sec. 8 supra. 

Corporations by prescription are those that have existed and exercised their corporate rights from time immemorial, and whose charter cannot be produced, or commencement shown under any special act of the legislature. It is presumed that by the accidents of time the charter and all direct proof of its existence has been lost. Robie v. Sedgewick, 35 Barb. 327; New Boston v. Durnbarton, 15 N. H. 

201; Hagerstown Turnpike Co. v. Creeger, 5 H. & J. 122.

The states of the United States have not in general reenacted the statutes of mortmain, or generally assumed them to be in force, and, with the possible exception of real property devised by will (G. C. L. 14), corporations may take in fee. Nicoll v. N. Y. & E. R. R., 12 N. Y. 121; Cady's 

Cases on Pri. Corp. p. 163. Easterday, The Law of Real 

Property, sec. 187. § 59.

Power to Have a Common Seal and to Alter the 

Same at Will.

Provisions permitting the use of an engraved or printed facsimile of the seal on a corporate bond or other corporate obligation for the payment of money, and a definition of the "seal" mentioned in G. C. L. 14 (2) supra, is contained in secs. 43 and 44, General Construction law in App. L.

The seal of the corporation attached to an instrument proves itself. Canandaigua Academy v. McKechnie, 19 

Hun 62. The notary or other officer before whom the instrument is acknowledged need not take proof that the one

affixing the seal had power to do it, or as to the title of the officer. Ib. The corporate seal on an instrument is prima facie proof that it was attached by proper authority. 

Whitney v. Union Trust Co., 65 N. Y. 576. Jourdan v. L. I. 

R.R. Co.; 115 N. Y. 380, 384. Quackenbos v. Globe & R. F. 

Ins. Co., 177 N. Y. 71. United Surety Co. v. Meenan, 211

N. Y. 39. The presumption is rebuttable. Gause v. Commonwealth Tr. Co., 196 N. Y. 134. Alexander v. Equitable 

Life Assur. Co., 233 N. Y. 300.

The corporate seal, like the seal of an individual, creates the presumption of consideration, rebuttable as between the parties to the instrument, but irrebuttable on collateral attack by a stranger to the instrument. Mut. L. Ins. Co. v. 

Yates Co. Nat. Bank., 54 N. Y. Supp. 743, 35 App. Div. 218, Richardson's Law of Evidence, sec. 86. The seal on a corporate bond does not remove or even affect the quality of negotiability. Weeks v. Esler, 143 N. Y. 74. Chase Nat'l 

Bank v. Faurot, 149 N. Y. 532. 

§ 60. Express Power to Acquire Property. 

For the accomplishment of any purpose authorized by its charter, the corporation always has had implied power to acquire real or personal property, the test being whether it was reasonably necessary for its business. 2 Kent 281. 

Nicoll v. N. Y. & E. R. R. Co., 12 N. Y. 121. Implied powers as to property will be treated in Chap. VI. infra. What we have here to consider is the express power contained in 

G. C. L. 14 (3).

So far as express powers are concerned, a corporation can not hold real property beyond the authority conferred by its charter. Riley v. Rochester, 9 N. Y. 64. Downing v. 

Marshall, 23 N. Y. 366. And within its express corporate purposes the power to acquire land is unlimited. Central 

Gold M. Co. v. Platt, 9 Daly 263. 

That portion of G. C. L. 14 (3) which limits the express power of a corporation to take property by "gift,...devise or bequest" "subject to such limitations as may be prescribed by law" is related to sec. 12 of the Decedent Estate 

Law (ch. 18, laws of 1909) which reads: "no devise to a corporation shall be valid, unless such corporation be expressly authorized by its charter, or by statute, to take by

devise." The interpretation is that domestic corporations may take by devise for corporate purposes; but a corporation which has no use for the land for corporate purposes may not take unless by apt words in the certificate of incorporation it is authorized to deal in land. 

A curious feature of this limitation is that at a time when the statute of the state allowed land in the state to be devised only to natural persons, a devise to the United 

States was held void. U. S. v. Fox, 52 N. Y. 530. It was also held that a corporation which could not hold land in its own name could not hold it in the name of another, nor take a beneficial interest in it. Clemens v. Clemens, 37 

N. Y. 75; Chamberlain v. Chamberlain, 43 N. Y. 434; White v. Howard, 46 N. Y. 144. Since a trading corporation has implied power to lend or sell on credit, it might mortgage or lend on real estate not needed for its business, and then buy in for the purpose of protecting its interest. But a contract of a corporation for the purchase of real property for the purpose of speculation, unless expressly authorized, is ultra vires, and unenforceable. Berwin & Co. v. Hewitt 

Rty. Co., 191 N. Y. Supp. 817, 199 App. Div. 453. If loss resulted, the officers might be liable to the creditors or stockholders for damages but the title to the property would be perfectly valid, except for intervention by the state. See

Chap. VII, infra. 

The statutory limitation is based upon the idea of those who favored the unfettered alienation of land and who, when this became impeded by large ownership by corporations that took in fee and never died, passed various acts to interpose obstacles to such transfers. The best known of these statutes were those of 13 Edw. 1, st. 1, c. 32 (Westminster, the second) which declared that no corporation, ecclesiastical or lay, should buy or sell, or in any way take land by gift, lease or otherwise, and 15 Rich. II, c. 5 which extended the provisions so as to cover uses. The corporation was allowed to hold the land for a brief prescribed period when the mesne lords or the crown might seize them.

Somewhat similar in effect is G. C. L. 221 limiting the right of a foreign corporation to hold for 5 years only real property in this state purchased under foreclosure sale, or under

execution, or taken by devise, from the date of the purchase, or from the date on which the right to possession vested in the devisee, and giving power to convey it by deed or otherwise in the same manner as a domestic corporation. G. C. L. 

221 does not require a foreign corporation to obtain from the court permission to sell, even tho it be a religious corporation. Muck v. Hitchcock, 212 N. Y. 283. Matter of 

McGraw, 111 N. Y. 85. Kerr v. Dougherty, 79 N. Y. 328. 

Downing v. Marshall, 23 N. Y. 366. Sherwood v. American 

Bible Soc. 4 Abb. Dec. 227. Draper v. Harvard College, 57 How. Pr. 269. 14 C. J. 512. 

Where a railroad corporation is authorized to purchase lands needed for its road, it will be presumed that all lands acquired were for that purpose. Yates v. Van de Bogart, 56 

N. Y. 526. For the power of certain corporations to acquire lands by condemnation, see Business Corporation Law, sec. 16.

Under G. C. L. 13, it has been held that a corporation incorporated for the purpose of "raising and smelting lead ore" has the power to purchase smelting works with all appurtenances necessary for carrying on the business, and also to assume a contract made by the vendors to provide means for transporting the ores, when smelted, to market. Moss v. Averell, 10 N. Y. 449. A lease executed by a corporation for a longer period than its corporate life is not invalid, nor will it cease upon the termination of the corporate life. Tate v. Neary, 52 App. Div. 78, 65 N. Y. 

Supp. 40.

The burden of proof is upon the one alleging the want of power, for the presumption is that the corporate act is valid, regular, and within the powers conferred. Ex parte Penn. 

Iron Co., 7 Cow. 540. 

§ 61. Power to Appoint or Elect Officers, Agents and 

Employees.

This express power is vested in the board of directors by 

S. C. L. 60. Abbott v. Harbeson Textile Co., 162 App. Div. 

405, 147 N. Y. Supp. 1031. The directors are agents and officers of the corporation and constitute its managing body only when assembled as a board, with a quorum present. 

Matter of N. Y. & W. T. S. Co., 145 App. Div. 623, 130

N. Y. Supp. 414, Cady's Cases on Pri. Corp. at p. 388. 

Matter of Ringler & Co., 204 N. Y. 30, Cady's Cases on Pri. Corp. at p. 520. Officers and agents may be appointed either by directors' by-law or by resolution. In the absence of a different requirement by statute, charter, or members' by-law, the appointment by the board of directors by mere words, without writing, or by implication of law, or by vote, or by writing without seal, is as valid as it would be if done by a natural person. The directors may delegate power to appoint agents and attorneys, but the appointees of one holding office by usurpation of power do not have good title to office, tho third persons and the public may hold the corporation liable for their acts within their ostensible power by reason of the holding-out. 1 A. L. R. 

1132. Perkins v. Wash. Ins. Co., 4 Cow. 645. Matter of 

Ringler, supra. Remington P. Co. v. London Assur. Corp., 12 App. Div. 218, 43 N. Y. Supp. 431. Granger v. Amer. 

Brew. Co., 55 N. Y. Supp. 695, 25 Misc. 701. The board may appoint officers or agents for a longer term than that of the appointing directors. Warner v. Morgan, 165 App. 

Div. 903, 149 N. Y. Supp. 1117. But while an officer may be elected to hold office for a longer term than the board, his term as an elective officer expires at the election by the stockholders of a new board. Granger v. Amer. Brew. Co., supra. 

§ 62. Power to Mortgage. Effect of Recording Usurious Loans. 

S. C. L. 16 gives a stock corporation, other than a moneyed corporation, the power to borrow money and contract debts, and to mortgage for intra vires purposes its property and franchises for any amount to secure the payment of its obligations. 

The papers required are: 

1. Written consents, or a favorable vote at a meeting called in the manner prescribed by S. C. L. 45, by 2/3 the outstanding stock that is entitled to vote on the proposition. 

The consents may be filed in the office of the corporation. 

2. The official certificate furnishing proof that the stockholders are bound. This must be properly filed or recorded in the office of the proper register or county clerk, dependent

upon the location of the property, and the office of the corporation, as set forth in the charter. 

3. The mortgage and the bond or bonds to which it is collateral. The mortgage should be recorded in the office of the county clerk or register of deeds of the county in which the land is situated, Real Prop. Law sec. 291, or, if a chattel mortgage, it must be filed and entered in the office of the clerk of the city, town or county or the register as set forth in detail in the lien law, secs. 230-235. A corporate mortgage affecting both real and personal property need only be recorded as a mortgage of real property, and one affecting choses to be delivered to the mortgagee trustee at a future date, need not be filed. Ib. secs. 230, 231. A chattel mortgage or a statement setting forth facts specified in the statute must be refiled annually, 30 days before a year from the date of first filing, or it becomes invalid as a lien as against creditors, subsequent purchasers, and mortgagees in good faith after the expiration of the year. 

Ib. sec. 235. 

4. The corporate certificate containing resolution of the board of directors to mortgage. 

5. Certified copy under corporate seal of resolution of board of directors appointing one or more officers to execute or deliver the mortgage and bonds with discretionary authority to insert or accept the terms thereof, and to receive the consideration therefor. 

6. The bond and mortgage.

The consents must be in writing. Leffert v. Jackman, 227 N. Y. 310. In re Astell &c. Corp., 284 Fed. 967. The consents need not specify the amount of the mortgage. 

Greenpoint Sugar Co. v. Whitin, 69 N. Y. 328. The assent of two stockholders owning two thirds is sufficient compliance. Welch v. Importers and Traders N. Bank, 122 

N. Y. 177. Treasury stock in the hands of the corporation cannot be counted to make up the two thirds. Vail v. 

Hamilton, 85 N. Y. 453. Those consenting are estopped from attacking the mortgage. Ga. B'ldg Co. v. Burdett, 150 N. Y. Supp. 27. A purchase money mortgage is expressly excepted, and may be made without the consent of stockholders. Farmers L. & T. Co. v. Equity G. Co., 32

N. Y. Supp. 385, 65 N. Y. St. Rep. 591. Black v. Ellis, 197 

N. Y. 402; Cady's Cases on Pri. Corp. at p. 184.

There must be a debt that has been contracted in order that the mortgage may be valid; but the bonds and the corporate mortgage may cover future advances and secure debts other than those created simultaneously with the giving of the security, and the corporation may pay interest in advance equally as well as at any other time. Lord v. 

Yonkers Fuel Gas Co., 99 N. Y. 547. Martin v. Niagara 

F. P. M. Co., 122 N. Y. 165. Flynn v. Coney I. & B. R. Co., 26 App. Div. 416, 50 N. Y. Supp. 74. The resolution of the directors ordinarily must be passed by a majority of a quorum. A formal resolution is not indispensable, and if the mortgage is executed by a majority at a meeting it is binding on the corporation. South B. S. v. Clapp, 18 Barb. 

35. Cohn v. Gersh Realty Corp., 242 N. Y. Supp. 671, 137

Misc. 245. The resolution must describe the property to be mortgaged by a description broad enough to cover the property pledged by the mortgage. In re Endicott Laundry Co., 219 N. Y. Supp. 632, 128 Misc. 413. Where the mortgage is made to a trustee for bondholders' bonds, a purchaser of bonds is bound and estopped by provisions in the trust deed or mortgage giving exclusive rights of foreclosure and suit to the trustee. An action by the bondholder to recover overdue coupons is an affirmation of the validity of the provisions of the mortgage. Guaranty T. Co. v. Troy Steel Co., 68 N. Y. Supp. 915, 33 Misc. 484. But where a proviso permits the calling of the mortgage on 90 days default, it is not implied that all the board must exercise the option. 

Atl. Tr. Co. v. Crystal Water Co., 72 App. Div. 539, 76 N. Y.

Supp. 647. See as to duties of the trustee, Tschetinian v. 

City Tr. Co., 186 N. Y. 432. Reynolds v. T. G. & T. Co., 240 

N. Y. 257. Patterson v. Gdn. Tr. Co., 144 App. Div. 863, 129 N. Y. Supp. 807.

S. C. L. 16 contains appropriate provisions for a convertible bond issue. The mortgage should recite the performance of the steps provided by S. C. L. 16 in detail. If it does so, S. C. L. 17 provides that the mortgage, with proof that it is duly recorded, is presumptive evidence of due execution, and as against an attack based on defect or inww

sufficiency of consent or authority of the stockholders, or in the filing or recording of such consent or authority. Proof of the additional facts that the mortgage has been recorded one year or more and that the corporation received value therefor, is made conclusive evidence that the execution of such mortgage has been duly consented to and authorized by the stockholders, and that it is a binding security for all valid obligations. Southern L. Ins. Co. v. Packard, 17 

N. Y. 51. North R. Mtg. Corp. v. 254 &c Corp., 240 

N. Y. Supp. 654, 136 Misc. 342. The loan however, must be made to the corporation and not to an individual. The lender can not evade the statute by disguising the borrower. Granis v. Stevens, 216 N. Y. 583. Schanz v. Sotscheck, 167 App. Div. 

202, 152 N. Y. Supp. 851. Even where the usurious loan was made to a one-man corporation, it was held that the receiver in bankruptcy could not avoid the mortgage for usury without returning the consideration received. Fort v. 415 &c 

Corp., 131 Misc. 774, 227 N. Y. Supp. 357. The section also makes a short statute of limitations of one year from the earliest recording for actions to declare the mortgage invalid for insufficiency of consent. The reason impelling the statute is said to be the greater risk in lending because of the stockholders' immunity from personal liability. The rule excluding the defense to usury extends to a case in which the corporation is the primary debtor of an obligation which is guaranteed by an individual. In such an instance even the indorser cannot set up usury for he occupies no better position than the corporation. Salvin v. Myles Realty Co., 227 N. Y. 51, 124 N. E. 94. In Union Estates v. Adlon Construction Co., 221 N. Y., reversing 167 App. Div. 979, a corporation executed a bond secured by a mortgage with interest at 6% and a written agreement was entered into coincidentally to the effect that the corporation in the event that the mortgage should not be paid at a certain time, was to pay additional interest at the rate of 17% per annum. 

The performance of this latter agreement was guaranteed by an individual who sought to interpose the defense of usury. It was held that inasmuch as the maker was a corporation, the written agreement was not void as being usurious; that the guarantor had guaranteed a lawful con-

tract; and therefore was liable within the obligations of his guaranty. It is interesting to note that the statute only prevents the avoidance by a corporation of its own contract upon the ground of usury; and where property was pledged by an individual to secure a usurious loan, a corporation succeeding to the rights of the pledgor may recover the property pledged, and the statute denying to a corporation the right to plead usury has no application. Merchants 

Exchange National Bank v. Commercial Warehouse Co., 

49 N. Y. 635.

For a peculiar situation in which a mortgage executed by a one-man corporation to its sole stockholder was held valid see Harvey v. Gty. Tr. Co., 226 N. Y. Supp. 37, 134 

Misc. 417. 

§ 63. Sale or Lease of Corporate Property, and of Fran chises.

As to corporate property, being that which the corporation was not chartered to deal in and including that bought for the use of the corporation in its business and integral to the business, the directors, at common law, could not sell against the wishes of a single member. A single member also had power at common law to hold up the sale of a department of the business accompanied by the good will, so that, if the sale went through, the corporation might not start up again; for, it was said, "a corporation cannot cease to exist of its own will." Matter of Timmis, 200 N. Y. 177, Cady's Cases on Pri. Corps. p. 253. Peo. v. Ballard, 134 

N. Y. 270. Sec. 15 (1) supra.

Particularly, a corporation could not sell or assign its corporate property, not kept for sale, together with its franchises to a competitor-a sale which would amount to the sale of the trade of the corporation-without express charter authority, as against the wish of the minority stockholder.

A lease of all the corporate property to one agreeing to carry on the same business at the same place, was held not to amount to a suspension of business, and was, therefore, within the powers of the directors, though two-thirds of the stockholders objected. Denike v. N. Y. &c. Co., 80 N. Y. 

599. But in projected sales of corporate property not au-

thorized to be dealt in by charter, or of the franchises, the minority stockholder held the balance of power, and, as a practical matter, those who dissented had to be bought out if the sale was to go through. The purchaser without the consent of all got a bad title. Ernest v. Nicholls, 6 H. L. C. 

401. Matter of Drosnes, 187 App. Div. 425, 175 N. Y. Supp. 

628. Murrin v. Archibald Consol. Coal Co., 232 N. Y. 541. 

Copeland v. Cits. G. Co., 61 Barb. 60. Taylor v. Earle, 8 

Hun 1. Welch v. O. D. M. & R. Co., 56 Hun 650, 10 N. Y. 

Supp. 174. Cole v. Millerton Iron Co., 133 N. Y. 164, Cady's 

Cases on Pri. Corps. p. 577.

The statutory remedies found in S. C. L. 20, 21, G. C. L. 

50 and 119 adjust the situation. The sale of franchises and corporate property may be made with the consent of twothirds the voting stock, given by vote at a stockholders' meeting, called pursuant to S. C. L. 45. The dissenting minority may have their stock appraised. Franchises within the state may be sold only to domestic corporations. 

S. C. L. 20. Peo. ex rel. Barney v. Whalen, 119 App. Div. 

749, 104 N. Y. Supp. 555, affd. 189 N. Y. 560. In re Heilbron 

Wolff & Co., 224 App. Div. 14, 229 N. Y. Supp. 325. The statute is constitutional. Brock v. Poor, 216 N. Y. 387.

If all the stockholders agree, the sale may be for the stock of another corporation. Holmes & G. Mfg. Co. v. Holmes & 

W. Metal Co., 127 N. Y. 252. Merrin v. Archibald Con. Coal 

Co., 187 N. Y. Supp. 606, Cady's Cas. on Pri. Corps. p. 182.

If the sale is consummated on consents irregularly obtained, or at a meeting not duly called pursuant to S. C. L. 

45, the dissenting minority stockholder, moving promptly, may avoid the sale, or may require the appraisal of his stock if the sale purports to be one under S. C. L. 20. In re 

MacDonald, 205 App. Div. 579, 199 N. Y. Supp. 873. Weingreen v. Michelbacher, 149 N. Y. Supp. 110. If the sale was not one under S. C. L. 20 or covered by other provisions of the statute, the common law rule remains. Peo. v. Ballard, supra.

The court may review and regulate the conduct of the appraisers, although it may not set aside the appraised value. Mtr. of Erlanger, 237 N. Y. 157, Cady's Cas. on

Pri. Corps. p. 180. Matter of Bickerton, 196 App. Div. 231, 

187 N. Y. Supp. 267.

The consent of the shareholders is not required to a lease made by virtue of power to lease contained in the charter. 

Matter of Knaisch, 203 App. Div. 725, 197 N. Y. Supp. 116; 

Cady's Cas. on Pri. Corps. p. 178. Where the certificate provides for "a sale and lease" the minority are not entitled to an appraisal under secs. 20 and 21 S. C. L. Matter of 

Drosnes, supra.

The sale of the franchises within the state cannot be made to individuals, but to a domestic corporation only. S. C. L. 

20. Wegman v. Levinson Shoe Mfg. Co., 195 N. Y. Supp. 

535. Cf. Peo. ex rel. Barney v. Whalen, 119 App. Div. 749;

Cady's Cas. on Pri. Corps. p. 52. This provision does not apply to reorganizations, S. C. L. 96-98. Chap. XVIII infra. 

Various statues applicable to religious, railroad and other corporations require other steps, such as leave of court to sell, mortgage or lease their real property, G. C. L. 50. 

Second Reformed v. Trustees, etc., 216 N. Y. Supp. 616, 127 

Misc. 498, affd. 220 App. Div. 244, 221 N. Y. Supp. 396. In a proceeding to restrain a sale and to set aside the deed, the title of the de facto officers cannot be questioned. Shavers v. Thomas, 171 N. E. 625 (Ill.). In re Long Acre Lt. & P. 

Co., 188 N. Y. 361. People v. N. Y. City Ry. Co., 57 Misc. 

114, 107 N. Y. Supp. 247.

Creditors' rights may not be violated by sale of all the corporate assets with the consent of the stockholders for the stock of another corporation, issued to an individual member. Hurd v. N. Y. & Conn. S. L. Co., 167 N. Y. 89, 60 N. E. 327. Harr v. Consol. C. R. D. Co., 62 Hun 622, 43 

N. Y. St. R. 1, 17 N. Y. Supp. 25.

A quasi public corporation is limited in its sales to such of its property as is not necessary to enable it to perform its duties to the public. A sale of that which will not bring about an abandonment of the corporate enterprise may be made by the directors without any action by the stockholders. Venner v. So. Pac. Co., 279 Fed. 832, certiorari denied 258 U. S. 628, 66 L. ed. 799. Town of Mamaroneck v. N. Y. Interurban Water Co., 198 App. Div. 396, 190 N. Y.

Supp. 580. 

N. Y. 24; Cady's Cas. on Pri. Corps. 269.

Compare Bath Gas Light Co. v. Claffy, 151 

The rule that requires the stockholders' consent to the sale of corporate property and franchises has no application to the sale of all the share stock. Stone v. The C. C. C. & St. L. Ry. Co., 202 N. Y. 352. 

§ 64. Same. The Federal Rule. 

Federal courts hold that corporate franchises are not transferrable but are transmissible by succession, as by merger or consolidation, in accordance with the statutes of the corporate domicile. Lane & Bodley v. Locke, 150 U. S. 

193, 14 Sup. Ct. 78, 38 L. ed. 1049. In Hapgood v. Hewitt, 119 U. S. 226, 7 Sup. Ct. 193, 30 L. ed. 369, the court held that a license to a corporation, afterwards dissolved, would not pass to a corporation which had been formed by the stockholders of the defunct corporation, where its charter did not expressly empower it to assign the license. In 

Niagara Fire Ext. Co. v. Hibbard, 179 Fed. 844, it was held that, by a sale of all its property, profits and goodwill by one corporation to another which did not assume the liabilities of the first, the assignee did not get title to a patent, held by the first, which, by the terms of the contract with the patentee, was not assignable without his consent. In like manner the federal courts hold that public service corporations cannot disable themselves by disposing of their franchises or property that is essential to the performance of their public duties, without express authority from the state. Penn Co. v. St. L., A. &c Ry., 118 U. S. 293. Ore. 

Ry. Co. v. Oregonian Realty Co., 130 U. S. 1. 

§ 65. Sale of Corporate Land. 

The directors, at common law, might make all sales, whether ordinary or extraordinary, of corporate realty which the corporation was chartered to deal in; except that, if the corporation was restricted by charter as to alienation, ownership, or user of lands, not only might the corporation successfully resist enforcement of a contract made by the directors to sell contrary to the charter, but also a single member, against the wishes of all the others, might restrain performance. Dulwich College case, 1 P. Wms. 655. Mc-

Carter v. Orphan Asylum Soc., 9 Cow. 435, 462. The situa tion is corrected by S. C. L. 20, 21, supra. 

§ 66. Dealings in the Corporation's Own Shares. 

Under the English rule, express power to deal in the shares of other corporations did not authorize dealing in its own shares; and a corporation's purchase of its own stock was void. Re London, H. & C. Exchange Bank, L. R. 5

Ch. 444. The risk is not that of ordinary business and tends inevitably to corrupt transactions to take back a stockholder's holdings, and to manipulation of the market, possibly in a direction contrary to the stockholder's advantage. 

In New York it was held at a common law that there was nothing to prevent a corporation from taking its own stock in payment, security or satisfaction of debt, or as a gift, or from holding or selling its stock thus acquired; and some cases held that at common law a corporation might purchase its own stock providing the transaction was bona fide and not in fraud of creditors. Talmadge v. Pell, 7 N. Y. 328. City 

Bank v. Bruce, 17 N. Y. 507. Lake Superior Iron Co. v. 

Drexel, 90 N. Y. 87. Barton v. P. J. & U. F. Plankroad Co., 17 Barb. 397. Verplanck v. Merc. Ins. Co., 1 Edw. Ch. 84. 

Cf. Moses v. Soule, 136 App. Div. 904; Cady's Cas. on Pri. 

Corps. p. 247.

Early statutes prohibited moneyed corporations from buying their own stock, except out of surplus profits. 

These statutes have been extended to all corporations. 

Under Penal Law, sec. 664, subd. 5, it is a misdemeanor for a director to apply any portion of the funds of the corporation, except surplus, to the purchase of shares of its own stock. An interesting situation was presented in In re 

Fechheimer Fishel Co., 212 Fed. 357. A New York corporation, while solvent, made a contract to purchase certain shares of its own stock, giving a promissory note for the purchase price. When the note matured, the corporation was insolvent. It was held that payment of the note should be postponed until after the claims of the general creditors had been satisfied.

The contract of a corporation to buy back its own stock is presumed valid, and the burden of pleading and proving a lack of surplus is on the corporation. Richards v. Ernst

Wiener Co., 207 N. Y. 59. Cady's Cas. on Pri. Corps. 249. 

Helburn T. Co. v. All Amer. Corp., 211 App. Div. 69, 206 

N. Y. Supp. 652.

A contract to sell the corporation's stock for installments, payable monthly, the purchaser to have the right to pay off at any time, and the company agreeing that after two years payments have been made, to return the money on six months' notice and cancel the contract, is a contract to sell and is not a sale of stock with an agreement to buy back, and hence does not infringe the statute, and the contract is valid. Hyman v. N. Y. U. R. Est. Co., 140 N. Y. Supp. 138, 79 Misc. 439. Robt. Dollar Co. v. Wentworth Sec. Corp., 

30 Fed. (2d) 98. A purchase of its own stock out of capital where no creditors' rights are affected, gives good title. 

Med. Arts Bldg. Co. v. So. Fin. & Dev. Co., 29 F. (2d) 969. 

Joseph v. Raff, 81 N. Y. Supp. 546, 82 App. Div. 47, affd. 

176 N. Y. 611. A contract by the president individually to repurchase stock is not forbidden. Quigley v. MacQueen & 

Co., 151 N. E. 487. Topken, Loring & Schwartz v. Schwartz, 249 N. Y. 206, 163 N. E. 735. Gross v. Beguelin, 226 App. 

Div. 349, 235 N. Y. Supp. 336. 

§ 67. Power to Guarantee bonds of Another Corporation. 

By statute, a stock corporation may guarantee the bonds of any other corporation engaged in the same general line of business if the unanimous written consent of the holders of all its outstanding shares entitled to vote thereon be given; or upon the unanimous vote of the holders of all its outstanding shares entitled to vote; or upon the vote of the holders of two-thirds of its outstanding shares entitled to vote thereon, if the guarantor corporation owns a majority of the voting shares of the other corporation. S. C. L. sec. 19. The votes aforesaid must be given at a meeting duly called pursuant to S. C. L. 45. Venner v. N. Y. C. & 

H. R. R. Co., 160 App. Div. 127, 145 N. Y. Supp. 725, affd. 

217 N. Y. 615. Peabody v. Interborough R. T. Co., 212 App. 

Div. 502, 209 N. Y. Supp. 380 and 893. 

§ 68. Issuance of Stock to Employees. 

With the written consent of all the stockholders entitled to vote thereon, or by a majority vote at a stockholders'

meeting called pursuant to 45 S. C. L., held on notice stating the object, the corporation may issue stock to its employees or to employees of a subsidiary, on such terms as the stockholders may impose. Four plans of payment and allotment are provided for: 1. Subscriptions. 2. Through the inter vention of a trustee for employees. 3. On installment payments. 4. From a share in the surplus profits for employees continuing in the ownership of the stock, and in the employment of the corporation. The capital stock may be increased by amending the certificate of incorporation for that purpose, pursuant to S. C. L. 36. "In case of the issuance to employees of increased stock," a stockholder not voting in favor, may object thereto at the meeting, or twenty days thereafter, and, within sixty days after the meeting, take proceedings for the appraisal of his stock under S. C. L. 21. The mere vote at the meeting will not entitle an objecting stockholder to have his stock appraised and taken over, unless the issuance of increased stock has taken place. The issuance of treasury stock to employees, or of non-issued stock antecedently authorized, will not entitle a dissenting stockholder to appraisal. Matter of 

Stockwell, 210 App. Div. 753, 206 N. Y. Supp. 834. 

$ 69. Power to Deal in Stock or Bonds of Another Cor poration.

The common law rule was that a corporation was without power to invest in the shares of another unless the nature of its business was conducive to the prosperous accomplishment of the corporate purposes of the first. One trading corporation might accept shares in another to carry out its own ends, but it was beyond its powers to do so for the purpose of affecting the management. Re Asiatic Banking 

Corp., Royal Bank of India case, L. R. 4 Ch. 252, 257. Berry v. Yates, 24 Barb. 199. Talmadge v. Pell, 7 N. Y. 348. The shares purchased were very generally transferred to the name of an individual, officer, agent or employee, who agreed to hold in trust for the corporation. Slade v. Bennett, 133 App. Div. 666, 118 N. Y. Supp. 278. Godley's Outline of Equity, secs. 30, 14. Nassau Bank v. Jones, 95 N. Y. 

115; Cady's Cas. on Pri. Corps. 209.

There is a rule for the construction of charters to the

effect that special powers override general powers; and express power is now conferred on all stock corporations (except moneyed corporations) by S. C. L. 18 to invest in the stock, bonds, notes, or choses in action of other corporations, domestic or foreign, provided either: (1) power to do so is conferred by express statement of said purpose in the certificate of incorporation or amendments thereto (Chap. VII, infra); or if (2) the corporation whose stock is purchased is engaged (a) in the manufacture, use or sale of property useful to the purchasing corporation; or (b) in the construction or operation of works necessary or useful in the business of the purchasing corporation; or if (3) the corporation in whose stock investment is made, may use the products or property of the purchasing corporation; or if (4) it is one with which the purchasing corporation might be authorized to consolidate. S. C. L. 86. 

S. C. L. 18 further provides that where authorized by its certificate of incorporation, the purchasing corporation might pledge the stock, etc. so purchased to secure the payment of a bond issue, or of notes; and might, when so authorized by the certificate, issue in exchange for the other's stock, bonds, notes or choses in action, its own stock, bonds or other obligations.

The officers of the purchasing corporation are expressly made eligible as directors of the other, the same as if they were individual stockholders therein, S. C. L. 18.

The effect of the section is to permit the control of one corporation by another by means of stock ownership, without transfer of the franchise. Thus, it was held that S. C. L. 

18 authorizes one railroad company to make another company's road part of its own line. Venner v. N. Y. C. & 

H. R. R. R. Co., 160 App. Div. 127, 145 N. Y. Supp. 725, affd. 217 N. Y. 615, Cady's Cas. on Pri. Corps. pp. 213, 221.

Said case also held that a railroad corporation might acquire the stock of foreign railroad corporations and assume such a large share in the management and corporate control thereof, that it became the equitable owner of such foreign corporations and become responsible for its proper operation. See also Wehrhane v. Nashville C. & St. L. R.

Co., 42 Hun 660, 4 N. Y. St. R. 660. Continental Sec. Co. v. 

Mich. Cent. R. Co., 217 N. Y. 617.

Holding companies have in recent years become popular as a means of controlling the management of other companies. The charter of a holding corporation specifies as one of its purposes, to invest in the stock, bonds and obligations of other corporations, and to issue its stock, bonds and obligations therefor, and to act as a holding company. To illustrate: A wishes to control A corporation, of whose stock he owns 26%. He induces B, who owns 25%, to come in with him. They form a holding company, the X Corporation, and transfer their stock in A Corporation to X 

Corporation, A receiving 26/51 of X Corporation's stock therefor, and B 25/51 thereof. X Corporation, the holding company, therefore, will have 51% of the stock of the A Corporation and will control it. A, having a majority of the stock of X Corporation, will thereby control the A 

Corporation, though he owned but 26% of its stock.

S. C. L. 18 which allows this to be done, has been held constitutional in New York. In some states, notably in 

Illinois, similar statutes have been held unconstitutional as tending to create a monopoly. Male v. A. T. & S. F. 

Ry. Co., 230 N. Y. 157, 129 N. E. 458. Continental Sec. Co. v. I. R. T. Co., 221 Fed. 44. Herman v. Brooklyn Sav. Bank, 196 App. Div. 269, 187 N. Y. Supp. 738. Stone v. C. C. C. & 

St. Louis R. R. Co., 202 N. Y. 352. It is the duty of the holding company, while enjoying all the rights of individual owners of stock, to exercise the franchises of the corporation for the lawful purposes thereof, particularly if there are creditors, or if it is a public service corporation. Green v. People's Gaslight & C. Co., 118 Misc. 1, 192 N. Y. Supp. 232. 

§ 70. Consolidation and Merger. 

It is only by virtue of legislative enactment that corporations may amalgamate, since amalgamation amounts to a transfer of the franchises and privileges. S. C. L. 86, 90, M. C. L. 50, 51 and G. C. L. 9, regulate consolidation and

S. C. L. 85, merger. Consolidation results in novation, a new company taking the place of its predecessor corporations, within the limitations of the statute, and the pre-

decessors then cease and determine. Peo. ex rel. Schurz v. 

Cook, 110 N. Y. 443. In merger, one company's assets are transferred to a possessor corporation which owns its shares and is absorbed in it, the latter corporation being the only one that continues to exist. These will be treated in Chap. XIX, infra. Consolidation cannot to be used as a blind for fraud. Small v. Sullivan, 245 N. Y. 343, 157 N. E. 

261. Consolidation and merger are distinguished from stock ownership. No consolidation or merger follows from the issuance by one corporation of stock in exchange for all the stock of another. Rafferty v. Buff. City Gas Co., 37 App. Div. 618, 56 N. Y. Supp. 288. The effect of merger and consolidation on creditor's rights is discussed in Syracuse Lighting Co. v. Md. Cas. Co., 226 N. Y. 25, 122 

N. E. 723. 

§ 71. Other Express Powers. 

Prohibited Combinations and Pools. 

Statutory Prohibitions. 

A distinction is sometimes drawn between contracts to do things that are prohibited by statute and things prohibited by the certificate of incorporation. Contracts to do acts prohibited by statute are void, because of the legislative will, a violation of which is malum in se, and comes under the maxim ex turpe causa non oritur actio. But where the purpose is lawful, and the contract merely one prohibited by the charter, it may be good by estoppel as to the party who has received the consideration, and it may be ratified, and thus made binding. Marshall v. K. O. T. M., 270 S. W. 418 (Mo.); Cady's Cas. on Pri. Corps. p. 287.

Those who deal with a corporation are bound to notice the restrictions and limitations upon the powers of officers contained in the charter, notice of which has been given them by public record. Sec. 4, supra. Gause v. Commonwealth 

T. Co., 196 N. Y. 134. Sanford v. Trust F. Ins. Co., 11 Pai. 

547. Three exceptions to this rule are: (1) negotiable instruments in the hands of a bona fide holder. Ellsworth v. St. 

Louis, A. & T. H. R. R. Co., 98 N. Y. 553. (2) Ratification 

Goss & Co. v. Goss, 144 App. Div. 698, 132 N. Y. Supp. 76, affd. 207 N. Y. 742; Cady's Cas. on Pri. Corps. p. 22. (3) 

Estoppel. Murray v. Smith, 166 App. Div. 528, 152 N. Y. 

Supp. 102, modfd. 224 N. Y. 40; Cady's Cases on Pri. Corps.

p. 201, 205. Perkins v. Hatch, 4 Hun 137, affd. 64 N. Y. 

634. Contracts prohibited by statute can not be validated by ratification or estoppel. Murray v. Smith, supra; Gause v. Commonwealth T. Co., supra.

The foregoing sections have covered many of the principal powers expressly provided by the statutes, which are a part of the charter of every corporation, unless clearly excepted by the provisions of the statute itself. Many of the powers which must be expressly set forth in the certificate of incorporation, if the corporation is to possess them, will be discussed in the following chapters. The express powers necessary for corporate activities will largely depend on the facts in any particular case.

One of the statutory prohibitions upon corporations concerns combinations and pools. At common law, contracts creating a monopoly, or tending to prevent competition in its broad sense, or to control prices to the detriment of the public, were held void as against public policy, even when granted by the sovereign power. Richardson's Outlines of 

Contracts, secs. 169 and 188. Powers granted a corporation must be construed, if possible, in such a way as to avoid a construction which would amount to creating a monopoly or a combination in restraint of trade. The presumption is against the implication of monopolistic powers. Charles 

River Bridge Co. v. Warren Bridge Co., 11 Pet. 420. See sec. 6, supra. The whole subject is covered in the course on "Anti-Trust law."

The principal statutes prohibiting combinations in restraint of trade are the so-called Sherman Act and the Clayton Act, which are printed in Cady's Cases on Pri. 

Corps. pp. 221 and 222; and S. C. L. 23. The Sherman and 

Clayton acts affect interstate operations only. Venner v. 

N. Y. C. & H. R. R. Co., supra. U. S. v. Southern Pacific, 259 U. S. 214, Cady's Cases on Pri. Corps. p. 215-228.

S. C. L. 23 applies only to corporations, domestic or foreign, doing business in this state and prohibits the following combinations: 1. for the creation of a monopoly, or, 2. for the unlawful restraint of trade, or, 3. for the prevention of competition in any necessary of life. Amer. etc. Corp. 

v. New Idria Corp., 293 Fed. 509. Continental Sec. Co. v.

I. R. T. Co., 221 Fed. 44.

Standard Oil Co. v. U. S., 221 U. S. 1. General Business Law, secs. 340 and 341, contain provisions avoiding, as illegal, contracts creating monopolies in the manufacture, production, or sale in this state of any article in common use, or restraining competition in this state in the supply or price of any such article, product or commodity, or the free pursuit of any lawful business, trade or occupation. Buff. Gravel Corp. v. Moore, 201 App. 

Div. 242, 194 N. Y. Supp. 225. The penalty for breach of

G. B. L. 341 by a corporation, is a fine not exceeding $20,000. G. B. L. 342 authorizes action by the attorney general in the name of the people to restrain or prevent illegal acts under the foregoing sections. 

One corporation may not buy the stock of another corporation for the sole purpose of controlling that other corporation. There must be some purpose of benefit for the purchasing corporation relative to its charter powers. In De 

La Vergne Co. v. German Sav. Inst., 175 U. S. 40, it was held to be lawful for one corporation to buy the stock of another where the lease of a line was desired. In New York, the restraint is held not to be unlawful unless it is general restraint. An agreement between the Lorillard S. S. Co. and the Old Dominion Co., by which the former agreed to discontinue its line of steamships and to leave the Lorillard Co. in undisturbed possession of the route from New York to Virginia was held not to be unlawful under S. C. L. 23, although no other line operated between the ports. It was held that the agreement was not void as being in general restraint of trade, since it merely acted to prevent one party from engaging or competing in the same business, and did not effectuate a general restraint of trade. Leslie v. 

Lorillard, 110 N. Y. 519. In Matter of Attorney General, 124 App. Div. 401, 108 N. Y. Supp. 823, it was held that the purchase of stock by one company in another was not in itself illegal unless it resulted in the creation of such a monopoly as would limit the supply and enhance the cost of the commodity. Peo. v. North R. Sugar Ref. Co., 121 

N. Y. 582. 

Under the Sherman Act and the Clayton Anti Trust Act, contracts in partial restraint of trade are not illegal, except

1 when unreasonable. When contracts in restraint of trade are incidental or ancillary to lawful business, and not unreasonable in scope and operation, they are not illegal. List v. Burley Tobacco Growers' Co-op. Ass'n, 151 N. E. 471 (Ohio). The recent decisions may be taken to have established that only such combinations are forbidden which, by reason of the inherent nature of the contemplated acts, prejudice the public interests by unduly restricting competition or unduly obstructing the course of trade. Northern Securities Co. v. U. S., 193 U. S. 197, 48 L. ed. 679. U. S. v. 

Southern Pacific Company, 261 U. S. 245. Standard Oil Co. 

v. U. S., 221 U. S. 1, 55 L. ed. 619. International Harvester 

Co. v. Mo., 234 U. S. 199, 58 L. ed. 1276.

The following cases illustrate the New York statute: 

(commodities) Peo. v. Amanna, 203 App. Div. 548, 196 

N. Y. Supp. 606. Finnegan v. Butler, 112 Misc. 280, 182 

N. Y. Supp. 671. (Importation and exportation); Export 

Lumber Co. v. South Brooklyn Sawmill Co., 54 App. Div. 

518, 67 N. Y. Supp. 626. (Transportation) Ives v. Smith, 55 Hun 606, 8 N. Y. Supp. 46, 28 N. Y. St. Rep. 917. Brook lyn El. R. Co. v. Brooklyn B. & W. E. R. Co., 23 App. Div. 

29, 48 N. Y. Supp. 665. Ceballos v. Munson S. S. Line, 93 

App. Div. 593, 87 N. Y. Supp. 811. (Not to compete) Brett v. Ebel, 29 App. Div. 256, 51 N. Y. Supp. 573. Peo. v. Amer. 

Ice Co., 120 N. Y. Supp. 443. N. Y. Motion Picture Co. v. 

Univ. Film Mfg. Co., 77 Misc. 581, 137 N. Y. Supp. 278. 

§ 72. 

Banking.

At common law, the right of doing banking was a common law right of individuals. Atty. Gen. v. Utica Ins. Co., 2 Johns. Ch. 371, cf. 15 Johns. 357. Peo. v. Doty, 80 N. Y. 

225. G. C. L. 18 prohibits a corporation other than one formed under or subject to the banking laws of New York or of the United States from carrying on the business of banking. Curtiss v. Leavitt, 15 N. Y. 1; Cady's Cases on

Pri. Corps. p. 160. The business of discounting paper was prohibited to other than banking corporations at an early date, but the purchase of a note, once issued for value, from the payee at less than face does not constitute banking. 

N. Y. State Loan & Tr. Co. v. Helmer, 77 N. Y. 64; Cady's 

Cases on Pri. Corps. at p. 286. In Nassau Bank v. Jones,

95 N. Y. 115, citing the Utica Insurance cases, 15 Johns. 

383 etc., banking powers were defined as "the right to issue bills, negotiate notes, and receive deposits." The statute specifies the businesses of buying and selling, exchange, discounting, deposits, and issuing a circulating medium, and the statute prohibits ordinary corporations from receiving or transmitting money by draft, travelers check, money order or otherwise, unless incorporated prior to 1850, or, unless they are express companies operating under contract with railways or transatlantic steamship companies, or telegraph companies. The statute was passed under the police power, and is constitutional for the business is one affected with a public interest. In re Bean, 207 App. Div. 276, 201 

N. Y. Supp. 827, 238 N. Y. 552 and 581. In re Morse, 247 

N. Y. 290, 160 N. E. 374. Natl. Liberty Ins. Co. of A. v. 

Bank of America, 217 App. Div. 691, 217 N. Y. Supp. 67. 

Jacobs v. Monaton Rty. Corp., 160 App. Div. 449, 145 N. Y. 

Supp. 611. Mere discounting of one or of hundreds of promissory notes is not of itself banking. Meserole Securities Co. v. Cosman, 226 App. Div. 21, 234 N. Y. Supp. 260, affd. 253 N. Y. 130, 170 N. E. 519. 

§ 73. Practicing Law. 

Penal law, sec. 280, and S. C. L. 7, forbid the practice of law by corporations. Contracts in violation thereof are il legal. U. S. Title Ins. Co. v. Brown, 166 App. Div. 688, 

152 N. Y. Supp. 470, affd. 217 N. Y. 628 (mem.). Peo. ex rel. Floersheimer v. Purdy, 221 N. Y. 481, 116 N. E. 390.

The retainer is void. In re City of New York (Bridge), 144 App. Div. 107, 128 N. Y. Supp. 999, affd. 204 N. Y. 625.

A partnership between a layman and an attorney to divide fees from proceedings to secure reduction of assessments through the medium of a corporation may violate the statute. Peo. ex rel. Trojan Rty. Co. v. Purdy, 174 App. 

Div. 702, 162 N. Y. Supp. 56. Cf. Tannenbaum v. Higgins, 190 App. Div. 861, 180 N. Y. Supp. 738.

The practice of law by a corporation is held malum in se and also malum probibitum. Meisel & Co. v. Natl. Jewelers &c., 90 Misc. 19, 152 N. Y. Supp. 913, affd. 173 App. Div. 

889, 157 N. Y. Supp. 1133. Mtr. of Coop. Law Co., 193 N. Y. 

479; Cady's Cases on Pri. Corps. p. 54. Peo. v. T. G. & T.

Co., 227 N. Y. 366, 125 N. E. 666, cf. 228 N. Y. 585, 127. 

N. E. 919. In re Kelsey, 186 App. Div. 95, 173 N. Y.

Supp. 860. 

Services in drawing legal papers are as much prohibited as the representation of clients in litigation through an attorney furnished by the corporation for litigation in which it has no interest other than the fee to be received. Peo. v. 

Peoples Trust Co., 180 App. Div. 494, 167 N. Y. Supp. 767. 

§ 74. To Practice Medicine or Dentistry. 

Education law, sec. 1263, makes the practice of medicine by any person other than a duly licensed physician a misdemeanor; and under Public Health Law, sec. 160, the administering of medicine by a business corporation in its own name is held to be practicing medicine, even though it does so under the advice of a licensed physician in each individual case. Godfrey v. Med. Soc. of N. Y. Co., 177 App. 

Div. 684, 164 N. Y. Supp. 846. A hospital incorporated under the membership corporations law is excepted from the prohibition, since it has legislative permission, if, as required by the statute, it has a staff of licensed physicians. 

Peo. v. John H. Woodbury Dermat. Inst., 192 N. Y. 454, 85

N. E. 697. The assignee of a patent medicine can not administer it for a fee. Thompson v. Staats, 15 Wend. 395. 

See Peo. v. Cole, 219 N. Y. 98, 113 N. E. 790. 

Pub. Health Law, sec. 203, makes it a misdemeanor to practice dentistry under an assumed name or a trade name. 

One who advertised under his own name adding "formerly

King Dental Offices" was held not punishable under this section. Peo. v. Hewson, 224 N. Y. 136, 120 N. E. 115. 

Education law, Sec. 1304-1313, limits the practice of dentistry to duly licensed dentists and provides penalties for the breach. Compare Hannon v. Siegel Cooper Co., 167 

N. Y. 244, 60 N. E. 597. 

§ 75. Other Licensed Crafts. 

General City Law, sec. 45a permits corporations to employ licensed master plumbers and engage in the plumbing business under their charters. Education law, Art. 55, permits corporations to engage in engineering if they employ duly licensed engineers; and sec. 1476 forbids corpora-

tions to practice architecture, except by the employment of a registered architect as the chief executive officer, and provided all the work is done under his personal supervision. Under the Insurance Law, sec. 143, a corporation may obtain a license to do an insurance brokerage business and be an insurance broker, provided the officers and directors are qualified to receive a license as brokers. Reference must be made to particular statutes relating to other crafts and arts. 

§ 76. Prohibition to Enter Into Partnership. 

At common law a corporation could not be a partner, and agreements to become such were void. Agreements to divide gross receipts, or an agreement whereby corporate premises were let for a rental equal to a moiety of the net profits of the business to be conducted therein, were held not partnerships, and valid. N. Y. & Sharon Canal Co. v. 

Fulton, 7 Wend. 412. Catskill Bank v. Gray, 14 Barb. 471. 

Breinig v. Sparrow, 80 N. E. 37, 39 Ind. App. 455. The reason assigned for the prohibition is the distinctive control, viz., in a partnership by the members, but in a corporation, by the directors only. "The business of a corporation shall be managed by its board of directors" G. C. L. 27. If a corporation became a partner there would be two principals, the legal person and a natural person, each having within the scope of the society's business, full authority to manage its concerns. The effect would be analogous to the assignment of the franchise. Whittenton Mills v. Upton, et als., 10 Gray (Mass.) 582. A possible penalty for partnership participation by a corporation is loss of its charter. Peo. v. 

North R. Sug. Ref. Co., supra. McCarter v. Firemen's Insurance Co., 74 N. J. Eq. 372.
