§ 77. Implied and Incidental Powers Defined. 

Implied powers are those necessary for the corporation to have in order to carry out the express powers. A corporation may transact all such matters as are ancillary to the express purposes and powers conferred by the charter, and which are necessarily transacted by ordinary individuals under similar circumstances. These powers are implied because they are bound up with the express powers. Thus, where the legislature has incorporated a telegraph company, it is implied that it may erect poles, string wires, buy materials, secure tools, employ help, etc. What is fairly implied is as much granted as what is expressed. Holmes 

Elec. Prot. Co. v. Williams, 228 N. Y. 407, 127 N. E. 315. 

Thomas v. R. R. Co., 101 U. S. 71. Peo. v. Utica Ins. Co., 15 Johns. 358. 

Incidental powers are practically the same as implied powers, and may be defined as those directly and immediately appropriate to the execution of the specific power granted. 7 R. C. L. sec. 513. For instance, a business corporation, whose business exposes it to sudden and immediate demands for the payment of money, has the incidental power of borrowing money, of having a bank checking account, and of drawing checks thereon, though such 120

powers are not expressed in the certificate. Curtis v. Leavitt, 15 N. Y. 1, Cady's Cas. on Pri. Corps. p. 159.

It is necessarily implied that a corporation which has embarked upon the business expressed in its charter may enter into the usual arrangements with its customers, and other parties, that obtain in the business, and adopt the proper means and make the requisite purchases for the success of the business. Thus a banking corporation may allow a depositor to overdraw his account; a merchandising corporation may loan its surplus funds, and the directors who are guiltless of fraud, will not be liable at the suit of a stockholder for losses subsequently occurring therefrom, even though the defaulting customer be himself a director; and a corporation formed to "raise and smelt lead” may build and rent shanties to their employees about the minehead in the wilderness, and tools for their gardens, as well as employ other concerns to smelt for them. Moss v. 

Averell, 10 N. Y. 451. Murray v. Smith, 224 N. Y. 40,

Cady's Cases on Pri. Corps. p. 200. It has implied power to compromise and settle claims, and to transport its goods to market in any reasonable way. Ib. The ability to make a contract implies the ability to make a negotiable promissory note for any proper corporate purpose. Ib. 

§ 78. Implied Powers Classified. 

Implied powers are classifiable as follows: 1. Acts in the usual course of business, i.e. to have a bank account, to borrow money, execute contracts within its powers to make, execute notes, take notes, hold land and buildings for its business. 2. Acts to protect debts owing to the corporation. For instance, the corporation may even run a business, temporarily, of a kind not authorized by its charter. 

Millbank v. N. Y. L. E. & W. R. Co., 64 How. Pr. 420. 

3. Embarking in a different business, provided it is ancillary, casual, temporary, or incidental to its main business. 

Metzger v. Knox, 77 Misc. 271, 136 N. Y. Supp. 681, affd. 

153 App. Div. 911, 137 N. Y. Supp. 1129. 4. Acts in part or wholly to protect or aid employees. 5. Acts to increase business, Holmes v. Willard, 125 N. Y. 75, 25 N. E. 1083.

Most of the conflict arises under this subdivision, but it is conceded that the act must be reasonably necessary to en-

able the corporation to accomplish the object of its incorporation. This means reasonably necessary, not indispensably so.

The tendency of the courts is to broaden the scope of the implied powers. Steinway v. Steinway & Sons, 17 Misc. 43, 40 N. Y. Supp. 718. Virgil v. Virgil Practice Clavier Co., 

33 Misc. 200, 68 N. Y. Supp. 335. Kochler & Co. v. Reuheimer, 26 App. Div. 1, 49 N. Y. Supp. 755. 

§ 79. Meaning of "Necessary.” 

The meaning of "necessary" has provoked much discussion. "Necessity is a word of flexible meaning. There may be an absolute necessity, a great necessity and a small necessity." Curtis v. Leavitt, 15 N. Y. 1, Cady's Cases on Pri. 

Corps. at p. 161. Gause v. Common. Tr. Co., 196 N. Y. 134.

Benefit or profit to the corporation is not a test. 

In Gause v. Commonwealth Trust Co., supra, the rule is succinctly stated as follows: "The unexpressed and incidental powers possessed by a corporation are not limited to such as are absolutely necessary to enable it to exercise the powers affirmatively granted. Whatever incidental powers are reasonably necessary to enable it to perform its corporate functions are implied from the powers affirmatively granted. But powers merely convenient or useful are not implied if they are not essential having in view the nature and object of the incorporation." "The authority of a corporation to perform a particular act is always dependent to a very considerable extent upon the facts and circumstances existing at the time when it is proposed to perform the act." 

In that case it was held that the guaranty by a bank of the sale of securities at designated prices in a fixed period, though done in aid of a proposed pooling agreement in which the bank was interested, and therefore presumably profitable when done, was neither within the express, implied, nor incidental powers of the bank. 

It is a general fundamental principle that when a right is given, all powers necessary to the exercise and enjoyment of the right are also given. Leavitt v. Blatchford, 3 N. Y. 

19. As a corollary, there must exist some scrap of language or implication in the grant of express power on which to hang a claim to implied power.

Neither implied nor incidental powers can avail to enlarge the express powers, and they exist merely for the purpose of enabling the corporation to carry out the powers expressly conferred. Fifth Ave. Coach Co. v. N. Y., 11 

N. Y. Supp. 759, Cady's Cases on Pri. Corps. at p. 258-262. 

Tracy v. Talmage, 14 N. Y. 162.

A railroad running to the seashore where there was no hotel, such point being mentioned as the terminus in its charter, was held to have power to build and run a hotel. 

Jacksonville Ry. and Nav. Co. v. Hooper, 160 U. S. 514.

The Pullman Car Co. was held not empowered to build a city for its employees with schools, churches, and theatres because there was no relation between the act for which it was created and these enterprises. Peo. v. Pullman's Pal. Car 

Co., 51 N. E. 664 (Ill.), 64 L. R. A. 366. The power will never be construed as implied where to pursue it would enlarge the express powers. Peo. v. Chi. Gas Trust Co., 22 N. E. 798 (Ill.). In Davis v. Old Colony R. R., 131 Mass. 

258, the appropriation by a railroad of money in aid of a 

"World's Peace Jubilee and International Musical Festival" 

conducted in its terminal city, and presumably to the advantage of the railroad's treasury, was held without its incidental powers because not necessary. Cf. Morris v. 

Ernst Wiener Co., 119 N. Y. Supp. 163, 65 Misc. 18.

A test frequently applied to ascertain the scope of incidental powers is the injury which the employment of the power in question may do to third persons. Thus, a corporation which had the power to make a railroad was enjoined from pulling down plaintiff's house for the purpose of extending its right of way as an accommodation to a large landowner in the neighborhood. The deviation could not be shown to be necessary. Dodd v. Salisbury, 33 L. T. 

254, 311. Bridge Co. v. Troy R. R., 7 Lans. 240. Rensselaer & Saratoga R. R. v. Davis, 43 N. Y. 137. So a water company was enjoined by a stockholder from laying pipes to connect with water pipes beyond the limits of their powers. 

Skaneateles W. W. Co. v. Skaneateles, 161 N. Y. 154. The burden of proof is upon the company to show that the challenged necessary power is such in fact. An affidavit by the engineer that the lands in question "are required or will be

required for the purpose of the corporation" is too vague to support the burden of proof which is on the corporation. 

Rensselaer & Saratoga R. R. v. Davis, supra. 

§ 80. Power to Own Real Property. 

An incidental power of all corporations at common law, unless specifically restrained by charter, was that of owning such real property as was reasonably necessary for its business, and that which had been taken in payment of a debt to the corporation. G. C. L. sect. 14, subd. 3. Nicoll v. 

N. Y. & Erie R. R., 12 N. Y. 121, Cady's Cases on Pri.

Corps. p. 163. A trading corporation has implied power to lend or sell on credit, and so it may lend on real estate not needed for its business, and take it, or buy in, for the purpose of protecting its interest. It is ultra vires for a corporation to buy real property for the purpose of speculation, unless it has express power. The officers might be liable to the creditors or stockholders for losses so incurred; but the title to the property would be perfectly valid, except for intervention by the state, before conveyance by the corporation. 

Where a railroad corporation is authorized to purchase lands needed for its road, it will be presumed that all lands acquired were for that purpose. Yates v. Van de Bogart, 56 N. Y. 526. A stockholder cannot restrain the consummation of a contract made for the purchase of lands ultra vires, unless he can show fraud. Burden v. Burden, 159

N. Y. 287. For the power of certain corporations to acquire lands by condemnation, see Business Corporations 

Law sec. 16.

A lease executed by a corporation for a longer period than its corporate life is not invalid, nor will it cease upon the termination of the corporate life. Tate v. Neary, 52 App. 

Div. 78, 65 N. Y. Supp. 40. 

§ 81. To Invest Surplus Funds. 

It has been held to be within the powers of a corporation, when not forbidden to do so by charter, to invest its idle funds in the stock of a dividend paying corporation, but without the implied power to subscribe for the stock of a corporation to be formed. Berry v. Yates, 24 Barb. 199.

Metcalf v. Amer. Sch. Furn. Co., 122 Fed. 115. Irvine v. 

Chi. &c. Coal Co., 200 Fed. 953. Converse v. Gardner Gov. 

Co., 174 Fed. 30. Richter v. Sea Gate Assn., 207 App. Div. 

573, 202 N. Y. Supp. 68. The court refused to order the performance of such a contract where the interest of the corporation would not be promoted thereby. A corporation may take the stock of another in payment of a debt. Hyde v. Equit. Lf. Assur. Soc., 61 Misc. 518, 116 N. Y. Supp. 219. 

§ 82. Power to Loan. 

The corporation may loan surplus moneys on safe security when it is inexpedient to distribute them among the shareholders. Murray v. Smith, 224 N. Y. 40, Cady's Cases on Pri. Corps. p. 201. 

§ 83. To Be Accommodation Endorser. 

A corporation has power to be a party to negotiable instruments taken in the course of its business; but it cannot issue or endorse simple accommodation paper in which it has no interest, unless expressly authorized by charter. It is no part of the ordinary business of a trading corporation, and still less so of a non-trading, for it to become a surety for others. Such endorsement will be void in the hands of those who have notice. Bank of Genesee v. Patchin Bank, 13 N. Y. 309. 

A holder in due course may enforce the contract against the corporation, and it is no defense that the corporate endorsement was without consideration. First Bank v. Jones, 222 N. Y. 579, 118 N. E. 1058. 

§ 84. To Borrow Money. 

Unless prohibited by charter, a corporation has implied power to borrow to carry on its legitimate business. Curtis v. Leavitt, supra. S. C. L. 16. To exempt the officers from liability, the circumstances must be such as to render borrowing useful. Corporate power to buy goods on credit does not always involve power on the part of the officer to borrow money to pay for goods bought, or for the contemplated purchase of goods, and it may often be more readily implied that the borrowing involved a wrong use of his power, in the case of borrowing, than when pledging credit.

§ 85. Power to Guarantee in General. 

Although a corporation has not the power to become a guarantor for any company or business, a corporation is bound on contracts of guaranty that are reasonably incidental to its business. The power to guarantee is not to be implied from general provisions authorizing a corporation to engage in any "similar line of business," or to "make contracts such as a private person could make." In Mtr. of Gilchrist, 278 Fed. 235, the court held that the guaranty by a dry goods corporation of the lease of dry goods firm was void. The object of the guaranty was to build up a shipping center around the street intersection on which the corporation's store was located, and, in the opinion of the board of the corporation, the purpose was definitely advantageous to it. See also Nat'l Park Bank v. German Amer. 

Sec. Co., 116 N. Y. 281. A corporation may not guarantee merely to increase its business. If the purpose of the guaranty is within its legitimate business (as of a saloon by a brewery which is not a retailer) it may guarantee. 

Hall v. Ochs, 33 App. Div. 103, 54 N. Y. Supp. 4; Harms 

Co. v. Leonhard Michel Brew. Co., 228 N. Y. 263. In 

Holmes v. Willard, 125 N. Y. 75, a corporation was held bound on its guaranty of the note of the manufacturer from whom it got its stock in trade, on the ground that the contract of guaranty was reasonably incidental to its business. 

A corporation selling stock or securities of another corporation may, in order to give such stock a market value, guarantee their payment. Arnot v. Erie Railroad, 67 N. Y. 

315. Where the payment of a dealer's debt to the corporation depended upon his prosperity in business, it was held that the corporation might guarantee his notes in order to assist him to get money with which to buy from the corporation. Hess v. Sloane, 66 App. Div. 522, 73 N. Y. Supp. 

313, aff'd 173 N. Y. 616 (mem.). A corporation may guarantee its own obligations, or the payment of dividends on its own stock, or on stock which it has lawfully acquired from another corporation. J. P. Morgan 

Co. v. Hall & Lyon Co., 34 R. I. 273. Where premises are used by an individual solely for the sale of the corporation's products, the corporation may guarantee the payment of

rent as an incident of its business. Holm v. Brewing Co., 47 N. Y. Supp. 518, 21 App. Div. 204. 

§ 86. Power to Agree to Submit to Arbitration. 

It has usually been held that the jurisdiction of arbitrators is absolutely exclusive of, and not concurrent with, that of any other tribunal, and that the whole world is bound to respect the adjudication of arbitrators, duly rendered, as binding and exclusive, and without appeal. In the enforcement of its rights a corporation has equal capacity with an individual to refer matters to arbitration. Alex andria Canal Co. v. Swann, 5 How. 83. Brady v. City of 

Brooklyn, 1 Barb. 584. In the absence of express power, a corporation should not emperil the stockholders investments by acting as arbitrator. The arbitration law, art. 2, sec. 8, requiring arbitrators to be sworn, may be waived; but if not waived, the award may be set aside on motion. Howard v. Sexton, 4 N. Y. 157. Day v. Hammond, 57 N. Y. 479. 

Hinkle v. Zimmerman, 184 N. Y. 114, 76 N. E. 1080. The "appraisal" clause of a fire insurance policy is binding on the insured corporation. Remington Paper Co. v. Louden 

Assur. Corp., 12 App. Div. 218, 43 N. Y. Supp. 431. 

§ 87. To Act as Agent, Trustee or Executor. 

Power to act as agent should be included in the certificate of incorporation. In the absence of express authority, there is no implied power, since the agency would not be directly connected with any express power, and would not be necessary to the accomplishment of any corporate purpose. Peo. v. Roberts, 145 N. Y. 375, 40 N. E. 7. So it was held that stockholders of a corporation organized solely for the manufacture of electric appliances were not liable for a debt incurred through an agreement of the corporation to act as sales agent for electric appliances, although their shares had not been paid, and therefore ordinarily the shareholders would be liable to creditors of the corporation for its debts by reason of S. C. L. 70. This debt, however, could not bind them, as it was a risk which was beyond the power of the corporation. Powell v. Murray, 3 App. Div. 273, 38 

N. Y. Supp. 233. Cf. United Press v. Abell Co., 58 App. 

Supp. 613. A savings bank cannot act 

Div. 611, 68 N. Y.

as agent in selling or buying stock on the exchange unless the power to act as agent is expressly given by its charter. 

Jemison v. Citizen's Nat'l Bank, 122 N. Y. 135, 140, 25 

N. E. 264.

The doctrine originally was that a corporation could not act as trustee or executor because it could not take an oath and because a court of equity could not enforce the trust by laying hold of the conscience of the corporation since it had no soul and could not be excommunicated. Also, the artificial legal entity could not be imprisoned. It was held, therefore, that a corporation which had assumed to act as a trustee under a deed of trust could not be compelled to execute the trust. A court of equity, upon request, would appoint another trustee. 1 Bl. Com. 477. This view has been abandoned, and a corporation, empowered to own real property, and under no express charter prohibitions, may hold real property in trust. Groesbeck v. Dunscomb, 41 

How. Pr. 302. Vidal v. Girard's Ex'rs., 2 How. (U. S.) 

127. Jones v. Habershaan, 107 U. S. 174, 27 L. ed. 40. In re Howe, 1 Pai. 214.

A business corporation is prohibited from acting as trustee under a corporate trust mortgage, for that power is reserved to banking corporations. Banking Law, sec. 185, subd. 4. G. C. L. 18.

If power to act as trustee is placed in the certificate of incorporation, it should not be filed. If filed, the provision is illegal and void. A corporation organized for the purpose of increasing the business of retail merchants, which proposes to issue checks, stamps, or other evidences of debt, and to sell them to merchants who in turn can place them in a bank to be eventually paid out of a fund which has been set aside by the corporation, thereby violates the provisions of this section. Rept. of Atty-General, 5 State Dept. Rep. 530.

At common law a corporation might be a guardian or executor. Ledwith v. Ledwith, 1 Dem. Sur. 154. Unless, however, it had some interest in the subject matter, it was without power to risk the capital stock on a purpose so foreign to its authorized powers. The power today is re-

served to banks. Banking law, sec. 185 (6). Matter of 

Bergdorf, 206 N. Y. 309. 

§ 88. Power to Act in Foreign Jurisdictions. 

A corporation has this power to carry on business, through agents or otherwise, provided the other state impliedly or expressly consents, and provided there is no restriction in the charter. Cary v. Cleveland & T. R. Co., 29 Barb. 35. It has no existence in the other state unless permitted by its laws. A New York corporation cannot exercise in Illinois powers permitted to corporations created in Illinois but denied in New York to New York corporations. Stockweathers' case, 72 Ill. 50. Express power to do business in other states is given by G. C. L. 17. 

The corporation carries its charter wherever it goes. 

This is true although the corporation is doing business in a state other than that wherein it is incorporated. Jemison v. 

Citizen's Savings Bank, 122 N. Y. 135, 25 N. E. 265, 92 

L. R. A. 78. 

§ 89. Power to Make Assignments for the Benefit of Creditors. 

At common law, a corporation in failing circumstances had the power of a natural person to make assignments for the benefit of creditors. Vanderpoel v. Gorman, 140 N. Y. 

563, 35 N. E. 932. Rogers v. Pell, 154 N. Y. 518, 49 N. E. 75.

In New York, S. C. L. sec. 15 prohibits a corporation which has failed to pay its obligations when due from transferring any of its property to officers, directors, stockholders, or creditors. Furthermore, no stockholder may assign his shares in contemplation of the insolvency of the corporation. 

This section also provides that the claims of laborers shall be preferred claims, and shall be paid before any creditors, out of the corporation assets in excess of valid prior liens or encumbrances.

The word "assignment" covers all appropriate means of creating a preference. Thus a confession of judgment when the corporation is insolvent or in contemplation of insolvency is a preference and void. If the corporation were solvent, there would be no confession of judgment, ordinarily; the debt would be paid instead. Also, it is held that after the corporation becomes insolvent, the di-

rectors are prohibited by the true construction of the statute from obtaining liens against the corporation's property by acquiring valid outstanding obligations of the corporation. 

So where a director sued on such a claim and obtained a writ of attachment, it was held that the writ must be set aside. Throop v. Hatch Lithographic Co., 125 N. Y. 531.

An insolvent corporation is not bound to defend a hopeless suit against it, though the obtaining of a judgment will give that creditor a preference. The only way the other creditors can prevent a judgment creditor from obtaining a preference is by having a receiver appointed before the sheriff has sold under levy under the judgment, or by an involuntary bankruptcy proceeding against the corporation. 

Varnum v. Hart, 119 N. Y. 101. The fact that another creditor has been granted a judgment by confession does not change that rule. See: Throop v. Hatch, supra. French v. Andrews, 145 N. Y. 441.

Receivers and counsel of an insolvent corporation are incapacitated from acquiring liens for themselves and enforcing them for more than they paid. And where a corporation, when insolvent, transferred its property without consideration to another corporation which issued its bonds to the receiver and counsel, the latter corporation, on its insolvency can secure no right as against the property of its seller, but must look for its compensation to the complainant in the suit in which receivers were appointed. Ciba 

Co. Inc. v. Interstate Tanning Co., 9 Fed. (2d) 632. An officer cannot gain a preference by indirection. Where a director was paid an excessive salary for acting as treasurer, general manager, and clerk, each on its own footing, the receiver may recover any grossly excessive payments in excess of the fair value of the services. Stratis v. Andreson, 150 N. E. 932 (Mass.), citing Godley v. Crandall & 

Godley Co., 212 N. Y. 121. Unfair compensation to directors for their services in the sale of corporate stock may be recovered back by the receiver. The corporation may sue the officer, and a stockholder may also recover for the resulting depreciation of his stock values. The decisions have held that even the United States government may not

get an illegal preference over creditors. U. S. v. Fletcher 

Savings & Trust Co., 151 N. E. 420 (Ind.).

The statute prohibits corporations from making political contributions. Penal Law, sec. 671. 

§ 90. Form and Mode of Corporate Contracts. 

It was at one time held that, save in a few cases, a corporation could not contract except under its corporate seal.

Today, unless the charter makes a seal necessary to the validity of the contract, a corporation may contract by resolutions or by parol, and without a seal, in any case where a natural person could contract without a seal. If the charter of a corporation or some statute specifies a particular form for corporate contracts, that form must be followed, but the statute must be mandatory, and not merely directory. Even where there is such a provision, and it is not complied with, the corporation may be liable. Thus, if a corporation enters into a contract not in the form prescribed by its charter, and receives the consideration, it cannot escape liability by saying that the contract is not in the prescribed form, though it might have defeated recovery if the contract had remained executory. In Pixley v. 

Pac. R. Co., 3 Cal. 183, the charter prescribed that no contract should be valid unless in writing. The defendant railroad company hired plaintiff under an oral contract to perform services for the corporation, and later when sued for the value of such services, set up the defense that the contract was not in the proper form. The court said: "While such contract remains executory on both sides, an action could not be maintained by either party to enforce it; but where one of the contracting parties has completely performed on his part, the party receiving the consideration cannot escape liability. See also: Fisler v. LaRue, 15 

Barb. 523. Curtis v. Piedmont Lumber & Mining Co., 109 

N. C. 403, 13 S. E. 944. Clowe v. Imperial Pine Products 

Co., 114 N. C. 304, 19 S. E. 153.

A corporation must use its corporate name on every obligation entered into, and the use of a fragment of its name in a real estate contract may be urged against the contract; and a check drawn to the payee in the same fragment of the corporate name was held insufficient to form the basis

for a recovery in an action by the corporation against the drawer. Scarsdale Publishing Co. v. Carter, 63 Misc. 271, 116 N. Y. Supp. 731. Nevertheless a misnomer is not necessarily fatal. In VanNorden Trust Co. v. L. Rosenberg, 62 

Misc. 285, 114 N. Y. Supp. 1025, a note indorsed “Louis

Rosenberg, Inc.," was held to be a sufficient indorsement for a corporation whose name was "L. Rosenberg, Incorporated." See also: Mail & Express Co., Inc., v. Parker, 204 

App. Div. 327, 198 N. Y. Supp. 20. The parol evidence rule allows the use of parol evidence to identify the real party. Richardson on Evi. § 446. A promissory note commencing, "For value received we promise to pay, etc." signed "W. Gilmore, Pres., D. C. Sharpe, Sec'y of the Hobart

Agricultural Horse and Cattle Show, Ass'n," and containing no reference in the body thereof to the corporation, is upon its face, the individual note of the two makers. Bush v. Gilmore, 61 N. Y. Supp. 682, 45 App. Div. 89.

§ 91. Origin and Definition, Reasons. 

At first, corporations were considered to have most of the powers and to be subject to most of the obligations of individual persons. For the protection of both state and investor there was introduced and developed in the courts within the last century the doctrine of ultra vires (“beyond the powers"), by which was laid down the rule (1) that a corporation exists for the attainment of powers granted and necessarily incident, and for those only; and (2) that the control and exercise of corporate powers by officers and agents, as well as the creation of corporate obligations, are limited to acts within the powers (G. C. L. 13). Hood v. 

N. Y. & N. H. R. R., 22 Conn. 1. Curtiss v. Leavitt, 15 N. Y. 

1, Cady's Cas. on Pri. Corps., 159. Dartmouth College v. 

Woodward, 4 Wheat. 518, Cady's Cas. p. 321. The doctrine necessarily arrived at was that the corporation could not be bound by liabilities springing out of acts ultra vires; but it has been whittled away by reasonings based on estoppel, pari delicto, public policy in relation to torts attributable to the corporation, novation, adoption and ratification, the rules for construction of directory provisions of the charter, 133

and efforts to protect title to property from being impaired by the working of a doctrine of law. Whitney Arms Co. v. Barlow, 63 N. Y. 62, Cady's Cas. on Pri. Corps. p. 266. 

Nassau Bank v. Jones, 95 N. Y. 115, ib. p. 212. Cits. Natl. 

Bank v. Appleton, 216 U. S. 196, 190 N. Y. 417, Cady's 

Cas. on Pri. Corps. pp. 279, 281. Bath Gas. Co. v. Claffy, 151 N. Y. 24, ib. p. 269. Bissell v. M. S. etc. Ry., 22 N. Y. 

259, ib. p. 289. Kerfoot v. Farmers Bank, 218 U. S. 281, ib. p. 264. Verplanck v. Merc. Ins. Co., 1 Edw. (N. Y.) 84.

Scandinavian Imp.-Exp. Co. v. Bachman, 195 App. Div. 297, 

186 N. Y. Supp. 860. 

In Whitney Arms Co. v. Barlow, 63 N. Y. 62, it is said: "When acts of corporations are spoken of as ultra vires, it is not intended that they are unlawful or even such as the corporation cannot perform, but merely those which are not within the powers conferred upon the corporation by the act of its creation, and are in violation of the trust reposed in the managing board of the shareholders, that the affairs should be managed, and the funds applied solely for carrying out the objects for which the corporation was created." 

In Leslie v. Lorillard, 110 N. Y. 519, it was said that "contracts of corporations are said to be ultra vires when they involve some adventure or undertaking not within the scope of their charter, which is their rule of corporate action." 

Jemison v. Citizens' Sav. Bank, 122 N. Y. 135. 

An act is said to be intra vires ("within the powers") when it is within the scope of a corporation's powers or authority. Pittsburgh, etc., R. Co. v. Dodd, 115 Ky. 176, 72 S. W. 827. 

§ 92. Diverse applications of the term ultra vires. 

Some confusion has resulted from the loose use of the term ultra vires. Fletcher on Corporations, p. 2567. A probable explanation of loose usage is that a court, engaged in deciding a controversy as distinguished from preparing a treatise, may often convey the desired meaning by paraphrasing in a way that parallels the exact sense of the term. 

Only acts not within the powers conferred by the charter or contrary to express prohibitions of the charter (chap. V, supra), are strictly within the doctrine of ultra vires; and this is the signification which will be given to the term

herein when it is employed without qualification. So. Pac. 

Ry. Co. v. Orton, 32 Fed. 457. Le Couteux v. Buffalo, 33 

N. Y. 333. Auburn & C. Plank Road Co. v. Douglass, 9 N. Y. 

444. Jacobs v. Jamestown Mantel Co., 211 N. Y. 154. Black v. Ellis, 129 App. Div. 140, 113 N. Y. Supp. 558; Schwab v. 

E. G. Potter Co., 194 N. Y. 409, Cas. p. 542.

Other uses of term: As instances where the term ultra vires has been employed in a loose sense might be listed the 

(1) Acts of officers, agents or other executives beyond the scope of their authority as such, but within the powers of the corporation; as where a treasurer without express authority from the directors gave the corporation's promissory note. The corporation might be liable on the note by ratification; or, for any portion of the consideration rightly laid out for the corporation, in a money had and received action; but the note is loosely said to be ultra vires. Castle v. Lewis, 78 N. Y. 131. Mitchell v. Forest City Printing Co., 187 App. Div. 743. Remington, etc., Pulp etc. Co. v. Coswell, 126 App. Div. 142. (2) In an euphemistic sense to designate illegal acts, merely malum prohibitum and innocently done, but which are beyond the powers of all corporations, such as acts in illegal restraint of trade, or creating monopolies, or acts contra bonos mores. Dyer v. Broadway Cent. Bank, 225 

App. Div. 366. Bath Gaslight Co. v. Claffy, 151 N. Y. 24, 35, 45 N. E. 390, Cady's Cas. on Pri. Corps. p. 269. Whitney 

Arms Co. v. Barlow, 63 N. Y. 62, ib. p. 266. (3) Acts of others—e. g., the shareholders or majority stockholders purporting to contract for the corporation—a power vested in the directors and executives only. G. C. L. 

27. Manson v. Curtis, 223 N. Y. 313, 322. (4) Acts as to which formal requisites of law were omitted, and which are therefore capable of being ratified. 

Sec. 62, supra. (5) Acts that do not bind all the shareholders, i. e., dissenting stockholders are not bound. This has nothing to do with the powers of corporations as such but only with the method of their exercise, as with the consent of the collective body of stockholders. Chap. XV, infra.

(6) Acts that bind the corporation but for which the stockholders may hold the executives liable in damages. As in Earl of Shrewsbury v. North Staffordshire Ry. Co., 35 

L. J. Ch. 156, 172, where the directors, having authority to build a railroad, applied the corporate funds for the purpose of a different speculation, to-wit, making a terminal harbor. See chap. XIV, infra. 

§ 93. Usual Actions Involving Ultra Vires Acts. 

(1) Cases in which one or more of the shareholders seeks to restrain the officers of the corporation from engaging in transactions unauthorized by the charter. (2) Actions brought by third persons against corporations to enforce their contracts, or by the corporation against third persons, in which the defense relied upon is, that in making the contract the corporation exceeded its corporate powers. (3) Actions in which the defense is that the directors had exceeded, not the powers conferred upon the entire corporation by law, but those conferred by the shareholders upon the directors or managing officers. (4) Actions against the corporation for torts and crimes committed by executives. See Bissell v. M. S., etc. R. Co., supra, Cady's Cas. on Pri. Corps. p. 289. 

§ 93a. Burden of Proof. Presumption of Intra Vires. 

Acts which on the face of the powers conferred by the charter appear to be authorized are, by inference of law, intra vires and valid; and the burden of proof will be on those claiming them invalid to plead and prove the defense of ultra vires. Omnia acta rite esse praesumuntur. Hess v. 

Sloane, 66 App. Div. 522, 73 N. Y. Supp. 313. Conn. Mut. 

Lf. Ins. Co. v. Cleveland, etc. R. Co., 41 Barb. 9, 26 How. 

Pr. 225. Akin v. Blanchard, 32 Barb. 527. Ellsworth v. St. 

Louis, etc. R. Co., 98 N. Y. 553. Burden v. Burden, 159 

N. Y. 287, 54 N. E. 17. Jacobs v. Monaton Rty. Co., 160 

App. Div. 449, 145 N. Y. Supp. 611. The burden is upon the defendant corporation to show that the person served with process was no longer the president and a director. 

Beck-Brown Rty. Co. v. Ansack Corp., 222 App. Div. 760, 225 N. Y. Supp. 792. The presumption is that a check

signed by the corporation was issued in the course of its business. Ferd. Ehrlich, Inc. v. Levine, 83 Misc. 136, 144 

N. Y. Supp. 818. In an action on a promissory note by an indorsee against a corporate indorser, since it does not appear on the face of the note that the note was the act of the corporation, the plaintiff must prove in his prima facie case the signature, and that the individual who indorsed the corporate name was authorized to do so. The corporation has the burden of proof to show lack of his authority. 

Secs. 50, 91, and 98 Neg. Insts. law sets forth the presumptions arising on further proof by the plaintiff that he paid value, and the burden is cast on the corporation to show lack of authority. Karsch v. Pottier & S. Mfg. & I. Co., 82 

App. Div. 230, 81 N. Y. Supp. 782. Cheaver v. Pittsburgh 

R. R. Co., 150 N. Y. 59. cf. Title G. & T. Co. v. Pam, 232 

N. Y. 441.

One who deals with a corporation is presumed to know the extent of its charter powers, but not its by-laws. 

Farmers & Mech. Bank v. Butchers & D. Bank, 16 N. Y. 

125, 14 N. Y. 623, 28 N. Y. 425, 69 Am. Dec. 678. 

§ 94. English Rule of Ultra Vires. Cardinal Principles. 

Under the English rule, transactions and contracts, both executory, or partly or wholly executed by either party, are wholly illegal and void, if they are not within the express or implied powers given the corporation by reasonable implications from the language of its charter, or if prohibited by charter or statute.

Courts in dealing with corporations will look to those capacities and powers only which they actually possess at the time.

The English rule further holds that corporations cannot be rendered directly liable upon ultra vires transactions, even though executed, but must account for benefits received therefrom. As long as the transaction remains executory, it is established that it cannot be enforced. (At this point the various rules known as the U. S., the Massachusetts, the New York and the Kansas rules, diverge from the English rule.) Under all rules and in both countries unquestionably the corporation must account for benefits derived. 

The English rule, in common with all American rules dis-

tinguishes between directory and mandatory provisions of the charter. Formalities are generally not imperative but merely directory and, therefore, the absence of them can be set up against those persons only who were cognizant of the defect. Formalities are useful as a protection but they may not be turned into instruments of dishonesty, either against or on behalf of a corporation.

The English rule, regards acts which amount to an assignment of franchises and special privileges, or powers in the nature of franchises as wholly void and not merely ultra vires, except as permitted by statute. Similiter, S. C. L. 20, 21, 96, 97 and 98.

By the English rule, any party to an ultra vires transaction may set up the defense thereof, and any one corporator may call upon the courts to restrain the corporation from engaging therein. This proposition has been, however, much modified in the various American rules. Under the 

New York rule, a stockholder cannot interpose in a wholly or partly executed transaction, his right being limited to contracts or acts which are wholly executory. Wormser v. 

Metropolitan St. Ry. Co., 184 N. Y. 83, 76 N. E. 1036. 

Treadwell v. United Verde Copper Co., 134 App. Div. 394, 119 N. Y. Supp. 112. 

§ 95. The United States Rule. 

The federal courts have repeatedly held that a contract with a corporation which is beyond its powers, or ultra vires, though it may not be otherwise illegal, is absolutely void and unenforceable for illegality; that the fact that the contract has been executed by one of the parties, and the other has thus received the consideration for his or its promise, cannot give the contract any validity, and that no action will lie on the contract itself by the party on whose part it has been executed. Bassick v. Aetna Explosives Co., 246 Fed. 

974. Central Transportation Co. v. Pullman's Palace Car Co., 139 U. S. 24, Cady's Cases on Pri. Corps. p. 274. De La Vergne Co. v. German Savings Inst., 175 U. S. 40. Pitts burgh, C. & St. L. R. Co. v. Keokuk & H. Bridge Co., 131 U. S. 371. Louisville, N. A. & C. R. Co. v. Louisville 

Trust Co., 174 U. S. 552. Pearce v. Madison & I. R. Co., 21 How. 441. Bowen v. Needles Nat. Bank, 94 Fed. 925.

By the U. S. rule, the ultra vires acts cannot be made valid by subsequent ratification by either stockholders or directors, in spite of the fact that the acts do not violate either statutory or express charter prohibitions. Park Hotel 

Co. v. Fourth Nat. Bank of St. Louis, 85 Fed. 742. California 

Bank v. Whitney, 167 U. S. 362. In the case of Central 

Trans. Co. v. Pullman's Palace Car Co., supra, a manufacturing corporation incorporated in Pennsylvania for “the transportation of passengers in railroad cars constructed and owned by the said company" and "to enter into contracts with corporations of this or any other state for the leasing or hiring and transfer to them or any of them of its railway cars and other personal property," carried on the business of manufacturing sleeping cars, hiring or letting the cars to railroad companies, and selling berths and accommodations to passengers. The corporation, at a time when its charter had 99 years to run, leased and delivered to defendant corporation, which was engaged in a similar business, all its cars, railroad contracts, patent rights and other personal property for 99 years; and covenanted not to compete. The lease was clearly ultra vires. The federal court held it to be void, and that no action could be maintained by the lessor upon the illegal contract for rent or otherwise. In pari delictu potior est conditio defendentis. 

Three reasons advanced by the courts for the U. S. rule, are: (1) The interest of the public that the corporation shall not transcend the powers granted. McCormick v. 

Market Nat. Bank, 165 U. S. 538, 549, 41 L. ed. 817. (2)

The interest of the stockholder that the capital shall not be subjected to the risk of enterprises not contemplated by the charter, and therefore not authorized by the stockholders by and in their subscription for stock. Pittsburgh C. & St. 

L. Ry. Co. v. Keokuk & H. Bridge Co., 131 U. S. 371, 33

L. ed. 157. (3) The obligation of everyone, when entering into a contract with a corporation, to take notice of limitations of its area of activity defined in its charter. A corporation carries its charter with it in every state it goes. 

Pennsylvania R. Co. v. St. Louis, A. & T. H. R. Co., 118 U. S. 

290, 317, 30 L. ed. 83. In St. Louis, Vandalia & T. H. Ry. 

Co. v. Terre Haute & I. Ry. Co., 145 U. S. 393, it was held

that where a statute of Illinois permitted a railroad corporation to lease its road to a railroad corporation of another state, and where the railroad corporation in such other state was not empowered to take such a lease by the law of its own state, a lease by the one railroad corporation to the other, ultra vires of one or of both, would not be set aside at the suit of the lessor, although the lessee had possession, paying the stipulated rent for 17 years, and had taken no steps to rescind or repudiate the contract. 

§ 96. Exceptions to the U. S. Rule. 

(1) Where the contract is fully executed on both sides, the court will not interfere, and the title of the one that has received the property is good. Kerfoot v. Farmers & Merchants Bank, 218 U. S. 211, 54 L. Ed. 1042. Cincinnati etc. 

R. R. Co. v. McKeen, 64 Fed. 44. Rogers v. Nashville etc. 

Ry. Co., 91 Fed. 316. (2) If the contract is fully executed on one side, the one who has performed may recover in quasi contract. 

Rankin v. Emigh, 218 U. S. 27. Merchants Nat. Bank v. First Nat. Bank, 238 Fed. 507. Cit. Nat'l Bank v. Appleton, 216 U. S. 196. See also L. R. A. 1917 A, 1040. (3) In cases of contracts which were made wholly beyond the scope of the corporation's powers, the courts have gone a long way to enable parties who have parted with property or money on the faith of such contracts to obtain justice by recovery of the property or the money specifically, or as money had and received to plaintiff's use, Thomas v. 

Railroad Co., 101 U. S. 71. Louisiana v. Wood, 102 U. S. 

294. Chapman v. Douglas County, 107 U. S. 348, 355. Salt 

Lake City v. Hollister, 118 U. S. 256, 263. (4) The corporation may be regarded estopped to repudiate the contract as ultra vires where it has received the benefit. Union Trust Co. v. Ill. Midland Co., 117 U. S. 434. 

Nat'l Bank of Xenia v. Stewart, 107 U. S. 676, Providence 

Engineering Corp. v. Downey etc. Corp., 294 Fed. 641. (5) Where the contract is ultra vires because of facts not known at the time the contract was made, and where it has been performed by the innocent party who is not in pari delicto, the federal court will allow redress. Thomas v. Richmond, 12 Wall. 349.

(6) If the contract is valid in part and ultra vires in part, the valid part will be upheld if separable. Ill. Trust & 

Sav. Bank v. City of Arkansas, 76 Fed. 271. See, however,

Cent. Ohio & Fuel Co. v. Cap Dairy Co., 64 L. R. A. 395, 

53 N. E. 711. (7) By means of an estoppel in pais, a corporation may be withheld from asserting ultra vires, and the innocent party is permitted relief. Citizens Natl. Bank v. Appleton, 216 U. S. 196. Cit. State Bank v. Hawkins, 71 Fed. 369. (8) Subrogation. When that which was received by the corporation was used to pay lawful debts, the party who has performed may be granted redress in the nature of subrogation. (9) Contracts fully executed and performed by payment or by conveyance cannot be relieved against for invalidity, if parties in equal fault. Harriman v. Northern Securities 

Co., 197 U. S. 296. Metcalf v. American School Furniture 

Co., 122 Fed. 124. 

§ 97. The Massachusetts Rule. 

The earlier decisions in Massachusetts seemed to favor the federal rule and to hold that ultra vires contracts were void even though fully performed on one side. Fletcher on 

Corporations, p. 2622. In Davis v. Old Colony R. Co., 131

Mass. 258, 41 Am. Rep. 221, it was held that no action was maintainable against a railroad on an ultra vires contract, by which it guaranteed a proportion of the expenses of a musical festival to be held in its terminal city. The later decisions of the state show a tendency to follow the New 

York rule, Nims v. Mount Hermon Boys' School, 160 Mass. 

177, 35 N. E. 776, Cady's Cases on Pri. Corps. p. 303. N. Y. 

Bank Note Company v. Kidder Press Mfg. Co., 192 Mass. 

391, 404, 78 N. E. 463. Slater Woolen Co. v. Lamb, 143 

Mass. 420, 421, 9 N. E. 823. Prescott Natl. Bank v. Butler, 157 Mass. 548, 549, 32 N. E. 909.

Ultra vires is a good defense to contracts wholly executory on both sides in Massachusetts as in every state except 

Kansas. Davis v. Old Colony R. Co., supra. If an ultra vires contract has been fully performed on both sides, neither party can maintain an action to set aside the transaction or to recover what has been parted with by reason

of being in pari delicto. Nantasket Beach Steamboat Co. v. Preston, 182 Mass. 147, 65 N. E. 57. $ 98. The New York Rule.

The New York rule proceeds upon the idea that the defense of ultra vires when pleaded for or against a corporation should not avail to impede or impair justice or work a legal wrong where a benefit has accrued by full or part performance. Whitney Arms Co. v. Barlow, 63 N. Y. 62, Cady's Cas. on Pri. Corps. p. 266. Curtis v. Natalie A. 

Coal Co., 89 App. Div. 61, 70, 85 N. Y. Supp. 413, affd. 181 

N. Y. 543. Jourdan v. L. I. R. R. Co., 115 N. Y. 380, 22 

N. E. 153. The rule may be expressed as follows: (1) To contracts wholly executory on both sides, the defense of ultra vires is available to either party to the contract. Nassau Bank v. Jones, 95 N. Y. 115, Cady's Cas. on Pri. Corps. p. 209. Jemison v. Cit. Sav. Bank, 122 N. Y. 

135. Doubleday P. & Co. v. Shumaker, 60 Misc. 227, 113 

N. Y. Supp. 83. DeVinne v. Rianhard, 9 Daly 406. With the foregoing phase of the New York rule most jurisdictions concur, and notably the federal courts and those of Alabama, California, Illinois, Massachusetts, Minnesota, New 

Hampshire, Ohio, and Wisconsin. (2) If the ultra vires contract is wholly executed, neither party can maintain an action to set aside the transaction or to recover back what has been parted with.

Parish v. Wheeler, 22 N. Y. 494, 508. Lancaster v. Amsterdam Improvement Co., 140 N. Y. 576, Cady's Cas. on Pri. 

Corps. p. 586. Woodruff v. Ry., 93 N. Y. 618. Parish v.

Wheeler, 22 N. Y. 494. Title so obtained is good. In accord are decisions of U. S., Ala., Iowa, Pennsylvania, Virginia and West Viriginia courts. (3) To ultra vires contracts which have been in good faith executed by either party to the contract, and of which the other has had the benefit, the defense of ultra vires is not available, and an action may be brought on the contract. 

Wormser v. Met. St. R. Co., 184 N. Y. 83. Vought v. Eastern 

Bldg. etc. Assn., 172 N. Y. 508. Linkauf v. United Lombard, 137 N. Y. 417. Treadwell v. United Verde Copper Co. 134

App. Div. 664. Davidson v. Cannabis Mfg. Co. 113 App. 

Div. 664. Usher v. N. Y. Cent. etc. R. Co., 76 App. Div. 472.

Fahey v. Ottenheimer, 219 App. Div. 668. Diamond Match Co. v. Roeber, 106 N. Y. 473. Rider Life Boat Co. v. Rodder, 

97 N. Y. 378. Bowers v. Ocean Accident, etc., 110 App. Div. 

691. Rowe Savings Bank v. Krug, 102 N. Y. 331. In accord are decisions in Arkansas, California, Georgia, Idaho, Indiana, Ky., Mich., Mo., N. J., Texas, Colorado, Penn., and

Wisc. A notable variation of this rule, of course, is the 

U. S. rule which is that the performance never precludes the other party from urging ultra vires. Sec. 95 supra. 

Three reasons advanced for the New York rule are (1)

The state alone may assert and protect against an injury to the public right; and by its silence and acquiescence in the ultra vires acts the state waives its rights and no citizen may speak in its place. Fulton Lt. H. & P. Co. v. Seneca 

R. P. Co., 119 Misc. 729, 731, 199 N. Y. Supp. 923. Starin v. S. I. R. T., 112 N. Y. 206. Thomas v. Musicians etc. Assn., 121 N. Y. 45. Bank of Lyons v. Ocean Natl. Bank, 60 N. Y. 

278. Smith v. Met. Gaslight Co., 12 How. Pr. 187. (2) The interests of stockholders will be given due consideration when they request it. Murrin v. Archbald Consol. 

Coal Co., 232 N. Y. 541. Where, however, the corporation is bound by benefits received or parted with under the ultra vires contract, the stockholders can not impair contract rights and are limited to the enforcement of the liability of the directors, if any. Chap. XIV, infra. Oelberman v. 

N. Y. & N. Ry. Co., 76 Hun, 613. Venner v. N. Y. C. & 

H. R. R. Co., 217 N. Y. 615, 111 N. E. 487. If the contract is wholly executory, the stockholder may enjoin performance. 

Schwab v. Potter Co., 194 N. Y. 409; Cady's Cas. on Pri.

Corps. p. 542. If there is an adequate defense at law, no injunction should be granted tho the contract is ultra vires. 

Minturn v. Farmers L. & T. Co., 3 N. Y. 498, 501. A different result is reached where the contract was made by the officers in fraud of the corporation, and not merely ultra vires. Guggenheimer v. Beaver Board Co., 136 Misc. 511, 240 N. Y. Supp. 15.

The stockholder must move promptly so that injury to strangers and creditors may be unlikely. Steinway v. Steinway & Sons, 17 Misc. 43, 40 N. Y. Supp. 718. Sheldon Hat 

Bl. Co. v. Eickemeyer Hat Bl. Mach. Co., 90 N. Y. 607.

New Britain Nat. Bank v. A. B. Cleveland Co., 91 Hun 447. 

Kent v. Quicksilver Mining Co., supra; Cady's Cas. p. 447. (3) The doctrine of notice is impracticable where the incorporation is incorporated under a general statute. It requires one dealing with a corporation to take notice of its certificate. Jemison v. Cit. Savings Bank, supra. 

§ 99. The Kansas Rule. 

In absence of special circumstances, such as illegality or immorality, the Kansas courts have held that neither party to an executory ultra vires contract may defeat its enforcement. The contract itself is a property right. This state stands alone in support of this rule. Fletcher on Corporations p. 2595. In Harris v. Independence Gas Co., 76 Kan. 

570, 92 Pac. 1123 it was held that one who leased land to a gas company to explore for oil and gas could not maintain a suit to cancel the portion thereof relating to oil, although the corporation had no authority to engage in the oil business and although the agreement was wholly executory. 

§ 100. The U. S., New York and Mass. Rules Contrasted. 

The most important distinction between the U. S. rule as to contracts fully executed on one side, and the N. Y. and present Massachusetts rules, is that under the federal rule, the one who has performed cannot recover in an action at law on the contract. Louisville, N. A. & C. R. Co. v. Louisville Trust Co., 174 U. S. 552, 43 L. Ed. 1081, while under the N. Y. and present Mass. rules it is held that a recovery may be had upon the contract itself on the theory of estoppel or otherwise. Linkauf v. Lombard, 137 N. Y. 417, 33 N. E. 

472. Woodruff v. Erie Ry. Co., 93 N. Y. 609. N. Y. Bank 

Note Company v. Kidder Press Mfg. Co., 192 Mass. 391, 78 N. E. 463. A corporation cannot under any rule retain what it has received under a contract with impunity. Appleton v. Cits. Natl. Bank, supra.

If the contract is fully executed on one side, the Mass. and N. Y. rules are now harmonious, and only the federal rule refuses to consider the contract.

All rules hold that contracts wholly executory in both sides may be avoided by either party, or by a stockholders suit, and their performance enjoined as ultra vires.

Where a corporation purchased intoxicating liquors beyond its powers the corporation was held estopped, by delivery of the chattel to it, from urging the defence of ultra vires. Schlitz Brewing Co. v. Missouri Poultry & Game Co. 

229 S. W. 813 (Mo.) In Griggs Manufacturing Co. v. 

Holmes & Wessal Metal Co., 127 N. Y. 252, it was held that where a corporation sold its plant to another corporation, taking as payment the stock of the purchasing corporation, which stock it then sold and delivered to a third party, in an action by the first mentioned corporation against such third party, ultra vires could not be set up. In Ring v. Long 

Island Inv. Co., 87 N. Y. Supp. 682, it was held that where an investment company received money for investment, it could not be heard to say, as against the investor, that the investment contemplated was ultra vires. 

All jurisdictions agree in leaving the parties as they found them in cases where ultra vires contracts have been entirely executed on both sides. No court will interfere to deprive either the corporation or the other party of money or property acquired under the ultra vires contract. Holmes & Griggs Mfg. Co. v. Holmes & Wessell Metal Co., 127 N. Y. 

252, 27 N. E. 831. Parish v. Wheeler, supra. First Natl. 

Bank of Xenia v. Stewart, 107 U. S. 676, 27 L. Ed. 592. 

Nantasket Beach Steamboat Co. v. Preston, 182 Mass. 147, 65 N. E. 57. Thomas v. W. Jersey R. Co., 101 U. S. 71, 25 

L. ed. 950. Nassau Bank v. Jones, supra. Davis v. Old 

Colony R. Co., supra. 

§ 101. Ultra Vires Conveyances. 

A conveyance or transfer of the title to a corporation of land which it has no power to own gives the corporation good title as against all persons but the state, and the title of the corporation's grantee is also good. Holmes & Griggs 

Mfg. Co. v. Holmes & Wessell Metal Co., 127 N. Y. 252, 27 

N. E. 831. Parish v. Wheeler, 22 N. Y. 494. Lancaster v. 

Amsterdam Improvement Company, 140 N. Y. 576, Cady's 

Cas. on Pri. Corps. p. 586. No collateral attack may be made upon the power of any corporation to be a conduit for title to any kind of property. Kerfoot v. Farmer's Bank, 218 U. S. 281. Barron v. McKinnon, 196 Fed. 933. Fritts v.

Palmer, 132 U. S. 282, 286, 33 L. Ed. 317. Nantasket Beach 

Steamboat Co. v. Shea, 182 Mass. 147, 65 N. E. 57.

The fee does not revert to the grantor of the corporation upon the dissolution of the corporation, although the transfer was ultra vires. Miller v. Flemingsburgh & F. Springs 

Turnpike Co., 109 Ky. 475, 59 S. W. 512. Fletcher on Corporations, p. 2640.

The rule regarding ultra vires sales of personalty is the same. Rogers v. Nashville, C. & St. L. Ry. Co., 91 Fed. 299.

St. Louis V. & T. H. R. Co. v. Terre Haute & I. R. Co., 145 

U. S. 393, 36 L. Ed. 738. 

§ 102. Who May Raise the Issue of Ultra Vires. 

Neither directors nor strangers may raise the question of ultra vires directly. Lewis v. Nat'l Bank, 274 Fed. 587. 

Clement v. Williams, 191 App. Div. 279, 181 N. Y. Supp. 

230. Dambman v. Empire Mill, 12 Barb. 341. Mut. Life Ins. 

Co. v. Stephens, 214 N. Y. 488.' The state which created the corporation may restrain the act. Peo. v. Utica Ins. 

Co., 15 Johns. 358. Peo. v. N. R. Sug. Ref. Co., supra;

Cady's Cas. p. 228. An injunction may be obtained by an individual or corporation when special injury is shown. 

Fulton Light, Heat & Power Co. v. Seneca River Power 

Co., supra. A stockholder may enjoin a threatened ultra vires act. Schwab v. E. G. Potter Co., 194 N. Y. 409. Murrin v. Archbald Consol. Coal Co., 232 N. Y. 541. N. Y. 

Cement Co. v. Consolidated Rosendale Cement Co., 178 N. Y. 

167. Directors or officers if loss results to the corporation from binding ultra vires contracts made by them may be required to make good the loss to the corporation. Great 

Western & Co. v. Harris, 128 Fed. 321. Roth v. Robertson, 64 Misc. 343, 118 N. Y. Supp. 351. That they acted under advice of counsel may be a defense to the directors if they in good faith believed the act intra vires and for the best interest of the company, in an honest mistake as to the extent of their authority. Wingert v. First Nat'l Bank, 223 

§ 103. Vires.

Contracts Apparently But Not Actually Ultra 

Where the act is a mere excessive exercise of the powers possessed by the corporation, as distinguishable from a con-

tract wholly beyond the scope of the charter, the rule of ultra vires does not apply, and the contract is valid. 

Citizen's State Bank v. Hawkins, 71 Fed. 369. Grand Water v. Zumbrum, 272 Fed. 943. Thus, a corporation when sued for rent can not defend on the ground that it has put the premises to a use in excess of its corporate powers, since it had power to lease for some purposes. Cambers v. Pac., 196 Pac. 488 (Cal). Jacobus v. Jamestown Mantel Co., 211 N. Y. 154. Mechanics Banking Ass'n v. N. Y. etc. 

White Lead Co., 35 N. Y. 505. Putnam v. Ensign Oil Co., 272 Pa. 301. Nat'l Park Bank v. German-American Mut.

Warehouse & Sec. Co., 116 N. Y. 281. Thompson v. Davis, 

297 Ill. 11, 130 N. E. 455. In Tracy v. Talmadge, 14 

N. Y. 162, an action was brought to recover the price of goods and it was held that the vendors knowledge that they were bought for an illegal purpose was no defense, the vendor having done nothing in furtherance of the unlawful design. 

§ 104. Duty to Restore Benefits Received. 

Both in law and equity it is held that upon the rescission of a repudiable ultra vires contract, there is an obligation to restore what has been received under the contract. 

Fletcher on Corporations, p. 2682. Higgins v. H. V. R. R.

Co., 188 App. Div. 685. McVity v. Albro Co., 90 App. Div. 

109. Seymour v. Spring Forest Cemetery Ass'n, 144 N. Y. 

339. Central Railroad & Banking Co. of Georgia v. Farm er's Loan & Trust Co., 114 Fed. 263. The obligation to return the property transferred under these contracts is mutual. U. S. Tel. Co. v. Boston Safe & Deposit Co., 147 

U. S. 431. Morville v. American Tract Society, 123 Mass. 

129, 25 Am. Rep. 40. 

§ 105. Remedies to Parties to Ultra Vires Contracts. 

Three remedies other than action on the contract, available for ultra vires contracts are: (1) Rescission in equity in which restitution is a neces sary preliminary. In McVity v. Albro & Co., 90 App. Div. 

109, it was held incumbent to show a tender to the defendant of the amount received on the property. He who seeks equity must do equity. Lewis v. 53rd Nat. Bank, 274 Fed. 587.

(2) Action on implied contract. This remedy is per mitted in all jurisdictions, but is particularly used in jurisdictions where the ultra vires contract, tho fully executed on one side, is void. The courts grant relief by allowing an action on implied contract for money had and received, or for the reasonable value of the property or services rendered. The action is in disaffirmance of the ultra vires con tract. Cit. Nat. Bank v. Appleton, 216 U. S. 196. Ports mouth Cotton Oil Ref. Corp. v. 4th Nat'l Bank, 280 Fed. 

879. Brunswick Gas Light Co. v. U. S. Fuel Co., 85 Me. 

532, 35 Am. St. Rep. 385. In jurisdictions wherein the 

N. Y. rule applies, it has also been held that where an act is ultra vires, the obligation to restore benefits received thereunder should be enforced, whenever possible, by allowing an action quasi ex contractu to be maintained. Jacobs v. Monaton Realty Investment Corp., 160 App. Div. 449, 465, rev'd on other grounds in 212 N. Y. 48. Day v. Spiral 

Springs Buggy Co., 57 Mich. 146, 23 N. W. 628. Paul v. 

Kenosha, 22 Wis. 266, 94 Am. Dec. 598. (3) Accounting in equity. The corporation may be required to account for money or property received in connection with an ultra vires contract or act of the corporation. Equitable Trust Co. of N. Y. v. Nat'l Bank of C. 

St. L., in St. Louis, 211 Fed. 688. Thus where railroad companies entered into a pooling contract, and the contract was carried out, and the profits therefrom collected and held by the receiver of one of the companies, a court of equity compelled him to account to the other company for its share. 

Central Trust Co. of N. Y. v. Ohio Cent. R. Co., 23 Fed. 306. 

§ 106. Illegal Contracts and Contracts Expressly Pro hibited by Charter.

Every illegal contract is necessarily ultra vires, though not every ultra vires contract is illegal. An illegal contract can never be made binding by ratification, nor may a corporation ever be estopped to set up illegality as a defense, for no one is permitted to justify an act which the legislature within its constitutional power has declared shall not be performed. Bath Gaslight Co. v. Claffy, 151 N. Y. 24.

Acts merely ultra vires may become binding by ratification or estoppel. Nadel v. Brillo Mfg. Co., 123 Misc. 952. Martin

v. Niagara Falls Paper Co., 122 N. Y. 165. Galdieri v. 

Arthur Waist Co., 98 Misc. 612. Skinner v. Smith, 134 N. Y. 

240. Schurr v. N. Y. etc. Suburban Investment Co., 18 

N. Y. Supp. 454. Wormser v. Met. St. R. Co., 184 N. Y. 83. 

Vought v. Eastern Bldg. etc., Assn., 172 N. Y. 508. Thus in the case of Dyer v. Broadway Cent. Bank, 225 App. Div. 

366, it was said where a contract appears to be not only ultra vires, but also illegal as contrary to public policy, the court will refuse to enforce it for it is absolutely void. 

Helmer v. N. Y. State Loan & Trust Co., 77 N. Y. 64. North 

River Ins. Co. v. Lawrence, 3 Wend. 482. No action may be maintained upon a contract in violation of a statutory prohibition. Pratt v. Short, 79 N. Y. 437. A stockholder may raise the issue of illegality. Williams v. Western Union Tel. 

Co., 93 N. Y. 162.

. THE CHARTER A CONTRACT. AMENDMENT AND REPEAL.

108. The charter as a contract. 109.

What amendments impair the charter.

112. 

Amendments by the majority.
