§ 107. 

Eminent domain. Taxation.

Visitation Defined. 

By visitation is meant the right of the state to examine into all internal arrangements of the corporation to require it to act not otherwise than in accordance with its charter powers and in subordination to the statutes. To a degree the ordinary corporation is an imperium in imperio. 

The members and directors of an ordinary corporation in the conduct of its business are supreme, and may determine what business shall be done, whether all or only a part of the corporate powers shall be exercised, and all matters relating to the internal arrangement; and, provided they act in subordination to the charter and statutes which form the corporate constitution, the corporation is exempt from the intervention of the courts. So long as they keep the corporation active and alive and solvent, they may extend its business under one power and contract it in another in the pursuit of profit; and, in the absence of an express or any necessarily implied legal obligation or duty, imposed by charter or general law, the state may not interfere by its courts. Peo. v. Alb. & Vt. R. Co., 24 N. Y. 

261. Peo. Tr. Co. v. O'Meara, 204 App. Div. 268, 197 N. Y. 

Supp. 795, app. dism. (mem.) 236 N. Y. 508.

In this respect a business corporation differs from a municipal corporation, for the latter may be compelled by the legislative or judicial visitor to exercise powers which · it holds for the benefit of the public. Flouton, Municipal 

Corporations, Chaps. III and IV. 

A further exception exists in the case of a public service 150

corporation, which, unlike an ordinary business corporation, is required to treat all with impartiality, and not to refuse to one a privilege granted to another. In Peo. ex rel. 

Western Un. Tel. Co. v. Pub. Serv. Comm., 230 N. Y. 95, 129 N. E. 220, it was held that the corporation was in duty bound to receive and transmit messages for a competitor, the Postal Telegraph Co., at the same rate and allowance of credit as messages sent by others; and Woodward, J., in an opinion in the case, citing 3 Kent. Comm. (14th ed.) 

458, said, "the acceptance of a franchise implies the execution of the conditions and duties prescribed in the grant." 

See also Peo. ex rel. N. Y. Telep. Co. v. P. S. Comm., 157 

App. Div. 156, 141 N. Y. Supp. 1018. Postal Teleg.-Cable 

Co. v. Assoc. Press, 228 N. Y. 370, 127 N. E. 256. Peo. ex rel. N. Y. Steam Co. v. Straus, 186 App. Div. 787, 174 N. Y. 

Supp. 868, affd. 226 N. Y. 704. Peo. ex rel. Woodhaven 

Gas Co. v. Nixon, 203 App. Div. 369, 196 N. Y. Supp. 623, affd. 236 N. Y. 530, 269 U. S. 244, 70 L. ed. 255.

The right of visitation, and the supervision of the visitor, is limited only by the principle that the visitor must act in accordance with the charter and the by-laws, legally adopted.

In case of insolvency, suspension of all its ordinary and lawful business for one year, or neglect or refusal to pay and discharge its notes or other evidences of debt for one year, the state may bring action to dissolve the corporation. G. C. L. 71, 72. French v. Andrews, 140 N. Y. 

441. Joseph v. Raff, 82 App. Div. 47, 81 N. Y. Supp. 546.

Further examples of the exercise of this power is found in statutes requiring corporations to make reports, in the state supervision of insurance and banking corporations by state heads, and of national banks by the comptroller of the currency. Originally this power was exercised by the king as to municipal public corporations, and by the founder, or his heirs and assigns, or, these failing, by the king, as to eleemosynary and ecclesiastical corporations. 

Rex v. St. Catherine's Hall, Cambridge, 4 T. R. 233. The legislatures have this power over all corporations formed under them respectively. Dartmouth College v. Woodward, 4 Wheat. 518, Cady's Cas. p. 321. State corporations,

however, are not subject to congress, except with respect to regulations relating to interstate and foreign commerce. 

Public Serv. Comm. v. N. Y. C. R. R., 230 N. Y. 149. Gibbons v. Ogden, 9 Wheat. 1. Courts have no special visitorial powers except as given by statute. Peo. v. Ballard, 136 N. Y. 639, and 134 N. Y. 269. Cushman v. Thayer 

Mfg. Jewel Co., 76 N. Y. 365. Schwab v. Potter Co., 194 

N. Y. 409, Cady's Cas. p. 542.

Among other acts of visitation, constituting part of the charters of the corporations affected thereby, are those provided for by G. C. L. 60 and 61, which affect generally all corporations. Some other pertinent statutes contain, in brief, the following:- Membership corporations shall be subject to the "visitation and inspection" of a justice of the supreme court, to be invoked by the verified petition of a member or creditor of the corporation, showing misappropriation or diversion of the corporate funds or property, or the acquiring of property in excess of that authorized, or the engaging in an ultra vires business; and authorizes the justice, after a hearing, to require an inventory, account and a detailed statement of its acts and transactions during twelve months last past, and to inspect books and vouchers. M. C. L. 26. A corporation subject to the visitation of the regents of the university, must make a sworn report to the comptroller each year. M. C. L. 25.

Membership corporations that require their members to take an oath are compelled by Civ. Rts. Law §531 to file with the secretary of state a sworn copy of its constitution, by-laws, rules, regulations and oath of membership, with a roster of members and officers, within 10 days after the adoption or election thereof, and within 10 days of any change; and by M. C. L. 54, it must also file every resolution, or the minutes of any action, providing for concerted action of its members to promote or defeat legislation, or any candidate, federal, state or municipal. The penalty is a fine of not less than $1,000 nor more than $10,000 for the corporation, the officers and directors participating, and members remaining such and attending a meeting after breach are each made guilty of a misdemeanor. Civ. Rts.

Law, §56. S. C. L. 107 is a specimen of acts passed from

time to time requiring a report of existence of every stock corporation, the object being to check up on the annual franchise tax reports. See also: (railroads and common carriers) Pub. Serv. Comm. Law, §§46-59; (banks) Banking Law, §§42-43a; (religious corporation, property holding) Religious Corps. Law, §14. And see particular statutes.

The court by reason of its equity powers, may investigate transactions wherein the directors are charged with having made themselves trustees by dealing for their individual advantage with corporate property and voting salaries to themselves. Carr v. Kimball, 153 App. Div. 825, 139 N. Y. 

Supp. 253, affd. 215 N. Y. 634. But in general, the powers of directors are discretionary and unless illegally or unconscientiously executed, or unless it is made to appear that the acts were fraudulent or collusive or destructive of the corporate interests or those of the stockholders, the court has no power to interfere. Peo. ex rel. W. U. Tel. 

Co. v. Pub. S. Comm., 230 N. Y. 95, 129 N. E. 220. 

§ 108. The Charter as a Contract. 

The charter of a corporation is not only similar to a law in its effect upon those who deal with the corporation as members, officers or strangers, but, as soon as it has been accepted at the organization meeting (§ 19, supra, and App. "F" infra) it becomes a contract between the state on one hand, and the corporation, its stockholders, subscribers, corporators and all who rely on the charter powers, on the other. The charter being a contract, once granted and accepted, it is held that the state impliedly has agreed not to alter the charter as a law, and that the state cannot interfere with the free exercise of the intra vires powers granted; and that the corporation may exercise all its lawful powers, within the limits contained in the grant, as freely as an individual, unless the power to amend or repeal the grant has been reserved by the state. Dartmouth Col lege v. Woodward, 4 Wheat. 518. Lord v. Equit. Life As sur. Soc., 194 N. Y. 212. In the Dartmouth College case an attempt was made by the legislature of New Hampshire to oust the trustees of the college from control by increasing the number of trustees, and making them subject to a board of overseers, provided for by the act, the mem-

bers of which were to include ex officio the governor and certain other state officials. It was expected that by so changing the control it would be possible to change the doctrines taught in the college. It was also provided that the name of the college should be changed to Dartmouth University. Pursuant to the terms of the act, the defendant 

Woodward was appointed secretary of the new university, and although he had been discharged as secretary and treasurer of the college, he refused to deliver to the new trustees the corporate books of the college on the ground that he properly held them under his appointment pursuant to the original charter, contending that the amendatory act of the legislature was void on the ground that it impaired the obligations of contract. The trustees, appointed under the amendatory act brought action against Woodward in conversion for the wrongful withholding of the books. The supreme court of the United States held that the charter was a contract; that the corporation, although the people of New Hampshire were most benefited by its teaching, was private, since its manner of formation and management made it such; that being a private corporation, and its charter being a contract, the act of the legislature attempting the material changes in the charter was unconstitutional and void.

Daniel Webster appeared for the old board, the plaintiffs in error; William Wirt for the defendant in error; and opinions were written by Chief Justice Marshall and Jus tices Story and Washington. Cady's Cas. on Pri. Corps. 

p. 321.

The principle has found application also in New York. 

Trinity Church which received its charter from the British crown in 1697, was held not to be affected by the religious corporations law, passed in 1895, which purported to change the powers and duties of trustees and the management of the property. No power to repeal or amend having been reserved in the charter, the obligations of contract thereby established could not be impaired by a statute later adopted. The opinion cites the Dartmouth College case. 

Burke v. Rector &c. of Trinity Church, 63 Misc. 43, 117 

N. Y. Supp. 255, affd. (mem.) 132 App. Div. 930. See

also, In re Church Ave., 100 Misc. 143, 165 N. Y. Supp. 

459. In People v. Manhattan Company, 9 Wend. 351, the court, considering the effect on the Manhattan Company, which was organized primarily as a water company (App. 

F, infra), of a statute prohibiting any corporation not expressly created or chartered as a banking institution, from acting as such, said: "Nothing has been considered better settled than that the rights and privileges conferred by these acts of incorporation or charters were held by the sacred obligation of a contract between the public and those on whom they were conferred; and that any attempt on the part of the legislature to repeal or to alter or modify any of their essential provisions, would be unconstitutional, as interfering with vested rights, and violating the obligation of a contract." See also Union Pac. R. R. v. U. S., 99

U. S. 700. Article I, Section 10, U. S. Constitution. Amend ments V and XIV, sec. 1, ib. 

The proposition that the charter of a corporation when accepted and acted on by incorporators and subscribers is a contract between the state and the corporation, has been criticised, mainly on the following grounds: 1. The rule deprived the states of power to regulate and restrain its creatures. 2. Lack of intent to contract. 3. No promise or obligation to perform on the part of corporation or members. 4. No valuable consideration is involved. Members receive stock for their investments. 5. The rule produces inequality, giving more protection to the corporation than natural persons enjoy. See Rose's Notes on U. S. Reports, pp. 959-961.

As to public corporations, however, the state may amend or repeal the charter at will. Its charter is not a contract, it being the theory that the state is the only party to the transaction. Dartmouth College v. Woodward, supra. 

Pawhuska v. Pawhuska Oil & Gas Co., 250 U. S. 394, 398, 63 L. ed. 1050, 1057. Quasi public corporations, such as gas, electric light, railroad, canal, bridge, hospital and water companies, are private corporations engaged in public enterprises, and their charters are protected as contracts. Greenwood v. Union Frt. R. Co., 105 U. S. 13, 26 L. ed. 961.

§ 109. What Amendments are Material. 

The obligation of the contract existing by reason of the charter is impaired either by a total repeal or by a material amendment of such nature as not to be in furtherance of the charter. Dartmouth Coll. case, supra. An amendment whereby the risks of stockholders are altered would constitute an impairment of their contract rights if the right to alter, amend or repeal the charter had not been reserved in either the certificate of incorporation or by statute. Thus the legislature may not authorize the majority to accept an amendment of the charter enlarging the business, even though the corporation offers to buy out the dissenting minority. Peo. ex rel. Cayuga Power Corp. v. Pub. Serv. 

Comm., 226 N. Y. 527, 124 N. E. 105. Zabriskie v. Hack. & 

N. Y. R. Co., 90 Am. Dec. 617 (N. J.). Allen v. Francisco 

Sug. Co., 110 Atl. 37 (N. J.). Nor may the state change by statute the method of voting so as to change the relative control exercisable by the shares, as by authorizing cumulative voting. Tucker v. Russell, 82 Fed. 263. Lord v. Equit. 

Life Assur. Soc., 194 N. Y. 212, 87 N. E. 443. A mere change in number of directors does not violate the stockholders' rights. Bond v. Atl. Terra Cotta Co., 137 App. 

Div. 671, 122 N. Y. Supp. 425. The liability of stockholders to creditors cannot be increased during the corporate life. 

Evans v. Nellis, 101 Fed. 920. 

In Mtr. of Mt. Sinai Hospital, 250 N. Y. 103, 164 N. E. 

871 it was held that c. 17 L. 1925 by which the legislature amended the charter to provide for filling vacancies on the board by the votes of the trustees whose terms had not expired, instead of election by the members as provided by the certificate of incorporation as originally granted, was not in violation of Art. 1, Sec. 10 of the U. S. Constitution, or Art. 8, Sec. 1 of the New York Constitution, forbidding acts "impairing the obligations of contracts." By reason of the reserved power to amend, the Dartmouth College decision was not applicable. Under the reserved power anything could be done, "which will not defeat or substantially impair the object of the grant, or any rights... vested under it." Const. § 10. The only limit of the power to amend under the reservation of power is that property

or property rights may not be taken away except under due process of law and with just compensation. Ib.

U. S. Constitution, Art. 1, Sec. 10, provides that no state shall pass any "law impairing the obligation of contracts." 

This provision does not apply to congress, but the constitutional prohibition against depriving anyone of his property without due process of law and just compensation, does. 

U. S. Const. Art. V, Sec. 1. The same prohibition is imposed upon the states by U. S. Const. Art. XIV, Sec. 1, reading, "Nor shall any State deprive any person of life, liberty or property without due process of law." Rights that have vested under a contract are held to be property rights under these prohibitions. The final decision, whether or not state statutes or state acts of visitation impair the obligations of contracts between a state and the corporation may rest with the Supreme Court of the United States, if the constitutional question was properly raised on the trial and in the appeals; and the decisions of that court on questions arising under the U. S. Constitution are binding on state courts. Secombe v. R. R. Co., 23 Wall. 108. A de cision by the state court that a state statute is in accordance with the state constitution binds the federal courts. R. R. 

Co. v. Georgia, 98 U. S. 359.

The obligations of contracts made by the corporations with third persons may not be impaired by legislative amendment. Boswell v. Sec. Mut. Lf. &c Co., 193 N. Y. 465.

Skaneateles Water Works v. Vill. of Skaneateles, 161 N. Y. 

154 (citing the Dartmouth Coll. case).

Statutes affecting procedural reforms and remedies are usually construed to be retrospective in effect as well as prospective, and do not as a rule impair vested rights of contract. However, the legislature cannot by a statute, procedural or otherwise, deprive creditors of their right to resort to the corporate property for the satisfaction of corporate debts. Peo. v. O'Brien, 111 N. Y. 1, 18 N. E. 692. 

Bank of Columbia v. Okely, 4 Wheat. 235, 4 L. ed. 559. The legislature may extend corporate life. In re Consol. Gas Co. of N. Y., 124 App. Div. 401, 108 N. Y. Supp. 823. 

§ 110. Reservation of the Power to Amend. 

The right of the legislature to repeal, alter or amend the

charter has been reserved in New York by constitutional provision and by statute. N. Y. Const. Art. VIII, Sec. 1 

and G. C. L. 5. The right also might be reserved by charter provision, and a reservation in any one of these ways is equal to the others. Tomlinson v. Jessup, 15 Wall. 454. 

Re Reciprocity Bank, 22 N. Y. 9. In re Oliver Lee's Bank, 21 N. Y. 9. "The right to withdraw a franchise includes every power or privilege which is a part of the franchise." Desty "On the Constitution of U. S." pp. 136-7. If reserved, the legislature may amend summarily and at will, as in the case of the passage of the prohibition amendment and laws. 

Hollender v. Roch. Food Prod. Corp., 242 N. Y. 490. Such general reservation of the right to amend, alter or repeal a corporate charter becomes a part of every corporate charter later granted, whether under a general or special statute. 

Peo. ex rel. Roosevelt Hospital v. Raymond, 194 N. Y. 189.

Where corporations whose charters the state had no power to amend are consolidated, a new corporation results, which is subject to constitutional or statutory reservations of the power to repeal or amend enacted prior to the date of consolidation. Their immunity did not pass to the new corporation. 8 Fletcher, Enc. of Corps. § 5444.

Where the legislature repeals, pursuant to the reservation of power to repeal, a court cannot scrutinize its motives. Calder v. Michigan, 218 U. S. 591, 54 L. ed. 1163.

The constitutional reservation of power to amend in the N. Y. constitution of 1821 required the concurrence of twothirds of the legislature. The charter of a corporation known as the "Reciprocity Bank" contained also a reservation of the power to alter, modify or repeal, and did not specifically require that the amendment be passed by a twothirds vote. The fundamental law of the state was changed by the constitution of 1846, which omitted the requirement of a two-thirds vote in enacting laws of that character. In 

1849, the legislature amended the company's charter by exempting it from the operation of a certain "Safety Fund Act." The amendment subjected the stockholders to a risk different from that preexisting. It was held that the constitution was no part of the charter of the corporation, though "every statute which adds to or takes from the

power of a corporation is a part of its charter," and that the amendment was valid. The bank having failed, the creditors enforced the personal liability of the stockholders. 

Mtr. of Reciprocity Bank, 22 N. Y. 9. Mtr. of Timmis, 200 N. Y. 177, Cady's Cas. at p. 255.

The amendment may increase the liability of stockholders as to future debts and contingencies (S. C. L. 71); but it may not impose a further liability for past debts. Close v. 

Porter, 11 Misc. 729, 34 N. Y. Supp. 1136, affd. 155 N. Y. 

145. The legislature without the interposition of a court, may repeal the corporate charter. Peo. v. O'Brien, 111 

N. Y. 1. Brooklyn Steam Transit Co. v. Brooklyn, 78 N. Y. 

524. The unfulfilled obligations of the corporation may be carried out through a receiver. Peo. v. O'Brien, supra. The risk of repeal of the charter is one of the risks to be contemplated by those who become creditors, for the reservation of the right to repeal or alter is a part of the charter, known to the public. Minna v. Potomac Co., 8 Pet. 281.

Peo. ex rel. Roosevelt Hospital v. Raymond, supra. Repeal does not divest the corporation of its vested rights. Colby v. Equit. Tr. Co., 192 N. Y. 535, 84 N. E. 1111. The amendment cannot diminish vested property rights unless provision is made for the taking under eminent domain proceedings. Rochester & C. Turnpike Co. v. Joel, 41 App. 

Div. 43, 58 N. Y. Supp. 346. "In respect to the effect of the power of repeal reserved in the acts of incorporation upon the property rights of a corporation, such power must still be exercised in subjection to the provision of the federal constitution." And such limitation accrues to the benefit of the stockholders and strangers dealing with the corporation. Peo. v. O'Brien, supra. Roswell v. Security Mut. 

Lf., 193 N. Y. 465. 

§ 111. Acceptance or Refusal of Amendments. 

When the amendment of the charter by the state makes an organic or fundamental change in the purposes of the corporation, the risk of the investment, or the power of the stockholder, the directors cannot make the amendment effectual by accepting it under their power to manage the business of the corporation. G. C. L. 27, cf. § 51a, supra.

Acceptance can only be made by the act of the members,

either express or implied. To make fundamental changes without the consent of the stockholders would be to make them members of an association in which they never consented to invest. In re Wheeler, 2 Abb. Pr. (N. S.) 361. 

Troy & R. R. R. v. Kerr, 17 Barb. 581. The stockholders may accept the amendment, or suspend business. But the repeal or amendment of general laws or statutes under which the corporation was formed, will not operate to dissolve the corporation by implication and the usual proceedings to dissolve must be taken. People v. Manhattan Bank, 9 Wend. 351. Chap. XIX, infra. 

Unless the stockholders accept, amendment can not change the purposes of the corporation by including some that could not have been originally granted, nor change fundamentally the corporate business or its control. Lord v. Equitable Life Assur. Soc., supra. Hollender v. Rochester

Food Prod. Corp., supra. People ex rel. Cayuga Power 

Corp. v. Pub. Serv. Comm., supra. The state cannot compel the corporation to accept the amendment and continue business. Troy & R. R. R. v. Kerr, 17 Barb. 581. Amendments made under S. C. L. 36 and 37 may be accepted by the board of directors, since the stockholders consents are obtained in advance. Matter of Excelsior Ins. Co., 16 Abb. 

Pr. 8. Bond v. Atl. Terra Cotta Co., 137 App. Div. 671, 122 N. Y. Supp. 425. § 112. Power of Majority to Amend. 

S. C. L. 35 permits amendments to (1) extend, limit or otherwise change the purposes and powers or other provisions; (2) increase or reduce the number of directors; (3) change the location of its office (if not a moneyed corporation). The amendment is effected by filing a certificate of such change in each office of the state in which the certificate of incorporation is filed, and a certified or duplicate copy in the county clerk's office of the county in which the corporate office is located and in the county to which the office is to be removed if the change is under subdivision 3. 

If the amendment is made before any stock has been issued, the certificate must be subscribed and acknowledged by all the subscribers to the stock and to the certificate of incorporation and have annexed an affidavit by one of the sub-

scribers to the effect that all the persons executing the certificate are all the subscribers to both the certificate of incorporation and to the stock. If there are many subscribers, the easier way is to issue some stock. If this has been done, the said certificate need only be subscribed and acknowledged in person or by proxy by the holders of all the outstanding shares of the corporation entitled to vote thereon, and this is filed, as aforesaid, with an affidavit by the secretary or assistant secretary that the persons who executed the certificate in person or by proxy, constitute the holders of record of all the outstanding shares entitled to vote thereon. The subscribers, to whom no stock has as yet been allotted, are not considered in the statute. By a material amendment a subscriber who does not consent is released from his subscription. Chap. IX, infra.

If the stockholders will not agree to amend, a meeting has to be held, called pursuant to S. C. L. 45, and the amendment for a change of purpose, voted through by a 2/3 vote of all the outstanding shares entitled to vote thereon; but for a change in the number of directors or of the location of the office a majority vote is sufficient. The said certificate to be filed, if a meeting has been held, must be subscribed and acknowledged by the president, or vice-president and secretary or assistant secretary, who must make and annex an affidavit stating that they have been authorized to execute and file such certificate by the votes cast in person or by proxy of the holders of 2/3 of the outstanding shares entitled to vote thereon, or by a majority as the case may require, and that such votes were cast at a stockholders' meeting called pursuant to S. C. L. 45.

The minutes of the meeting provide the evidence for the protection of all concerned and should cover all the requisite features, such as, 1. The organization of the meeting; 2. The call for the meeting, and proof of its due service under S. C. L. 45 and the by-laws; and the filing of such waivers of notice as are obtainable. 3. Inspectors appointed as set forth in Chap. XII infra. 4. Proxies listed and filed. 

5. Challenges, see Chap. XII. 6. The announcement of the result of the vote. Votes recorded. 7. Resolution adopted directing the execution of the certificates aforesaid in triplicate original, the filing, and the payment of fees. The

secretary of state's fee is $20 (Exec. law § 26 [10] and the county clerk's filing charges are per folio C. P. A. 1554, 1557, 1557a, etc.) The certificate is not required to be recorded. 8. Minutes read and resolution approving same passed. 9. Minutes certified by president and secretary under corporate seal.

Other amendments that may be made by the action of a majority of a specified size are set forth in S. C. L. 36. 

These are: (4) To increase or reduce capital stock where all shares have a par value. (5) To increase or reduce the par value. (6) To increase or reduce the number of shares. The added shares may be with or without par value. (7) To change all or any previously authorized par value shares issued or not, into shares without par value. The number of shares and also a classification may be added or changed. Chap. XI, infra. 

(8) To change all or any shares without par value, issued or unissued, into par value shares, and to increase or reduce the number, and to classify, or reclassify. (9) To reclassify stock without par value, issued or unissued, and specify a different number of the same class or any other class or classes. (10) To classify or reclassify shares with or without par value; and to authorize the issuance from time to time of one or more series of any class with preferences as to dividends or assets subject to S. C. L. 11. (11) If the certificate of incorporation authorized the issuance of stock without par value, to change the statements respecting capital. See S. C. L. 12. (12) To reduce the amount of capital where it has issued shares without par value. See S. C. L. 12.

The foregoing amendments 8-12 inclusive are effectuated in a manner similar to amendments 1-3 as set forth above. 

Before any stock is issued, the subscribers to the certificate of incorporation and the subscribers to stock may make and file the certificate and affidavit. S. C. L. 37 (1). If some stock has been issued and all the stockholders authorized to vote, subscribe and acknowledge the certificate of amendment in person or by proxy, no meeting need be held.

S. C. L. 37 (2). Their consent with the necessary affidavit, as before, is sufficient. 

If there is a dissenting minority the certificate of the president or vice-president, and secretary or an assistant secretary, with the annexed affidavit, must show that the stockholders meeting was held pursuant to S. C. L. 45 and that the following majorities authorized the amendments:- (a) 8, 9, and 12, in brief, to increase or reduce the capital stock, or to reduce the capital, a majority. (b) For any of the other changes, 10-12 inclusive, by two-thirds. (S. C. L. 37)

Amendments other than the foregoing cannot be made by a stock corporation in New York without the consent of all the stockholders; and the power to amend the purposes given by S. C. L. 35 is not interpreted as being sufficiently broad to permit the 2/3 majority to make amendments in the purposes or powers so drastic as to constitute a new business or new corporation. Peo. ex rel Cayuga Power 

Corp. v. Pub. Serv. Comm., 226 N. Y. 527. Hollender v. 

Roch. Food Prod. Co., 242 N. Y. 49. News Pub. Co. v. Blair, 29 Fed. (2d) 955.

The amendment of the charter of a membership corporation requires the approval of the supreme court. Re Creditors Audit & Adjustment Ass'n, 72 Misc. 461, 131 N. Y. 

Supp. 263. 

§ 113. Police Power. 

The powers of eminent domain, of taxation, and the police power, are necessary to the welfare of the state, and one legislature cannot, by a grant to a corporation, grant or abridge these rights, so as in any way to bind its successors or even itself. N. Y. C. & H. R. R. R. v. Williams, 199 N. Y. 108. The area of regulation of matters affecting the public health, morality and welfare, comprising the police power, is held not to impair the obligation of the contract expressed by the corporate charter, because the charter is taken subject to the police power. So the state may control railroads and their rates. Peo. v. B. & A. R. R., 70 N. Y. 569. In Public Service Commission v. N. Y. C.

R. R., 230 N. Y. 149, the court affirmed a reduction of rates after the railroad was released from federal control fol-

lowing the war. In Peo. v. N. Y. C. & H. R. R. R., 28 Hun 

543, the railroad was held to be obliged, under the police power, to receive and transport freight when it had refused to do so because of a strike, the court there holding that there was a duty of a public trust conferred by the state and accepted by the corporation, which could be enforced for the public benefit.

By virtue of police power the state regulates the use of corporate property, but takes nothing; by taxation the state takes property without making direct compensation; and by eminent domain, it takes property for a public purpose, making just compensation. The assessed valuation for the purpose of taxation may be reduced for overvaluation of the premises or inequality of distribution of the tax, by means of a timely protest followed by a certiorari proceeding; but under eminent domain, the state may take more of one person's property than it does of another's. 

Where the business is lawful and open to all, and beyond the power of the legislature to prohibit, police power regulations must be confined to reasonable requirements for the conservation of public health, safety, morals, peace and order. The state may not classify persons and objects for the purpose of regulating employers contrary to their constitutional and common law rights, unless the distinction is based on proper and justiciable grounds. Ives v. So. Buff. 

Ry. Co., 201 N. Y. 271 (employers liability acts). Peo. ex rel. Wineburgh Adver. Co. v. Murphy, 195 N. Y. 126 (ordi nance limiting height of advertising signs held reasonable). 

Peo. ex rel. Niger v. Van Dell, 85 Misc. 92, 146 N. Y. Supp. 

992 (statute punishing officers of membership corporations who initiate novices into higher degrees, on condition of payment of dues, held invalid). Under the police power the state may not appropriate one's property for the public benefit (pumping water from other's premises by wells bored into the rocks in one's premises) Peo. v. N. Y. 

Carbonic Acid Gas Co., 196 N. Y. 420. See also, Village of 

Carthage v. Frederick, 122 N. Y. 268. Peo. ex rel. Appel v. 

Zimmerman, 102 App. Div. 103, 92 N. Y. Supp. 497 (trading stamps). Crittenden Co. v. N. Y., 224 N. Y. 607 (patent medicine labels to state ingredients). Noble State Bank v.

Haskell, 219 U. S. 104 (requiring state banks to guarantee

each other's solvency held constitutional). Germ. Alliance 

Ins. Co. v. Lewis, 233 U. S. 389 (fixing rates chargeable by fire insurance companies using the standard fire insurance policy, held reasonable). Peo. v. Klinck, 214 N. Y. 121 (giving one day's rest in seven). Peo. v. Brakes Dairy Co., 222 N. Y. 416 (restricting handling of milk for shipment to New York to citizens of New York or to corporations organized or authorized to do business in New York). 

Rafice v. Peo., 264 U. S. 292 (fixing hours of employment for women in cities of the first class in restaurants, with a provision that the statute should not apply to females employed as singers or in ladies cloak-rooms or in dining rooms or kitchens of hotels-held valid). Banton v. Belt 

Line Ry. Corpn., 45 U. S. Sup. Ct. Repr. 534 (the state cannot arbitrarily select one kind of traffic for regulation; requirement of transfers from the Central Park Co. and 59th 

St. R. R. Co. in New York between lines on 1st, 2d and 3rd and certain other avenues held unconstitutional). Legislation abrogating valid exclusive privileges of slaughtering animals was held a valid exercise of the police power in 

Butchers Union Slaughter House v. Crescent City Co., 111 U. S. 746. The Slaughter House Cases, 16 Wall. 361, a previous decision, had held the exclusive feature of the privileges valid. 

§ 114. Eminent Domain. 

In the exercise of its inherent power of eminent domain the state may take the property and franchises of corporations on making just compensation, just as the state may take other property; e. g., a bridge built by a private corporation, and its franchise to operate it. West R. Bridge 

Co. v. Dix, 6 How. 507. Peo. v. Adirondack Ry. Co., 160 

N. Y. 225, affd. 176 U. S. 335. Board v. F. J. & G. R. Co., 249 N. Y. 445, 250 N. Y. 559. The state's or federal government's exercise of this power is subject to but three restrictions: (1) no person shall be deprived of his property without due process of law; (2) private property shall not be taken without just compensation. U. S. Const. Amendments V, which does not apply to the states and XIV which applies to the states. The provision for just compensation is not in the Amendment XIV, but is in most of the state

constitutions. See Appendix A; (3) and the purpose must be a public purpose. Peo. ex rel. Horton v. Prendergast, 248 N. Y. 215, affd. 49 U. S. Sup. Ct. 77. In re N. Y. C. & 

H. R. R. Co., 66 N. Y. 407. The state having given by general statutes power to various kinds of corporations to take by eminent domain, may thereafter amend the power, though no express power to repeal or amend was reserved. 

The amendment is not exercisable under the police power, without compensation, but only under the power of eminent domain.

The corporation itself has no power of eminent domain unless granted by the state, Golde Clothes Shop v. Loew's 

Buff. Theatres, 236 N. Y. 465, but where that power has been granted the court will not interfere with its exercise, if the corporation keeps within its authorized powers and acts bona fide. Re N. Y. C. & H. R. R. R., supra. 

The federal government may exercise the right of eminent domain over a state corporation without violating the Fifth 

Amendment. The "due process of law" clause has reference to the law of the land as that term is used in the Magna 

Charta. Murray's Lessee v. Hoboken Land Co., 18 How. 

272.

And as the state may under its power of eminent domain take the charter and franchises of a corporation, so also a corporation, if given the power of eminent domain, under its charter, may take the property of another corporation on making just compensation. Greenwood v. Union Freight 

R. Co., 105 U. S. 13.

But where a corporation was granted a franchise not exclusive, and another was given to a second corporation, thereby rendering practically useless the franchise of the first, it was held not to be an impairment, nor a taking un der eminent domain. Skaneateles Water Works Co. v. 

Skaneateles, 161 N. Y. 154, affd. 184 U. S. 354.

However, where the right of eminent domain has been granted to one corporation, it may not transfer this power to another person, firm or corporation. Ontario Knitting 

Co. v. State, 205 N. Y. 409. 

§ 115. Taxation. 

Corporations are taxable on their real and personal prop-

erty in the same manner as individuals (Tax Law § 3), but the taxing power is to be strictly construed. Peo. ex rel. 

National Park Bank v. Metz, 141 App. Div. 600, 126 N. Y.

Supp. 986. Certain exemptions, however, are given to cemetery, religious and eleemosynary corporations (Tax Law § 4), but if the property of such corporations is income producing and not used exclusively for religious purposes, they forfeit the exemption. Tax Law § 4, Peo. v. Wells, 180 

N. Y. 534. And the use of the property at the time of the assessment governs the right to the exemption. Matter of 

Mary Immaculate School, 188 App. Div. 5. Mtr. of Montefiori Home, 159 App. Div. 644, 144 N. Y. Supp. 952, affd. 

211 N. Y. 549. The exemption must be in clear language, and cannot be presumed, and any doubt as to the exemption will be resolved in favor of the state. Peo. v. Commissioners, 82 N. Y. 459. There may also be an exemption from assessment, but such an exemption is not included in an exemption from taxation. Roosevelt Hospital v. Mayor, 84 N. Y. 108. If such immunity from taxation is granted, it is not transferable. Rochester v. Roch. Ry. Co., 182 N. Y. 

99, Cady's cases p. 344. Since the Emerson Act, foreign corporations paying the franchise tax are exempt from all taxes on personal property to local assessors. Peo. ex rel. 

United Shoe Co. v. Cantor, 112 Misc. 603, 184 N. Y. Supp. 214. 

Under the federal Constitution, Article I, Section 8, the tax must be uniform, and capitation and direct taxes are prohibited unless in proportion to the census. Articles exported from any state are free from the imposition of any tax or duty (Section 9). Under the provisions of the Four teenth Amendment, a state cannot deny the equal protection of its laws nor impose unequal taxation. Under the 

N. Y. state constitution, Article III, Sec. 18, the legislature is prohibited from enacting any private or local bill which grants any exemption from taxation on real or personal property to any corporation.

The following seven subjects of taxation are usually found in the corporate tax laws of all states: 1. Franchise; 

2. Capital stock in hands of corporation; 3. Corporate property; 4. Shares of capital stock in hands of stock-

holders; 5. Dividends in hands of stockholders; 6. Stock transfers; 7. Organization. 

There is no special tax on dividends in New York.

For discussion and construction of "dividend" in this particular see Chattanooga Savings Bank v. Brewer, 9 Fed. (2d) 982. Contract obligations are not to be considered as debts. Peo. ex. rel. Butterick Pub. Co. v. Purdy, 138 N. Y. 

Supp. 707. Double taxation, in the absence of any constitutional prohibition, is constitutional, but is not to be presumed. Thus the state may tax the corporation for the value of its property and also tax stockholders, for the value of the stock holdings. Klein v. Board of Tax etc., 51 U. S. 

Sup. Ct. Repr., 15. Appendix M, infra, tabulates the various tax reports required from New York corporations. 

Under the Tax Law, the tax imposed on a foreign corporation is not a tax on the franchise. What is taxed is the business of the corporation, or its capital or property, employed or located within the state. Peo. v. Knapp, 229 N. Y. 

502. Peo. ex rel. Griffith v. Loughman, 249 N. Y. 369.

The state cannot tax interstate commerce, and so cannot require solicitors and salesmen, from door to door, of foreign corporations, or foreign corporations engaged in interstate commerce, to take out a state license. Robbins v. 

Shelby Co. Taxing Dist., 120 U. S. 489. Brennan v. Titus ville, 153 U. S. 289. Crenshaw v. Arkansas, 227 U. S. 389. 

Real Silk Hosiery Mills, Inc. v. Portland, 45 Sup. Ct. 525. 

Cudahy Packing Co. v. Hinckle, 49 Sup. Ct. 204. Ruby 

S. S. Corp. v. American Merch. M. Ins. Co., 231 N. Y. Supp. 

503. For what is "doing business within the state" see 

Peo. ex rel. Buff. Union Furnace Co. v. Gilchrist, 213 N. Y.

Supp. 307 and Chap. XX infra. The franchise tax, on the business or capital of the foreign corporation, becomes a lien on November 1 on its corporate property here tho the amount of the tax has not yet been completed, and, until it is paid, the title is unmarketable. Cary v. Keith, Inc., 250

N. Y. 216. The property of federal corporations within the state may be taxed by the state, but not the franchise. 

In New York they are domestic corporations. See sec. 13 (a) supra.

State court papers, referee's deeds, and the like, cannot

be taxed by the federal government, and likewise the state cannot tax federal bonds, and royalties received under copyrights. Neldick v. Chicago & R. I. & P. R. R., 153 N. Y.

Supp. 658. But by act of congress the states can tax the stock of national banks.

Stock of a domestic corporation, held by a non-resident decedent, is subject to taxation here since the situs of the corporation is deemed to be the situs of the stock. Matter of Cooley, 186 N. Y. 220. Stock owned by a resident decedent is taxable here, even though it is of a foreign corporation. Matter of Merriam, 141 N. Y. 479, affirmed 163

U. S. 625. Matter of Hollenbeck, 231 N. Y. 409. U. S. 

Radiator v. State, 135 N. Y. Supp. 981.

The tax assessed, is presumed to have been paid after a lapse of twenty years after it became a lien. Fisher v. 

Mayer, 67 N. Y. 73.

§ 116. Membership Defined. (a) In a Stock Corpora tion.

The terms "member," "shareholder" and "stockholder" are used synonymously with respect to stock corporations, to designate an owner of the stock of the corporation. 

Burges v. Seligman, 107 U. S. 20. Peo. v. Sec. Lf. Ins. & 

Ann. Co., 78 N. Y. 114. "A person may become the owner of shares of stock of a corporation by subscription or by purchase. In the former case he becomes a member, and takes all the rights as such, by his subscription to the original stock, and no offer or delivery of a certificate is essential to his liability to pay the amount of the shares for which he has subscribed; but if his relation is that of a purchaser, the delivery of the certificate and payment for the stock are in contemplation concurrent." Kohlmetz v. Calkins, 16 App. 

Div. 518, 44 N. Y. Supp. 1031, citing 1 Morawetz on Private 

Corporations, sec. 61. 170

Where membership is acquired by purchase, that is, by buying the certificates representing the shares as saleable choses in action, the member does not become such until he has received the certificate. If he refuses to accept it, or if the company wrongfully refuses to recognize his rights, an action may be brought for the damages suffered, but a necessary allegation of the breach is that the certificate was tendered the member, or refused him by the corporation, as the case may be; and the damages which the corporation has suffered is the difference between the subscription price and the value of the shares, if less, and the converse of that proposition constitutes the damages of the purchaser. His purchase may consist of stock previously authorized or of a new and later issue. Ib.

His subscription alone to the stock after organization renders him a member when accepted by the company through its proper agents. Beals v. Buff. Expanded Met. 

Const. Co., 49 App. Div. 589, 63 N. Y. Supp. 635. In re 

Automotive Mnfrs. Assn., 120 Misc. 405, 199 N. Y. Supp. 313. 

§ 117. Membership Defined. (b) In a Membership 

Corporation.

In a non-stock corporation all are members who have signed the certificate of incorporation, and also each person admitted to membership therein pursuant to the certificate or act of incorporation and by-laws. G. C. L. 4 (13). 

Preston v. Reinhart, 109 App. Div. 781, 96 N. Y. Supp. 851.

Generally speaking the charter, rules or by-laws of membership corporations require election, or some formal kind of admission, as initiation, but provisions in the by-laws as to formal steps to be taken to acquire membership may be waived by the corporation.

The charter may consist of a special act of the legislature. In that case the special act together with the Membership Corporations Law and the General Corporation Law, constitute the charter; and a constitution, and regulations adopted by the order are not the charter, but bylaws. In re Monroe Chapter, O. E. S., 132 Misc. 100, 228 N. Y. Supp. 248. Unlike stock corporations, no one can acquire membership in a membership corporation with-

out the consent of the corporation, express or implied.

In 

American Live Stock Commission Co. v. Chicago Live Stock 

Exchange, 143 Ill. 210, 32 N. E. 274, a certificate of membership in the exchange was sold and delivered to the plaintiff by a member. Plaintiff had neither then applied for membership under the rules, nor had he been elected by directors and members as required by the by-laws, nor had he bound himself to abide by the rules, etc., as required thereby. It was held that mere ownership of the certificate was insufficient to constitute him a member and that application in accordance with the by-laws was necessary. 

The charters of mutual benefit and other membership corporations may prescribe qualifications for membership, which in that case, are exclusive, such as, a limited membership to persons of certain age. Pirrung v. Supreme 

Council C. M. B. A., 104 App. Div. 571, 93 N. Y. Supp. 575; or of a certain religious denomination, or residence. 

If the member admitted was not of the age, religion, residence, etc., the action of the officers in admitting him was null and void. Pirrung case, supra. No rights accrued to the member improperly admitted and his estate or beneficiary can not share in death or other benefits, though dues were paid by him. Ib. The directors have no implied power to change rules or by-laws governing eligibility to membership. Croughan v. N. Y. Mut. Benev. Soc., 179 App. Div. 211, 166 N. Y. Supp. 161. Any member may take the remedy of a summary application to the court against the initiation of a member not regularly elected, Thompson v. Soc. of Tammany, 17 Hun 305. Injunction will not be granted unless some pecuniary loss will be sustained by the petitioner through the wrongful admission of the "member." Ib. 

§ 118. Membership. How Secured in a Stock Corpora tion. 

Since ownership of stock is the test of full membership, it follows that one who has secured stock as either corporator, purchaser, or transferee of shares from a member, is a full member of a stock corporation. East 110th St. Corp. v. Wolinski, 198 App. Div. 414, 190 N. Y. Supp. 626. Pers.

Prop. Law, § 162.

Whether the proof in a given case is sufficient to establish membership so as to render the subscriber liable to pay for his stock, depends upon the rules of contract. Christensen v. Eno, 106 N. Y. 97, Cady's Cas. at p. 350. There is no membership without the legal consent of the member. 

Richards v. Robin, 178 App. Div. 535, 165 N. Y. Supp. 780.

The elements of consideration and promise must be present. 

Eastern Plank Rd. Co. v. Vaughan, 14 N. Y. 546. The different steps towards membership may be grouped, for convenience of discussion, as, 1. tentative; 2. inchoate and imperfect; and 3. full and perfect membership. 

Membership is tentative when one subscribes for stock in a corporation not yet formed. There is no consideration to support the offer, which is unilateral. The due formation of the corporation and the allotment of stock to the tentative member cannot turn the offer which is as yet unilateral, into a contract by acceptance by the corporation de jure after it has been formed. Avon Springs Sanitarium v. Weed, 119 App. Div. 746, 104 N. Y. Supp. 58, Cady's 

Cas. p. 358, affd. 194 N. Y. 567. Keyser v. Miller, 236 

N. Y. 561.

Membership is inchoate and imperfect when the intending member has entered into such relation with the corporation or with the other members that he can be compelled by it or them to complete his membership, and will be liable to creditors who became such through faith in his subscription. Thus, a subscriber for stock after the process of incorporating has been completed, has an inchoate membership upon allotment. If the corporation becomes insolvent, his contract is corporate property, enforceable at the instance of creditors for the amount unpaid. Granger & Co. v. Allen, 214 App. Div. 356, 212 N. Y. Supp. 356, affd. 244 

N. Y. 587, Cady's Cas. p. 383. Allen v. Ryan, 219 App. 

Div. 634, 221 N. Y. Supp. 77.

The acceptance of the charter turns the inchoate subscription of the corporators into full membership. Bates 

Co. v. Winters, 112 U. S. 325. Where a statute requires the subscription to a number of shares as a condition precedent to the grant of the charter, the change from inchoate to full membership between the said subscribers is

accomplished from the time of the filing of the certificate of incorporation with the required subscriptions. Erie & 

N. Y. C. R. Co. v. Owen, 32 Barb. 616. Thereafter, after the filing, they may vote at corporate meetings, claim a share in the profits, and exercise all the rights and privileges of members. The issuance of a certificate of stock is not essential to constitute the said subscriber a member, but he may demand it and maintain specific performance by virtue of his rights of membership. Buff. & N. Y. City 

R. R. Co. v. Dudley, 14 N. Y. 337. Lake Ont. A. & N. Y. 

R. R. Co. v. Mason, 16 N. Y. 451-463. Phoenix Warehousing Co. v. Badger, 67 N. Y. 298. Burr v. Wilcox, supra, Cady's Cas. p. 380. Wheeler v. Millar, 90 N. Y. 353. Rutter v. Kilpatrick, 63 N. Y. 604. The rights of inchoate members cannot be disregarded in favor of tentative members, as where there is an over-subscription before incorporation, or in a case where the charter permits a distribution in case of over-subscription after incorporation. Buff. & N. Y. City R. R. Co. v. Dudley, 14 N. Y. 336, 346. Poughkeepsie &c. P. Rd. Co. v. Griffin, 24 N. Y. 150.

Membership is full and perfect when the stock has been issued to the member; or when stock that has been issued is endorsed and delivered to him by the owner. P. P. L. 

§ 162, S. C. L. 65. The lawful possession and ownership of shares of stock confers membership without the knowledge and even against the wishes and to the detriment of the other members. Rice v. Rockefeller, 134 N. Y. 174.

Playa De Oro Mining Co. v. Gage, 60 App. Div. 1, 69 N. Y. 

Supp. 702, affd. 172 N. Y. 630 (mem.). In Collins v. Caldwell, 29 F. (2nd) 329, a widow, who became owner of stock in a national bank under the last will of her deceased husband, was held properly assessed as a stockholder on the bank becoming insolvent, notwithstanding that her name did not appear on the books of the bank as owner of the stock. 

Allotment may take the place of delivery of the certificate; but where the subscriptions equal but do not exceed the capital stock authorized by the charter, the subscriber's title becomes perfect when the books are closed, which, presumably, occurred when all the stock was subscribed. 

Buffalo & N. Y. City R. Co. v. Dudley, supra. The defini-

tion of "member" in G. C. L. 4 (13) as a "stockholder of record having the right to vote" comprehends the elements of full and complete membership set forth in the above definition, and does not exclude from the definition those who stock has only limited voting rights by reason of provisions of the certificate of incorporation. Peo. ex rel. Browne v. 

Koenig, 133 App. Div. 756, 118 N. Y. Supp. 136, 137. Membership is secured by the contract with the corporation, and though the stock certificate is the best evidence of that relation, it is not essential that it be issued. Kohlmetz v. Calkins, 16 App. Div. 518, 44 N. Y. Supp. 1031. Stevens v. 

Epis. Ch. Hist. Co., 140 App. Div. 570, Cady's Cas. p. 115. 

Powers v. Knapp, 71 Hun 371, 25 N. Y. Supp. 19. 

§ 119. Subscriptions Before Incorporation. 

These may include: 1. subscriptions in the certificate of incorporation; 2. in separate agreements; 3. subscriptions on condition precedent; and 4. subscriptions on condition subsequent. 

§ 120. Subscriptions in the Certificate of Incorporation. 

The corporators, who are the subscribers to the certificate of incorporation, are liable to pay for their subscription when the certificate of incorporation is filed by them, without the formal issuance of certificates to them. Either the corporation or a receiver for the corporation may enforce payment. Richmondville Union Sem. v. McDonald, 34 N. Y. 

379. Buff. & J. R. R. Co. v. Gifford, 87 N. Y. 294, Cady's 

Cas. p. 363. Dorris v. French, 4 Hun 292. 

Where defendant subscribed the certificate of incorporation for the purpose of organizing a railroad corporation, which at the time of signing was incomplete, in that the names of the directors were not inserted, it was held that there was no implied consent upon his part to the insertion of the names of any persons as directors; and that by the insertion of such names without his consent, the instrument was not made binding upon him. Dutchess & Columbia 

R. Co. v. Mabbett, supra. 

§ 121. Subscription by Separate Agreement. 

An agreement between the subscribers, made before incorporation, to form an identified corporation and take its

stock in amounts set opposite the subscribers' names, may be turned into a binding contract by the corporation by acceptance; for the mutual promises of the subscribers are sufficient consideration for the promise to pay the subscription to a third party, the corporation, when the latter comes into being as a de jure corporation, fully organized. ton v. Wilson, 2 Hill 153. Stan It is held in New York that an action may be maintained by a third person on a promise made by the defendant to another for the benefit of the plaintiff, without any consideration moving towards the plaintiff. Barker v. Buck lin, 2 Den. 47. Richardson's Outline of Contracts, § 306. 

A further consideration is the advantage to be derived from being a member, and the consequent right to participate in the pecuniary profits. On the due formation of the company, the objection of want of consideration is without basis. The subscribers before incorporation who subscribe by agreements separate from the certificate of incorporation, are not bound unless a de jure corporation is formed. 

Jermyn v. Searing, 225 N. Y. 525. However, if a person subscribes for stock in a corporation after its organization and assumption of corporate powers, it is sufficient to show a de facto corporate existence to support an action on the subscription, Cayuga Lake R. Co. v. Kyle, 64 N. Y. 185; 

Aspinwall v. Sacchi, 57 N. Y. 331; Buffale & A. R. Co. v. 

Cary, 26 N. Y. 75.

But where there is no clear agreement between the subscribers to form the corporation and take its stock, the subscription by separate instrument to the stock of an identified corporation thereafter to be formed, is a nudum pactum and cannot be turned into a binding contract by acceptance by the corporation after it is formed. Sanders v. 

Barnaby, 166 App. Div. 274, 151 N. Y. Supp. 580. Gen. 

Elec. Co. v. Wightman, 3 App. Div. 118, 39 N. Y. Supp. 

420. Avon Spr. San. v. Weed, supra. Non-Electric Fibre 

Mfg. Co. v. Peabody, 21 App. Div. 247, 47 N. Y. Supp. 677.

Compare Yonkers Gazette Co. v. Taylor, 30 App. Div. 334, 

51 N. Y. Supp. 969, Cady's Cas. p. 341. Hamilton & D.

Plank Road Co. v. Rice, 7 Barb. 157. The distinction is that before the corporation is formed there is no party with

whom the subscriber can contract, and unless he contracts with the other subscribers to form the corporation and take its stock, there is no consideration. 

§ 122. Subscriptions on Conditions Precedent. 

These are subscriptions so phrased as not to take effect until the condition is performed; for instance, a subscription "provided $200,000 be subscribed by citizens of Buffalo." 

Union Hotel Co. v. Hersee, supra, Cady's Cas. p. 339.

The parol evidence rule prevents the subscriber from proving a condition unless the condition is set forth in the subscription agreement. Yonkers Gazette v. Jones, 30 

App. Division 317, 51 N. Y. Supp. 973, Cady's Cas. p. 375.

The condition, if it relates to time of payment, must be one permitted by our corporation statutes. Gen. Elec. Co. v. 

Wightman, 3 App. Div. 118, 39 N. Y. Supp. 420. Lyell Lumber Co. v. Lighthouse, 137 App. Div. 422, 121 N. Y. Supp. 802.

Contrary to the weight of authority, it has been held in 

New York, under New York statutes relating to railroads, etc., conditional subscriptions to the effect that the road pursue a stated route have been held void for public policy, since transportation is intended to be for the benefit of the public in general, and the evils resulting from competitive bidding between communities to secure the road. Lake 

Shore v. Curtis, 80 N. Y. 219. Craig v. Town of Andes, 93 N. Y. 405. Conditional subscriptions to the stock of a corporation, after it has been organized, are valid, though on condition precedent, providing the charter or enabling act does not forbid, and providing the conditions do not require the performance of ultra vires acts or acts in violation of law, or acts contrary to public policy. Wing v. Smith, 170 App. Div. 57. Burrows v. Smith, 10 N. Y. 550. Stone v. Young, 210 App. Div. 303, 206 N. Y. Supp. 95, Cady's

Cas. p. 366. Compare General Electric Co. v. Wightman, supra. See, however, Lauer v. Raymond, 190 App. Div. 319, 180 N. Y. Supp. 31. Conditions that require the whole or a certain percentage of the capital stock to be subscribed for are valid. Subscriptions may thus be qualified as to manner, or means of payment, or made to depend upon the completion of work, or be limited in time. Meyer v. Blair, 109

N. Y. 600. Bray v. Farwell, 81 N. Y. 600. Meyers v. 

Sturgis, 123 App. Div. 470, 108 N. Y. Supp. 528. Stuart v. New York Community Mausoleum Const. Co., 179 N. Y. 

Supp. 73. Brewers Fire Ins. Co. v. Berger, 10 Hun 56.

A person who has contracted to take shares upon performance of a lawful condition, can only be compelled to do exactly what he has contracted to do. The subscription cannot be enforced unless the condition is performed or waived. Chesbrough v. Wright, 51 N. Y. 662. Southworth v. Morgan, 205 N. Y. 293, Cady's Cas. p. 370. If he subscribes for 25 shares, the corporation cannot make him accept 20. Knowlton v. Congress and Empire Spring Company, 57 N. Y. 519. As soon as the condition is performed, the subscriber is bound. Union Hotel Co. v. Hersee, supra. 

In Pennsylvania the void condition is regarded as separable and the subscription is held valid and enforceable without the condition. Boyd v. Peach Bottom Ry. Co., 90 Pa. St. 

169. Bavington v. Pittsburg R. R. Co., 34 Pa. St. 358.

In Pennsylvania, the subscription is treated as absolute and unconditional; while in New York, it has been held that the entire subscription is bad, if the condition set forth therein is unlawful. Ft. Edwards & Ft. M. Plank Road Co. v. 

Payne, 15 N. Y. 583, Cady's Cas. p. 374.

Private arrangements, not expressed in the subscription paper, giving peculiar privileges to the subscriber, are fraudulent upon the other subscribers, and therefore null on this ground, as well as by reason of the parol evidence rule. The invalidity of the secret agreement does not release the subscribers. Yonkers Gazette v. Jones, supra. 

In Jones v. Dodge, 97 Ark. 248, L. R. A. 1915, A472, the secret agreement was that the eight corporators should only be liable for one-half their subscriptions. The corporation having failed, the court held that the agreement was a fraud upon the other defendant stockholders and that the eight were liable for the full amount of their shares. See 

Upton v. Englehart, 3 Dill. (U. S.) 389. Mann v. Currie, 

2 Barb. 294.

Substantial performance of a condition precedent binds the subscriber. The subscription may be withdrawn by

the subscriber at any time before the condition is performed. 

Faris v. Beck, 222 Pac. 652 (Col.)

The subscriber may waive the conditions of his subscription. Hutchins v. Smith, 46 Barb. 235.

The member may be estopped to deny his relation to the corporation, though conditions have not been performed, (Received and retained stock). Pray v. Todd, 71 App. Div. 

391, 75 N. Y. Supp. 947; (endorsed the certificate of stock) 

Richards v. Ackerman, 175 App. Div. 746, 162 N. Y. Supp. 

657, affd. 223 N. Y. 721; (held stock and acted as director) 

Beals v. Buff. Expand. Met. Const. Co., 49 App. Div. 589, 63 N. Y. Supp. 635.

If the subscriber dies or becomes incapacitated before his membership becomes full and perfect, his estate is not liable on the contract, since there was no contract in force. 

Fletcher on Corps. p. 1235. 

§ 123. Subscriptions on Conditions Subsequent. 

A subscription on condition subsequent is one that purports to be conditioned on a promise of the corporation to perform an act, which, by the terms employed in the subscription, does not have to be performed before the subscription becomes valid.

Thus, in a subscription for hotel stock, which provided that the hotel be "built and located on the southeast corner of block 44," the condition was one that was not settled at the outset, but was merely a special term of the contract, breach of which would still leave the subscriber a stockholder, but would afford him a cause of action for damages for the breach of the independent condition. See Richardson's

Outline of Contracts, Section 454. Red Wing Hotel Co. v. 

Friedrick, 1 N. W. 827 (Minn.).

The distinctions between a subscription on condition precedent and one on special terms may be classified as follows: 

Subscription on condition precedent. 

1. Becomes a stockholder on performance of the condition. 

2. May withdraw at any time before complete performance of the condition. 

Subscription on condition subsequent (on special terms). 

1. Becomes a stockholder upon acceptance of subscription, or upon subscription as the case may be. 

2. May not withdraw.

3. Is not liable for assessments until condition has been performed. 

4. Ordinarily no remedy except withdrawal of subscription. 

5. Will ordinarily withdraw if corporation becomes insolvent before performance of condition. 

6. Are construed as subscriptions on special terms rather than conditions precedent, unless apt words are employed. 

3. May be required to pay for his stock. 

4. Upon non-performance may sue for damages. 

5. Even though the damages to the subscriber equal the assessments unpaid, the subscriber cannot escape the liability of a stockholder to creditors. 

6. Will be construed as a subscription on special terms whenever possible.

The corporation on breach of its promise expressed in the condition subsequent, will be liable to the subscriber in damages. In Jewett v. Lawrenceburgh &c. R. R. Co., 10 Ind. 539, the subscription was on the condition that the road should be located at a certain point. A different location was adopted. The subscriber, who had paid his subscription, sued for damages and it appearing that the promise for the location formed practically the whole consideration for the subscription, so that there was a failure of consideration, it was held that the subscriber might recover the whole amount paid by him. As against corporate creditors the subscriber on special terms is estopped to withdraw, though there has been failure of consideration for his subscription. Upton v. Tribilock, supra. Schulte v. Boul. Gardens, 129 Pac. 582 (Cal.). Paducah & M. R. Co. v. Parks, 8 S. W. 842 (Tenn.). Morrow v. Nashville &c. Co., 3 

L. R. A. 37 (Tenn.).

A subscription contract may contain terms providing for its discharge upon the happening of certain events, or at the option of one of the parties. These stipulations are conditions subsequent and valid, unless creditors rights intervene.

In Cook, Assignee v. Chittenden, 25 Fed. 544, the defendant agreed to take 50 shares of stock with the understanding that he might, if he chose, withdraw within a certain time. 

He elected to withdraw within this time, notified the company's agent, and was released. The release was held effectual. Compare Zittel v. Schwartz, 192 App. Div. 353,

182 N. Y. Supp. 638. Kent v. Quicksilver Min. Co., supra, Cady's Cas. p. 453. 

bership.

Subscription After Incorporation. Proof of Mem- 

Transactions in shares of stock for $50 or more are within the statute of frauds. Nichols v. Clark, 40 Misc. 107, 81 N. Y. Supp. 262. Libaire v. Feinstein, 133 Misc. 27, 231 N. Y. Supp. 3. To "subscribe" has been defined as equivalent to an "agreement to pay" and in circumstances where subscription creates a debt, the statute of frauds, it seems, would not apply. Bullock v. Falmouth, 3 S. W. 129 (Ky.). Decisions, precisely in point, are lacking. Oral subscriptions would seem to be valid and not subject to the defense of the statute of frauds if they constitute agreements to pay for stock; but invalid, under the statute of frauds, if they constitute an agreement to take stock. The one is a debt, the other a sale of choses in action. Sales are within the statute, but not debts. It is not an agreement to pay for stock, but a sale, if the subscription contract is either to form a corporation and take its stock (Yonkers 

Gazette Co. v. Taylor, supra, Cady's Cas. p. 341); or to buy treasury stock. A subscription for unissued stock would seem a mere agreement to pay, and not within the statute. 

The distinction between a sale of treasury stock, and a subscription for unissued stock, is emphasized by the rule which requires a certificate of treasury stock to be tendered in order to put the subscriber in default, whereas no tender is required on a subscription for unissued stock, but only a call. S. C. L. 68. Kohlmetz v. Calkins, 16 App. Div. 518, 44 N. Y. Supp. 1031. Compare Sanders v. Proctor, 172 

App. Div. 713, 158 N. Y. Supp. 433, affd. 225 N. Y. 682 (where, however, the statute of frauds was not in issue). 

In Mills v. Friedman, 111 Misc. 253, 181 N. Y. Supp. 285, affd. (mem.) 194 App. Div. 942, affd. (mem.) 233 N. Y. 517, the defendant subscribed orally to stock of the Playthings

Corporation, the trustee in bankruptcy of which brought suit to enforce his subscription. Ten per cent was paid down with the oral subscription, in accordance with the statute as it then read, so that it might have been thought, though it was not discussed, that the part payment had

taken the contract out of the statute of frauds. Overruling a demurrer to the complaint, the court said in part, "Shares of joint stock companies are neither goods, wares, nor merchandise within the meaning of the statute of frauds." See 

14 A. L. R. 394.

S. C. L. 67, authorizing the opening of subscription books, is permissive and not mandatory. Donovan v. Power Film 

Products, 111 Misc. 157, 181 N. Y. Supp. 157. An entry of a subscription or a transfer on the corporation's books passes legal title to the stock regardless of delivery. Wheeler v. Miller, 90 N. Y. 353. In

Though an agent was the subscriber, the principal is entitled to the shares, and is liable on the subscription. re N. Y. L. & W. Ry. Co., 99 N. Y. 12. Burr v. Wilcox, 22 N. Y. 551, Cady's Cas. p. 380. On the question of the agent's personal liability, there is a conflict of authority. 

Fletcher on Corporations, p. 1211. The New York rule seems to be that the agent makes himself liable as a subscriber and stockholder. Union Hotel Co. v. Hersee, 79 

N. Y. 454. Where the investment is not proper for the trust funds, a trustee, subscribing as trustee, does not bind the cestui que trust, but the trustee is personally liable as a subscriber. Bagnell v. Ives, 184 Fed. 466.

An unaccepted subscription may be revoked by death or insanity of the subscriber or laches in accepting subscription, Armleder Motor Tk. Co. v. Barnes, 202 N. Y. Supp. 

472. Fletcher on Corporations, p. 1235. Where the subscription books do not contain sufficient matter to identify a party, they cannot be used against him, Allen v. Ryan, 125 Misc. 521, 211 N. Y. Supp. 405.

The best evidence of membership is the certificate of stock. S. C. L. 65, 75. It is the transfer of the certificate that passes title to the transferee. Gideon v. Rep. Sec. 

Corp., 232 Fed. 184, P. P. L. 162, 164, 166, 178. The stockbook entry is prima facie evidence, Hoagland v. Bell, 36

Barb. 57, but it is rebuttable. Allen v. Ryan, 219 App. Div. 

634, 221 N. Y. Supp. 77, 246 N. Y. 609. The stock subscription is relevant and competent evidence (Partridge v. 

Badger, 25 Barb. 146) and, as to the corporators, the certificate of incorporation, or a certified copy, or the recorded

copy, Strong v. Wheaton, 38 Barb. 618, G. C. L. 12. Where the stock certificate has been endorsed and delivered to the present holder by the person to whom it was issued, the execution of the endorsement must be proved by competent evidence. Thompson v. Stanley, 72 Hun 248, 25 N. Y. 

Supp. 890, affd. 147 N. Y. 713. Acts as a stockholder, on the road towards estoppel, may be proved. Brech v. Brewster, 150 App. Div. 202, 134 N. Y. Supp. 697. The legal presumption is that a director is a stockholder, but it is rebuttable. Butterfield v. Radde, 58 N. Y. 489.

A stockholder who was such at organization is presumed to have continued until the contrary is shown. 

Wesley, 13 Hun 492. 

§ 125. Who May Subscribe. 

Herries v.

Subscriptions by infants, or of others incapable of contracting, are governed by the law of contracts. Richardson's Outline of Contracts, Chap. VIII. If an infant elects to rescind his subscription, he must return what has been received by him. Wuller v. Chuse Grocery Co., 241 Ill. 398.

But if it has been lost or expended, he need not return it. 

Danziger v. Iron Clad Realty & Trading Co., 80 Misc. 510, 141 N. Y. Supp. 593. If the infant disaffirms and repudiates his contract, he cannot be held liable either to the corporation or to creditors. A married woman now subscribes for stock as a femme sole. In re Reciprocity Bank, 22 N. Y. 9.

A corporation may subscribe for shares of stock in another corporation, if it is expressly authorized to do so, or if such a contract is a necessary or proper means of accomplishing the purpose for which it was created. Union Hotel 

Co. v. Hersee, supra, Cady's Cas. p. 339. The subscription in that case was made by authority of the directors, with the consent of all the stockholders, and was subsequently ratified by the payment of calls. See sec. 69, supra.

Officers of the corporation may purchase its stock from it, providing they are not the sellers. Dusenberry v. Sagamore Development Co., 164 App. Div. 573, 150 N. Y. Supp. 

229 (president). F. Gilbert Paper Co. v. Prankard, 204 

App. Div. 83, 198 N. Y. Supp. 25 (directors). Where the directors vote a dividend to permit some of their members to purchase stock, directors who purchase must not vote.

Hartley v. Pioneer Iron Works, 87 App. Div. 107, 84 N. Y. 

Supp. 79, rev. 181 N. Y. 73. The subscription by the officers must not be unfair to the stockholders. East N. Y. & 

J. R. Co. v. Elmore, 5 Hun 214. 

§ 126. Mortgagees and Pledgees as Members. 

No person holding shares as collateral is personally liable to creditors, but the pledgor is considered the holder and is liable. S. C. L. 72. This changed the common law. Johnson v. Underhill, 52 N. Y. 203. U. S. Trust Co. v. U. S. 

Fire Ins. Co., 18 N. Y. 199. Roosevelt v. Brown, 11 N. Y. 

148. The pledge of shares of stock carries with it, as an incident of the pledgees special ownership, the right to receive dividends afterwards declared, to be applied on the debt, or held in trust for the pledgor. Booth v. Consolidated Fruit Jar Co., 62 Misc. 252, 114 N. Y. Supp. 1000. 

Brightson v. Claflin, 225 N. Y. 469. § 127. Executors, and Trustees under Voting Trust 

Agreement, as Members.

Executors, administrators, guardians, and trustees, who receive stock by virtue of their duties as such and have it transferred on the books to their names are not personally liable as stockholders. S. C. L. 72. Trustees named in voting trust agreements entered into by virtue of power conferred by S. C. L. 50, are not liable as members. Under the voting trust agreement the stock of stockholders is transferred to a trustee, who causes the old certificates to be cancelled and a new certificate to be issued to himself, issuing in turn his trust certificates to those stockholders who transferred their stock to him. When this has been done the right to vote is vested in the trustee, but the beneficial interest is in the stockholders. In re Morse, 247 N. Y. 

290, 160 N. E. 374. If the trustee is divested of his interest, as by the foreclosure of a mortgage on the stock in his hands, or of sale under pledge, the owner of the beneficial interest ceases to be a stockholder upon the foreclosure sale. 

The holder of the beneficial interest may be a director. In re Hassam Paving Co., 152 App. Div. 610, 137 N. Y. Supp. 

453. Mtr. of Ringler & Co., 204 N. Y. 30, Cady's Cas. p. 516.

§ 128. Subscriptions Induced by Fraud. 

Subscriptions induced by fraud are voidable at the option of the subscriber, except as to creditors who have extended credit in reliance on the subscriptions. Mack v. Latta, 178 

N. Y. 525. Bosly v. National Mach. Co., 123 N. Y. 550.

Canadian Agency v. Assets Realization Co., 165 App. Div. 

96, 150 N. Y. Supp. 758. Ritzwoller v. Lurie, 176 App. Div. 

100, 162 N. Y. Supp. 475. Kent v. Quicksilver Mining Co., 78 N. Y. 159, Cady's Cas. p. 447. McDermott v. Harrison, 56 Hun 640. A fortiori, he cannot withdraw if there are creditors, this being a defense to the corporation. Buker v. Leighton Lea Association, 63 App. Div. 507, 71 N. Y. 

Supp. 610. The applicant may withdraw a tentative or inchoate subscription before it becomes binding. Hecksher v. Edenborn, 203 N. Y. 210. Haessig v. Gregory, 197 App. 

Div. 111, 188 N. Y. Supp. 500. Woods v. Dudley, 188 App. 

Div. 136, 176 N. Y. Supp. 494. Turner Lumber Co. v. 

Lacey, 199 App. Div. 534, 191 N. Y. Supp. 774. That the officers have wasted the corporate assets is not ground for recission. Brown v. Ransdell, 227 App. Div. 224, 237 N. Y. 

Supp. 573.

The subscriber may rely on the representations of duly constituted officers or agents of the company. New York 

Exchange Co. v. De Wolf, 31 N. Y. 273. The test of fraud in a stock transaction is the same as in any other. Fletcher on Corporations, p. 1350. Keeler v. Seaman, 47 Misc. 292, 95 N. Y. Supp. 920. Specimen false representations are the following: That the corporation has purchased or owns certain property or rights. Lehman-Charley v. Bartlett, 135 App. Div. 674, 120 N. Y. Supp. 501. Cawthra v. Stewart, 109 N. Y. Supp. 770. That all or a certain amount of the capital stock of a corporation has been subscribed for. 

Talmadge v. Sanitary Security Co., 31 App. Div. 498, 52 

N. Y. Supp. 139. On statements of the value of property of a corporation, present or prospective, or of the value of its assets and stock, the subscriber may not rely; but on representations of extrinsic facts affecting value or quality he may rely. Van Slochem v. Villard, 207 N. Y. 587. That the officers of a corporation would use their best efforts to make the corporation a success is an expression of opinion.

Stein v. Freund, 215 App. Div. 149, 213 N. Y. Supp. 9, as is a representation of the future acts and desires of the corporation, Wilson v. Meyer, 154 App. Div. 300, 138 N. Y. Supp. 

1048; or that the management of a corporation was efficient, Hill v. International Products Co. 129 Misc. 25, 220 N. Y. 

Supp. 711.

There are three remedies which may be pursued by a subscriber who has been induced to subscribe through fraud, viz., (1) recision, (2) damages, (3) keep the stock and sue for damages. Heckscher v. Edenborn, 203 N. Y. 210. Haessig v. Gregory, 197 App. Div. 111, 188 N. Y. Supp. 500. 

Wood v. Dudley, 188 App. Div. 136, 176 N. Y. Supp. 494. 

Turner Lumber Co. v. Lacey, 199 App. Div. 534, 191 N. Y. 

Supp. 774. Sec. 45 supra. The subscriber may be estopped to assert his rights to recision by ratification, evidenced by such acts as attending meetings, receiving dividends, giving proxies, etc. Buker v. Leighton Lea Ass'n, 63 App. Div. 

507, 71 N. Y. Supp. 610. Davis v. Gifford, 182 App. Div. 

99, 169 N. Y. Supp. 492. Brennon v. Nat'l Equitable Investment Co., 247 N. Y. 486. Ratification, implied from the acceptance of benefits, is ratification of the contract alone and not of the fraud which induced the contract, and does not bar an action for damages for deceit. Potts v. Lambie, 138 App. Div. 144, 122 N. Y. Supp. 935. § 129.

Consideration Required for the Issuance of Stock. 

It has always been held a breach of duty for the directors to give away shares, or to allot them save for money or money's worth. Continental Sec. Co. v. Belmont, 222 N. Y. 

673, Cady's Cas. p. 456. The capital is an essential element for the functioning of the corporation, without the tangible existence of which subscribers ought not to be tolled into the company, nor dealers inveigled into giving credit. "The capital paid in, and promised to be paid in, is a fund which the trustees cannot squander or give away." Van Cott v. 

Van Brunt, 82 N. Y. 535. 

At the start stock was issued only for cash or on promise to pay cash on call. Later it was held that a holder of stock, for which he subscribed, and which was issued to him for work or property, would be credited only for the actual value received by the corporation, and in the absence of

unanimous consent of the stockholders, the subscriber would be chargeable with the par value of the stock. Ib. Expedients designed to let one stockholder get his stock at a less price than another, were disregarded and full liability enforced. Thus where a note given for the statutory subscription was surrendered up after incorporation and one for less accepted, the stockholder was held liable for the benefit of creditors on the first note. Tuckerman v. Brown, 33 N. Y. 297. But it was also held that shares or bonds issued merely to get money might be sold at a discount. 

Gray's Case, 1 Ch. Div. 664 (1876); Re Anglo-Danubian &c. 

Co., L.
