R. 20 Eq. 339 (1875); and that a contract to take shares of any kind bound both parties to what they agreed, so that, if the corporation issued paid-up $100 shares on payment of $25, the corporation could be enjoined, on the one hand, from cancelling the stockholder's name on the stockbook as the holder of fully-paid shares and, on the other, could be compelled to register the stock as fully paid (Ashworth v. Bristol & N. S. Ry. Co., 15 L. T. [N. S.] 561); it could not sue the stockholder for the balance; a succeeding transferee of stock issued as fully paid was protected, even though the delusive nature of the consideration could have been discovered from an inspection of the contract on file, the original holder still remaining liable; and that since the company had no rights against the said stockholder, creditors who gave credit in reliance on the apparent capital stock, could not sue him, since their rights arose only by subrogation or other succession to the rights of the corporation. Christenson v. Eno, 106 N. Y. 97, Cady's Cas. p. 348. 

Southworth v. Morgan, 205 N. Y. 293, ib. p. 370. 

Stone v. Young, 210 App. Div. 303, 206 N. Y. Supp. 95, Cady's Cas. p. 366. Bash's case, L. R. 9 Ch. 554.

The conflict of interest between the associates in the corporation who are anxious to raise funds for the enterprise, the promoters who want profits, and the investors who want sound investments, has lead to the system of checks and remedies to prevent losses by watered stock. It has been a historical development. The promoters' desire for full-paid stock, costing them less than par, but saleable at a profit, changed the original fashion of issuing stock only

for money payable on call to an issue for services, even those performed before incorporation, and valuable to the corporation. This lead to the enactment of the provisions of statutes similar to S. C. L. 69, found in the constitutions of some states, and in the laws of practically all states, that "no corporation shall issue either shares of stock or bonds except for money, labor done, or property actually received for the use and lawful purposes of such corporation," thus preventing the issuance of stock or bonds save for the enumerated considerations when received after incorporation, and prohibiting their issuance for expenditures and services performed before incorporation. Herbert v. Duryea, 34 App. Div. 478, 54 N. Y. Supp. 311, affd. 164 N. Y. 596.

The B. & C. Electrical Const. Co. v. Owen, 176 App. Div. 

399, 163 N. Y. Supp. 351, Cady's Cas. p. 453. Parol evidence may be received to show that the true consideration was not that recited in the stock certificate and that the shares are. not in fact fully paid. Ib.

The remedy applies to stockholders who became such after April 16, 1901. S. C. L. 69 to 73, embraces the following propositions: 

1. Stock may be issued for three kinds of consideration only: (a) Money, equal to par value, if any. (b) Labor done. (c) Property actually received by the corporation for intra vires purposes. 

2. If the consideration received by the corporation for stock issued as fully paid is equal to its par value, both the holders thereof and the shares, are exempt from liability for debts of the corporation. 

3. In the absence of fraud the judgment of directors as to the value of the property received for shares shall be conclusive. 

4. Every holder of shares, except those mentioned in

S. C. L. 72, shall be personally liable to creditors for corporate debts for the amount unpaid on the shares held by him for debts contracted while such shares were held by him; unless some special act fixes a different liability (e. g., banking corporations, Mosler Safe Co. v. Guardian Tr. Co., 153 App. Div. 117, 138 N. Y. Supp. 298, affd. 208 N .Y. 524).

5. He may, nevertheless, be liable to laborers, servants and employees if the steps required by S. C. L. 71 are complied with. 

6. The holder of not fully paid stock is liable for corporate debts only under the following conditions: (a) The debt must have been payable within two years from the date when contracted. (b) Action must have been brought against the corporation to collect it within two years after the debt became due. (c) Judgment must have been recovered in that action, and execution issued against the corporation and returned unsatisfied in whole or in part. (d) Under a short statute of limitations, liability of the stockholder terminates two years after he parted with his stock. (e) The debt must have been contracted while he held his shares. 

7. The holder of not fully paid shares is not liable for more than the unsatisfied portion of the judgment against the corporation nor for more than the difference between the par value of his stock and the value received by the corporation at any time for the shares.

The law as set forth prior to 1901 has been resettled by the statute. The statute has the following general import: (a) The liability of the directors and the subscribers for stock has not been changed by the statute. (b) One to whom stock, having par value and appearing on its face, contrary to fact, to be fully paid is issued or transferred, has been made liable to creditors, but not to the corporation. Similarly, the holder of stock that appears on its face to be partly paid stock is liable to the extent of the unpaid residue. S. C. L. 74. (c) The language of the statute, S. C. L. 70, is applicable to holders of shares without nominal or par value, where the capital representing them has not actually been furnished in accordance with the statement in the certificate of incorporation made pursuant to S. C. L. 12-A or the "additional statement" permitted by S. C. L. 12-B. (d) The New York statutes do not affect the liability

of stockholders of foreign corporations. The laws of the state wherein the company was incorporated, or, if these are not alleged or proved, then the common law rule, determine their liability. Sec. 3, supra.

The contrasted liability of a stockholder of a foreign corporation incorporated in a state where the old rule applies, of a stockholder of a domestic corporation, and of a subscriber, is illustrated by the respective facts of Milliken v. Caruso, 205 N. Y. 559, Breck v. Brewster, 150 App. 

Div. 202, 134 N. Y. Supp. 697, and Granger & Co. v. Allen, 214 App. Div. 367, 212 N .Y. Supp. 356, affd. 244 N. Y. 587.

In the Milliken case, Caruso, who paid the Nitrogen corporation of North Dakota $2,000 for full paid stock of the face value of $5,000, was held not liable to creditors for the difference. In the Breck case, it was indicated that the jury might decide whether the defendant, whose name was entered on the stockbook of a domestic corporation for 100. shares for which he had not subscribed, was a stockholder, in the sense that he, as owner, held the stock, and, if so, the receiver in bankruptcy of the corporation might have a verdict for the amount unpaid on his stock. And in the 

Granger case, a subscriber for the stock of a domestic corporation was held to pay the balance unpaid of his subscription to the trustee in bankruptcy, except as affected by the short statute of limitations.

The statute does not make liable a stockholder of record if he in fact was not the owner or holder of the certificate. 

Breck v. Brewster, supra. In the Breck case it appeared that the stock was entered in the stockbook in the name of an employee, the defendant, who had no beneficial interest, but who endorsed the stock certificate at the request of someone else who was the beneficial owner of the stock and who actually held the certificate. The court noted that the statute made holders, and not mere stockholders of record, liable to creditors.

The fact that the directors' minutes recite that they fixed the value of property taken for stock before they took it over and came to the conclusion that its value was equal to the stock, which was then issued as fully paid stock, neither precludes evidence of the facts and circumstances of

which they had or should have had knowledge, nor other competent evidence of the value of the property. Boynton v. Hatch, 47 N. Y. 225. The question is whether there has been an evasion of the law and a fraudulent issue of stock, and while proof of inadequacy is competent evidence, if it appears on the whole that the directors in the honest exercise of their judgment, were guilty of no more than an error of judgment as to the value, the holder of stock issued as fully paid will not be liable to creditors. Schenck v. Andrews, 57 N. Y. 133. Thurston v. Duffy, 38 Hun 327. Where a going partnership is incorporated, stock may be issued against the reasonable value of the good will. There is a presumption that stock has been regularly issued and for a valuable consideration unless the contrary is shown. Matter of Seneca Oil Co., 153 App. Div. 594, 138 N. Y. 

Supp. 78. White, Corbin & Co. v. Jones, 79 App. Div. 

373, 79 N. Y. Supp. 583. The law makes allowances for variations of the judgments of men, but does not countenance intentional over-valuations. Flour City Nat'l Bank v. Shire, 88 App. Div. 401, 84 N. Y. Supp. 810, affd. 

179 N. Y. 587. The good faith and the amount which the directors thought the property to be reasonably worth to the corporation are matters of inference, to be drawn from the circumstances. The plaintiff creditor has the burden of proving the amount of fraudulent over-valuation. Rathbone v. Ayer, 121 App. Div. 355, 105 N. Y. Supp. 1041, rev. on opinion of Kellogg, J., 196 N. Y. 503. Gamble v. Queens 

Water Co., 123 N. Y. 104. In the Rathbone case, supra, the associates bought an idle tin plate mill for $85,000. They then incorporated the Elmira Steel Company, and drew their checks to it for $500,000, in return for all its capital stock, issued as full paid. The corporation paid this sum for a conveyance of the mill to one Baird, who redistributed the money to the associates. The purchase was made pursuant to resolution of the directors passed at the same meeting at which the shares were issued. The resolutions recited with ponderous formality, that in the judgment of the directors the value of the property was equal to the aforesaid sum, and that the plant could be made profit producing at once to the corporation. For the failure of the plaintiff

creditor to prove the value of the property to the corporation, the complaint was dismissed, a stipulation having been entered into enabling the court to dispose of the case on the question of law. The value of the property to the corporation as compared with the par value of the stock received by them, determines the liability of the stockholders, but the price paid by them for the property which they turned in for the stock is competent, but not conclusive, evidence of what they considered the intrinsic value to be. Ib. Compare secs. 43 and 44 supra.

A "secret process," if it has a provable value, may be sufficient consideration to validate the corporation's agreement to issue shares therefor: but if the value is too speculative to be susceptible of proof, or, a fortiori, if the proof establishes a lack of value, the agreement of the corporation to issue the stock can not be enforced. Berger v. Burden, 173 App.

Div. 680, 160 N. Y. Supp. 331. The speculative element in the issuance of stock for the purchase of a patent is to be considered. The judgment of the directors may be helped by appraisals, and their judgment, exercised honestly, fairly and without fraud, will be held final and conclusive. Alpha 

Portland Cement Co. v. Schratweiser, 221 Fed. 258. Before the creditor obtains judgment against the corporation, the charter may be amended so as to reduce the amount of stock. Randall v. Havemeyer, 49 N. Y. Super. 520 (17 

J. & S.). "Property" under the statute S. C. L. 69 is delimited by the charter. To a corporation authorized by charter to "manufacture and sell" electrical apparatus, an ultra vires contract to sell as agent is not property "necessary for the use and lawful purposes of such corporation," for which full paid stock can be issued. Powell v. Murray, 3 App. Div. 

273, 38 N. Y. Supp. 233, affd. 157 N. Y. 717 (mem.). 

§ 130. Release of Subscribers. 

The corporation has no implied power to release or discharge a holder of partly paid stock, or a subscriber, from liability, if there are creditors. If there are no creditors to be affected, the directors, if they have express consent of all stockholders, may cancel the stock, or permit the stockholder to transfer it to the corporation. Hollingshead v.

Woodward, 107 N. Y. 96. The fact that there are differences between the stockholder and the corporation, and that it is to the manifest interest of the company that he should retire, cannot weigh against the fact that as to creditors, or dissenting stockholders, the corporation cannot cancel or diminish the capital, but only forfeit shares for nonpayment of calls for the benefit of all. S. C. L. 68. Lake Ont. 

A. & N. Y. R. Co. v. Mason, 16 N. Y. 451. Even a subscription made after incorporation on condition precedent, cannot be cancelled after acceptance by the corporation until after a reasonable time has elapsed within which the company may perform the conditions. Hutchins v. Smith, 46 Barb. 235. Since the subscriber, who subscribes after incorporation, may insert any condition in his subscription he may insert a condition entitling him to withdraw. A subscriber who subscribed to the stock of a real estate corporation formed to improve, etc., a tract in the city of New 

York with an apartment building, inserted in his subscription a condition which permitted him to cancel the subscription on 60 days' notice and receive back what he had paid. 

It was held that he thus became a simple contract creditor and might withdraw as against a prior mortgagee, subject to whose mortgage the corporation took the property. Mc- 

Comb v. Barcelona Apt. Assn., Ltd., 134 N. Y. 598. Cf. sec. 

66 supra.

Whether the corporation or a creditor may hold a subscriber in a case where the charter was altered or amended during the period when the subscription was merely inchoate, depends upon the materiality of the amendment. 

Amendments authorized by statute, and not changing the scope of the business or the risk, will not permit the subscriber to cancel. Buffalo & N. Y. C. R. Co. v. Dudley, 14 

N. Y. 336. Kelsey v. Northern Light Oil Co., 45 N. Y. 505. 

Union Htl. Co. v. Hersee, supra, Cady's Cas. p. 339. Buff. & 

J. R. Co. v. Gifford, 87 N. Y. 294. The mere fact that the corporation has entered into illegal projects will not permit cancellation. U. S. Vinegar Co. v. Schlegel, 143 N. Y. 537, 38 N. E. 729. Same v. Foehrenbach, 148 N. Y. 58, 42 N. E. 403. 

A material change in the certificate of incorporation will

release a subscriber from his obligation to the corporation. 

Dutchess & Columbia County R. R. Co. v. Mabbett, 58 N. Y. 

397. Thus, he will be released by a change in purposes of its incorporation, Dorris v. Sweeney, 60 N. Y. 463: or a change in proposed business, Woods Motor Vehicle Co. v. 

Brady, 181 N. Y. 145. Stern v. McKee, 70 App. Div. 142, 75 

N. Y. Supp. 157. In the last mentioned case, subscriptions were obtained in connection with a prospectus stating that the object of the corporation was "to acquire all patents and rights for all countries, except the United States and 

Canada, to metal turning machines, known as 'Hoffman machines'." The corporation was authorized by its charter, however, to make contracts for the manufacture, or purchase of, or to buy, use, sell, lease or rent such machines. 

The subscriber was held released. Change of name without substantial loss of good will, will not release a subscriber,- 

Yonkers Gazette Co. v. Taylor, supra, Cady's Cas. p. 341.

For a case where a change in capitalization did not release the subscriber see Myers v. Sturgis, 123 App. Div. 470, 108 

N. Y. Supp. 528. 

§ 131. Treasury Stock. 

This term has been used indifferently in two senses to denote stock authorized, but unissued and held in treasury with the stockholders' consent, or stock once validly issued and later bought in by the corporation (sec. 66, supra), or donated to it. The latter is the significance attached to the term when used without qualifications herein.

Stock held in treasury is kept with the idea of selling it at or above par when investors shall have been attracted. 

When sold above par it is sometimes called "assessable" stock. Cf. the words "full paid and non-assessable" in the stock certificate. Stock held in treasury being unissued stock cannot be sold below par without subjecting the directors and holders to liability. Sec. 128 supra. 

The usual purpose and reason for the donation of treasury stock is to enable the corporation to realize money by its sale below par, and to safeguard the purchaser from all liability for the debts of the corporation. For instance, A sells the corporation a mine, patent, tract of land, or a going business with the goodwill, and donates to the cor-

poration gratis, a part of the stock issued to him therefor. 

The transaction does not demonstrate that the property was overvalued, for over-valuation depends upon a fair appraisal of the value of the property, to the corporation. A's expectation of profit from turning Blackacre, potentially worth $180,000, into active operation, may be sufficient inducement to him to yield up $20,000 of the stock received, in order that the corporation may give away the $20,000 of stock as a bonus for a bond issue of, say, $40,000, to realize capital for building. This is the true use of the term "treasury stock." The bonus stock would not be "watered stock" in law or in fact, and the holders would be immune from liability if the corporation failed in business. 

Fletcher, Cyc. of the Law of Pri. Corps. pp. 5830-5950. 

The use of the term "treasury stock" to denote stock originally authorized but unissued, and remaining in the treasury, is illustrated by Dusenberry v. Sagamore Development Co., 164 App. Div. 573, 150 N. Y. Supp. 229, where the appellate division reversed a judgment which had set aside an election. In that case the president, a stockholder, and his associates, had purchased at par 175 shares of the unissued stock held in treasury after the directors had, by resolution directed the president to sell it at par; and, by voting the stock so purchased, the president was able to control the election. It was held that the president was not disqualified by reason of being an officer, from purchasing. 

The appellate court applied the parol evidence rule to exclude testimony offered to show that the October 23 resolution which was the one that directed the sale, was intended to be revoked and made inoperative by a resolution subsequently passed on November 14, 1911, which did not in terms refer to the prior resolution. See also Archer v. Hesse, 164 App. Div. 493, 150 N. Y. Supp. 296. The corporation is not injured by the issuance of stock remaining in the treasury at par contrary to the agreement between the stockholders, unless in fact a larger price was obtainable. Waters v. Waters & Co., 201 N. Y. 184, Cady's 

Cas. at p. 445. 

The more correct use of the term "treasury" stock to denote shares once validly issued, that have been transfer-

red to the corporation, is illustrated in Hartley v. Pioneer 

Iron Works, 181 N. Y. 73, 73 N. E. 576. There a corporation had bought in 70 of its shares which it held as treasury stock in the true sense of the term. A dividend of $87.38 per share on each and all of its shares, including the 70 shares, was declared. It will be noted that if the 70 shares had been unissued stock, no dividend thereon could have been declared. S. C. L. 74. The treasury stock having been sold to plaintiff on the same day as the entry of the dividend, a dispute arose as to whether the sale was "dividend on" or "ex-dividend." It appeared that after the sale the books were altered so as to show no dividend on the treasury stock. 

It was held that the rights of plaintiff were fixed by the declaration of dividend. See Chap. XI. Treasury stock may be issued for the promissory note of a responsible purchaser. 

Furlong v. Johnson, 239 N. Y. 141, Cady's Cas. p. 350. The corporation is as free to issue it as it was to issue stock before it was curbed by statutes which were intended to protect the investor. S. C. L. 69. Lake Sup. Iron Co. v. 

Drexel, 90 N. Y. 87. Otter v. Brevoort Pet. Co., 50 Barb. 

247. 14 C. J. 455.

During the time that the corporation holds treasury stock it cannot exercise in regard to those shares the privileges that belong to an ordinary stockholder. It cannot vote them and thus perpetuate the directors in office, or provide thereby the required number of consents for a mortgage, even through the subterfuge of registering the stock in the name of a trustee or a director, who, by virtue thereof, are trustees for the corporation. Vail v. Hamilton, 85 N. Y. 453. 

Ex parte Holmes, 5 Cow. 426. The corporation cannot cancel treasury stock where the result would amount to a reduction of stock, except by going through the proceeding outlined in S. C. L. 37. If a bank takes its own stock in payment for a debt it must hold it, and may reissue it. Bank of Columbus v. Bruce, 17 N. Y. 507. 

The statutory safeguard S. C. L. 69-73 lead to a maze of decisions distinguishing between evasion and avoidance of the statute. The use of treasury stock, and contracts whereby stock was issued for services performed after as well as before incorporation, were popular expedients

and a fertile source of litigation. Morgan v. Bon Bon 

Co., supra, Cady's Cas. p. 147. Then came the Blue Sky laws, sec. 46, supra. These provided, in general, for commissions to pass on the soundness of proposed issues of stock or bonds-the Public Service Commission for public service corporations, the Interstate Commerce Commission for interstate railroads, and the "blue sky" commission, whose jurisdiction, in most states, is limited to the securities of industrial corporations. But the operations of a commission are slowed up by the necessity of affording a hearing in each case, with almost infinitesimal detail, before deciding. Interstate Com. Com. v. Louisville etc. R. R., 227 U. S. 18, 88. Pub. Serv. Com. cases, 40 Abbott's New 

York Digest, Consol. ed., p. 1164. The outstanding feature of these hearings is that the public do not and cannot learn the real inside facts necessary for an intelligent choice of investments.

A foil to the blue sky laws is the use of stock without nominal or par value, since it is issued for a fixed capital, with such additions as the directors may from time to time transfer thereto, the minimum amount per share being $1. 

S. C. L. 12. That the no-par-value plan may readily lend itself to stock selling schemes for corporations that have slight capital will appear from the following considerations: 

Pen. Law sec. 664 (1), in 1909, prohibited the declaration of a dividend except from "surplus profits arising from the business." In 1923, when the no-par-stock statute was passed, the penal section was changed to prohibit dividends from "capital or capital stock" (note the same terms in S. C. L. 58), and in 1924 the section was further changed to read "except from surplus." Therefore, at present it is no crime to issue stock without nominal or par value for $50 a share, credit $49 to surplus, and declare a dividend out of the latter, thereby inflating the market value of the non par to, say, $75 a share, for which further treasury stock may be issued, and so on until the stock sells for $100 a share, but is, in fact, largely water. To illustrate: in 

Cunliffe v. Consumers Assoc. of America, 124 Atl. 501 (Penn.), it appeared that 100,000 shares of non par stock without voting rights were authorized, the corporation being controlled by 1,000 voting shares, also without par value,

held by the insiders. The 100,000 shares were at first sold for $25 a share, but rose to $27.50, the insiders retaining 

71% of the sales price as their commission for marketing the shares. At this stage, in an action by some of the stockholders, the Supreme Court of Pennsylvania appointed a receiver and wound up the corporation. 

The remedy of public reports in specified detail has been advocated, but so far has not been adopted, even for investment corporations.

Other means of watering stock is by release of subscribers when the stock has been only partly paid, the release being brought about by a resolution unanimously adopted that no more calls shall be made; or by consolidation of two or more corporations with a liberal valuation for good will. S. C. L. 

89. Sec. 119 supra. Where it is done by release of subscribers the proceedings should be made as open as possible, formal resolutions spread on the minutes of a meeting called pursuant to S. C. L. 45, a record kept of the vote, and stock certificates reciting on their face that they are fully paid and non-assessable issued in place of the partly paid certificates (S. C. L. 74) and a receipt therefor signed by the stockholder, by which he specifically consents to the change. 

All inquiries at the corporate office should be truthfully answered. 

Dissenting stockholders may enjoin a threatened watering, and creditors have even greater rights. Chap. XVII, infra. In states (other than New York, where the liability is statutory), in which the trust fund theory obtains, those who have not paid for their stock must pay it to satisfy debts, despite releases. Richardson v. Green, 133 U. S. 30.

The New York statute, Pen. Law § 662, renders the per son in the service of the corporation criminally liable and punishable by imprisonment up to 7 years, or by fine of $3,000 or both, for selling or issuing shares or bonds "in excess of the power of such..corporation or of the limit imposed... upon its power to.. issue stock or evidences of debt." S. C. L. 69 specifically prohibits the issuance of shares of par value stock for money in an amount less than the par value, but does not prohibit the issuance of bonds for less than face. Proof of criminal intent, requisite for

conviction, would be so difficult in the average case as to be insurmountable. Pen. Law § 664 (3) punishes the director who concurs in a vote or act of directors to discount or receive a note or other evidence of debt in payment of a call. 

Officers, directors and others in the service of the corporation may be punished criminally for the illegal issuance of stock. Furlong v. Johnson, supra, Cady's Cas. at p. 351.

Stone v. Young, supra, Cady's Cas. at p. 369. Their responsibility as regards the issuance of bonds is considered separately in § 132, infra. Fraud in selling watered stock may further be classifiable penally as grand larceny, conspiracy, obtaining money under false pretenses, or using the U. S. mails to defraud.

The liabilities of persons receiving watered par value stock, stated conversely from its treatment in sec. 129 supra, may be grouped as follows:- 

1. Persons receiving the stock: Liable to creditors, but not to the corporation, unless they subscribed. S. C. L. 

§§ 69-73. Whalen v. Hudson Hotel Co., 183 App. Div. 316, 

170 N. Y. Supp. 855, 256 Fed. 546. If they subscribed, they may be liable on subscriptions to the corporation, or to the assignees of the corporation, or to creditors. Furlong v. 

Johnson, supra. Marston v. Deither, 49 Minn. 423. 

2. Transferees: Liable to creditors only, subject to the limitations in S. C. L. 73. Where the laws of the state wherein the corporation was incorporated do not impose liability, transferees with notice have the same liability as their transferors. Upton v. Tribilcock, 91 U. S. 45.

Transferees of bonds with bonus stock are not presumed to have known that it was watered or to have been put on inquiry. Dickerman v. Northern Tr. Co., 176 U. S. 

181. Transferees without notice are not liable, but the word "non-assessable" on a certificate reciting that the shares are partly paid, does not prevent notice from attaching, nor does the statement of the agent that no more need be paid. Webster v. Upton, 91 U. S. 65. The purchase of a certificate silent on its face as to whether it is fully paid, is a purchase without notice if in the open market, in good faith. The presumption is against fraud. Dickerman v. Northern T. Co., supra.

3. Officers of the corporation may be liable to purchasers, or criminally, Where officers receive stock as promoters they have all the liability of a promoter as well as liability as an officer. Secs. 43, 44 and 49, supra. 

4. Vendors of watered stock are not liable to their transferees in the absence of fraud, deceit, or express warranty. 

Ersfeld v. Exner, 128 App. Div. 135, 112 N. Y. Supp. 561, Cady's Cas. p. 376. 

5. The liability of stockholders for debts is not several, and cannot be enforced against a part of the stockholders. 

Bottlers Seal Co. v. Rainey, 243 N. Y. 333, 153 N. E. 437. 

§ 132. Transfer of Stock. 

The right of a stockholder to transfer his stock is an incident to the ownership of stock, as it is to the ownership of any personal property. By-laws regulating the power of transfer and amounting to more than a reasonable regulation of the method of transfer are held void, and even proper regulations are construed as being for the protection of the corporation only, and not as affecting the ownership of a transferee, to whom the stock was transferred by an irregular method. Gilbert v. Manchester etc. Co., 11 Wend. 

627. Mech. Bank v. N. Y. etc. R. R. Co., 13 N. Y. 599. N. 

Y. etc. R. R. Co. v. Schuyler, 34 N Y. 30, Cady's Cas. p. 473.

An acquiescence of the corporation in a transfer that is irregular in that it was not made in conformity to the bylaws, charter, or statute, is binding on it, and the original stockholder, who is still the stockholder of record, will not be liable on calls made after the corporation had notice, and it will be liable to the irregular transferee for dividends thereafter wrongly paid to the transferor. Isham v. Buckingham, 49 N. Y. 216. Moses v. Soule, 63 Misc. 203, 118 

N. Y. Supp. 410, affd. 136 App. Div. 904, (mem), Cady's 

Cas. p. 247. A transferee by an irregular transfer, not in accordance with by-laws, risks the payment of dividends to the holder of record who, unless challenged, is potentially in a position to vote, give consents, receive notices of calls, etc. 

Early by-laws forbade transfer if the owner was indebted to the corporation or had not paid calls theretofore made; and provided that shares should be transferrable only on the books of the company, to do which would involve the

surrender to the company and the cancellation by it of the certificate, and the issuance of a new certificate to the transferee. These have been reduced to statutes. S. C. L. 66, 10. 

The corporation is given power to regulate transfer by bylaws, but the statute is affirmative of the common law, G. C. 

L. 14, S. C. L. 65; and a transfer, acquiesced in by the corporation is binding, and renders the transferee liable for the debts. S. C. L. 10. Regardless of the method adopted for the transfer, the transferee becomes a member. 

The principal methods of transfer are (1) by indorsement and delivery of the certificate of stock. Pers. Prop. Law, 

§ 162 (a); (2) by assignment and delivery. Ib. § 162 (b). 

Grimes v. Hone, 49 N. Y. 17. Schmids Cas. on Wills, p. 1. (3) By delivery of an indorsed certificate by another than the owner. Ib. 166. Turnbull v. Longacre Bank, 249 N. Y. 

159. (4) By words of gift and manual delivery, though unindorsed by the donor. Miller v. Silverman, 247 N. Y. 

447, 100 N. E. 910. (5) By death of member, or by his last will. Bailey v. Hollister, 26 N. Y. 112. (6) By transfer by a voting trust agreement. S. C. L. 50. 

§ 133. Issuance and Transfer of Corporate Bonds. 

Familiar types of bonds are indenture, gold, registered, prior lien bonds, adjustment bonds, bonds issued in series, railroad, public utility, industrial, guaranteed, collateral, equipment trust bonds, convertible, callable, and refunding bonds. The great distinction between stockholders and bondholders is that stockholders are associates in the enterprise, while bondholders are creditors. Bonds represent a debt of the corporation, shares an interest in it. Smith v. Westchester Bronxville Rly. Co., 156 App. Div. 920, 141 N. Y. 

Supp. 1147. Consequently, though bonds, like stock, must be issued for money, labor done or property actually received, there is no prohibition on issuing bonds at less than par. 

While the statute provides that no stock "shall be issued for money in an amount less than the par value of such shares," there is no similar provision relating to bonds, and there is no provision of the penal law imposing a criminal liability for the issuance of bonds at less than par, assuming that the corporation authorized the obtaining of the loan. Pen. Law 

§ § 662, 890, 926. Blue Sky Law, § 352 (Gen. Bus. Law.)

Of necessity, the investor in bonds, knowing he is a mere lender, supposedly knows the high risk of lending to a corporation. Gamble v. Queens Co. Water Co., 123 N. Y. 91, 25 N. E. 201. In McQuoid v. Queens, 143 App. Div. 134, 

127 N. Y. Supp. 867, it was held that the issuance of a corporate bond for a sum less than its par value did not violate the provisions of a statute which is now S. C. L. 69. 

It was said: "As the statute stood before 1901, it read, 'No such bonds shall be issued for less than the fair market value thereof'. This qualification was omitted by the Act of 1901 (now 69 S. C. L.). Therefore, the issuance of corporate bonds at a price below their par or face value was a valid act in the absence of fraud; the act of 1850 (354 G. 

B. L.) repealing the usury law as to corporations enabled them to issue bonds at a discount." Gamble v. Queens Co.

Water Co., supra. Under the statute as it now stands, considered in the light of its history and language, there is no reasonable basis for asserting that the issuance of a corporate bond for a price less than its par value violates the statute. Westinghouse Elec. Co. v. Bklyn etc. Co., 288

Fed. 221. As a sort of corollary to the foregoing considerations, the agreement between the corporation and the lender or underwriter, which is not exhibited to the public, may provide for the payment of any part of the interest in advance, and that, in order that the corporation's credit may not suffer, the bonds shall bear interest at not more than 6%, the remaining interest being represented by bonds which are accepted by the lender pursuant to the aforesaid agreement, as and for payment of interest in advance. Sec. 62 supra.

The formal minutes authorizing the loan need reveal none of the details, provided only that the agreement is such as to bind all the associates, and that all prior creditors are taken care of.

Corporate bonds issued as security for debts and mortgages may run for any time, say from six months to 50 years, but most bond issues provide an option to the corporation to pay off and retire the bonds before maturity. 

A contract of guarantee is frequently inserted in the bond, in which case the bond is called "stamped or endorsed."

A clause usually inserted in the corporate mortgage cov-

ers after acquired property. Its effectiveness may be considerably diminished by the corporation by such expedients as (1) Purchasing subject to a purchase money mortgage. 

Secs. 62 and 84 supra; (2) Forming a subsidiary to acquire new property: (3) Taking new property by lease with appropriate renewal clauses; (4) Consolidating with another corporation before acquiring the new property. 

Bonds, being debts, must be liquidated. Three methods of liquidation are conversion, refunding and redemption. 

Conversion is the exchange of the bonds for certain other forms of security, usually stock. Refunding is the exchange of the bonds for other bonds whose maturity is deferred to a date later than that of the original issue. Redemption is the exchange of cash for bonds. The conversion privilege, which adds a speculative note to the bond issue, gives additional security to the investor, and thus renders convertible bonds easier to sell. Convertibility is generally inserted to give bondholders control of the corporation, if default is suffered. Refunding will arise in a case wherein the bonds to be retired were issued when the market was tight and money rates high. Redemption enables the corporation by reason of a clause in the bonds, to rid itself of its debt, either at a stipulated price or at par. 

The statute, 374 G. B. L., specifically denies to a corporation the right to interpose a defense of usury. By implication, a minority stockholder may not sue to set aside a bond and mortgage executed by the corporation on the ground that it provided for usurious interest. McQuoid v. 

Queens Estates, supra. § 69 S. C. L. 

It has been held that neither the possibility of the acceleration of the due date of maturity of corporate bonds by provisions in trust mortgages securing them, nor on default, nor provisions for a sinking fund, nor the fact that bonds are payable to bearer, or, if registered, to registered holders, affect the negotiability of corporate bonds. Dickerman v. Northern Trust Co., supra. Higgins v. Hocking Val. 

R. Co., supra. Chi. Ry. Eq. Co. v. Merchants' Bk., 136

U. S. 268, 34 L. Ed. 349. 

The simplest form of a corporate bond is that of a promissory note under the seal of the corporation. Neg. Inst.

Law § 20, controls the negotiation or transfer of such a bond, which would be termed a debenture bond. No consents of stockholders would be required to validate it, since it would be issued by resolution of the directors under their power to borrow. Sec. 84 supra. The one taking it would need to know that he was lending for intra vires purposes, but the endorsee would be protected by the Negotiable In struments Law, or the Corporate Bonds statute, Art. 8 of the Personal Property Law. Pearce v. Madison etc. R. R., 

21 How. 441. Fairbanks v. Sargent, 104 N. Y. 108. Hibbs v. Brown, 190 N. Y. 167, Cady's Cas. p. 38. A mere transferee of an unregistered corporate bond, payable to bearer, or negotiable in form, from one having possession, however acquired, is protected by P. P. L. 261, 262, if he takes for present or antecedent value without notice of prior defenses or equities or claims of ownership of the endorser, or any prior holder. Where the bond was endorsed by a restrictive or special endorsement, as well as where it was endorsed in blank by the person specified on its face and by none of the later holders, any subsequent holder is aided by a presumption of title arising from possession, but the presumption is rebuttable. 

There are, therefore, two diverse analyses of the situation presented where a bond has changed holders irregularlyone under the negotiable instruments law, if the bond was a negotiable instrument, and the other under the personal property law. Negotiability requires that the bond (1) 

Must be in writing and signed by the maker or drawer; (2) Must contain an unconditional promise or order to pay a sum certain in money; (3) Must be payable on demand, or at a fixed or determinable future time; (4) Must be payable to order or to bearer: (5) Where the instrument is addressed to a drawee, he must be named or otherwise indicated therein with reasonable certainty. Reynolds v. Title 

G. & T. Co., 240 N. Y. 257. Higgins v. Hocking Valley R. 

Co., 188 App. Div. 68, 177 N. Y. Supp. 444. 

A purchaser of negotiable bonds from a thief may get good title which a holder in due course may enforce. Enoch v. Brandon, 249 N. Y. 263, 164 N. E. 45. Other provisions may be contained in the bond without impairing its negotiability. For instance, a statement of the transaction giving

rise to the instrument (N. I. L. 22), a statement as to collateral security (N. I. L. 24), or a reference to a trust mortgage which fixes the remedies, and usually provides that no action shall be brought on the bond except after action by the trustee do not necessarily preclude negotiability. Chelsea Bank v. Warner, 202 App. Div. 499, 195 N. Y. 

Supp. 419. Old Colony Tr. Co. v. Stumpel, 247 N. Y. 538, 161 N. E. 173. There may be an acceleration clause, without affecting negotiability, for this is construed as making the instrument payable at a determinable future time. 

N. I. L. § 21. Dickerman case, infra.

No stipulations in the bond, or in the accompanying certificate issued by the transfer agent, will suffice to render it negotiable if, in fact, any element of negotiability is lacking. 

The recital that it is a negotiable instrument and that the transfer agent may treat the holder as the absolute owner, is of importance for the protection of the agent under P. P. 

L. 261. Manhattan Co. v. Morgan, 242 N. Y. 38, 150 N. 

E. 594.

If the bond was not negotiable, or if it was transferred instead of being negotiated, the early equity cases held that unless there was something in the surrounding circumstances, or in the agreement between the corporation and the lender antecedent to the issuance of the bond, or in the construction of the language of the bond itself, to show an intent to forego the ordinary rule of assignment, the transferee took the bond subject to equities between the original parties. Re Natal Investment Co., L. R. 3 Ch. 355, 366. 

Western Bank v. Sherwood, 29 Barb. 383. The corporation, however, might be estopped, in equity, either by the contract with the lender, or by a holding out, from setting up the equities which existed between it and the first holder. 

Re Imperial Land Co., L. R. 3 Ch. 758. In law, however, early decisions, based upon the general custom of lenders to interest their friends to purchase bonds from them, held that assignees of bonds were free from prior equities. 

Higgs v. Northern Assur. Tea Co. Ltd., L. R. 4 Ex. 387. 

Mann v. Eckford, 15 Wend. 502.

In the sale of bonds in advance of issuance, the agent issues "scrip," which is a certificate by which the holder is to be entitled to delivery of the bond when executed. Man-

hattan Co. v. Morgan, supra. Scrip, by the usage of bankers and dealers in public securities, passed by mere delivery to bona fide holders for value without title. The enactment of P. P. L. 260, 261, probably does not affect the right of the agent to treat the holder of scrip as the true owner under a clause in the scrip so providing, Ib. 

If the provisions of the bonds and the trust deed or mortgage are inconsistent, the provisions of the bonds prevail. Enoch v. Brandon, 24 N. Y. 263, 164 N. E. 45. Innocent purchasers for value of stolen negotiable bonds acquire good title. Ib. Interest coupons, payable to bearer, are not negotiable if they refer to non-negotiable bonds to which they were attached, e. g., if the bonds refer to the trust mortgage conditions limiting or explaining them. 

McClelland v. Norfolk etc. R. Co., 110 N. Y. 469, 18 N. E. 

237. Levy v. Cleveland C. & C. & St. Louis R. Co., 210 App. 

Div. 422, 206 N. Y. Supp. 261. Greene v. Minzisheimer, 110 N. Y. Supp. 429. Upon default, the overdue coupons constitute a cause of action independent from the bonds. 

Bailey v. Buchanan Co., 115 N. Y. 297, 22 N. E. 155.

Bonds, like shares of stock, if endorsed by the person who appears on the face to be the owner, pass by delivery, and the purchaser, suing the corporation for the debt, need not, in his prima facie case, give evidence connecting his purchase with the original payee's blank assignment. Brainerd v. N. Y. & H. R. Co., 23 N. Y. Super. (10 Bosw.) 332. Conn. 

Mut. Lf. Ins. Co. v. Cleveland R. Co., 41 Barb. 9. The owner of stolen negotiable bonds has no title as against a bona fide purchaser from the thief. Newton v. Porter, 69 N. Y. 

133. But where the instrument when stolen was incomplete, the certification or necessary signatures being lacking and being supplied by a forgery, the purchaser is not protected. (Seal and certificate of trustee forged) Maas v. Mo. K. & T. Ry. Co., 83 N. Y. 223. Ledwith v. McKim, 53 N. Y. 307. Chester Co. G. & J. D. Co. v. Sec. Co., 219 

N. Y. 599. But see Manhattan Sav. Inst. v. N. Y. Nat. 

Exch. Bank, 170 N. Y. 58. The burden of proof as to the bona fides of the purchase is on the innocent purchaser. 

Manh. Sav. Inst. v. N. Y. Nat. Exch. Bank, 42 App. Div. 

147, 59 N. Y. Supp. 51. Where the mortgage given as collateral security for a bond issue has been paid or foreclosed

and the judgment has been paid, a corporation is entitled to have the bonds surrendered and the deficiency judgment assigned to it. Butterly-Maribert Realty Corp., 245 N. Y. 

Supp. 341. 

§ 134. Expulsion of Members. 

A membership corporation, from the earliest times, has been recognized as possessing implied or incidental power to disfranchise or expel a member for sufficient cause, subject to charter restrictions. People v. New York Board of 

Fire Underwriters, 7 Hun 428. People v. New York Com mercial Ass'n., 18 Abb. Pr. 271. National League of Commission Merchants v. Hornung, 148 App. Div. 355, 132 N. 

Y. Supp. 871. It may expel for any of the following: (1) For committing a heinous offense indictable at common law, although without relationship to a member's duty as such; (2) For an offense in violation of his duty as a member; and (3) For an offense combining both the above. 

Peo. v. Medical Soc. of Erie Co., 32 N. Y. 187. Matter of 

Barr, 147 App. Div. 704, 133 N. Y. Supp. 59. In Cunningham v. Supreme Council, R. A., 165 App. Div. 52, 151 N. 

Y. Supp. 83, a member was expelled after conviction for perjury. The power of expulsion may not be exercised without notice to the person charged, or without giving him an opportunity to be heard. Wachtel v. Noah Widows, etc. 

Benev. Soc., 84 N. Y. 28. Matter of Reed, 95 Misc. 695, 160 N. Y. Supp. 907. See Van Campen v. Olean General 

Hospital, 210 App. Div. 204, 205 N. Y. Supp. 554, Cady's

Cas. p. 24. Mandamus is the proper remedy to compel the reinstatement of a member wrongfully expelled. Matter of Haebler, 149 N. Y. 414. Wiedenfeld v. Keppler, 84 App. 

Div. 235, 82 N. Y. Supp. 634. Taufer v. Brotherhood of 

Painters, Dec. & P. H. of Am., 137 App. Div. 838, 122 N. Y.

Supp. 527. A by-law of a musical union punishing members for employing or playing with non-members or amateurs at public performances, was held invalid as arbitrary, where express power was not given by the charter in Thomas v. 

Mus. Mut. Prot. Union, 121 N. Y. 45, 24 N. E. 24.

Stock corporations possess no rights of disfranchising members except for non-payment of calls, (S. C. L. 68, Matter of New York, etc., Site Co., 145 App. Div. 623, 130 N.

Y. Supp. 414), or of assessments duly levied on the stock of moneyed corporations, unless such power is conferred by its charter, or by the general law in force at the time of its creation, or perhaps by a by-law consented to by all the stockholders. In re Long Island Railroad Co., 19 Wend. 37.

Instalments of subscriptions, except from the subscribers to the certificate of incorporation, do not become due until a resolution has been passed by the board of directors, fixing the time and the instalment. S. C. L. 68.

Bouton v. Dry Dock etc. Co., 4 E. D. Smith 420. No notice of this resolution is required to be given preliminary to bringing action to collect the instalment. Lake Ont. etc. 

Co. v. Mason, 16 N. Y. 451. United Growers Co. v. Eisner, 22 App. Div. 1, 47 N. Y. Supp. 906. Though the subscription agreement of a foreign corporation provides that subscriptions shall be payable only as required by the board of directors, the subscription is deemed payable on demand, and a court of the corporations domicile may direct the payment to an assignee of the corporation of the entire amount. Subscriptions are assignable. McNelies v. Stillman, 172 App. Div. 307, 158 N. Y. Supp. 428. Where otherwise limited by charter, stockholders by-law, or the subscription agreement, the board's resolution may not require payment in toto, at once, nor, where the subscription agreement required one-third to be paid down and the remainder as called for by the board, neither the board nor the court may regard the contract as one for the absolute payment of the entire subscription at once, or as soon as all the stock is subscribed. Williams v. Taylor, 120 N. Y. 244. 

Failure to pay any call for instalments on unpaid shares of stock may result in forfeiture. S. C. L. 68. Sigua Iron 

Co. v. Brown, 171 N. Y. 488. The call is the preliminary corporate act to forfeiture of stock. It consists of (1) a notice, (2) served on the stockholder in default, requiring payment within 60 days from service at a place specified, and stating that unless the aforesaid instalment is paid his shares and previous payments will be forfeited. 

The call must (1) be in writing; (2) be served personally or by mail, and if by mail, be directed to the stockholder's last known post office address; (3) state the place where payment is to be made; (4) state that on failure to pay, his

shares and all previous payments will be forfeited; (5) after the expiration of the sixty days, the board of directors should pass a resolution declaring the forfeiture. Mat ter of New York etc. Site Co., supra. Armleder Motor Truck 

Co. v. Barnes, supra. Stock thus forfeited may be reissued. S. C. L. 68. If the stock of a corporation is not shown to have a market value, an action may properly be maintained for an accounting and to restrain the corporation from forfeiting the stock for non-payment of an assessment. 

Schultz v. German-American Real Estate Co., 21 App. Div. 

163, 47 N. Y. Supp. 500. (6) The call must be uniform and equally imposed. If some subscribers have paid more than their share equity will give relief. Nassau Bank v. Anglo- 

American Land, M. and A. Co., 189 U. S. 221. Great Western Tel. Co. v. Purdy, 162 U. S. 329. The words in S. C. L. 

68, "subscriptions to the shares of a corporation” limit the application of the section to subscriptions made after incorporation. (7) All calls must be for lawful purposes of the corporation. The presumption of regularity applies in favor of the call, but the presumption may be rebutted. 

Proper purposes include, among other things, expenses of incorporating and organizing, debts, expenses of business, exhaustion of funds, or creation of a fund to carry on business. Bank of China v. Morse, 168 N. Y. 458.

The resolutions must be passed at valid meetings where a quorum was present, and must be supported by a majority of a quorum. The resolution need not state the person to whom payment is to be made, for the statute only requires that the notice served shall state the place. Schenectady & 

Saratoga P. R. Co. v. Thatcher, 11 N. Y. 102. In re N. Y. & Wschtr. Townsite Co., supra. The statute for forfeiture is against common right and is strictly construed. Eastern 

Plank Rd. Co. v. Vaughan, 14 N. Y. 546. Mitchell v. Vt. 

Cop. Min. Co., 67 N. Y. 280. Though the "call" has been served, the corporation may sue on the subscription, forfeiture being only a cumulative remedy. Rensselaer & 

W. P. R. Co. v. Wetsel, 21 Barb. 56. Goshen & M. T. R. v. 

Hurtin, 9 Johns. 217. Herkimer M. & H. Co. v. Small, 21 Wend. 273. Mann v. Currie, 2 Barb. 294. Harlem Canal 

Co. v. Spear, 2 N. Y. Super. 548. 

Stock may be sold at forfeiture sale for less than par.

14 C. J. § 642 (75). But under the statute, no sale is necessary to avoid the stockholders rights. If a sale is had and the amount realized plus the sums paid is either less or greater than the amount which the defaulting shareholder subscribed, the latter is not liable for the deficiency, nor entitled to any overplus. Jenkins v. Union T. Rd., 1 Cai. 

Cas. 86, Ft. Edwd. etc. Plk. Rd. Co., supra, Cady's Cas. p. 

374. Weeks v. Silver Islet Consol. Min. Co., 55 N. Y. 

Super. 1, 8 N. Y. St. Rep. 110, affd. 120 N. Y. 620. The stockholder is liable for his subscription tho the capital stock has been reduced by amendment. Myers v. Sturges, 197 N. Y. 526, 90 N. E. 1162. In Mills v. Stewart, 41 N. Y. 

384, the court, speaking of collusive forfeitures made for the purpose of affording the subscriber a defense against creditors of the corporation, said: "The power to forfeit, like the power to manage all the affairs of the corporation, is vested in the directors upon the assumption that they will exercise it in the best manner practicable for the promotion of the interest of the company and its creditors; that they will not forfeit the stock unless the interest of all will be promoted thereby. Should they forfeit it for the purpose of defrauding the corporation, or any creditor, such forfeiture would, for that reason, be set aside.”

A delivery of stock to one who is not a subscriber, (or when the subscription is invalid), at the request of the promoter, does not render the one receiving it liable. The doctrine of Lawrence v. Fox, 20 N. Y. 268, has no application. Sanders v. Proctor, 172 App. Div. 713, 158 N. Y. 

Supp. 433, affd. 225 N. Y. 682. If it were treasury stock, its mere receipt would imply a contract to pay. Ib. An agent who subscribes for an undisclosed principal, pledges his own credit and may be held as a subscriber by the corporation or by creditors. Mann v. Currie, supra. Stover v. Flack, 30 N. Y. 64. Orr v. Bigelow, 14 N. Y. 556. Union 

Hotel Co. v. Hersee, supra. Burr v. Wilcox, supra.

The subscriber's own omission to follow the form prescribed by his subscription agreement is no defense to him to an action to collect calls. Thus, where he had omitted to pay down 10% in cash on subscribing as at that time required by the statute, his subscription was held binding. 

Jeffery v. Selwyn, 220 N. Y. 77, 115 N. E. 275.
