§ 135. To Act in Relation to the Ordinary Business of the Corporation.

The charter of every corporation determines the extent to which stockholders, individually or acting as a collective body, can interfere in the management. The statute in most states confines the management and control to the board of directors, the presence of all the members being required on comparatively few occasions, when acts are to be authorized vitally affecting the corporate interests. G. C. L. 27, M. C. L. 

45, 46. The board of directors are the agents of the corporation strictly, and not of the stockholders, having original and not derived authority, but like other officers of the corporation, they are special and not general agents. 

Adriance v. Roome, 52 Barb. 399. G. C. L. 14 (5). See generally, Bank of China, etc. v. Morse, 168 N. Y. 458, 56 

L. R. A. 139, 61 N. E. 774. Jacobus v. Diamond Soda W. 

Mfg. Co., 94 App. Div. 366, 88 N. Y. Supp. 302. The whole title to corporate property is in the corporation, and the shareholders are neither tenants in common, nor in any 211

legal sense the owners of it. U. S. Radiator Co. v. State, 208 N. Y. at p. 152.

The general rule, as more fully stated in Continental Sec. 

Co. v. Belmont, 206 N. Y. 7, Cady's Cas. p. 456 may be summarized under the following heads: 1. The stockholders cannot interfere or act in relation to ordinary business, and have no general power of initiative. Stockholders acts, with reference to details of corporate business, amount only to an assent, request, or recommendation. The decision rests with the board of directors. For instance, the stockholders cannot bind the corporation by making a lease, even though the directors are also stockholders. Couro v. Port Henry 

Iron Co., 12 Barb. 27, cf. Simmons v. Sisson, 26 N. Y. 264. 

Palmer v. Ring, 113 App. Div. 643, 99 N. Y. Supp. 290. 

2. Statutes vest certain authority in stockholders, such as consenting to the mortgage, lease or sale, amending the certificate of incorporation, etc. S. C. L. 16, 35, 36, 37, 86, 105; G. C. L. 50, 215 etc. These statutes are mainly permissive or confirmatory, and the acts under and necessary to effectuate the consent are performed by the board of directors, not by the stockholders. 

3. Stockholders indirectly control the corporation through their power to elect directors. This is the stockholders' "supreme right and main protection." Stokes v. 

Continental Tr. Co., 186 N. Y. 285, Cady's Cas. p. 436. Any number of stockholders may act in concert to control corporate policy through the directors, provided their agreement to do so does not contravene the charter or a statute, or involve a fraud upon the corporation or upon the other stockholders for the benefit of the contracting stockholders or strangers. Havemeyer v. Havemeyer, 43 N. Y. Super. 

506, affd. 86 N. Y. 618. In re Mitchell's Est., 114 Misc. 370, 186 N. Y. Supp. 666. Venner v. Chi. City R. Co., 258 Ill. 523.

Thompson v. Thompson Carnation Co., 279 Ill. 54. Palm baum v. Magerlsky, 217 Mass. 306. Winsor v. Commonwealth Coal Co., 63 Wash. 62. 

4. Stockholders by a majority vote may ratify acts of directors that are irregular, such as acts passed by less than a majority of a quorum, or by irregularly elected directors, or by directors having an interest adverse to the corporation

-in other words, acts that are legal but voidable and their ratification is binding on the dissenting minority. Stockholders cannot bind the minority by ratifying acts that were illegal or a fraud upon the rights of minority. Pollitz v. Wabash R. R. Co., 207 N. Y. 113, 176 Fed. 333, Cady's 

Cas. at pp. 466, 468. Schwab v. Potter Co., 194 N. Y. 409, Cady's Cas. p. 542. 5. 

Performance of powers inherent in the corporation, but, for some peculiar circumstance, not vested in the board of directors, may be authorized or even performed by the stockholders. Thus, where the board, by reason of personal interest, could not properly vote to discontinue an action, the majority of stockholders might authorize its discontinuance by their vote. Socorro Mt. Min. Co. v. Preston, 17 Misc. 220, 40 N. Y. Supp. 1040.

The foregoing rules must not be confused with the principle that permits a stockholder to sue in his own right to restrain or annul acts fraudulent as to him. Kelly v. 

Mariposa Land & Min. Co., 4 Hun 632. Whatever the stockholders might have done by the requisite vote at a formal meeting they may generally do by unanimous consent by agreement between themselves without holding a meeting. 

Elyea v. Lehigh Salt Min. Co., 169 N. Y. 29, 61 N. E. 992.

Thus, they may authorize that the corporation's assets be disposed of, all creditors being taken care of. Ib. The statute expressly authorizes a waiver in writing by every member in person or by proxy of notice of meetings. 

G. C. L. 31, 19. 

§ 136. Right to a Stock Certificate. 

While it is true in a legal sense that it is not necessary for the subscriber, in order to be a stockholder, to have the certificate of the stock which was entered upon the stockbooks in his name, nevertheless among business men, the certificate of stock is regarded as representing the stock and the title thereto, and the failure of the stockholder to demand it is some evidence to show that he did not regard himself as the owner. Jackson v. 23rd St. Ry. Co., 88 N. Y. 520. 

Burr v. Wilcox, 22 N. Y. 551, Cady's Cas. p. 380. Brown v. 

Superus Co., 181 App. Div. 420, 168 N. Y. Supp. 918. The

certificate, duly issued, estops the corporation. A certificate of stock must be issued by the corporation on demand by a subscriber who has paid his subcription, and, if refused, either the subscriber or the transferee of the subscription may compel issuance by suit in equity against the corporation, or may sue at law in assumpsit for the value of the stock at the highest market price between the time of the refusal and the commencement of the action, or, in his equity suit, he may ask in the alternative for the stock certificate or for damages if it cannot be delivered. Moores v. Cits. Natl. Bank, 111 U. S. 156, 165. Kortright v. Buff. 

Com. Bank, 20 Wend. 91, 22 Wend. 348, 34 Am. Dec. 317. 

Rice v. Rockefeller, 134 N. Y. 174. Natl. Bank v. Watsontown Bank, 105 U. S. 217. Pacific Natl. Bank v. Eaton, 141 U. S. 227. Thayer v. Butler, 141 U. S. 234. Butler v. 

Eaton, 141 U. S. 240. Butler v. Wright, 186 N. Y. 259. 

Rawl v. Baker-Vawter Co., 187 App. Div. 330, 176 N. Y. 

Supp. 189.

The damages for refusal to deliver a stock certificate is the market value of the shares at the date of refusal. Kortright v. Buff. Com. Bank, supra. Bank of Attica v. Mnfgrs. 

Bank, 220 N. Y. 505. If the complaint is in the alternative for specific performance or for damages, a judgment for damages is improper unless it appears that the corporation is unable, all its authorized shares being issued, to deliver the shares. Otter v. Brevoort Pet. Co., 50 Barb. 247. If the one whom the corporation refuses to recognize elects to treat the refusal as a conversion, he thereby regards his ownership as ended, and cannot maintain action for dividends declared after the commencement of his suit and before the entry of judgment. Hughes v. Vt. Copper Mfg. 

Co., 72 N. Y. 207. Mandamus will not lie to compel the issuance of the certificate. Travis v. Knox Terpezone Co., 215 N. Y. 259, Cady's Cas. p. 470.

On the other hand, if the plaintiff is only the equitable owner of shares standing in the name of another who claims title, and the plaintiff has no proof of legal title in the corporate records, he cannot recover damages from the corporation on its refusal to issue the certificate, for the corporation is not bound to take on itself the peril of deciding between

rival claimants. Natl. Bank v. Lake Shore, etc., R. R. Co., 21 Ohio St. 221.

As to creditors of the corporation, the entry of the subscriber's name in the stockbook is prima facie evidence, and the stockholder has the burden of proving the transfer of the stock by him to another. Richards v. Robin, 175 App. 

Div. 296, 162 N. Y. Supp. 12, affd. 225 N. Y. 719.

Under familiar principles of equity, the purchaser of stock from a stockholder cannot succeed in maintaining an action of specific performance to compel the seller to deliver the stock certificate unless the stock has a special or peculiar value which is not readily obtainable in the market, or it otherwise appears that compensation in damages is not a complete and adequate remedy. Butler v. Wright, supra. 

Waddle v. Cabana, 220 N. Y. 8. Donovan v. Powers Filius 

Products, Inc., 111 Misc. 276, 181 N. Y. Supp. 157. Bateman v. Strauss, 86 App. Div. 540, 83 N. Y. Supp. 785.

Godley's Outl. of Equity, Ch. XV. 

The necessary statutory requirements of all stock certificates are: (1) In writing; (2) Signatures; (3) Seal of corporation; (4) All preferences of all classes of stock to be stated in every certificate; and they may further contain (5) a copy of S. C. L. 66 or of its substance if stock is not to be transferred while a debt by the stockholder to the corporation is unpaid; (6) A provision that it is transferable only on the books of the corporation; (7) A statement that it is fully paid and nonassessable, or only partly paid; and (8) Any matter of which it is desired to give notice to the stockholders. S. C. L. 65, 66, 47, 10, 74. G. C. L. 14.

Cowles v. Cowles Rty. Co., 201 App. Div. 460, 194 N. Y. 

Supp. 546. Hassel v. Poole, 214 App. Div. 654, 212 N. Y. 

Supp. 561, Cady's Cas. p. 391. In Hassel v. Poole, supra, it was held that a by-law printed on the face of the certificate requiring stockholders to offer stock to the corporation before selling it to others was binding upon the purchaser; and in Moses v. Soule, supra, Cady's Cas. p. 247, that a similar provision giving the corporation and also other stockholders opportunity to purchase was binding on purchasers and was not void as against public policy. See

Claude Neon Lights v. Fed. Elec. Co., 135 Misc. 113, 236 

N. Y. Supp. 692.

The statute permits the corporators to provide in the certificate of incorporation for the issuance in the discretion of directors of subsequent series of preferred stock, provided the designations, preferences, privileges and voting powers, and the restrictions and qualifications, be stated both in the certificate of incorporation and in every certificate of stock issued. S. C. L. 65.

S. C. L. 65 requires the stock certificate to be signed by two executive officers of the classes named, except where it is signed by a transfer agent or transfer clerk, when the signatures of the executive officers named may be in facsimile. These and the further provision of the statute that, if an officer's term of office terminates in any way before the certificate which he has theretofore signed in blank or on which the facsimile aforesaid has been placed, the certificate shall nevertheless be valid, are affirmative of provisions once ordinarily found in by-laws; pursuant to which it was held that the ordinary rule that an officer employed to sell might not sell to himself, did not require another or different form of certificate where the officer was the purchaser, and that the aforesaid officers might issue certificates to themselves in the same manner as to other stockholders. Titus v. Grt. W. Turnp. Rd., 61 N. Y. 237. 

§ 137. Right to Transfer Shares. 

This right is so inherent to the ownership of stock, considered as personal property of the stockholder, that any by-law restraining transfer and amounting to more than a reasonable regulation of the method is void, unless contained in the charter or consented to. G. C. L. 14 authorizing a corporation to make by-laws for the transfer of its stock, and a somewhat similar provision contained in S. C. L. 65 must be construed to permit reasonable regulation only. Thus, it has been held, that even a consent in advance by the stockholder to be bound by bylaws thereafter regularly passed, does not empower the corporation to do more in the way of regulating the transfer of stock than to prescribe the officer by whom the stock shall be transferred and the mode of its transfer, and does not au-

thorize the corporation to require as a prerequisite of transfer that the stockholder accept a stock certificate containing a new by-law, making the stock assessable at $10 per year. 

Kinnan v. Sullivan County Club, 26 App. Div. 213, 50 N. Y.

Supp. 95. Bloomingdale v. Bloomingdale, 107 Misc. 646, 

177 N. Y. Supp. 646.

No private corporation by repeal or amendment of a bylaw may impair the rights which have been given and be come vested. Cowles v. Cowles Realty Co., 201 App. Div. 

460, 194 N. Y. Supp. 546.

S. C. L. 10, providing that no transfers shall be valid until registered, is affirmative of the common law and is construed to be effectual only for the protection of the corporation in such matters as the payment of dividends and giving notices to the registered holder. Gilbert v. Manchester etc. Co., 11 Wend. 627. N. Y. etc. R. R. Co. v. 

Schuyler, 34 N. Y. 30, Cady's Cas. p. 473. Moses v. Soule, supra.

No share is transferable unless all previous calls are fully paid. S. C. L. 65. Since the stockholder's indivisible interest in the assets upon dissolution subject to creditor's rights is what is represented by his stock certificate, and since this interest is salable despite the prohibition of the statute, it follows that an assignee of stock, who becomes such before a call duly made is paid, has all the rights of the original stockholder; and therefore the assignee may sue in behalf of the corporation to set aside a fraudulent conveyance of its assets. Gilbert v. Manchester Iron Mfg. 

Co., 11 Wend. 627. Pollitz v. Gould, 202 N. Y. 11, 94 N. E. 

1088, Cady's Cas. p. 462.

If the vendee neglects to have the transfer registered, he is liable to the vendor for calls thereafter made, which the vendor has been obliged to pay by reason of his name still remaining upon the books. Gaffney v. Peo. Tr. Co. of Bing., 191 App. Div. 697, 182 N. Y. Supp. 451, affd. 231 N. Y. 

577. Johnson v. Underhill, 52 N. Y. 203. If the corporation registers the new owner, the vendor is exonerated from liability to the corporation for calls thereafter made by reason of its acceptance of the other, and the liability is shifted to the vendee. Signa Iron Co. v. Brown, 171 N. Y.

488. Isham v. Buckingham, supra. Roch. & K. F. Land 

Co. v. Raymond, 158 N. Y. 576, 53 N. E. 507. This principle does not affect the accrued liability of the vendor to creditors. S. C. L. 73.

The transferror, even if the transfer is registered by the company, remains liable to it for all calls made at any time up to the date of registration, but the transferee is impliedly liable to the vendor for all calls made after the date of sale.

The transferee is not liable to the corporation upon a call made before the transfer, but the transferror is liable to it although the said call, though made before the sale, was not payable until after the transfer. The corporation has the right to require the one to pay the call, whose name appears on its books as stockholder at the time when the call is made, Schdy. etc. Plank Rd. v. Thatcher, 11 N. Y. 102.

If the transferror should later pay the call, the corporation would be obliged to credit the shares of the transferee with the amount, and, therefore, there would seem to be an implied obligation of the transferee to indemnify the transferror. In the absence of an express agreement, the fair implication is that the vendee contracted to buy only the interest which the vendor at that date possessed. The rights and liabilities of the vendor and the vendee should appear by the terms of their contract and not be left to implication. 1 Morawetz on Corps. § 176. Roch. Dry Goods 

Co. v. Fahy, 111 App. Div. 748, 97 N. Y. Supp. 1013, affd. 

188 N. Y. 629.

Transferrors of stock must provide and pay for stock transfer stamps, and the transferee may insist on registration of certificate with necessary stamps provided. T. L. 

270. In re Shelley's Est., 134 Misc. 265, 234 N. Y. Supp. 497. 

It is not essential that an assignment of shares of stock of the corporation shall be inscribed on the certificate itself or on its back. If contained in a separate paper which identifies by description the stock intended to be assigned, it is sufficient to pass title to the transferee. Such separate powers and assignments are sometimes called "fly powers." 

Talcott v. Standard Oil Co., 149 App. Div. 694, 134 N. Y.

Supp. 617. 

Smith v. Savin, 141 N. Y. 315. Carlisle v. 

Norris, 215 N. Y. 400, 109 N. E. 564. 

By T. L. 278 a transfer of stock not having affixed a transfer stamp, cannot be received in evidence, though it is a valid conveyance of the stock. Ambrasius v. Ambrasius, 167 App. Div. 244, 152 N. Y. Supp. 562. Bean v. Flint, 204 

N. Y. 153, 97 N. E. 490. 

§ 138. Right to Transfer as Affected by Insolvency of Corporation. 

S. C. L. 15, which forbids a transfer of stock in contemplation of the insolvency of the corporation, must be construed as only restraining the transfer in a case where the transfer of stock would tend to hamper creditors. Hence, if the subscription is fully paid, the stockholder may transfer for the purpose of terminating his position as director and the transfer is valid. The effect of S. C. L. 15 was to change the burden of proof of the bona fides to the transferee. Before the section was passed, a transfer to a responsible party terminated the liability of the stockholder to creditors, but the burden of proof was on the creditor. 

Nathan v. Whitlock, 9 Pai. Ch. 152. Billings v. Robinson, 94 N. Y. 412. S. C. L. 15 puts the burden on the transferee to prove the bona fides. Sinclair v. Fuller, 158 N. Y. 607. 

Richards v. Robin, 175 App. Div. 296, 162 N. Y. Supp. 12, affd. 225 N. Y. 719. A binding "option" when "accepted" does not operate as a transfer of stock, but only as creating another "contract." Heller v. Pope, 250 N. Y. 132, 164 

N. E. 881. All-Amer. Securities Co., Inc. v. Foundation Co., 211 App. Div. 684, 208 N. Y. Supp. 328. 

§ 139. Right to Transfer as Affected by Agreement. 

The existence of an agreement between the vendor and a director that stock held by either should be for their joint benefit binds only the parties thereto, and does not bind their estates. Cole v. Levy, 212 App. Div. 84, 208 N. Y. 

Supp. 481. Moses v. Soule, supra; Hassel v. Poole, supra. 

Havemeyer v. Havemeyer, supra. See Chap. XIV. infra. 

§ 140. Same. Lost or Stolen Certificates. 

Certificates of stock were not negotiable instruments at common law. Mech. Bank v. N. Y. & N. H. R. Co., 13 N. Y.

599. Hudson Trust Co. v. Amer. Linseed Co., 232 N. Y. 

350, Cady's Cas. p. 488. Amer. Press. Assn. v. Brantingham, 75 App. Div. 435, 78 N. Y. Supp. 305.

At common law, it was held that where a certificate endorsed in blank by the first owner, though bearing on its face "transferable only on the books of the company," was entrusted by the owner to one who wrongfully transferred it by larceny of misappropriation to a bona fide holder, the legal title passed. The possession of the certificate, thus properly endorsed, was prima facie evidence of either the ownership or the authority of the wrongdoer, so that the owner, who put the wrongdoer in a position to commit the fraud, should be the one to suffer. McHenry v. Jewett, 90 N. Y. 58. Leitch v. Wells, 48 N. Y. 585. McNeil v. 10th 

Natl. Bank, 46 N. Y. 325, Cady's Cas. p. 494. But a bona fide purchaser of a certificate stolen by larceny of taking, or where the facts did not estop the owner, got no title. 

Barstow v. Savage Mfg. Co., 64 Cal. 388. Anderson v. 

Nicholas, 18 N. Y. Super. 121, affd. 28 N. Y. 600. Knox v. 

Eden Musee A. Co., 148 N. Y. 441, 42 N. E. 988. Treadwell v. Clark, 190 N. Y. 51, 82 N. E. 505. Hannahs v. Ham. 

Typ. Co., 158 App. Div. 620, 143 N. Y. Supp. 939. Mere possession of a stock certificate unendorsed and without a fly power, gives no apparent authority to the person in possession to transfer it, and a transferee would get only such title as the transferror had. Wood v. Stoneham, 206 

App. Div. 507, 201 N. Y. Supp. 483. 

C. P. A. 333 providing for recovery upon a lost negotiable instrument does not apply to an action by a bondholder to recover on lost interest coupons which were non-negotiable, but only to negotiable bonds. Erb v. Banco di Napoli, 243 

N. Y. 45, 152 N. E. 460. Rolston v. Cent. Pk. N. & E. R. R. 

Co., 21 Misc. 439, 47 N. Y. Supp. 650. 

S. C. L. 75, 76, and P. P. L. 1178, empower the supreme court to order the corporation to issue a new certificate in place of one that has been lost. The necessary steps are as 

1. Demand a new certificate from the corporation, giving proof of the facts establishing the loss. The corporation's refusal is a necessary preliminary to the proceeding. In

re Coats, 75 App. Div. 469, 78 N. Y. Supp. 425. If the corporation grants the demand it will be liable to any third person who, by reason of fraud or mistake is the true owner of the certificate, allegedly "lost." Harvey v. Guar. Tr. 

Co., 134 Misc. 417, 236 N. Y. Supp. 37, 56. Reynolds v. 

T. G. & T. Co., 240 N. Y. 257, 148 N. E. 514. 

2. Get an order to show cause from special term on a verified petition by the owner stating the facts mentioned in S. C. L. 75. Serve a copy of the petition and show-cause order ten days before the return day mentioned therein on the corporation, and file the original order with proof of service in the office of the clerk of the court. 

3. Upon the return, the court may not proceed further without taking testimony to prove the facts of the petition. 

In re Speir, 69 App. Div. 149, 74 N. Y. Supp. 555. S. C. L. 

76 then provides that if the court is satisfied that, a) the petitioner is the lawful owner of the shares or any part thereof; b) the certificate is lost and cannot after due diligence be found; c) no sufficient cause is shown why a new certificate should not be issued, it shall order the corporation to issue a new certificate upon the deposit by the petitioner in a public office of indemnity for the true owner if he should be thereafter found. Judicial orders under which a court by virtue of a statute transfers property belonging to one who was not a party or privy, to another who is not entitled to it, have usually been held nullities, on which no one has a right to rely. Losee v. Stanley, 147 N. Y. 560. 

Howell v. Leavitt, 95 N. Y. 617, resulting in Mygatt v. 

Coe, 124 N. Y. 212, 142 N. Y. 78, 147 N. Y. 456, 152 N. Y. 

457. S. C. L. 75 and 76 are, however, component parts of the charter of the corporation of which the stockholder has notice when he became such, and by which he is bound. 

It has been held that the court may direct the publication of notice either before or after making the show-cause order, so as to give some publicity for the benefit of nonparties. In re Coats, supra. The proceeding is constitutional as to domestic corporations only. Mtr. of Ostrander, 206 App. Div. 362, 201 N. Y. Supp. 423. In re Bernhard, 209 App. Div. 808, 205 N. Y. Supp. 195. If some of the shares are shown to be in the possession of another, the

petition may be denied. 

Biglin v. Friendship Assn., 46 

Hun 223, 11 N. Y. St. R. 566. 

P. P. L. 178 expressly provides that if the corporation has transferred the original certificate, or if it has come into the hands of a holder for value without notice of the proceedings or of the issuance of the new certificate, the bond aforesaid shall not relieve the corporation from liability in damages to him. Thus the corporation may be liable under facts similar to those in the Coats or Reynolds cases, supra, where it issued duplicate non-negotiable bonds in a case where the original bonds had not, as it was eventually proved, actually been lost; or where the stock endorsed in blank, has been transferred and delivered to a bona fide purchaser for value and without notice by a finder of the endorsed certificate that was lost. Sec. 139 infra. In 

Giffon v. Amer. Safety Razor Corp., 134 Misc. 140, 234 N. Y.

Supp. 646, plaintiff's husband abstracted her stock certificate, forged her endorsement and obtained new certificates which then passed from him into the hands of bona fide purchasers, and these last obtained a registry. The court held that, on the weight of authority, the purchasers were to be protected in their possession of the stock, and that the plaintiff, the original owner, was limited to money damages. As to intermediate dividends paid the purchasers, the court held, without so deciding, that the plaintiff would be sufficiently compensated by an allowance of interest from the date of conversion.

The common law rule was that the party who purchased from the thief and obtained registry had no rights except as against his transferror. But subsequent innocent transferees, who purchased from the said innocent transferee and received from him the certificates issued by the corporation were fully protected, both as against the corporation, and against the true owner, who lost his stock by the forgery. The decisions were based on the rule of estoppel which operated against the corporation, that issued the new certificates, on trade customs, and on the relationship existing between the rightful stockholder and his corporation. 

The purchaser from a registered owner need only search the corporate records back to the issuance of the certificate

bought by him. This rule is applied in New York in cases of lost or stolen stock of foreign corporations formed in states which, unlike New York, have not adopted the Uni form Stock Transfer Act. Such a state is Delaware. Rand v. Hercules Powder Co., 129 Misc. 891, 223 N. Y. Supp. 383.

If the corporation has unissued stock, the original stockholder may enforce his rights to a stock certificate from that supply. Giffon and Rand cases, supra. 

The burden of proof is on the original owner to defeat the legal title of the person having possession of certificates of stock, duly issued by the corporation. Lewis v. Canadian 

P. Ry. Co., 39 F. (2d.) 834, citing Travis v. Knox Terpezone 

Co., 215 N. Y. 259, Cady's Cas. p. 470.

The degree of diligence in the search necessary to satisfy the court of the loss of the certificate is proportioned to the value of the certificate. Richardson on Evi. § 222. In most cases the court will require, at least, proof of enquiry of all persons shown in the stockbook as prior owners of the shares, and of all persons proved to have been ever in possession. 

§ 140a. Same. Effect of the Uniform Stock Transfer Act. 

The statute, adopted by many states and by New York in 1909 as Art. VI of the Personal Property Law, codifies some parts of the law relating to transfers, and affects changes in the direction of providing a kind of negotiability of the same nature in the case of stock certificates duly endorsed, or "bearer" certificates, and corporate securities not negotiable in form, as provided for other instruments by the Uniform Bill of Lading Act, the Uniform Warehouse Receipt Act, etc. The general scheme of the Uniform Stock 

Transfer Act is to make delivery of the certificate the transfer thereof, irrespective of the unlawfulness of the possession of the one making delivery, provided only that the certificate was either endorsed, in blank or to a specified person, by the person named in the certificate as owner, or was accompanied by the usual fly power signed by said person, assigning the certificate in blank or to a specified person. P. P. L. 162, 166. The result, summarized, is an estoppel of the original owner to claim as against an honest purchaser, mortgagee, or pledgee, "for value in good faith

without notice," an endorsed certificate or one in the form aforesaid (§§ 183, 168), even though the original owner was not guilty of negligence. The delivery by a person "having no authority from the owner or from the person purporting to transfer the title" (§ 166) transfers the certificate, permitting a thief, finder, or impersonator to give better title than he had, and extinguishing the distinction between the effect on title where the certificate had been obtained by larceny of taking as distinguished from larceny of misappropriating. The act supersedes all inconsistent provisions in the statutes, charter, or by laws, such as those requiring registering or other things than delivery, and is to be construed as declaratory of the common law, and uniformly with the construction of similar statutes of those states which enact it. P. P. L. 185, 180, 186c. The statute preserves common law rights of the original owner (where the rights of a purchaser for value in good faith without notice have not intervened) where endorsement or delivery was procured by fraud, duress or mistake, or delivery made without authority or without consideration, providing there has been no waiver or laches, and provides the remedies of enjoining transfer, or impounding the certificate. P. P. L. 

167-169. The powers of infants and of others lacking full capacity are declared not to be enlarged by the statute, nor those of executors, trustees, administrators or guardians, etc. P. P. L. 163. Casey v. Kastel, 237 N. Y. 305. Certificates of stock issued prior to 1909, the date of adoption of the statute, are not affected by it, but are governed by the common law as before. P. P. L. 184.

Under the uniform stock transfer act, the common law rule as to title obtained by a purchaser by a larceny of misappropriation, remains unchanged. Nicholson v. Morgan, 196 N. Y. Supp. 147, Cady's Cas. p. 497. Turnbull v. 

Longacre Bank, 249 N. Y. 159, 163 N. E. 135. 

In Iowa Securities Corporation v. Ridgewood Nat. Bank, 106 Misc. 335, 175 N. Y. Supp. 776, Cady's Cas. p. 503, rescission or reclamation under the statute was denied where the certificate had come into the hands of a holder for value in good faith without notice.

The stockholder who takes the precaution of having only

the unendorsed certificate, free from fly power, in his possession, avoids the risks entailed on him by the statute, and one who steals such certificate from him can give no better title than a thief of any chattel (excepting only where new certificates have been obtained from the corporation by a later holder and transferred to bona fide purchasers, sec. 

138 supra). In Wood v. Stoneham, 206 App. Div. 507, 201

N. Y. Supp. 483, it was held that a transferee of unindorsed stock certificates who relies on a mere delivery is not protected by the provisions of the uniform stock transfer act, since the absence of either an indorsement or a written assignment or power of attorney gives notice to the transferee that he is taking only such title as the person had in whose name the certificates were issued. Consequently, where such certificates were issued by the corporation, but not delivered, and remained in its possession, and subsequently were pledged for a corporate debt by one of the corporation's agents acting without authority, a transferee of the certificates obtained only such rights as his transferor had, and was not entitled to hold them as against the corporation's receiver. See also Donaghue v. Di Giorgio 

Fruit Corporation, 225 App. Div. 81, 232 N. Y. Supp. 78. 

Ohio Match Sales Co. v. Everard, 211 N. Y. Supp. 856.

By P. P. L. 167 the indorsement of a certificate by the proper person is effectual though the indorsement or transfer was induced by fraud, duress or mistake. Jelenk v. 

Albert, 133 Misc. 28, 231 N. Y. Supp. 31. For a discussion of provisions of the factors act, warehouseman's receipt act, etc. similar to the uniform stock transfer act, see Sealy on

Bailments, and General Business Law, § § 90-147. 

The apparently drastic limitations on an owner's rights imposed by the statute are justified.

The purchaser in good faith for value without notice from a finder or a thief is entitled to be protected in some such way as others are protected by the factors act, or by purchase in market overt. The principle that "When one of two innocent parties must suffer through the fraud of a third, he shall bear the loss who enabled the fraud to be perpetrated," is justly applicable to an owner who does not surrender an endorsed stock certificate forthwith for

cancellation.

The latter has done something more than suffer loss by a sneak thief or a finder. He has allowed the innocent corporation to hold out the original owner to the world as the true owner, knowing that the corporation, by its books, still regarded him as the owner. 

Shares of stock are not negotiable instruments under the N. I. L. and are given only a limited negotiability by the statute. P. P. L. 186c. This negotiability is based on contract and estoppel in that the U. S. T. A. embodied in the P. P. L. is a part of the charter of every domestic corporation to which, of course, the stockholder impliedly assents. The familiar term "holder in due course," applicable to negotiable instruments, is nowhere used in the U. S. T. A. 

Orth v. Bell, 215 App. Div. 738, 212 N. Y. Supp. 726.

By P. P. L. 164 the corporation's common law right to hold the registered owner liable for calls and assessments, to pay him dividends, and to permit him to vote the shares, is expressly retained. 

§ 141. Same. Spurious Certificate or Forged Transfer. 

One who buys and pays value for spurious stock to an agent of the corporation who is duly authorized to issue stock, does not become a stockholder, and can not be admitted to a participation with the genuine and bona fide stockholders. The stock is equally spurious and void in the hands of his transferees. Mech. Bank v. N. Y. & N. H. 

R. R. Co., 13 N. Y. 599. 

Where the officer or agent, authorized to issue stock, forged the necessary signatures of other officers, and issued the stock to a bona fide purchaser, the latter, if the deception was not due to his own want of care, may hold the corporation liable in damages, or, if there is treasury stock that could be legally issued, require it to recognize him as a stockholder. Fifth Ave. Bank v. 42nd St. and Grand St. 

Fy. Co., supra, Cady's Cas. p. 484. Knox v. Eden Musee, supra. Jarvis v. Manhattan Beach Co., supra, Cady's Cas. p. 480. 

If the officer or agent had no authority to issue certificates of stock, but was employed to cancel certificates surrendered for transfer, and, instead of doing so, fraudulently issued the surrendered certificates or stole certificates signed in

blank and issued them, the purchasers deceived by him cannot recover damages from the corporation unless they are able to establish its negligence, for there was no agency of fact to issue the certificates, and no estoppel of the corporation by a holding out. Hudson Trust Co. v. Amer. Linseed Co., supra, Cady's Cas. p. 488.

The officers who issue spurious stock are liable therefor to every bona fide holder. Bruff v. Mali, 36 N. Y. 200. Also the purchaser has a cause of action against his vendor for breach of his implied warranties. P. P. L. 172. Shotwell v. Mali, 38 Barb. 445. These warranties are continuing warranties. Bassett v. Perkins, 65 Misc. 103, 119 N. Y. 

Supp. 354.

The corporation is liable to the lawful owner, if it transfers shares on a forged endorsement or power. Brisbane v. Del. &c. R. R. Co., 94 N. Y. 204. The corporation must pay to the lawful owner the dividends paid to the wrongful transferee. Pollock v. Natl. Bank, 7 N. Y. 274. The corporation may cancel the certificate which it issued on the surrender of the one that bore the forged transfer, for the transferee did not take it on faith of the corporation's act. 

If the new certificate has been transferred to a holder for value in good faith, the company cannot cancel. Pollock v. 

Natl. Bank, 7 N. Y. 274, P. P. L. 162, 168 (1), 177, 169.

The corporation is also liable if it transfers in violation of its own regulations to the stockholder's injury, for the performance of these is part of its contract; for instance, if it transfers stock and issues a new certificate without requiring a transfer on the books. Conklin v. 2d Natl. Bank, 45 N. Y. 655. Cushman v. Thayer Mfg. Co., 76 N. Y. 365, Cady's Cas. pp. 478-9. 

§ 142. Same. Overissued Stock. 

Stock issued by a corporation in excess of that authorized by the charter is void in the hands of the holder, and the fictitious certificates cannot make the holders stockholders. 

The corporation may bring suit to cancel the certificates, making all the holders thereof parties defendant; and the holders have a cause of action against the corporation for the damages they have suffered. N. Y. & N. H. R. R. v. 

Schuyler, supra, Cady's Cas. p. 473. Amer. Mac. Co. v.

Saumer, 174 N. Y. Supp. 183. Subsequent purchasers and transferees of the fictitious stock may also recover damages.

The holders have the burden of proving that the officer or agent who issued the stock had apparent authority to issue it; and it is no defense to the corporation that it, in fact, limited his authority to the issuance of valid stock, for the principle of agency applies that where an agent is authorized to act upon the concurrence of facts the existence of which are peculiarly within the personal knowledge of the agent, the apparent exercise of this power, accompanied with all the indicia of genuineness, renders the principal liable to those who act in good faith in the ordinary course of business. 5th Ave. Bank v. 42nd St. &c. Co., supra, Cady's Cas. p. 488. If the fictitious certificates are delivered upon the surrender of good stock, they may be valid. The corporation will not be liable to persons who have suffered no damages, such as those who took the fictitious stock as security for an antecedent debt, or those who have not paid for it. N. Y. & N. H. R. Co. v. Schuyler, supra, Cady's Cas. at p. 474. Ryder v. Bushwick R. Co., 134 N. Y. 83. The issuance of the fictitious certificates does not impair the legal rights of owners of the genuine stock that was issued under the charter; but if an owner deposits his genuine stock with another as collateral, and the latter receives stock issued in its place, which turns out to be fictitious, and the genuine certificate is then or later delivered by the corporation to a bona fide holder, the latter gets good title. Ib. p. 477. 

§ 143. 

Right of Members to Inspect Stock Books. 

At common law a stockholder had the right to inspect the stock books of his corporation. Matter of Steinway, 159 N. Y. 250. Hitchcock v. Union Ferry Co., 157 App. Div. 

328, 142 N. Y. Supp. 247. Statutory legislation has amplified this right. S. C. L. 10, 113. Peo. v. Consol. Natl. Bank, 105 App. Div. 409, 94 N. Y. Supp. 173. Peo. v. Kelseville, etc., R. Co., 106 App. Div. 349, 94 N. Y. Supp. 355. At common law the power to compel an exercise of the right was discretionary, while in a case brought within the terms of the statute it is mandatory. Peo. v. Consol. Natl Bank, supra. The right of the stockholders to inspect is not affected by the fact that his interest in the corporation is

small. Matter of Steinway, 159 N. Y. 520. The officers of a corporation before granting the right of inspection may require reasonable proof of an unknown demandant that he is the person named in the certificate of stock presented. 

Theile v. Merlis, 85 Misc. 351, 147 N. Y. Supp. 405.

A writ of mandamus was the early remedy to compel the exhibition of stock books for inspection, but the present remedy is motion at Special Term. C. P. A. 1313. Matter of Steinway, supra. Matter of Taylor, 230 N. Y. 556. An application for the order when not in good faith but for an ulterior purpose should be denied. Peo. v. American Press Ass'n, 148 App. Div. 651, 133 N. Y. Supp. 216; 

Peo. v. National Park Bank, 122 App. Div. 350, 107 N. Y.

Supp. 369. People ex rel. Britton v. American Press Ass'n, 

133 N. Y. Supp. 216.

S. C. L. 113 gives the right of inspection of the stock book of a foreign corporation. Henby v. Babcock, etc. Co., 196 N. Y. 302.

The statutory inspection is not open to all stockholders but only to persons who are either: 

1. Stockholders of record for at least 6 months preceding the demand; or, 2. Persons authorized by the holders of 5% of all the outstanding stock of a domestic corporation (3% of a foreign corporation); or, 3. A judgment creditor.

The inspection is limited to 3 business hours per day. 

The corporation that neglects to keep a stock book, or to permit inspection, forfeits to the state $50 for each day it shall so refuse, and the agent $50 for each refusal to the person entitled to inspect. It is a defense to any action for penalties that the person suing has within 2 years offered for sale any list of stockholders of any corporation or has aided or abetted another in doing so. Bartels v. Borgstede, 169 App. Div. 421, 155 N. Y. Supp. 322. Poleti v. Poleti, 193 App. Div. 738, 184 N. Y. Supp. 368. Skinner v. Home 

Bank, 190 App. Div. 187, 179 N. Y. Supp. 567.

The refusal of a proper demand to inspect the stockbook is a misdemeanor under Penal Law, § 665, and the officer is guilty even though he refrained from refusing the

inspection and merely prevented it. Peo. v. Bowie, 166 

N. Y. Supp. 905. 

§ 144. To Inspect Other Corporate Books and Papers. 

Stockholders, being the real owners, are entitled by natural right to know all about the affairs of the corporation. 

Farmers L. & T. Co. v. Pierson, 130 Misc. 110, 222 N. Y. 

Supp. 532. E converso, the business cannot well be managed by the board if stockholders are permitted to meddle. 

G. C. L. 27. The common law allowed the stockholder to inspect only such books and papers as would be necessary for the stockholder's proper information, after due request by him to the corporation, setting forth a proper purpose, a proper time and a proper place. In re Steinway, 159 

N. Y. 250, 53 N. E. 1103. The early rule, that one cannot examine the books of his adversary to obtain evidence against him, gave way to the interest of stockholders to ascertain that corporate affairs were not wastefully mismanaged. Burden v. Burden, 42 Hun 655, 3 N. Y. St. Rep. 

776, affd. 106 N. Y. 668. The purpose assigned by the stockholder as a ground must relate to the interests of the stockholders as such, and not to adverse personal interests of the stockholder. Peo. ex rel. Lehman v. Consol. Fire A. 

Co., 145 App. Div. 427, 127 N. Y. Supp. 348. Where there are any extraordinary circumstances, the right of inspection is readily granted, even to a small stockholder: such as, that he has been unable to get any information of the company's condition; that no dividends have been paid; that no financial report has been made for more than a year; and the hearsay statements made by officers that the corporation has suffered losses. In re O'Neill, 47 Misc. 495, 95 

N. Y. Supp. 964. If the stockholder's sole ground for examination is that dividends have not been declared, his application should be denied, for the declaration of dividends rests in the sound discretion of the directors; but this ground, with slight additional reasons, will ordinarily be sufficient. Farmers L. & T. Co. v. Pierson, supra. Dodge v. Ford Motor Co., 170 N. W. 668 (Mich.), 3 A. L. R. 413.

If it appears that any purpose prejudicial to the rights of the corporation may be served, the court will only grant the order of inspection upon such terms as will protect the cor-

poration. In re Coats, 75 App. Div. 567, 78 N. Y. Supp. 8.

S. C. L. 10 and 113, requiring corporations to keep books of account, do not require that stockholders be given access to them. The early English rule, abrogated there by St. 

8 and 9, and 25 and 26 Vict., and never applied in New

York, required the stockholder, as a prerequisite for obtaining a writ of mandamus to examine books and papers, to show a specific dispute existing between him and the management. Somewhat similar is C. P. A. § § 295, 296 and 

289, relating to the taking of the deposition of a corporation as an expected party to an action not yet brought under special circumstances rendering it proper. Carmody's 

New York Practice, 1st ed., p. 364. Walsh v. Press Co., 48 

App. Div. 333, 62 N. Y. Supp. 833. Snyder v. De Forest 

Wireless Tel. Co., 113 App. Div. 840, 99 N. Y. Supp. 644.

The common law right is enforced by motion made at special term for an order requiring the corporation to permit an inspection. The right to inspect general business books rests solely upon the common law basis, and the granting or withholding of it, on refusal of the corporation, rests solely in the sound discretion of the court. Matter of Steinway, supra. The moving papers must show a proper demand duly made. Latimer v. Herzog Teleseme 

Co., 75 App. Div. 522, 78 N. Y. Supp. 314. Matter of Steinway, supra. Peo. v. Produce Exchange Trust Co., 53 App. 

Div. 93, 65 N. Y. Supp. 926. The stockholder is entitled to inspect books for information even tho his purpose is to require his corporation to move against the directors for actionable wrongs committed by them. In re Hitchcock, 142 N. Y. Supp. 247. An order for the inspection of books of account will ordinarily not be granted unless he has previously made a written request to the treasurer for a statement of its affairs under oath. S. C. L. 77. Peo. ex rel. 

Clason v. Nassau Ferry Co., 86 Hun 128, 33 N. Y. Supp. 

244. The right to inspect a voting trust agreement filed with the corporation is granted to any stockholder or his attorney by S. C. L. 50, and to inspect a financial statement on file in the office of the corporation by S. C. L. 77. 

If the stockholder shows grounds for suspecting that the management has been guilty of waste or other illegal or

ultra vires acts, the fact that the officers, in their answering affidavits, give an explanation, duly sworn to by them, which, if true, ought to satisfy the stockholder, does not necessarily defeat his motion. Peo. ex rel. Ludwig v. Ludwig & Co., 126 App. Div. 696, 111 N. Y. Supp. 94, Cady's

Cas. p. 397. It is within the court's discretion to apply any of the remedial provisions of the C. P. A. relating to examinations of adverse parties or expected parties in view of C. P. R. 1569. Bell v. Gilbert Paper Co., 117 Misc. 610, 193 N. Y. Supp. 26, affd. 201 App. Div. 867, 193 N. Y. 

Supp. 867. Gilbert v. Same, 117 Misc. 610, 193 N. Y. Supp. 

26, affd. 193 N. Y. Supp. 933. Richmond v. Josephthal, 117 

Misc. 610, 193 N. Y. Supp. 26, affd. 193 N. Y. Supp. 951. 

Where stockholders are granted an inspection at a time when their action against the corporation is pending, a referee will usually be appointed under C. P. R. 142, to superintend the inspection granted by the court; and the stockholders' rights are those of a litigant rather than those of a stockholder. Bell v. Gilbert Paper Co., supra.

The motion to inspect books and papers is an appeal to the grace of the court, and may be denied to a stockholder if his purpose is shown to be hostile to the corporation and its stockholders. A director of the corporation, however, cannot be denied access to its books and papers, even though he becomes an officer of a competitor. Peo. ex rel. 

Stauffer v. Bonwit Bros., 69 Misc. 70, 125 N. Y. Supp. 958. 

§ 144a. Right to a Financial Statement. 

S. C. L. 77 gives the stockholders, owning 3% of the shares, this right. The requirements of the complaint in an action to recover a penalty under this section are: (1) corporation is a stock corporation and not a moneyed corporation: (2) ownership, 3%; (3) written request duly made to the treasurer or other fiscal officer; (4) expiration of time limit of thirty days; (5) failure to comply with the demand; (6) no prior delivery and filing of statement in the current year. The complaint must allege that the defendant failed to deliver the financial statement to the plaintiff or other stockholder during the fiscal year within which demand was made. Troughton v. Grace, 151 App. Div. 655, 136 N. Y. Supp. 200. Tighe v. Lavery, 162 N. Y. Supp.

1005. A director who is also a stockholder is entitled to the benefit of this section. Townsend v. Davis, 153 App. Div. 

599, 138 N. Y. Supp. 758, Cady's Cas. p. 435. The stockholder may waive verification of the statement. Sutton v. 

McBride, 162 N. Y. Supp. 1023. The statute, being in the nature of a penal statute, is strictly construed, and the written request must be delivered in person and not by mail. 

Troughton v. Grace, supra. The wilful refusal to allow inspection by a stockholder who has an order of the court or is otherwise entitled to inspect the books of a corporation is a misdemeanor. Penal Law, § 665 (4). 

§ 145. Rights of Members to Protect the Corporation from Wrongful Acts.

The member has no right to sue or to defend for wrongs to the whole corporation. For instance, he cannot sue in his own name and right to restrain or correct an intra vires transaction that is detrimental to the corporation by reason of mismanagement or bad judgment, or a trespass on the corporate property. Transactions that are not illegal or ultra vires may be ratified; and the decision to enforce or to forego a legal right must be left to the management. Chaps. 

XIV and XV, infra. Hawes v. Oakland, 104 U. S. 450. 

For a matter that especially affects the stockholder, or a bloc of stockholders, one stockholder may sue, in behalf of himself and other stockholders. If the corporation is the one naturally entitled to the benefit of the judgment, the corporation, together with the guilty parties, must be made parties defendant. Robinson v. Smith, 3 Pai. 222. Ver planck v. Merc. Ins. Co., 1 Edw. Ch. 84. Cunningham v. Pell, 

5 Pai. 607. Butts v. Wood, 37 N. Y. 317. Greaves v. Gouge, 69 N. Y. 154. Facts showing misappropriation of funds or losses through the negligence of officers or directors, or fraud or bad faith in departure from charter powers, warrant a court's intervention at the instance of a stockholder. 

Nauss v. Nauss Bros. Co., 195 App. Div. 318, 187 N. Y. 

Supp. 158, Cady's Cas. p. 404.

Acts that infringe the contract or other vested rights of the member will sustain an action by him against officers or corporation, as the case may require. Thus, the member may sue if dividends are not declared out of surplus profits

in derogation of a contract with the member, contained, for instance, in the charter or the stock certificate, Collins v. 

Portland Elec. Power Co., 7 F. (2d) 221; Godley v. Crandall and Godley, 212 N. Y. 121; or if calls are unfairly levied, or unlike as to time, convenience, amount, or other circumstance, upon all members. Bank of China v. Morse, 168

N. Y. 458. If elections, provided by the charter, are not held, the shareholder may compel them. Peo. ex rel. Miller v. Cummings, 72 N. Y. 433. If the right of transfer of stock is unlawfully denied, he may restrain the illegal issue of the shares to others. Ernst v. Elmira M. I. Co., 24 Misc. 583, 54 N. Y. Supp. 116. If stock is issued without consideration, he may compel its return and cancella tion. Ernst v. Rutherford etc. Gas Co., 38 App. Div. 388, 

56 N. Y. Supp. 403. And, if the majority break their contract with the other subscribers to pay for stock, and unite in turning over the corporation's assets to creditors, or otherwise to render their agreements unenforcible by the corporation, the aggrieved stockholder may sue the majority for his damages. Higgins v. Applebaum, 186 App. Div. 682, 174 N. Y. Supp. 807. Cole v. Levy, 212 App. Div. 84, 208 

N. Y. Supp. 481. Berkmire v. Campus Rty. Corp., 223 App. 

Div. 226, 227 N. Y. Supp. 226. But a stockholder cannot sue the associates for a debt due from the corporation. 

Bailey v. Bancker, 3 Hill, 188. The plaintiff stockholder must bring his action on account of himself and of all the other members similarly affected by the acts complained of. 

C. P. A. 194, 195. Sec. Tr. Co. v. Pritchard, 201 App. Div. 

142, 194 N. Y. Supp. 486. Brown v. Deposit Nat. Bank, 125 Misc. 247, 211 N. Y. Supp. 366. 

§ 146. 

To Restrain Ultra Vires Acts. 

If, in a domestic corporation, a strictly ultra vires act is contemplated, every stockholder has a right to sue to prevent its being done, or, in a case where the corporation is not bound, to prevent the continuation or repetition of the the act. Schwab v. Potter Co., supra, Cady's Cas. p. 542. 

Secs. 100, 102, supra. 

§ 147. Right to Vote on Stated Matters. 

S. C. L. 5 (4) authorizes the restriction of voting rights by charter provision. A general restriction of the voting

right in the charter purporting to exclude designated classes of stockholders from voting, will not affect their right to vote in the following specified instances, which right, however, may be taken away by specific exclusion in the charter:-(1) to mortgage property and franchises,

S. C. L. 16; (2) to guarantee the bonds of another corporation, S. C. L. 19; (3) for sale of franchises or property, S. C. L. 20; (4) for classification or reclassification of shares, S. C. L. 36; (5) for consolidation, S. C. L. 86; (6) for voluntary dissolution, S. C. L. 105; and (7) for change of name, G. C. L. 40, S. C. L. 51. At these meetings, the resolution must be passed by a two-thirds majority of those entitled to vote, except as to change of name, for which a mere majority vote suffices, and excepting classification of stock, which may in some instances be authorized by a majority vote, and in others by a two-thirds vote. S. C. L. 37. 

§ 148. Same. Restrictions on Voting. Vetoing. 

The usual purpose of issuing preferred stock is to invite investment of capital by a guaranty or a preference in respect to dividends. The management, exercisable by voting right, is generally reserved to the common stock, which is entitled to no dividend unless they have first earned and paid the dividend contracted to be paid to the preferred stock out of surplus profits only. S. C. L. 58. 

A usual clause in the preferred stock provides that if the dividends are not paid, the preferred stockholders may vote, to the exclusion, it is sometimes provided, of the common stock, or by cumulative voting, thus vesting the preferred stockholders with the management or with representation on the board on the happening of a failure to pay dividends. The permission to issue preferred stock practically allows the stockholders to divide the corporation's profits in any manner that they see fit. Peo. ex. rel. Cohn v. Miller, 180 N. Y. 16.

Frequently, veto powers are inserted in the preference to guard the preferred stock against methods which might operate to avoid or minimize the preferential rights granted, such as a special contract that without the express consent of the majority or other portion of the preferred stockholders, there should be no increase or reclassi-

fication of preferred stock; or that no claim should be created on the earnings, as by mortgage or the like, that might be prior to the rights of the preferred stock to dividends; or that common stock shall not be increased without the consent of the preferred stock. The preferences constitute a contract between the corporation and the preferred stockholder, comprised in the stock certificate and in the proceedings from the moment the preferred stock was authorized to the time when it was issued. Hackett v. 

Northern Pac. Ry. Co., 36 Misc. 583, 73 N. Y. Supp. 1087, 1090. Boardman v. Lake S. & M. S. R. Co., 84 N. Y. 157. 

Utica Tr. & Dep. Co. v. Kellogg etc. Co., 126 App. Div. 176, 110 N. Y. Supp. 1048. Prouty v. Mich. So. & N. I. R. R. 

Co., 1 Hun 655. There may be classes of common stock, but stock entitled to preference in dividends or in assets at distribution cannot be termed common stock. S. C. L. 11. 

It follows that a corporation may be formed under the statute without common stock, but with two classes of preferred stock. S. C. L. 5, 11. 

§ 149. Right to Receive Dividends. 

So long as the corporation carries on business, the individual shareholder has no general right in the corporate funds, except to have them applied for corporate purposes with a reasonable zeal for gain. When profits have accrued, shareholders have no unconditional right to them as divi. dends, and the directors in their honest discretion may decide to hold them as surplus, or for debts, taxes, depreciation, maintenance, upkeep, expansion of business, or the like. McNab v. McNab & H. Mfg. Co., 62 Hun 18, Cady's

Cas. p. 403. Chap. XI, infra. When the dividend fund has been severed, or a dividend actually declared by the directors out of surplus earnings, the dividend becomes thereupon the individual property of the stockholder, to be received by him on demand. Kane v. Bloodgood, 7 Johns. 

Ch. 90. Hyatt v. Allen, 56 N. Y. 553. Peo. ex rel. Jam.

Water Supply Co. v. State Board of Tax Coms., 196 N. Y 

39. Godley v. Crandall & Godley Co., 212 N. Y. 121, 105 

N. E. 818. If the declaration of dividend be fraudulent or unjust, the stockholder may sue to prevent the declaratior or distribution. Williams v. Western Union Tel. Co., 93

N. Y. 162. A particular stockholder, whose stock is of the class included by the dividend resolution, but who is unjustly excluded from payment, may recover at law his aliquot share of the dividend. 

R. R., 57 N. Y. 196.

Jones v. Terre Haute etc. 

§ 150. Right to Subscribe to New Issues. 

The amount of capital stock may be increased pursuant either to a provision therefor in the certificate of incorporation, or by an amended certificate. S. C. L. 36. Apart from statute, a corporation has no power of itself to increase its stock, for the increase would change the amount of control exercised by stockholders who had already bought stock, and thus vary the terms of their contract with the corporation as expressed in the charter and stock certificate. N. Y. & N. H. R. R. v. Schuyler, supra, Cady's 

Cas. p. 473. Wood v. Dummer, 3 Mason, 308. Mech. Bk. v. N. Y. & N. H. R. Co., 13 N. Y. 599. Sec. 108, supra. 

In Hartford Ry. Co. v. Croswell, 5 Hill 383, it was held that where the legislature amended the charter by increasing the capital stock, the amendment could not take effect unless unanimously accepted by the stockholders. Under

S. C. L. 36, it is held that a stockholder has "an inherent preemptive and vested right of property" to an aliquot proportion of the new stock, issued for money, in the ratio of his holdings to the total original stock, or in some other equitable way. Stokes v. Continental Tr. Co., 186 N. Y. 285,

Cady's Cas. p. 436. The stockholder may waive this right, as by voting in favor of a resolution to issue it to others. 

He cannot be deprived of the right by acts of the majority, and he must be given opportunity to buy or to sell his rights to his proportionate share, commonly called his "stock rights." Ib. Schramme v. Cowin, 205 App. Div. 

20, 199 N. Y. Supp. 98. The amount that he must pay for the new stock may be fixed by agreement with the corporation made at any time, and if there is no agreement, by the majority. Stokes case, supra. Einstein v. Roch. 

Gas & Elec. Co., 146 N. Y. 46. Where the charter provides that certain shares shall be issued at once, and other shares, authorized by the certificate of incorporation as originally filed, shall be held for future expansion, the stock rights

attach to the original authorized unissued stock by reason of the inherent right of the minority to have their voting status preserved. Dunlay v. Ave. M Garage & R. Co., Inc., 253 N. Y. 274, 170 N. E. 917. As to the initial authorized issue, the case is different, and those shares may be issued to anybody in order to raise money. Ib. Waters v. Horace 

Waters & Co., 201 N. Y. 184, Cady's Cas. p. 443. Also there are no stock rights where the shares are issued for the purchase of property for the corporation. Bond v. Atl. 

Terra Cotta Co., 137 App. Div. 671, 122 N. Y. Supp. 425.

The majority may fix a date within which the stock rights must be exercised and payment made, and a failure to comply therewith, after due notice, amounts to a waiver. The law does not require actual notice to every stockholder of the proposed increase, and a notice duly mailed to the stockholder to the address last known to the corporation, in Japan, was held due notice. Hoyt v. Grt. Amer. Ins. Co., 201 App. Div. 352, 194 N. Y. Supp. 449.

The damage suffered by a stockholder from the deprivation of his stock rights is the difference between the reasonable price fixed by the majority stockholders for the stock and its market value, if greater, on the day of sale.

Stokes case, Cady's Cas. at p. 443. The majority stockholders may provide that the new issue be sold at public auction; and the stockholder is entitled to bid at the sale, or to his proportion of the money resulting. Ib. p. 442.

The alternative remedy of enjoining an intended sale is available. Noble v. Grt. Amer. Ins. Co., supra.

A sale of stock held for future expansion (treasury stock, sec. 131, supra) may be sold for full value and in good faith to discharge a corporate debt. The sale does not entitle the stockholder to damages, and the directors may issue the stock to themselves at that price if the primary result and purpose is not to give them a majority of votes. 

Dunlap case, supra. 

§ 151. To Be a Creditor. 

A member may occupy the two relations of stockholder and creditor, and, if his stock has been paid for, he will be entitled as a creditor to receive his due proportion of the corporate assets. His transactions with the corpora-

tion will be scrutinized to prevent all inequitable attempts to shield the stockholder from loss at the expense of the general creditor. But if calls are unpaid, the stockholder's position is nearly akin to that of a partner in an ordinary partnership, who, on general principles, may not at common law claim any debt owing to him from the partnership estate until all claims of creditors have been satisfied. So a stockholder cannot set off debts due him from the corporation against calls, nor set off against calls a dividend that, after creditors' claims were satisfied, might come to him. McLaren v. Pennington, 1 Pai. 102. Mtr. of Empire 

City Bank, 18 N. Y. 199. Mathez v. Neidig, 72 N. Y. 100. 

Wheeler v. Millar, 90 N. Y. 353. A creditor who is also a stockholder cannot sue his fellow stockholders for more than contribution, where both are liable to creditors. Bailey v. Bancker, 3 Hill 188. Chap. XVII, infra. 

§ 152. To Share on Dissolution. 

The contract between the stockholder and the corporation includes the idea that whenever the corporation shall give up business and dissolve, each stockholder shall receive his share of the property determined, unless consent or waiver is proved, in the ordinary way of a winding up, by a public sale, in the manner recognized by law. McVicker v. Ross, 55 Barb. 247. Frothingham v. Barney, 6 Hun 366; 

Tayler v. Earle, 8 Hun 1.
