Definition, Nature, and Kinds of Dividends.

The word dividend signifies that portion of accumulated surplus which the directors may deem expedient to be distributed to the stockholders. Hastings v. International 

Paper Co., 187 App. Div. 404, 175 N. Y. Supp. 815. Dividends are payable on demand or at a fixed time. Peo. ex rel. Pullman Co. v. Glynn, 114 N. Y. Supp. 460, affd. 198 

N. Y. 605. Notwithstanding a provision in the declaration of the dividend that it is payable at the pleasure of the corporation, payment must be made within a reasonable time. 

Billingham v. Gleason Mfg. Co., 101 App. Div. 476, 91 

N. Y. Supp. 1046, affd. 185 N. Y. 571. Every distribution of profits to stockholders is to all intents and purposes a dividend. Peo. ex rel. Queens County Water Co. v. Travis, 171 App. Div. 521, 157 N. Y. Supp. 943, affd. 219 N. Y. 571.

Dividends are only payable out of surplus profits arising from business carried on. Roberts v. Roberts Wicks Co., 184 N. Y. 257. Thompson v. Erie R. R., 11 Abb. Pr. (N. S.) 188. 

Dividends may be (1) cash; (2) stock; (3) bond; (4) scrip; or (5) property dividends. A cash dividend is usually declared and paid from cash profits on hand. Hastings v. 

International Paper Co., 187 App. Div. 404, 175 N. Y. Supp. 

815, Cady's Cas. p. 405. A stock dividend is the distribu- 240

DIVIDENDS 

241 tion of an authorized increase of capital stock or the distribution of unissued stock on hand. The new stock certificate so issued represents income and not capital, provided the issue does not exceed in amount the value of the surplus. Williams v. Western Union Telegraph Co., 93

N. Y. 162, Cady's Cases, p. 416. In the resolution declaring the dividend, the directors may decide to retain profits earned for the purpose of the company in making improvements or payment of floating or funded debts, taxes, plant, overhead, extension of business or other contingencies, and in that case may issue stock dividends. Howell v. Chicago & 

N. W. R. Co., 51 Barb. 378. The issue must not exceed in amount the value of the surplus. Williams v. Western 

Union Tel. Co., supra. If it does, then it is an impairment of the capital stock and violates S. C. L. 58. The stock dividend may be of the corporation itself or that of another corporation held as part of the surplus or the undivided profits. Liebman v. Auto Strop Co., 241 N. Y. 427. A bond dividend consists of corporate bonds, issued as dividends.

They may be issued only against actual profits. Wood v. 

Lary, 124 N. Y. 83. This method is not usually practical, inasmuch as bonds carry the corporation's obligation to pay interest, and also to pay the face amount at maturity. Both the interest and principal of bonds are fixed charges, whether profits are made or not. Where bonds contain a provision permitting the owner to convert them into stock, and the stock is paying regular dividends, it is the custom to provide that the bondholder who surrenders his bond and takes stock shall be allowed the interest on his bond up to the date of the conversion, and shall be charged with interest on the stock at the rate of the regular dividend, from the date of the last dividend declaration up to the date of conversion. In Jones v. Terre H. & Rich. R. R. Co., 57 N. Y. 

196, the resolution declared a 20% stock dividend and also a 7% cash dividend out of surplus earnings for the six months ending November 30, payable the following January 6.

This resolution was passed on December 17, 1856, and the plaintiff converted his bonds into stock on December 3, 1856, and received an interest check for interest on his bonds computed to December 1, 1856, together with the

stock certificate. It was held that plaintiff was entitled to receive both of the dividends also. That the effect was to permit plaintiff to gain a substantial advantage over the other stockholders was urged in vain, for the right, nominated in the bond, to convert the bond into stock, was silent as to adjustments of interest; and it is a cardinal principle that after a dividend is declared, each stockholder who is such at the date of declaration of dividend, has a right in severalty to his particular portion. This legal right does not depend upon the question of whether he is a stockholder of long standing or of recent date. The failure to include, in the clause that permitted conversion, apt words to equalize the rights of both classes of investors, could not be rectified by a by-law closing the stock and transfer books for fifteen days from November 30, for the closing of the books, while it might delay bondholders who wished to convert their bonds, could not impair the right of plaintiff, as a stockholder, to receive the dividend. Ib. See also, Ford v. 

Snook, 205 App. Div. 194, 199 N. Y. Supp. 630, affd. 240 

N. Y. 624, Cady's Cas. p. 412.

A scrip dividend is a certificate stating that the owner is entitled to certain rights specified therein, generally, a certain sum at a future date. Billingham v. Gleason Mfg. 

Co., 101 App. Div. 476, 91 N. Y. Supp. 1046. Being in the nature of a deferred dividend, it usually represents existing profits, but not in a realizable form. It is also resorted to when directors determine that though there is cash available for distribution, it can be used to better advantage in making improvements or payment of debts. "Scrip" also denotes a writing issued by promoters, entitling the holder to shares, and is ordinarily transferable.

A property dividend is a distribution of the property of the corporation. Howell v. Chicago & N. W. R. R. Co., 51 

Barb. 378. Williams v. W. U. Tel. Co., supra., Cady's Cases, p. 416. Equitable Lf. Assur. Society v. Union Pac. R. R. 

Co., 212 N. Y. 360. It may be of properties owned outright by the corporation, or received by it on the sale of certain of its rights. Peo. ex rel. Queens County Water Co. v. 

Travis, supra. Liebman v. Auto Strop Co., 241 N. Y. 427.

Generally property dividends are declared when the cor-

DIVIDENDS 

243 poration is in the process of liquidation, having sold all its assets and received in return property of the purchasing corporation. Under such circumstances, the distribution is not truly payment of a "dividend" but a distribution of assets. The requirement that a dividend can be declared only out of accumulated profit does not apply in a case where creditors are not concerned.

A cumulative dividend is one with regard to which it is agreed that if at any time it is not paid in full, the difference shall be added to the following payment, the idea being that arrearages of one year are payable out of the surplus earnings of subsequent years. Lockwood v. Gen. Abrasive Co., 210 App. Div. 141, 205 N. Y. Supp. 511, affd. 240 N. Y. 592.

In absence of agreement, express or implied, that dividends shall be cumulative, unpaid dividends for past years cannot be collected. Lockwood v. Gen. Abrasive Co., supra. 

McNab v. McNab & Harlin Mfg. Co., supra, Cady's Cases, p. 402. 

The term "preferred stock," unless expressly limited, implies that dividends are cumulative at the vote specified in the stock certificate. Ib. 

Dividends may be regular or "extra." Dividends àt a rate declared by the corporation to be its "dividend policy" -for instance, in either the charter, a by-law, or by the usage of the corporation-are "regular" dividends. If there are unusual or aggregated profits which the directors deem wise to distribute, an "extra" dividend will be declared, sometimes called a "melon." Whether a dividend is a regular or "extra" sometimes is denoted by the directors in the language of the declaration. No special by-law is necessary to declare such a dividend.

The term interest when applied to preferred stock, may mean a dividend. If so, it can only be paid out of profits earned. Thompson v. Erie R. R. Co., 11 Abb. Pr. (N. S.), 188. 

§ 154. Right to Declare Dividends. 

The board of directors constitute the sole authority to declare dividends. Cuppy v. Ward, 176 N. Y. Supp. 233, 187 App. Div. 625, affd. 227 N. Y. 603. It is an incident of their general powers to manage the affairs of the corporation, and is part of the trust placed in them as wise,

prudent and honest men. The power to declare dividends is subject to the provisions of the charter, by-laws, and statutes. Avedon v. Gem Dress House, Inc., 185 N. Y. 

Supp 871, affd. 232 N. Y. 205. 

In Liebman v. Auto Strop Co., 241 N. Y. at p. 433, the court set forth the rule as follows: "It is a fundamental rule relating to the management of corporations that it is within the discretion of the directors to determine when and to what extent a dividend shall be made, subject of course to the qualification that the same shall not encroach on the capital. Courts will not interfere with such discretion, unless it be first made to appear that the, directors have acted or are about to act in bad faith and for a dishonest purpose. It is for the directors to say, acting in good faith of course, when and to what extent dividends shall be declared. Dividends when declared must be out of the surplus or undivided profits." 

See McNab v. McNab & Harlin Mfg. Co., supra, Cady's 

Cas. p. 402. Miller v. Crown Perf. Co., 125 App. Div. 881; 

Shaw v. Ansaldi Co., 165 N. Y. Supp. 872, 178 App. Div. 

589; Hastings v. International Paper Co., supra; Nauss v. 

Nauss Bros. Co., supra; Kranich v. Bach, 204 N. Y. Supp. 

320, 209 App. Div. 52.

The American Rule contrary to the English Rule does not require the whole of the profits to be periodically divided unless that obligation is created by charter or contract. 

The charter or by-law may state the dividend policy of the corporation. Avedon v. Gem Dress House, Inc., 185 N. Y. 

Supp 871, affd. 232 N. Y. 505.

Dividends and profits are not synonymous. A shareholder has no legal title to the property or profits of the corporation until a division is duly made. Declaration of this division results in a dividend. Hyatt v. Allen, 56 N. Y. 

553; Braxman v. Olpp, 135 N. Y. Supp. 1091. A corporation which has earned profits is not precluded from distributing them as dividends because some of its assets are in such a form that it must borrow money for its business. 

Holmes v. Saint Joseph Lead Co., 84 Misc. 278; Bankers 

Trust Co. v. Dietz Co., 157 App. Div. 594, 142 N. Y. Supp. 

847. A corporation may declare and pay dividends upon the

DIVIDENDS 

245 basis of the amount actually paid upon the respective shares. S. C. L. 74. 

§ 155. Dividends Once Declared Cannot Be Revoked. 

The general rule is that once a dividend is declared it cannot be revoked. Beveridge v. N. Y. R. R. Co., 112 

N. Y. 1. The amount of a dividend when declared is not one of the assets of a corporation constituting a part of the "surplus profits or reserved funds" but is an obligation perfect and complete in its character and is regarded as a debt. Billingham v. Gleason Mfg. Co., 101 App. Div. 476, 91 N. Y. Supp. 1046, affd. 185 N. Y. 571; Ohle v. Chittenango Bank, 24 N. Y. 548; Staats v. Biograph Co., 236 Fed. 454.

To the effect that a declaration of dividends gives stockholders vested interest therein see New York Trust Co. v. 

Edwards, and United States v. Rockfeller, both reported in 274 Fed. 952. However Ford v. Easthampton Rubber 

Thread Co., 158 Mass. 84, holds that a dividend does not become an irrevocable fact until notice of the resolution declaring it has been given or the fact that it has been adopted has become known. If the directors have voted the dividend but the fact has not been made public in any way, the action may be rescinded. 

§ 156. What is a Surplus. 

Dividends may be declared only out of surplus.

Surplus is any excess of value of the assets of a corporation over its liabilities and capital stock. Equitable 

Life Assur. Soc. v. Union Pac. R. R. Co., 212 N. Y. 360.

From the value of the "property" owned by the corporation, subtract the sum total of the capital stock, debts (liabilities) and losses. The remainder is "surplus," which, in the discretion of the directors, may be divided. Equitable 

Life Assur. Soc. v. Union Pac. R. R. Co., supra; Strong v. 

Brooklyn Cross Town R. R. Co., 93 N. Y. 426; Roberts v. 

Roberts Wicks Co., 184 N. Y. 257; Williams v. Western 

Union Tel. Co., 93 N. Y. 162; Russel v. American Gas & 

Electric Co., 152 App. Div. 136, 136 N. Y. Supp. 602; 

Barry v. Merchants Exch. Co., 1 Sand. Ch. 280; Searles v.

Gebbie, 199 N. Y. 533, Cady's Cas. p. 409; Lockwood v. 

Gen. Abrasive Co., supra.

The "capital" of a corporation at any specified time consists of all the property owned by it at the time, consisting of funds, securities, credits receivable, and property of whatever kind, excluding expected profits of unperformed contracts. Its "capital stock" is the amount stated in its charter as the sum for which shares were to be issued at the aforesaid time. The difference between the capital stock and the capital, if the latter is the greater, may be termed "net earnings," "profit," "gain" or "gain" or "income." 

Where debts, current expenses, etc., have been deducted from the "gain," that which is left is "surplus." Christensen v. Eno, supra, Cady's Cas. at p. 349; Peo. v. Supervisors, 4 Hill 20. "Profits" and "income" are not synonymous.

Profits generally mean the gain which is made upon any business or investment when both receipts and payments are taken into account. Income generally means that which comes in, or is received from any business or investment of capital, without any reference to the outgoing expenditures. Ib.

Where a dividend is declared and about to be paid and in fact there is not any surplus out of which it could be paid, a stockholder may maintain an action to enjoin payment thereof. Carpenter v. N. Y., New Haven R. R. Co., 5 Abb. Pr. 277. Payment of dividends from capital stock instead of surplus renders those directors voting therefor liable to the extent of the loss sustained by the corporation or its creditors by such wrongful declaration and payment. 

S. C. L. 58, 15. The directors who concur are penally liable. 

Pen. L. 664 (1). Dykman v. Kierney, 16 App. Div. 131, 45 N. Y. Supp. 137, affd. 160 N. Y. 677; Hutchinson v. 

Young, 80 App. Div. 246, 80 N. Y. Supp. 259; Cox v. Leahy, 204 N. Y. Supp. 741. The penal liability extends to foreign corporations doing business in New York. Germ. Amer. 

Coffee Co. v. Diehl, 216 N. Y. 57. The liability of the directors is joint and several, Cox v. Leahy, supra. Dividends declared may be credited to the amount unpaid on stock, so long as the dividends do not encroach on capital. Shaw v. Ansaldi Co., 178 App. Div. 589, 165 N. Y. Supp. 872.

DIVIDENDS 

247 When losses have reduced capital, no dividends can be paid until the deficiency has been made up. Williams v. 

Western Union Tel. Co., 93 N. Y. 162; Roberts v. Roberts

Wicks Co., 184 N. Y. 257. An apparent exception exists in the case where the corporation is formed to operate property that is destroyed in the using; for instance, mines, oil wells, patent rights and copyrights. No deduction need be made from the value of the capital as depleted by use, before declaring a dividend. Lee v. Newchatel Asphalt Co.,

L. R. 41 Ch. D. 1. 

§ 157. To Whom are Dividends Payable. 

Record holders of stock or their legal representatives at the time of the declaration are severally entitled to receive dividends. Robertson v. De Brulatour, 188 N. Y. 301; 

Hopper v. Sage, 112 N. Y. 530; Brisbane v. D. L. & W. R. R. 

Co., 94 N. Y. 204; Jurnam v. Lake Shore & M. S. Ry. Co., 91 N. Y. 483; Jones v. Terre Haute R. R. Co., 57 N. Y. 196.

Where there are diverse claims to stock, the declaration or payment of dividends may be restrained until a true list of genuine stockholders is established by a court of competent jurisdiction. Underwood v. N. Y. & New Haven 

R. R. Co., 17 How. Pr. 537.

In the absence of contract provision, all stockholders share in the dividend proportionate to their holdings. Jones v. Terre Haute & Rich. R. R. Co., 57 N. Y. 196.

The charter is a contract between the different classes of stockholders determining, by its language, their respective rights to the dividends declared. Lockwood v. General 

Abrasive Co., 210 App. Div. 141, 205 N. Y. Supp. 511, affd. 

240 N. Y. 592; Roberts v. Roberts Wicks Co., 184 N. Y. 

257, Cady's Cas, p. 454; Michael v. Cayey-Caguas Tobacco 

Co., 190 App. Div. 618, 180 N. Y. Supp. 532. The contract may be found in the stock certificate or in the by-laws of the corporation in effect when the stockholder purchased his stock, but a private corporation cannot by passing or repealing a by-law, impair vested rights of stockholders, even tho the power to amend the by-laws is reserved by charter. 

Kent v. Quicksilver Mining Co., 78 N. Y. 159; Presbyterian 

Church v. City of New York, 5 Cow. 538; Mechanics Bank

v. N. Y. & C. R. R. Co., supra; Avedon v. General Dress 

House, Inc., 232 N. Y. 205.

Preferred stockholders are entitled to receive dividends on their shares, to the extent agreed upon, before any dividends at all are paid to the holders of the common stock. 

People v. Miller, 180 N. Y. 16; Kent v. Quicksilver Mining 

Co., supra; People v. N. Y. Building Co., 189 N. Y. 547. 

If the contract with the preferred stockholders entitles them to be paid annual dividends at a certain rate per annum, or by any method short of making the dividend payable each year dependent on profits of that year, the dividends are cumulative; and if the profits at the time of declaration are not sufficient to pay the dividend, the unpaid arrears must be paid in addition to dividends subsequently declared out of the profits of subsequent years, before any dividends can be paid to the holders of common stock. Jermain v. Lake Shore & M. S. R. Co., 91 N. Y. 483; Boardman v. Lake Shore & M. S. R. Co., 84 N. Y. 157. The directors have a discretionary power to withhold dividends from the common stockholders, and to accumulate a surplus; but as laid down in Boardman v. Lake Shore &c. Ry Co., 84 

N. Y. 157, "While, as a general rule, courts of equity will not exercise visitorial powers over a corporation, and its officers are the sole judges of the propriety of declaring dividends, and in this respect the court will not interfere with a proper exercise of their discretion, yet where the right to the dividend is clear and fixed by the contract, and requires the directors to take action before it can be asserted in a court of law, and a restraint by injunction is essential to maintain the right of the stockholder, the injunction of a court of equity is a proper exercise of its power, and should be upheld." 

To illustrate: assume that the preferred 6% stock and the common stock were each $500,000 and the profits each year were normally $30,000. If the preferred stock was not cumulative stock, and the directors by device of bookkeeping, showed no profit on odd years and $60,000 profit on even years, the common stock and the preferred would each get $30,000 of dividend every second year. Whereas, if the preferred stock was cumulative, it would get the whole

DIVIDENDS 

249 $30,000 each year, and the common would get nothing. 

Sometimes stock is issued as noncumulative, but by the terms of the certificate becomes cumulative after a few years, thus giving the corporation a chance to expand before the necessity of clearing up arrearages arises. 

As between vendor and vendee, the one who owned the stock at the time the dividend was declared is entitled to the dividend to the exclusion of the other, although the dividend is not payable until a later date by the terms of the declaration, and although the stock does not stand in his name on the corporate books. Hopper v. Sage, supra, Cady's Cas. p. 414. Ford v. Snook, supra, Cady's Cas. p. 

412. N. Y. Trust Co. v. Edward, 274 Fed. 952. A sale of stock prior to the declaration of the dividend, passes to the vendee whatever interest in earnings the vendor has, as an incident to the transfer of the stock. Robertson v. De- 

Brulatour, 188 N. Y. 301. Jones v. Terra Haute & Richmond R. R. Co., supra. Where the transfer of the stock to the vendee has not been registered in the books of the corporation, any dividends declared subsequent to such transfer and received by the vendor are held by him in trust for the vendee. Locke v. Farmers Loan & Trust Co., 140 

N. Y. 135. Sigua Iron Co. v. Brown, 171 N. Y. 488. Johnson v. Underhill, 52 N. Y. 203.

As to the legatee under a last will, dividends declared before the decedent's death go to the personal representative; those declared after the decedent's death and before the stock is transferred to the legatee on the books of the corporation go to the personal representative to be held for the benefit of the legatee. Payment in good faith to the owner of record protects the corporation. Brisbane v. Del. 

L. & Western R. R. Co., 94 N. Y. 204. Seymour v. 

Mechanics Nat. Bank, 199 App. Div. 707, 192 N. Y. Supp. 

588. Though the dividend was earned in prior years, only those who owned the stock at the time of the declaration are entitled to take it. Peo. ex rel. Fraser v. Gt. West. Sugar 

Co., 29 Fed. (2d) 810. Jones v. Terre Haute R. R. Co., supra.

A contract for the sale of shares of stock at a specified price "payable and deliverable, seller's option, in this year”

is a sale in presenti provided the option is exercised in time and the contract operates as an equitable assignment to the purchaser of all the dividends accruing on such shares thereafter. Currie v. White, supra. Rowe v. White, 98 

N. Y. Supp. 729, affd. 189 N. Y. 523. 

Where a customer gives an order to a broker, knowing that it will be executed on a board of trade or exchange, he contemplates conformity to rules and customs that prevail there. Wilhite v. Houston, 200 Fed. Rep. 390. Springs v. 

James, 137 App. Div. 110, affd. 202 N. Y. 603. Custom and usage may be resorted to for the purpose of explaining contracts, to remove ambiguity, to amplify terms, if necessary to the statement of the parties' intentions, but not to alter the obligations between the parties resulting as a legal effect of their agreement. Ford v. Snook, supra. Hart v. Cort, 165 App. Div. 584, 151 N. Y. Supp. 54. O'Donough v. 

Leggett, 134 N. Y. 40. Hopper v. Sage, 112 N. Y. 530.

Britain v. Ferrin, 171 N. Y. 235. Home Ins. Co. v. Cont. 

Ins. Co., 180 N. Y. 389. Richard v. Credit Suisse, 242 

N. Y. 346. 

§ 158. 

Discrimination Between Stockholders. 

While a court of equity will not interfere with the internal arrangements of the corporation to require the declaration of a dividend, it will interfere to prevent injustice where it is apparent that the corporation has wronged some of its stockholders. Liebman v. Auto Strop Co., 241 N. Y. 

427; Roberts v. Roberts Wicks Co., 184 N. Y. 257, Cady's

Cases on Priv. Corp. p. 454. Greef v. Equitable Life Assur. 

Soc., 160 N. Y. 32. Williams v. Western Union Tel. Co., supra, Cady's Cas. p. 416; Hastings v. International Paper 

Co., supra, Cady's Cas. p. 405. As between the members of any one class of stock dividends must be paid with impartiality, proportionate to the number of shares owned by each stockholder. The time and method of payment must be the same for all. Jones v. Terre Haute etc. R. R. Co., supra; 

Godley v. Crandall & Godley Co., supra. 

§ 160. Actions to Require Declaration of Dividends. 

A shareholder can not sue the corporation for his share of the accumulated profits until a dividend is declared.

DIVIDENDS 

251 

Beveridge v. N. Y. El. Ry. Co., 112 N. Y. 1; Hyatt v. Allen, 56 N. Y. 553; Jones v. Terre Haute R. R. Co., 57 N. Y. 196.

While corporate officers are the sole judges as to the propriety of declaring dividends, and the courts will not interfere with a proper exercise of the discretion of the directors, yet where the right to a dividend is clear and fixed by the contract and requires action to be taken by the directors before the right can be asserted at law, a court of equity will interpose and compel such action and whenever necessary restrain by injunction any action violative of the rights of the stockholders. Boardman v. Lake Shore & 

M. S. Ry. Co., 84 N. Y. 157; Hastings v. International 

Paper Co., 187 App. Div. 404, 175 N. Y. Supp. 815; Greef v. Equitable Life Assur. Soc., 160 N. Y. 19; Nauss v. Nauss 

Bros. Co., 195 App. Div. 318, 187 N. Y. Supp. 158; Roberts v. Roberts Wicks Co., 184 N. Y. 257. The discretion of the directors will not be interfered with except for fraud, oppression, and unreasonableness. In re Brantman, 244 Fed. 

101; Kassel v. Empire Tinware Co., 178 App. Div. 176, 64 

N. Y. Supp. 10, 33; Logan v. N. Y. Sugar Refining Co., 176 

App. Div. 660, 163 N. Y. Supp. 214; Matter of Rogers, 161 N. Y. 108. The mere fact that there is a large surplus will not be grounds for the intervention of the courts. Burden v. Burden, 159 N. Y. 287; Reynolds v. Bank of Mt. 

Vernon, 158 N. Y. 470. Stockholders of shares guaranteeing dividends, may compel the declaration of dividends. 

Prouty v. Michigan, Southern & Northern Indiana R. R. 

Co., supra.

A suit in equity will only lie against the directors when the amount of the dividend has been segregated into a distinct fund and is under domination of directors who refuse to use it as intended. Searles v. Gebbie, 190 N. Y. 533, Cady's Cases on Priv. Corp., p. 409. Le Roy v. Globe Ins. 

Co., 2 Edw. Ch. 657; Kink v. Patterson etc. R. R. Co., 29 

N. J. Law, 89. If no time is set for payment an action may be brought to compel the board of directors to fix a time. 

§ 161. Dividends on Preferred Stock. 

That dividends on preferred stock are "guaranteed" authorizes the interpretation that they are cumulative; and all arrears must be paid before any dividends can be paid

on the common stock. Boardman v. Lake Shore &c. Ry. 

Co., 84 N. Y. 137. It should be expressly provided that dividends on preferred stock are not cumulative, or this may be inferred from the language used. Where the preferred stock purports to be interest bearing, the right of the preferred stockholders, in the absence of limitations is that of sharing in the profits, with arrears, at the stipulated rate, before anything is paid to the common stock. Bailey v. 

R. R. Co., 17 Wall. 96. Where the preferred stock was entitled to 7% cumulative dividends, and any further amounts of surplus was to be divided pro rata among the preferred and common stockholders, it was held that common stockholders were not entitled to receive the amounts that the directors, in their discretion, might have given them in past years before the preferred stockholders were fully paid. 

Lockwood v. Gen. Abrasive Co., supra.

If preferred stock is legally reduced when payment of dividends thereon is in arrears, payment of the arrearage accruing prior to the reduction must be made on the basis of the number of shares held by each stockholder prior to such reduction rather than on the number of shares as reduced. Roberts v. Roberts Wicks Co., 184 N. Y. 257.

Holders of common stock cannot enjoin the payment of dividends to holders of noncumulative preferred stock out of the surplus which might have been distributed to them during the years it was earned but was not. Wood v. Lary, 47 Hun 550; Moran v. U. S. Cast Iron Pipe Co., 95 N. J. 

Eq. 389 affd. 96 N. J. Equity 698; Barclay v. Wabash R. R., 30 Fed. (2nd) 259. The decision rests with the board.

Likewise, if dividends to the preferred stock are not in arrears, where the preferred stockholders seek to enjoin the payment of dividends to holders of common stock of the funds involved in the same situation, they will not be successful. Norwich Power Co. v. Southern Ry., 11 Va. Law

Reg. 203. This decision was based on the traditional assumption that if no dividends were declared on non-cumulative preferred stock for a particular year, such dividends were lost forever to the preferred stockholders. Contra, Day v. U. S. Cast Iron Pipe & Foundry Co., 126 Atl. Rep. 

302, holding that, where the statute imposed an obligation

DIVIDENDS 

253 on the directors to pay a fixed dividend to the preferred stockholders whenever there were earnings available, the satisfaction of the obligation may be postponed at the discretion of the directors, but its discharge was necessary before the common stockholders could receive current dividends. 

§ 162. Life Tenant and Remainderman. Pledgor and 

Pledgee.

Grants or bequests of income, i.e., dividends to a life tenant, with remainder to another whose enjoyment is to be postponed until the termination of the life estate, sometimes raise nice questions as to what the testator intended to be done with the extra dividends. If the donor has clearly expressed his intention, there is no difficulty. His intent governs. Thus a gift of the "full income" to the life tenant gives him extraordinary as well as ordinary dividends. McLouth v. Hunt, 154 N. Y. 179, 48 N. E. 548.

So also, where the will gave the "entire income" with a further provision that no part of the income should be diverted to "a sinking fund to replace loss... depreciation," the testator's words clearly gave extra dividends declared after testator's death from surplus accumulated 10 years before testator's death to the life tenant, as well as ordinary dividends. Lowry v. Farmer's L. & T. Co., 172 N. Y. 137. 

Dividends, ordinary or extra, declared before the testator's death but payable after his death, go neither to the remainderman nor to the life tenant, but to the executor, as part of the personal estate of the testator. Mtr. of 

Mercer, 117 Misc. 371, 192 N. Y. Supp. 317. The principle here involved is that dividends go to the stockholder who owned the stock at the date of declaration of the dividend. 

Peo. ex rel. Fraser v. Grt. Western Sug. Co., 29 F. (2d) 810.

Ordinary dividends are those paid from current net profits. They go to the life tenant, even tho the market value of the stock that constitutes the corpus depreciates. 

Ordinary dividends can not be kept by the executor to make up the depreciation in the value of the corpus for the benefit of the remainderman. Thus, Enz's will, in the residuary clause, bequeathed to his wife for life the "use and income" of the residue of his estate. In the said residue was stock

of a real estate corporation in which the dividend policy for many years had been to reappraise the corporate real estate, which was of a speculative nature and increasing in value, and to declare a cash dividend for the amount of the increased value, payable out of cash received from sales of land sold. This policy was continued by the corporation after testator's death and it was held that the dividends so declared after his death were ordinary dividends and went to the life tenant. In re Enz's Will, 204 App. Div. 

634, 198 N. Y. Supp. 802, affd. 237 N. Y. 577, affd. (mem.) 

237 N. Y. 577. See Mtr. of Eddy, 236 N. Y. Supp. 275.

Greater care is required to discover the donor's intention where the will or deed of gift does not in apt words state the disposition as between life tenant and remainderman of extra dividends. When a long accumulated surplus earned wholly or in part before testator's death is to be distributed as a dividend-consequent, perhaps on a change of policy of the corporation since the testator's death-several possibilities then arise: It is obvious that the distribution of a cash surplus that has been accumulated for a long period of years will have a tendency to depress the value of the stock; and that if the accumulated surplus is distributed in the form of a stock dividend, it is likely that the shares that formerly composed the corpus will be diluted by the substitution of the new and increased stock. If the situation has not been foreseen and provided for by donor's will or deed of gift—an oversight that too frequently occurs,the absence of expression of the testator's actual intent requires a construction in accordance with the legal intent signified by his mere words of gift of income. Four diverse rules to ascertain intent are known as the (1) English; (2) Massachusetts; (3) Pennsylvania; and (4) New 

New York rules.

The English rule appears to be based upon the power of directors to shift at one time a part of the net earnings to the capital account of the corporation, and at another to shift it back again and declare a dividend out of it. Therefore, "What the company says is income, shall be income, and what it says is capital shall be capital." McLouth v. 

Hunt, 154 N. Y. at p. 197, quoting Sproule v. Bouche, 29

DIVIDENDS 

255 

Ch. Div. 635, 653. In New York, the dividend resolution is competent evidence to prove the source of the fund, but is not necessarily conclusive, and is subject to contradiction. 

U. S. Trust Co. v. Heye, 224 N. Y. 242, 120 N. E. 645. In re Perkins Est., 133 Misc. 863, 234 N. Y. Supp. 596. cf. 

245 N. Y. 478. Where the dividend resolution throws no light on the question, the English rule, at first, was that all extraordinary or unusual dividends declared during the continuation of a life estate, whether payable in cash or stock, belonged to the corpus of the fund and not to the income. Brander v. Brander, 4 Ves. Jr. 800. Later, it was held that, prima facie, cash dividends belong to the life tenant and the stock dividends to the remainderman, subject to an examination of the facts and circumstances in each case, so as to give the life tenant the current profits since the testator's death, and the remainderman the profits earned prior to testator's death. Bouche v. Sproule, supra. 

U. S. Trust Co. v. Heye, supra. In re Jowit, L. R. 2 Ch. 

Div. 442 (1922).

The United States rule follows the English rule. If in effect it is only a distribution of assets or surplus of the corporation it goes to the remainderman. In Gibbons v. 

Malion, 136 U. S. 549, the court said: "When a distribution of earnings is made by a corporation among its stockholders the question of whether such distribution is an apportionment of additional stock representing capital, or a division of profits and income, depends upon the substance and intent of the action of the corporation as manifested by its vote or resolution; and ordinarily, a dividend declared in stock is to be deemed capital and a dividend in money is to be deemed income of each share." The federal rule further holds that it is a question to be determined by the action of the corporation itself, at such times and in such manner as the fair and honest administration of its whole property and business may require or permit, and by a rule applicable to all holders of like shares of its stock. Ib. 

Similarly, in income tax proceedings, a stock dividend is deemed to be capital and not taxable as income. Eisner v. 

Macomber, 252 U. S. 589.

Under the Massachusetts rule, as laid down in early cases,

cash dividends are regarded as income, however large, and stock dividends as capital, however made. Minot v. Payne, 99 Mass. 108. The courts, however, have taken to themselves the right to determine whether a stock dividend is in effect a distribution of cash to be treated the same as a cash dividend. Connecticut, Delaware, Georgia, and Illinois follow the Massachusetts rule. Under the Massachusetts rule, the settlement of the directors in the resolution declaring the dividend will govern the court.

The Pennsylvania rule, as laid down in the case of Earps 

Appeal, 28 Pa. St. 368 and called the "American Rule" is that (1). The surplus property accumulated by the corporation at the date of the testator's death belongs to the remainderman regardless of when the dividend was declared and whether in the form of cash or otherwise. (2). Accumulations after the testator's death are income and go to the life tenant, whether the dividend is in the form of cash, scrip or stock. Thus, this rule is confined to the condition at the testator's death.

Under the New York rule, the tests to be applied are the source of the dividend, (current profits going to the life tenant) and the language of the instrument creating the estate. 

In re Roberts est., 191 N. Y. Supp. 527. In re Osborne, 209 N. Y. 450, Cady's Cas. p. 420. The New York rule gives the life tenant all dividends declared after the testator's death and the setting up of the trust, provided the distribution will not dilute the corpus of the trust. If to give the life tenant an extra stock dividend would result in a lessening of the value of the stock per share which constitutes the corpus of the trust, enough of the new stock is to be retained in the fund so that the remainderman's estate will not be diminished through the new issue of stock. U. S. Trust Co. v. Heye, 120 N. Y. 645. The burden of proof is on the life tenant to show that the stock dividend was earned subsequent to the creation of the trust. Macy v. Ladd, 219 N. Y. Supp. 449. The testator may avoid litigation by stating in his will an arbitrary valuation to be put on the stock. In re Cory's Estate, 164 N. Y. Supp. 956.

When a corporation is liquidated and dissolved, so much of the proceeds as represent earnings since the creation of

DIVIDENDS 

257 the trust is income, going to the life tenant. Matter of 

Schaeffer, 178 App. Div. 117, 165 N. Y. Supp. 19. If the trustee sells the stock to the corporation itself, such part of the price received by him as represents profits since the creation of the trust is income. Any increase upon the sale of the corporate assets, not caused by the expenditure of the profits of the business, is capital. In re Bemis' Will, 205 N. Y. Supp. 367. A stock dividend representing earnings accumulated is not income to the beneficiary thereof so as to be subject to tax under the state Tax Law. Peo. ex rel. 

Clark v. Gilchrist, 243 N. Y. 173. The income of the life beneficiary in a trust can be reached by sequestration proceedings brought by a wife for nonpayment of alimony. Metropolitan Trust Co. v. Bishop, 200 N. Y. Supp. 649. See also, Riggs v. Cragg, 89 N. Y. 479. In re Rogers, 161 N. Y. 

108. Chester v. Buff. Car Mfg. Co., 183 N. Y. 425. Clarkson v. Clarkson, 18 Barb. 646. Richmond v. Richmond, 196 N. Y. 535. Tuttle v. 1st Nat. Bank, 44 Misc. 318, 89 

N. Y. Supp. 820. Gould v. Gould, 126 Misc. 54, 213 N. Y.

Supp. 286. Olcott v. Est. of Hoffman, Inc., 220 App. Div. 

713, 221 N. Y. Supp. 871. Bunker's Est., 77 Misc. 320, 137 

N. Y. Supp. 104. Mtr. of Bourne, 119 Misc. 43, 195 N. Y. 

Supp. 500, rev. 237 N. Y. 341, 143 N. E. 214.

As between pledgor and pledgee of stock the pledgee is entitled to collect dividends declared thereon, and it is his duty to apply them to the reduction of the indebtedness for which the stock is held as security. He represents not only his own interests as pledgee but also owes a duty to the pledgor to protect the security. Brightson v. Claflin, 225 

N. Y. 469. Gillet v. Bank of America, 160 N. Y. 549.

Where the pledgor of stock as collateral security for the payment of an indebtedness has defaulted in its payment, the pledgee of the stock is in duty bound to collect the dividends declared thereon, and apply them towards the reduction of the indebtedness for which the stock is held as security. When a pledgee sells the stock pledged, by virtue of his lien, the purchaser at the sale takes, with the stock, all dividends, declared before the sale, but payable later. 

Waterloo First National Bank v. Exchange National Bank, 226 N. Y. 663.

As between transferror and transferee the dividend, so far as the corporation is concerned, is payable to the owners of shares as shown on the books of the corporation at the time when the dividend is declared. Richter & Co. v. Light, 97 Conn. 364, 116 Atl. 600. Ford v. Snook, supra. Since an unrecorded transfer is good as between transferror and transferee, where a dividend is declared payable to owners of record on a certain future day, and stock is transferred before that date without being transferred on the books, the corporation may not pay the registered holder if it has knowledge of the true ownership. Ford v. Snook, supra.

The ownership of dividends may be made the subject of contract between the transferror and transferee. Jermain v. Lake Shore etc. R. Co., 91 N. Y. 483. A transfer passes all dividends declared subsequent to the transfer, tho earned before. Kane v. Bloodgood, 7 Johns. Ch. (N. Y.) 90. Hopper v. Sage, supra, Cady's Cases p. 414. 

§ 163. Same. As Between Classes of Stock. 

After the dividends, cumulative or otherwise, have been paid on the highest class of preferred stock, the distribution of the balance depends on contract. Preferred stockholders can not claim more than their percent of dividends even tho resulting from profit derived from dealings in the stock of other corporations. Graham v. 1st Natl. Bank, 84 N. Y. 

393. If the surplus is derived from a reduction of the capital stock, all stockholders share alike. Equit. Lf. Assur. 

Soc. v. Union Pac. R. R. Co., 212 N. Y. 360. Interest should be allowed on passed dividends of cumulative preferred stock before giving dividends to common stock. Boardman v. Mch. So. Ry. Co., 84 N. Y. 157. § 164. Recovery of Dividends Wrongfully Paid or Paid to the Wrong Person.

The remedy of a stockholder who is wrongfully excluded from his pro rata share of the dividends declared is against the corporation. The stockholder is not entitled to follow the assets of the corporation into the hands of parties to whom it has made payments and to recover the dividends from them, until at least the stockholder has established his right as a creditor of the corporation and exhausted his

DIVIDENDS 

259 legal remedies against it. The plaintiff could not, in the first instance, resort to a common law action against the persons whom the corporation had recognized as its only stockholders, to recover a portion of the dividends admitted to be due and actually paid to them in their own right and try his title to the share in an action against them. Peckham v. Van Wagener, 83 N. Y. 40. Godley v. Crandall & 

Godley, 212 N. Y. 121.

If the stockholder's shares are divided as a dividend, he may sue in assumpsit. Avedon v. Gem Dress House, supra. 

Demand for payment of the dividends must be made before an action is begun. Scott v. Central R. R. & Banking 

Co., 52 Barb. 45. Ehle v. Chittenango Bank, 24 N. Y. 548.

If an illegal dividend has been paid the stockholder, a judgment creditor of the corporation may generally sue the stockholder and recover, at least to the extent of the dividend received and not exceeding the judgment. In states where the 'trust fund" theory applies to the assets of a corporation the suit should be in the nature of a creditors bill. Bartlett v. Drew, 57 N. Y. 587. In some jurisdictions, such as England, and New York, the trust fund theory is enforced through the operation of a statute the "Winding

Up" Act in England, and S. C. L. 15 in New York. In re 

Phillips, 18 Beav. 629. Hamburger v. Cornell Univ., 240

N. Y. 328, Cady's Cas. p. 311. Even a preferred stockholder is not a creditor, for it is a dividend that is guaranteed and not a debt, and hence, when dividends have been paid out of capital to an innocent stockholder he is not in the position of a creditor who has received his debt in good faith out of funds in the hands of his debtor belonging to another. See however, McDonald v. Williams, 174 U. S. 397. First Natl. 

Bank v. Supervisors, 106 N. Y. 488. If the dividend was declared out of surplus the stockholder may recover his interest in it although he has let the dividend lie in the hands of the corporation until it became insolvent. From the moment the dividend was declared, it became the property of the stockholders. LeRoy v. Globe Ins. Co., 2 Edw. Ch. 

657. Van Dyck v. McQuade, 86 N. Y. 88.

Where assets of even solvent corporations were wrongfully transferred by the directors, such directors were re-

sponsible jointly and severally to the creditors for the loss occasioned by their acts. Giles Dyeing Machine Co. v. 

Klander Weldon Machine Co., 190 N. Y. Supp. 726. Saranac & Lake P. R. Co. v. Arnold, 167 N. Y. 368. Hurd v. N. Y. & Comm. Steam Laundry Co., 167 N. Y. 89.

Where dividends are improperly declared, as between the claims of the creditors and the stockholders, the creditors have the first right. Scott v. Eagle Fire Co., 7 Pai. 198.

Dividends improperly declared and paid out of the capital may be recovered back by the corporation and its creditors. 

Cottrell v. Albany Card and Paper Mfg. Co., 142 App. Div. 

148, 126 N. Y. Supp. 1070.

When a dividend is declared and paid out of the capital and the corporation then is solvent but later becomes insolvent, creditors cannot recover from stockholders, dividends so paid. McDonald v. Williams, 174 U. S. 397; Sweet v. 

Lang, 14 Fed. (2nd) 762; Little v. Garabrant, 90 Hun 404, affd. 153 N. Y. 661.

If the directors act in good faith and exercise reasonable care and diligence, they are not liable for losses resulting to the corporation from mistakes or mere errors of judgment on their part. Hun v. Carey, 82 N. Y. 65; Holmes v. 

Crane, 191 App. Div. 820, 182 N. Y. Supp. 270, affd., 232 

N. Y. 571; Holmes v. St. Joseph Lead Co., 168 App. Div. 

688, 154 N. Y. Supp. 513, affd. 217 N. Y. 619; Cass v. Realty 

Securities Co., 148 App. Div. 96, 132 N. Y. Supp. 1074, affd. 206 N. Y. 649.
