How Called. Regular and Special Meetings. 

The intangible legal entity can manifest its wishes only through individuals. Consequently, meetings are essential. 

Every member, unless his contract denies the right, is entitled to be present. S. C. L. 45, G. C. L. 31. Failure to give due notice to any member, therefore, will invalidate the proceedings at the meeting, even though the omission be accidental, provided only that he does not attend or otherwise waive notice or estop himself to object. To hold a meeting without due notice is as bad as denying to members, entitled to participate, that privilege. N. Y. Elec. W. U. v. Sullivan, 122 App. Div. 764, 107 N. Y. Supp. 886. The absence of a member from home will not excuse the want of notice. Jackson v. Hampden, 20 Me. 37. The burden is on the corporation to prove that notice was given, but the fact that notice was given to a member whose mental imbecility rendered him incapable of receiving it was held not to invalidate the proceedings at the meeting. Stebbins v. Merritt, 10 Cush. (Mass.) 27. Directors need be given no notice of stated meetings of the board; but the rule is different as to corporators and members. The latter must take notice of all adjourned notified meetings, but they are not bound to take notice of a special meeting called by a vote at a regular meeting at which they were absent. Peo. ex rel. Loew v. Batchelor, 22 N. Y. 128. The presumption of regularity, which attaches to every meeting's records, vanishes when it is shown that the meeting was not duly 261

called, and the burden of proof of the giving of notice is on the one who alleges the validity of the proceedings. Ib. p. 

134. Beardsley v. Johnson, 121 N. Y. 224, 228, 24 N. E. 380.

The directors should proceed under the statute and the by-laws, if any, not inconsistent with the charter, to call the meeting, and, where the stock is changing hands so rapidly that the statutory method of giving notice would be inadequate, they may bind the corporation to pay the expense of publishing notice; but they can not pledge its credit for the unusual expense of continued advertising, or of dispatching special messengers for the purpose of procuring proxies for one party. Lawyers Ad. Co. v. Con. Ry. L. & R. 

Co., 187 N. Y. 385. Whether they attend or not, stockholders are chargeable with notice of all that was done at duly notified meetings. Kranich v. Bach, 209 App. Div. 52, 204 N. Y. Supp. 320. On the other hand, if they attend and do not object they are estopped. Peo. ex rel. Smith v. Peck, 11 Wend. 604. But if one person is absent, or refuses his consent, the proceedings are invalid. Peo. Ins. Co. v. Westcott, 14 Gray, 440. Failure to comply with a by-law prescribing the method for calling the meeting to elect directors was held, in one case, to invalidate the election of directors, and a suspension of members in another. Stein v. 

Marks, 44 Misc. 140, 89 N. Y. Supp. 921. Harris v. Magrill, 131 Misc. 380, 226 N. Y. Supp. 621.

The statutory notice, S. C. L. 45, has not fully superseded all other provisions, and it may be said that the notice, to be proper, must comply with (1) the statutes, S. C. L. 45, 55, G. C. L. 14, 26; (2) the charter; (3) the by-laws, S. C. L. 

5 (11); and (4) the common law, to the extent that it has not been changed by statute. Meetings to elect directors should be held annually. S. C. L. 55. On failure to elect successors, the old board holds over. G. C. L. 21. If the directors for the first year, who became such by being named in the certificate of incorporation, hold over after the expiration of the term by reason of their failure to adopt proper by-laws calling the meeting to elect their successors, the disadvantage suffered by them is that in any action of stockholder or creditor to disaffirm the board's acts thereafter performed, and to charge the directors personally

STOCKHOLDERS' MEETINGS 

263 for any detriment that may have come to the corporation thereby, the said acts will be prima facie presumed fraudulent and not binding on the corporation, casting thereby the burden of proof on the directors to prove by a fair preponderance of evidence the bona fides. S. C. L. 57. The statute has not been construed, and the foregoing interpretation is based on the following considerations:-The statute is penal, and must be strictly construed. What is involved by that term as applied to directors was determined under somewhat similar statutes, now repealed in most part, imposing a liability on them for failure to make reports. 

Hoboken Beef Co. v. Hand, 104 App. Div. 390, 93 N. Y. 

Supp. 834. Huntington v. Attrill, 118 N. Y. 365, 23 N. E. 

544. Such statutes are construed as imposing no liability where the plaintiff is unable to prove that injury resulted.

Though the statute provides that all the acts after the expiration of the term shall be fraudulent and void, an action for damages for fraud can not succeed if no damage has been sustained. Arthur v. Griswold, 55 N. Y. 400. It follows, therefore, that the statute creates merely a presumption. Presumptions created by statute are, wherever possible, construed as rebuttable rather than conclusive. Siegel v. Dubinsky, 56 Misc. 681, 107 N. Y. Supp. 678. Schneitzer v. Kessler, 191 N. Y. Supp. 199. Therefore, the probable effect of the statute, S. C. L. 57, is merely to cast the burden of proof on the defendant directors. Plaintiff, therefore, would make out a prima facie case of fraud under the statute by proving (1) Holdover; (2) Acts done while holding over; (3) Injury to plaintiff. 

The requirements for the notice of the meeting are:—(1) 

Written; (2) Signed by either president, vice-president, secretary or assistant secretary; (3) Must state the purposes, time and place of the meeting; (4) Must be served personally or by mail upon each stockholder of record entitled to vote at the meeting, and upon those who would be entitled to have their stock appraised if the indicated purposes of the meeting should be carried out, S. C. L. 21, 87; (5)

The time of service is not less than 10 nor more than 45 days before the meeting; (6) If served by mail, the address must be that specified in the stockbook, unless the stock-

holder has indicated otherwise by a written request filed by him with the secretary; (7) The by-laws may require publication of the notice. G. C. L. 5 (13), 27. Directors by-laws regarding the call of the meeting must be published as required by G. C. L. 14 (5), or the proceedings of the meeting may be annulled at the suit of a dissenting minority stockholder, and the election of directors at the meeting held illegal, the old board and its officers holding over. Mtr. of Emp. St. Sup. Lodge, 53 Misc. 344, 103 N. Y. Supp. 465, affd. 118 App. Div. 616, 103 N. Y. Supp. 1124. The addition of further and unnecessary material to the notice, such as the location of a corporation's business which the meeting is to vote to merge, will not invalidate the notice unless someone is misled. Langan v. Francklyn, 29 Abb. N. C. 

102, 20 N. Y. Supp. 404. Where the purpose stated in the notice was the consideration of an amalgamation with another corporation, and a member, who was absent from the meeting, was not thereby informed that the meeting would consider the issuance of stock to a director, he was permitted to succeed in a proceeding to invalidate that act of the meeting. United G. & P. Mines Co. v. Smith, 44 Misc. 

567, 90 N. Y. Supp. 199.

By-laws relative to the call must not be unreasonable, and are readily construed as directory rather than mandatory so that a violation will not invalidate the meeting.

Thus, the by-laws of a bank requiring that directors should be nominated ten days before the meeting, and that none should be voted for, except those so nominated, are void, for stockholders should be permitted to vote for any qualified person, and the restriction on eligibility to the particular class was unreasonable. In re Farrell, 205 App. 

Div. 443, 200 N. Y. Supp. 95.

A stockholder may mandamus the directors to call the annual meeting for the election of their successors. Peo. ex rel. Miller v. Cummings, 72 N. Y. 433. While the president was absent on business, the minority held a meeting surreptitiously, as he claimed, and removed him. On his return, he demanded of the secretary that he call a special meeting for the purpose of electing new directors, which was refused on the ground that, as he held a majority of

STOCKHOLDERS' MEETINGS 

265 the voting shares, he would be in a position to control the election in his own favor, and by successive steps, decrease the board of directors by holding meetings and amending the charter for that purpose (S. C. L. 35, 37), and thus vote his enemies out of office, reinstate himself as president, and cause the new board, which would be favorable to him, to ratify his prior acts—all of which things he threatened to do. It was held that he was entitled to a mandamus to compel the special election, for no act of the meeting, ratifying the ex-president's acts, could take away from the minority stockholders the right to sue the president for an accounting of all of his dealings with the corporate property, if improper. Lersner v. Adair Mach. Co., 137 N. Y.

Supp. 565. The same notice is required for special as for regular meetings. G. C. L. 26.

The time of the meeting should be precisely stated, and no business should be transacted either before the meeting or after it has adjourned. Peo. v. Albany etc. R. R. Co., 55 Barb. 344. Only the proper officers may call the meeting—an aggrieved stockholder has no power. Peo. v. Board of Governors, 61 Barb. 397. Stein v. Marks, supra.

Waiver of notice may be by act, or by the statutory waiver, G. C. L. 31. The statutory waiver must be in writing, and may be executed by all the members, irrespective of whether they hold common or preferred stock, and whether their presence is required as voters or merely because they might have the right to have their stock appraised as the result of action proposed to be taken at the meeting. Waivers are ineffectual unless a quorum is present at a meeting; but if there is a quorum, those not present may execute a waiver of notice either before or subsequent to the time of the meeting, and are bound by its acts; and those present and attending are estopped to complain of the lack of notice. Peo. ex rel. Smith v. Peck, supra. Hallett v. Met. Messenger Co., 69 App. Div. 258, 74 N. Y. 

Supp. 639.

Stockholders' meetings of domestic corporations must be held within the state, and, by common law, at the corporation office, unless all waive or are estopped. S. C. L. 45. If all stockholders are non-residents, the use of proxies will

obviate the difficulty of personal attendance. Sec. 171, infra. Directors' meetings may be held without the state unless the by-laws or charter forbid. S. C. L. 5 (11). The organization meetings of the corporators, by clear weight of authority, must be held within the state of incorporation even though state laws are silent on the subject. Incorporation is not complete in every respect until the organization meeting has been held, so that until the corporation is organized, it may not operate in the foreign state even tho a provision of charter or statute permits it to conduct its operations in all states. The corporation is not a citizen under Art. IV., Sec. 2, U. S. Const., guaranteeing to the citizens of each state all the privileges and immunities of citizens in the several states, but is solely a creature of the state which incorporated it, and can have no powers except by the law of the state that made it. Consequently, altho the law of the foreign state like G. C. L. 223, permits meetings of foreign corporations to be held therein, its organization meeting held without the state of incorporation is an illegal meeting. Franco-Tex. Land Co. v. Laigle, 59 Tex. 

339. Miller v. Ewer, 27 Me. 509, 46 Am. Dec. 619. Aspinall v. O. & C. R. R., 83 Am. Dec. 329 (Ind.). Smith v. Silver 

Valley Mfg. Co., 20 Atl. 1032 (Md.). Hening & Hagedorn v. Glanton, 108 S. E. 256 (Ga.). In the leading case of

Miller v. Ewer, supra, the organization meeting of stockholders was held in New York, the corporate charter having been granted by the state of Maine. Property was acquired for the corporate business at this meeting. The directors organization meeting was held immediately afterwards, also in New York, and a mortgage on the corporate property executed. It was held, in an action to foreclose, that the mortgage was invalid, the corporation being invalidly organized, and no officer, therefore, having authority to act for it. This, and correlated principles relating to the law of place, may be summed up as follows: 1. Corporations exist only within the state in which they were chartered; 2. They can only be organized within that state; 

3. Corporate acts, strictly so called, can not be done outside the state of incorporation; 4. Duly authorized agents of the corporation may act anywhere. This includes meetings of

STOCKHOLDERS' MEETINGS 

267 directors, unless forbidden. Courts differ as to what are strictly corporate acts. The statute, S. C. L. 5, declares the policy of New York so far as directors' meetings are concerned, and the acts of directors without the state do not bind or estop those who did not participate, since the meeting was not legal. Ormsby v. Vt. Cop. Min. Co., 65 

Barb. 360, rev. (mem.) 56 N. Y. 623. Russian Reinsurance Co. v. Stoddard, 240 N. Y. 149, 147 N. E. 703. Repub.

Art Printery v. David, 173 App. Div. 726, 159 N. Y. Supp. 

1010. If the corporation could take action on strictly corporate matters without the state, the hardship and fraud that might be entailed on shareholders unable to attend might be irreparable. No one but a stockholder may sue to invalidate action so taken, and, if all the stockholders have estopped themselves by participating in the meeting, no one may complain, since there is no cause of action where no injury can be proved. Volenti non fit injuria. 

The single situation where a member may call a special meeting is where a meeting duly called failed to convene; or, if a quorum was present and it convened, no action was taken; and no further call for a meeting has been sent out by the regularly constituted officers for one month. G. C. L. 

22. The notice sent out by the member must be (1) Written; (2) Published; (3) Comply with by-laws, if any; (4) Delivered or mailed. Coghlan v. Coghlan &c. Inc., 226 

App. Div. 764, 234 N. Y. Supp. 273. Though no officers remain to call a meeting, the corporation is not dissolved thereby, and it is held that the stockholders may call a meeting. In the celebrated case of Foss v. Harbottle, 2 

Hare 461, 16 L. J. (Ch.) 217, some of the shareholders brought a proceeding in equity for the appointment of a receiver to wind up the corporation. The petition showed that there were insufficient members of the board to hold a meeting, that the company had no office or secretary, and that therefore, general meetings could not be held to fill the vacancies for the lack of a proper officer to call them. 

The Vice-Chancellor, however, held that, assuming the truth of all these statements, there was no ground shown for the interposition of the powers of a court of equity, and that it would be sufficient to fill vacancies if some of the stock-

holders, having given notice to the others of the meeting, met together and purported to elect directors. 

§ 166. Conduct of the Meeting. Inspectors. 

It will be noted that in many cases the action taken may destroy rights of the minority without making compensation, such as a compulsory sacrifice of the good will by majority amendment of the charter. Matter of Hinds, 172 

App. Div. 140, 158 N. Y. Supp. 249, affd. (mem.) 218 N. Y. 

715, Cady's Cas. p. 78. All formalities adapted to conserve existing rights must therefore be observed strictly. Extensive powers, capable of abuse, are exercisable by the meeting. A great and respected corporate name may be discarded by the will of a mere majority of a quorum present, G. C. L. 40. All changes in capital structure and in the relative rights of the holders of different classes of stock must be made under S. C. L. 36 and 37. These changes can not be made under any other general law, and must be made in the manner required by the statute. For instance, they can not be included in a certificate made under S. C. L. 35. 

All technicalities of this sort are for the protection of the minority stockholder, and his rights must be further sustained by carefully conducting the meeting in a lawful manner.

At common law, it was held that a corporation might, by by-laws, provide and enforce penalties by fines for nonattendance of members, in person or by proxy. Tobacco 

Pipe Makers Co. v. Woodroffe, 7 B. & C. 838. S. C. L. 55, if the charter is silent on the subject, permits one stockholder owning two shares, to hold the meeting, since it provides that the directors "shall be chosen by a plurality of votes cast." The reluctance of stockholders, in America, to attend meetings, or even to execute a proxy, is proverbial, and has produced this result. The charter, or its amendments, or the bylaws, may "fix the number of shares not exceeding a majority, necessary to constitute a quorum." 

S. C. L. 55. Unless the statute had specified this limit, designing promoters might perpetuate themselves in office if they had succeeded in influencing the corporators to insert a provision requiring a larger attendance. The meet-

STOCKHOLDERS' MEETINGS 

269 ing may take action on all matters stated in the notice of meeting if a quorum is present. At special meetings, two members must be present to constitute a quorum, and this statutory enactment can not be varied by the certificate of incorporation or by by-laws. G. C. L. 23, S. C. L. 55. To illustrate:-Assume that the charter is silent as to what number of shares will be required to constitute a quorum, and that A and B, directors, own all the stock, C being the third director, the certificate of incorporation or by-laws providing that directors need not be stockholders. S. C. L. 

55, G. C. L. 27. If both A and B attend the meeting, and disagree, no election will result; if B stays away, A may elect a board consisting of A and any two other persons, and, since B can not control a plurality of votes, this board may remain in office until death, removal (G. C. L. 136), or other incapacity, and thus A will control the corporation forever afterwards.

In the absence of a provision in the by-laws, the president has no implied authority to preside. It is a stockholders' meeting, and they may elect one not a stockholder. 

Fletch. Enc. Corps. p. 2759. The by-laws, prepared by counsel, should contain provisions governing the conduct of the meeting. Peo. ex rel. Godwin v. Amer. Inst. of N. Y., 44 How. Pr. 468. Secs. 57, 57a, supra.

S. C. L. 46 provides for two special officers for the election, called inspectors. The requirements are: 1. Appointed in the first instance by board of directors, pursuant to by-laws; if not appointed, or appointment is ineffectual, stockholders present at meeting may elect by a per capita vote; 2. A majority may act; 3. At least two; 4. May be a director or officer if the corporation is not "moneyed"; 

5. Oaths, filed in county clerk's office. If the oath is not administered to the inspectors, or if an improper oath is administered, any stockholder voting without objection waives the informality, and, if the election or other matter before the board was carried by a plurality of a quorum, it is valid. Mtr. of Mohawk &c. Ry., 19 Wend. 135. Union 

Nat. Bank v. Scott, 53 App. Div. 65, 66 N. Y. Supp. 145.

In a case wherein the voters elected one board, and the seceders walked out and held a separate meeting and elected

another, it was held that the president might call another person to the chair to sit in his absence, without invalidating the election at the meeting held pursuant to the notice. 

Peo. v. Albany &c. Ry. Co., 55 Barb. 344, mod. 57 N. Y. 161.

The duties of inspectors are both ministerial and judicial. 

Generally, they have the power to pass upon eligibility of voters but not eligibility of candidates for office. S. C. L. 

47. Mtr. of Clarke, 186 App. Div. 216, 174 N. Y. Supp. 313. 

Inspectors may be candidates at the meeting. Ex parte

Willcocks, supra. The stockholders cannot bind a dissenting stockholder by waiving the requirement of two inspectors. Mtr. of Rem. Type. Co., 234 N. Y. 295. If a vote is challenged, G. C. L. 20, the inspectors administer the oath, which is merely to the effect that the stockholder voting has not received "directly, indirectly or impliedly," a bribe to influence his vote, and, if the voter presents a proxy as his warrant for voting, that he has not given or promised any consideration for the appointment as proxy. The transfer books of the corporation are the evidence of membership to the inspectors and the sole criterion for the determination of the right to vote or to give proxies. Inspectors may not go beyond the books. Mtr. of Clarke, 186 App. Div. 216, 174 N. Y. Supp. 214. Mtr. of L. I. Ry. 

Co., 15 Wend. 37. A transferee of shares cannot vote unless his transfer is registered. McNeil v. 10th Natl. Bank, supra, Cady's Cas. p. 494. 

Stockholders do not elect officers other than directors.

S. C. L. 60. The quorum must remain throughout the meeting, and if one of the persons departs, even wrongfully, the meeting can only adjourn. Ex parte Rogers, 7 Cow. 526, 530, note. 

§ 167. Records of the Meeting. Presumptions. 

The omission of the New York statutes to prescribe that the records and minutes of the corporation should be in English, while making that requirement for the certificate of incorporation, is of some importance. G. C. L. 8. When kept, the minutes are the best evidence of what was done, tho they may be contradicted by parol. Richardson, Law of Evi., § 669. Woodhaven Bank v. Bklyn. Hills Imp. Co., 

69 App. Div. 489, 74 N. Y. Supp. 1023. Abernethy v. Soc.

STOCKHOLDERS' MEETINGS 

271 

of Ch. of Puritans, 3 Daly 1. Clark v. Farmer's Wool Mfg. 

Co., 15 Wend. 256. St. Geo. Vineyard Co. v. Fritz, 48 App. 

Div. 233, 62 N. Y. Supp. 775. Union Nat. Bank v. Dean, 154 App. Div. 869, 139 N. Y. Supp. 835.

Usual provisions of the by-laws require that the minutes of stockholders' meetings shall be kept by the secretary. 

If kept, they should be kept with due order and regularity, be signed and certified by him, and record the notice of meeting, all waivers, the names of stockholders present in person or by proxy, the filing of the latter, the appointment or presence and oath of inspectors, nominations, votes, resolutions, the plurality of votes by which any measure was carried, the adjournment, and in general give an account of the proceedings with sufficient fullness to show the validity of the action taken. By-laws requiring the keeping of minutes are construed as directory, and the failure to keep them does not invalidate the proceedings. Bank of U. S. v. 

Dandridge, 12 Wheat. 75. Woodhaven Bank v. Bklyn. Hills 

Imp. Co., supra. Leonard v. Faber, 52 App. Div. 495, 65

N. Y. Supp. 391. Imperfect minutes may be amended so as to cause them to show what actually happened. Fletch., Enc. Corps. p. 4045.

The ordinary form of waiver is as follows: 

.......on the.. and con- .day of

We, the undersigned, stockholders of X Corporation, do hereby waive service and publication of notice of a meeting of the stockholders of said corporation, for the purpose of.. sent that said meeting be held at.. 

19 at......o'clock in the ..M., and approve any and all action that may be lawfully taken thereat. (Dated and signed). 

§ 168. Ratification of Acts of Officers, Directors, and 

Agents.

The meeting may ratify acts of officers within the power of the corporation. Sec. 92 (1) supra. Acts of the majority at a meeting which was illegally held may be ratified by the majority at a regular and legal meeting. Schenectady & S. Pl. Rd. Co. v. Thatcher, 11 N. Y. 102. The stockholders may ratify a resolution of directors fixing their own salaries or fixing a rate of commission to be received by them on sales. Trimyer & Co. v. Noel, 28 F. (2d) 781. 

§ 169. Adjourned Meetings. 

Business that might have been transacted under the

notice of meeting given for the meeting that was adjourned, may also be transacted at an adjournment of said meeting; but no other business can be done without special notice. 

A minority of the stock attending may hold the meeting, unless there is a provision in the by-laws or charter requiring a majority to be present. S. C. L. 55. Smith v. Law, 21 N. Y. 296. Peo. ex rel. Loew v. Batchelor, supra. Re 

Rapid Trans. Ferry Co., 15 App. Div. 530, 44 N. Y. Supp. 

539. Ashcroft v. Hammond, 132 App. Div. 3, 116 N. Y. 

Supp. 362, at p. 365. Adjournments may be from day to day, or for many days, or from time to time; but all the meetings are regarded as one meeting, so far as the proceedings are concerned. In re Chenango Co. Mut. Ins. Co., 19 Wend. 635. Smith v. Law, supra. 

§ 170. Voting at the Meeting. Cumulative Voting. 

Every shareholder of record has the right to vote as many votes as he has shares, unless deprived thereof by charter, valid by-law, or contract. S. C. L. 51. The stockholders' by-law may close the transfer books not more than 40 days prior to meetings, thus depriving subsequent transferees of their voting rights at that meeting; or the stockholders' by-law may authorize the directors to fix a day not exceeding 40 days before a meeting as a day as of which the qualified voters are to be determined. S. C. L. 47. A transferee subsequent to the date set would need a proxy from the record owner of the stock in order to vote. The pledgor is entitled to a proxy from his pledgee; and if the pledgee has not had the stock registered in his name, the pledgor may vote it. Elyea v. Lehigh Salt Min. Co., 45 

App. Div. 231, 60 N. Y. Supp. 1050. The majority of fiduciaries who hold stock may decide how the stock shall be voted, and if the fiduciaries are evenly divided, an application may be made to the court for direction. Townshend v. 

Weinburn, 107 Misc. 443, 177 N. Y. Supp. 757. S. C. L. 48.

The right to vote is a property right, and depriving a stockholder of his right to vote for directors is depriving him of an attribute of his property. Lord v. Equit. Lf. 

Assur. Soc., 194 N. Y. 212, 87 N. E. 443.

A person who appears on the books of a corporation as the absolute owner of stock clearly has the right to vote it,

STOCKHOLDERS' MEETINGS 

273 although he really holds as trustee. Shares registered in the name of trustees may be voted by them. S. C. L. 48. 

The cestui que trust may prevent the trustee from voting if the shares are registered in the latter's name. Haines v. 

Kinderhook & H. Ry. Co., 33 App. Div. 154, 53 N. Y. Supp. 

368. Lewisohn Bros. v. Anaconda Copper Min. Co., 26 Misc. 

613, 56 N. Y. Supp. 807. Elger v. Boyle, 69 Misc. 273, 126 

N. Y. Supp. 946. Byington v. Piazza, 131 App. Div. 895, 115 N. Y. Supp. 918. Elias v. Schweyer, 27 App. Div. 69, 50 N. Y. Supp. 180. Shares held by the corporation cannot be voted, irrespective of whether they are unissued stock or treasury stock, for the will of the shareholders desiring to elect new directors would be frustrated. Vail v. Hamilton, 85 N. Y. 453. Ex parte Holmes, 5 Cow. 426. Ex parte 

Deddoity, 1 Wend. 98. The directors of a corporation which holds shares in another may vote them at a meeting of the second and may elect themselves to office. Oelbermann v. 

N. Y. R. Co., 77 Hun 332, 29 N. Y. Supp. 545. Farmers' 

Loan & Trust Co. v. N. Y. & N. R. Co., 150 N. Y. 410, 44

N. E. 1043. The personal interest of the stockholder adverse to the corporation does not disqualify him from voting. Gamble v. Queens County Water Co., 123 N. Y. 91, 25 

N. E. 201. Socorro Mountain Min. Co. v. Preston, 17 Misc. 

220, 40 N. Y. Supp. 1040.

Cumulative voting is permitted by S. C. L. 49 providing there is provision therefor in the charter. This method of voting permits the shareholder to cast the whole number of his votes for one candidate at an election for directors, or distribute them among two or more candidates as he may prefer. The purpose is to permit a minority to get together and secure representation of their interests on the board. In re Jamaica Consumers Ice Co., 229 N. Y. 516.

Under cumulative voting, a shareholder has as many votes as will equal the product obtained by multiplying the number of voting shares he owns, by the number of vacancies to be filled. On a motion to adjourn, the stockholder would have only as many votes as he has shares of stock standing in his name on the books. In re Roch. Dist. Tel. Co., 40 

Hun 172. A formula has been devised by which the minority group may determine the number of directors for whom they may successfully vote.. Let A equal the number of

voting shares outstanding, D the number of directors that the group wishes to elect, B the total number of directors to be elected to fill the vacancies, and X one less than the number of shares which the group must control in order to elect. The equation then is as follows:-(A times D) divided by (B plus one) equals X. In other words, divide the product of A multiplied by D, by one more than B. The quotient will be one less than the number of votes required to elect your candidates. No fractional votes may be cast unless provided for by charter. Peo. ex rel. Browne v. 

Koenig, 133 App. Div. 756, 118 N. Y. Supp. 136.

In the case of classified stock, such as preferred and common, the shares of all series of the same class having voting power will not have more than one vote each. S. C. L. 11. 

Hassel v. Pohle, 214 App. Div. 654, 212 N. Y. Supp. 561. 

Matter of Morse, 247 N. Y. 290, 160 N. E. 374. Matter of 

Silberkrauss, 224 App. Div. 268, 229 N. Y. Supp. 735. Peo. v. Koenig, 133 App. Div. 756, 48 N. Y. Supp. 136. 

Cumulative voting is unusual. Rudiger v. Coleman, 129 

App. Div. 916, 114 N. Y. Supp. 689. Bond v. Atlantic Terra 

Cotta Co., 137 App. Div. 671, 122 N. Y. Supp. 425. 

§ 171. Proxies. Voting Trusts and Other Agreements. 

A "proxy" to vote shares given by one corporate stockholder to another is an authority, by one having the right to vote, to another to do it. Manson v. Curtis, 223 N. Y. 

313, 119 N. E. 559. A "voting trust agreement" accumulates in the hands of a trustee the corporate shares of several owners, in trust for the purpose of voting them, in order, through the selection and election of directors, to control the corporate business and affairs in the interests of the cestuis que trustent. Ib. It was held at common law that shareholders had no implied right to vote by proxy, for the corporation was entitled to have the intelligent action of its stockholders, who were in duty bound to vote in person; but it was held competent in New York to confer the right by by-law. Phillips v. Wickham, 1 Pai. 590. Peo. v. Twaddle, 18 Hun 427. Some states hold by-laws, when not passed by virtue of express charter power permitting proxies, void; and in New York a proxy-holder may not vote at meetings of religious corporations. G. C. L. 19. Taylor v. Griswold,

STOCKHOLDERS' MEETINGS 

275 7 Am. Dec. 33 (N. J.). By-laws restricting the right of voting by proxy, conferred by charter, are void. White v. 

N. Y. St. Agric. Soc., 45 Hun 580, 10 N. Y. St. Rep. 594.

A by-law providing that one not a stockholder may not vote under a proxy is void. In re Lighthall Mfg. Co., 47 

Hun 258, 13 N. Y. St. R. 381. Until the enactment of

G. C. L. 19, a director could not vote by proxy unless expressly permitted by by-law. Craig Med. Co. v. Merch. 

Bank, 59 Hun 561, 14 N. Y. Supp. 16. As the law now stands, a director may vote by proxy at stockholders meetings; but proxy voting is unlawful at meetings of directors. 

The proxy holder, tho not a stockholder, has all the rights of a member at the meeting, and may be elected to preside at the meeting. Peo. v. Alb. & Sus. R. Co., 57 N. Y. 161.

Pen. L. 668 makes the issuance of a proxy for money or thing of value a misdemeanor. The issuance of a proxy makes the proxy holder the temporary agent of the stockholder who appointed him, and the proxy is therefore revocable at will by the stockholder, as by the issuance of another proxy at a later date, or by the death of the stockholder prior to the voting. Sullivan v. Parkes, 69 App. 

Div. 221, 74 N. Y. Supp. 787. By virtue of the said statute,

Pen. L. 668, it became the policy of New York that proxies could not be made irrevocable even under the familiar principle that an agency coupled with an interest is irrevocable -at least where that interest arises from a consideration paid or given by the proxy holder. Mtr. of Germicide Co., 65 Hun 606, 20 N. Y. Supp. 501. Hey v. Dolphin, 92 Hun 

230, 36 N. Y. Supp. 627. The right to vote stock is dependent on stock ownership, and, therefore, one who has only illegal or overissued stock can not execute a valid proxy. The right to vote is likewise inseparable from stock ownership. 

In Smith v. San Francisco &c. Ry. Co., 47 Pac. 582 (Cal.), a stockholder brought suit to set aside an election of directors, and showed the essential fact that votes rejected would have changed the result of the election. It appeared that a proxy vote for three stockholders had been rejected on the ground that an agreement between them, by virtue of which the proxy was given for a period of 5 years, recited, as a consideration to support the agreement, that they should

vote as a unit for that period, in order to control the corporation, and that a ballot taken among themselves before the meeting should govern the voting of the proxy holder.

The court, holding the proxy valid, said in part:-"It was within the power of the parties to contract in reference to this property as fully as with regard to any other property. 

They were at liberty to make as a condition of their purchase that its management should be held by either of them, or by a majority of the three, and the terms of the agreement for such purchase could not be repudiated by either after the purchase had been made. It may be assumed that neither of the parties would have entered into the transaction, or agreed upon the purchase of the stock, except upon these conditions, and it must be held that each contributed his money to the purchase of the stock upon the promise made to him by the others. There was thus a sufficient consideration for the agreement granting the right to vote the stock. It was in the nature of a power coupled with an interest, and, being given for a valuable consideration, could not be revoked at the pleasure of either. (Hey v. Dolphin, 92 Hun 230.. We have been cited to no instance where the purpose of a proxy given upon a sufficient consideration was lawful, and the person by whom the proxy was created continued to be the owner of the stock, in which the agreement has been held invalid. The stockholder cannot separate the voting power from his stock by selling his right to vote for a consideration personal to himself alone, any more than he could agree for the same consideration to cast the vote himself, and an agreement with others to appoint a proxy upon the same considerations would be equally invalid. . It was upon this principle that the agreements in Guernsey v. Cook, 120 Mass. 

501, and Fennessy v. Ross, 5 App. Div. 342, (39 N. Y. Supp. 

323), were held invalid. The same principle was declared in Gage v. Fisher, 65 N. W. Rep. 809." The proxy must be in writing; but any paper writing, regardless of form, which gives another the right to represent a stockholder in any corporate matter, for instance, to consent to a mortgage, is a proxy. Manson v. Curtis, supra. 

The proxy is revocable except in case of a valid pledge or an

STOCKHOLDERS' MEETINGS 

277 executory sale of the stock, but the revocation need not be in writing (G. C. L. 19), and it is revoked if the stockholder dies before the meeting, or sells his stock, or executes a different proxy at a later date, or attends the meeting and votes, or in any other manner indicates his revocation. Rossing v. Bode St. Bank, 165 N. W. 254 (Iowa). An infant or incompetent can not appoint a proxy. A general proxy authorizes the agent to ratify any irregularities in the call or conduct of the meeting which the stockholder might have waived, but attorneys attending under a general power of attorney to vote have no authority to ratify a sale of corporate property by a director. Cumberland Coal & I. Co. v. Sherman, 50 Barb. 553. The proxy's vote of stock for a director at the meeting will estop the stockholder; but where the director has induced the proxy to enter into a conspiracy adverse to the stockholder's interests, the stockholder may succeed in setting aside the act on the ground of fraud, assuming that the vote of the proxy, if changed, would alter the result. Wellington Bull &c Inc. v. Morris, 132 Misc. 

509, 230 N. Y. Supp. 122. The proxy is informal, and not void, where the corporation is identified by a misnomer, the same name being set forth in the notice of meeting. Langan v. Francklyn, 29 Abb. N. C. 102, 20 N. Y. Supp. 404. A proxy for three years is revocable, but where the agreements provided that the parties would vote together to control the corporation, the revocation prior to termination is a breach, entitling the aggrieved parties to damages. 

Brown v. Britton, 41 App. Div. 57, 58 N. Y. Supp. 353, 356. 

In re Argus Co., 138 N. Y. 557, 34 N. E. 388. The said transaction is vulnerable, however, if it amounts to a proxy given for a consideration. Mtr. of Glen Salt Co., 17 App. 

Div. 234, 45 N. Y. Supp. 568, affd. 153 N. Y. 688. A proxy need not identify the meeting at which the vote is to be cast by mentioning the date, but there should be some identification. A reference to the purpose of the meeting with the year and month, is sufficient. In re Townshend, 64 

Hun 636, 18 N. Y. Supp. 905, 48 N. Y. St. R. 294.

If a proxy is fair on its face and thus apparently the act of the stockholder, the inspectors have no power to determine its validity. Mtr. of Cecil, 36 How. Pr. 477.

Penal Law sec. 668 provides that any one entitled to vote at any meeting of the stockholders or bondholders, or both, of a stock corporation, who sells his vote, or issues a proxy to vote to any person for any sum of money or thing of value except as expressly authorized by law, is guilty of a misdemeanor. Cont. Sec. Co. v. N. Y. C. & H. R. R. R. Co., 168 App. Div. 345, 153 N. Y. Supp. 879. An agency based on a consideration paid by the agent is ordinarily irrevocable. Steele on Agency, sec. 156. But a proxy, given for a consideration, is not an agency coupled with an interest, but is void. Matter of Glen Salt Co., 17 App. Div. 234, 45 

N. Y. Supp. 568. Matter of Elect. of Dir. of Germ. Co., 65 Hun 606, 20 N. Y. Supp. 495. Hey v. Dolphin, 90 Hun 

230, 36 N. Y. Supp. 627.

Voting trust agreements are permitted by policy of law in New York by S. C. L. 50. The statutory requirements for the creation of the voting trust are: 1. Writing; 2. Term, 10 years or less; 3. Open, to let in other stockholders; 

4. Stock transferred to voting trustees; 5. New stock certificates issued to voting trustee with recitals; 6. Duplicate filed in office of corporation, open to inspection; 7. Not a banking corporation. A proxy creates a temporary relation of principal and agent, terminable at will; but a voting trust agreement cannot be avoided except for fraud, mistake, duress, illegality or breach of contract by the voting trustees, and vests a qualified title in the voting trustee with irrevocable power to vote the stock. Tompers v. Bank of 

America, 217 App. Div. 691, 217 N. Y. Supp. 67. Manson v. 

Curtis, 223 N. Y. 313, 119 N. E. 559. In re Morse, 247 

N. Y. 290, 160 N. E. 374. "Trustees certificates" are usually provided for by a separate agreement between the signatory stockholders, to be issued by the trustee to represent their various interests, and to entitle them to receive from the voting trustee their share of dividends. These are negotiable. Death or removal of the trustee from office will terminate the trust, since it, being wholly statutory, is not of the kind that equity will effectuate by designating trustees to carry it out. Tompers case, supra. Rice v. Rockefeller, supra.

The ingenuity of counsel has been taxed to devise ade-

STOCKHOLDERS' MEETINGS 

279 quate voting trust agreements to solve problems of corporate finance and control. See Berle's Cases and Materials for Corporate Finance, pp. 160 ff. "The Legality of Corporate Voting Trusts and Pooling Agreements," 18 Columbia L. Rev. 123. "The Validity of Voting Trusts," 22 Col. 

L. Rev. 627. Simeon E. Baldwin, "Voting Trusts," 1 Yale 

L. J. 1. Cushing, "Voting Trusts" (Macmillan). Clauses in the voting trust agreement purporting to release the trustee from liability for losses incurred through his negligence, probably will not be construed to release the trustee from an act of affirmative negligence in his performance of duties imposed by the voting trust agreement; but the trustee would not be liable for failure to take steps which he was not specifically obligated to take by the terms of the agreement, or for failure to include in the voting trust agreement, when drawn by the trustee, clauses that would have afforded further protection to the stockholder. Green v. 

T. G. & T. Co., 223 App. Div. 12, 227 N. Y. Supp. 252, affd. 

248 N. Y. 627.

There are decisions holding a voting trust illegal on the ground of public policy in that a corporation is entitled to the exercise of the judgment of its stockholders. Warren v. Pim, 66 N. J. Eq. 353, 59 Atl. 773. Consol. etc. Corp. v. 

Dickey, 269 Fed. 942. In New York, voting trusts are expressly authorized and valid. Union Trust Co. v. Oliver, 214 N. Y. 517, 108 N. E. 809. Knickerbocker Inv. Co. v. 

Voorhees, 100 App Div. 414, 91 N. Y. Supp. 816. The compensation of the trustee should be provided for in the agreement. The corporation, as such, has no interest as to who shall be its stockholders, and has no implied obligation to pay the compensation of the voting trustees. United Water 

Works v. Omaha Wat. Co., 164 N. Y. 41. The trustee may be a stockholder, a creditor, or a stranger. A trustee is not disqualified to act as such by reason of possessing a personal interest in the stock. If his duties are alike to all, he may act, though interested. Thompson-Starrett Co. v. Ellis 

Granite Co., 86 Vt. 282, 84 Atl. 1017. Sec. 87, supra.

The test of validity of a voting trust agreement is twofold: Does it come within the terms of the statute, and is its purpose legal? In re Morse, supra. The ten year period

on its expiration may be extended by a new agreement. 

Waters v. De Mossin, 176 App. Div. 711, 164 N. Y. Supp. 

82. An agreement which provided that no title or beneficial interest should vest in the trustee was held void in 

Internat. Paper Co. v. State, 210 App. Div. 253, 206 N. Y. 

Supp. 57, affd. 241 N. Y. 535. The minority stockholder may also attack the voting trust agreement for fraud if the majority in control mismanage the property in bad faith for the benefit of themselves or for strangers. If it is shown that the voting trustees or committee have little personal interest in the corporation, and the surplus has been decreased, and dividends have ceased, slight evidence of bad faith might suffice to prove the agreement illegal. Knick. 

Inv. Co. v. Voorhees, 100 App. Div. 414, 91 N. Y. Supp. 816.

It must be confessed that where the control has been changed by virtue of a voting trust agreement, all that has been accomplished, in the way of corporate action, in order to make this radical change in the conduct of its affairs, is a few entries in the stock transfer book. The statute does not state for what ends a voting trust agreement may be made, and does not even require that the policy, so far as it affects the course of the corporation and the interests of others, shall be stated in the agreement. As a matter of fact, the policy and end pursued by those who surrender their voting rights to the voting trustee are generally stated in another agreement between themselves as parties, to which the corporation is a stranger, and which is not made public. If the purpose stated in the separate agreement is hostile to the duties owed to the corporation by the parties, the agreement is illegal, and breach of it will not support an action for damages. Bonta v. Gridly, 77 App. Div. 33, 78 N. Y. Supp. 961. Thus, in Hellier v. Achorn, 151 N. E. 

305 (Mass.), an attorney who sold stock to a law clerk in his office was held not liable to the clerk for breach of his agreement to unite with the clerk in forming a voting trust, which was to give the clerk control of both corporations, and a lucrative office with each. The complaint was dismissed. The relation of a stockholder who has surrendered his stock to the voting trustee is comparable to a partner who has retired from the firm and yet retains his profit-

STOCKHOLDERS' MEETINGS 

281 sharing status as a partner. Harper v. Roe, 3 Bosw. 29. 

Waters v. De Mossin, supra. "No rule of law or of public policy is offended" by the relationship. Elger v. Boyle, 69 

Misc. 273, 126 N. Y. Supp. 946, citing Peo. ex rel. Browne v. Koenig, supra. The rule against perpetuities is not applicable to the voting trust agreement, and the death of a party to the agreement does not terminate it. Waters v. 

De Mossin, supra.

A third method to control voting, less successful in most cases than the voting trust, is a contract between certain stockholders. These stockholders, without creating a proxy or a voting trust, may enter into contracts, on sufficient consideration, to vote for designated ends, provided the latter are not illegal, or a fraud on the corporation or the other stockholders. While specific performance of such contracts will not readily be granted, an action for damages will lie for breach. The contracts may embody the idea of controlling the management and course of policy to be advocated. Where, however, the agreement is a deal for office, or provides that the duly elected officers shall not function as such, so as, on its face, to be an abuse of trust, it is illegal, although not a corrupt agreement morally. Manson v. Curtis, supra. Fabre v. O'Donnell, 185 App. Div. 179, 173 N. Y. Supp. 472. Havemeyer v. Havemeyer, supra. 

Fisher v. Bush, 35 Hun 641. Scruggs v. Cotterill, 67 App. 

Div. 583, 73 N. Y. Supp. 882. Snow v. Church, 13 App. 

Div. 108, 42 N. Y. Supp. 1072. Fennessy v. Ross, 5 App. 

Div. 342, 39 N. Y. Supp. 323. Barnes v. Brown, 80 N. Y. 

527. Rosenthal v. Light, 227 N. Y. 587, 125 N. E. 924. 

De Groff v. Amer. Linen Thread Co., 21 N. Y. 124. Contracts, by which a stockholder agrees not to sell his stock to strangers without first offering it to the corporation, or to sell it to the corporation or to other stockholders at a price to be fixed from the corporate books, with or without an allowance for good will, are valid and binding on the stockholder, if for a valid consideration. But negative covenants are not usually binding on the stockholder's next of kin. 

Purchasers of the stock for value in good faith without notice, unless the lien or restriction is stated upon the certificate, are not bound. P. P. L. 176, 168 (1) Ib. Drucklieb v.

Topken, L. & S. v. 

Weber v. Climax- 

Harris, 209 N. Y. 211, 102 N. E. 599. 

Schwartz, 249 N. Y. 206, 163 N. E. 735. 

Molybdenum Co., 127 Misc. 470, 216 N. Y. Supp. 481 (4).

Ford v. Snook, supra. Cady's Cas. p. 412. Cross v. 

Beguelin, 252 N. Y. 262, 162 N. E. 168. 

§ 172. Illegal Voting. Challenges. 

The receipt of illegal votes in favor of a candidate who has already received a majority of legal votes will not defeat the election, for a majority of legal votes determines the election at a meeting duly called. The inspectors are to determine the right to vote on the basis of the challenges and the stock transfer books. The directors have the right to direct a new stock transfer book to be prepared for the purposes of the election, and any stockholder not appearing to be such by the new books, is without voting rights. 

If the inspectors permit those to vote whose stock ownership is not registered, the voting is legal unless it appears that the voter, or, if the voting was by proxy, the proxy giver, was not the equitable owner. Thus an election was sustained where the stock was voted by the proxy of the one who had purchased it in violation of a contract by the seller's intestate, by which the latter had agreed not to sell the stock without first offering it to the ones now objecting to the vote, at the fair market value, to be ascertained by arbitration. Mtr. of the Argus Co. v. Manning, 138 N. Y. 

561, 34 N. E. 388. Re Trustees of Wash. Ave. Bapt. Church, 215 App Div. 529, 214 N. Y. Supp. 259. The challenge provided by G. C. L. 20 does not require either the stockholder or the proxy to swear to ownership of the stock. If the vote is not challenged, the objections, it would seem, are waived, for G. C. L. 23, now repealed, requiring the inspectors to call for the stock books upon a challenge being interposed, did no more than state the usual practice of inspectors in such cases. Cf. Pen. L. 668. By contrast, a stockholder who fails to offer his vote for the reason that he sees others in like case unjustly prevented from voting, waives, and is estopped from questioning the election. In re Chenango Co. v. Mut. 

Ins. Co., 19 Wend. 65.

Inspectors of election have no right to try the genuine-

STOCKHOLDERS' MEETINGS 

283 ness of proxies, apparently executed by stockholders of rec ord. Matter of Cecil, 36 How. Pr. 477. In re Townshend, 

18 N. Y. Supp. 905. Mtr. of Mt. Vernon Dye Casting 

Corp., 127 Misc. 169, 216 N. Y. Supp. 317. Oaths should be filed by the inspectors, and if, due to an oversight, they fail to file them, the election is nevertheless valid. The duty is ministerial, and the requirement is directory. Union 

Natl. Bank v. Scott, 53 App. Div. 65, 66 N. Y. Supp. 145. 

§ 173. Ineligible Directors Elected. 

Directors who do not possess the requisite qualifications under S. C. L. 55, may nevertheless act as such, if elected by the majority of a quorum at a duly called meeting, unless the election is set aside by the court on the application of a stockholder who is not estopped. Directors for the first year are not elected under the statute, but are those specified in the certificate of incorporation under S. C. L. 5. 

Nevertheless, if other directors are elected at the first meeting, a mortgage authorized by the board will bind the corporation, and may come before junior liens. Hamilton Tr. 

Co. v. Clemes, 163 N. Y. 423. Davidson v. Wschstr. Gaslight Co., 99 N. Y. 558. In re Pioneer Paper Co., 36 How. 

Pr. 105, 110. Mtr. of Ringler, 204 N. Y. 30, Cady's Cas. p. 

516. Where two parties each succeeded in organizing a meeting, the first regular and formal organization, first completed in point of time, was held the first in right. In re Newcomb, 42 N. Y. St. Rep. 442, 18 N. Y. Supp. 16. If a meeting that has elected ineligible stockholders as directors adjourns, the qualified directors elected at the adjourned meeting are alone entitled to sit. Ib. The stockholders present at the meeting can not be heard to object that the directors elected thereat were ineligible, where the objection is made for the first time in a statutory proceeding by the directors to dissolve the corporation. In re 

Manoca Temple Assn., 128 App. Div. 796, 113 N. Y. Supp. 172. 

The limitation upon eligibility may be manifested by resolution, by bylaw, or by certificate of incorporation; and if by resolution, no formal resolution of stockholders is necessary to rescind it; the election of a director, ineligible under the resolution, will operate as a rescission. Sorrentino v.

Giletti, 75 App. Div. 507, 78 N. Y. Supp. 322. Unless either the bylaws or the certificate of incorporation provide that directors need not be stockholders, stockholding is a necessary qualification, and is not satisfied by the fact that another holds stock for the director, or as his representative. 

The intendment of the statute is that he shall have beneficial ownership, and this is not satisfied by a merely nominal ownership, shown by the books. If a director parts with his stock, he automatically ceases to be a director. One who retains title to the stock as a trustee is duly qualified for the office. Though the certificate provided that the management should be in the hands of the common stockholders, a preferred stockholder is a stockholder eligible to election under the section. S. C. L. 55. In re Elias, 17 Misc. 718, 40 N. Y. Supp. 910. In re Hassam Pav. Co., 152 App. Div. 

610, 137 N. Y. Supp. 453. Haines v. Kinderhook &c Co., 33 App. Div. 154, 53 N. Y. Supp. 368. In re Haecker, 212 

App. Div. 167, 207 N. Y. Supp. 561.

A failure to object to the validity of a bylaw, providing that directors should be elected by the delegates of the members, estops those having notice of the meeting from questioning the election. George v. Holstein-Friesian Assn., 238 N. Y. 513, 144 N. E. 776. Acquiescence for a period of years in the elections of non-stockholders was also held to estop the member in Mtr. of Ringler, supra. 

§ 174. Power of the Supreme Court over Elections. 

The Supreme Court is the sole tribunal for the review of elections in all kinds of domestic corporations. G. C. L. 25. 

C. P. A. 1208. Hudson R. W. S. R. Co. v. Kay, 14 Abb. Pr. (N. S.) 191. Mtr. of Newcomb, 19 N. Y. Supp. 16. Mtr. of Empire St. Sup. Lodge, 53 Misc. 344, 103 N. Y. Supp. 

465. Unless specially authorized by statute, a court of equity has no power to try the question of corporate office, and pronounce judgment of removal, when that question is the only one before the court. Mech. Nat. Bank v. Burnett 

Mfg. Co., 32 N. J. Eq. 236. Merch. L. & Inv. Corp. v. 

Abramson, 242 N. Y. 587, 152 N. E. 438. Hudson Riv.

W. S. R. Ry. v. Kay, supra. But when the issue is as to the validity of corporate acts, any court that has jurisdiction

STOCKHOLDERS' MEETINGS 

285 of the issue has power to determine whether the quasi officer had power to represent the corporation, and, in doing so, it may pass upon his right to hold office, without, however, pronouncing judgment of amotion. Ib.

The application under G. C. L. 25 may be made by the corporation, a director, a stockholder who was such at the time of holding the election, or an elector, or someone who has been admitted to the exercise of duties as an officer. In re Pioneer Paper Co., 36 How. Pr. 111. In re Syr. C. & N. 

Y. R. Co., 91 N. Y. 1. In re Argus Co., supra. Mtr. of 

Moscowitz, 206 App. Div. 289, 200 N. Y. Supp. 630. Mtr. of Sheel, 134 App. Div. 442, 119 N. Y. Supp. 295. The motive of the petitioner is not material. Peo. v. Alb. & 

S. R. Co., 57 N. Y. 161. Mtr. of North. Dispensary, 26 

Misc. 147, 56 N. Y. Supp. 784. The burden of proof is on the petitioner to establish that the election was illegally called without due notice, or held contrary to the corporate custom, or that the votes were illegally cast or miscounted. 

The power of the court is limited by G. C. L. 25 to ordering a new election, but where it is apparent that the petitioner counted out was duly elected, the court may order that he be seated. Where it is apparent that a new election would not change the result, the application may be denied. 

The mere receipt of illegal votes, where insufficient in number to change the result, will not sustain the petition. In re Timen, 120 Misc. 815, 200 N. Y. Supp. 488. Mtr. of 

Argus Co., supra. Mtr. of Mut. Fire Ins. Co., 164 N. Y. 

10, 58 N. E. 29. Ex parte Murphy, 7 Cow. 153. Mtr. of 

Wash. Bapt. Ch., 215 App. Div. 529, 214 N. Y. Supp. 259. 

Mtr. of Keogh, 192 App. Div. 624, 183 N. Y. Supp. 408. 

Mtr. of Keller, 116 App. Div. 58, 101 N. Y. Supp. 133. Mtr. of Bogart, 215 App. Div. 45, 213 N. Y. Supp. 137. The court can not order the inspectors to recount the votes. 

Peo. ex rel. Putzel v. Simonson, 61 Hun 338, 16 N. Y. Supp. 

118. Directors de jure may oust directors de facto, and enjoin their threatened interference with corporate property. 

Ciancimino v. Man, 1 Misc. 121, 20 N. Y. Supp. 702. The corporation must be made a party defendant where it is not a petitioner, and also those whose votes are sought to be thrown out, as well as the allegedly unqualified directors,

even though the latter are not members of the corporation. 

Jones v. Nassau Sub. Homes Co., 53 Misc. 63, 103 N. Y.

Supp. 1089. Walker v. Devereaux, 4 Pai. 229. In re Scho harie R. Co., supra. The election of directors in excess of the number fixed by the charter, or the failure to accept proxies, may be reviewed by the court. Mitchell v. Forest 

C. Pr. Co., 107 Misc. 709, 176 N. Y. Supp. 157. Mtr. of 

Hammond Lt. &c. Co., 131 Misc. 747, 228 N. Y. Supp. 70. 

Mtr. of Vernon Dye Castg. Corp., 127 Misc. 169, 216 N. Y. 

Supp. 317.

Where the facts are contested, the usual practice is for the court to appoint a referee to hear and report. C. P. A. 80. 

By the weight of authority, it is held that entries in corporate books are not conclusive upon the court in a proceeding under G. C. L. 25. Mtr. of Ringler, supra. Strong v. 

Smith, 15 Hun 222. In re Robt. Clarke, Inc., 186 App. Div. 

216, 174 N. Y. Supp. 423. The decision in Trustees of

The action under C. P. A. 1208 may be maintained by the attorney general only, upon his own information or upon the complaint of a private person, against a person who unlawfully holds an office in a domestic corporation. The purpose is to try title to corporate office only, as between contending factions, and the equitable relief of injunction, which is obtained in proceedings under G. C. L. 25, is not available in this action. Merch. L. & Inv. Corp. v. Abramson, supra. The rector of an Episcopal church is not an "officer" of the corporate entity under this section. 

v. Beaty, 206 App. Div. 349, 201 N. Y. Supp. 441.

§ 175. Function of the Board of Directors. 

The exact position filled by the board of directors, in contemplation of law, is that of agents of the artificial legal entity, invested with the sole power and duty of management and control, without, however, being under any duty to perform operative functions. The authority of the board, and the appointment of the first board as such, is determined by the charter, consisting of the certificate of incorporation and the statutes governing the corporation, by which the legislature divides the powers of corporators, stockholders, and the board of directors. The legislature has power to vary the relation between stockholders and directors by giving more power to the stockholders. Chief Justice Marshall, in Bank of U. S. v. Dandridge, 12 Wheat. 113, said "the directors, though elected by the stockholders, are 288

constituted the agents of the corporation, not of the stockholders, and derive all their authority from the act or charter." The stockholders have no power to hold a general meeting for a purpose other than the election of directors, for the board, and not the stockholders, is the collective agent of the corporation. A lease made by the stockholders at a meeting was declared void in Conro v. Port Henry Iron 

Co., 12 Barb. 27, the court saying: "The stockholders in the case had no power to make a lease, or do any other administrative act in the management of the affairs of the corporation. If a lease could be made at all, it could be executed only in pursuance of the act of the directors, who are the body appointed by the charter for the management of its affairs. It is no answer that individual stockholders who were present at the meeting when the lease was ordered, were also directors. They did not meet or act as directors, but as stockholders." Cf. Cont. Sec. Co. v. Belmont, supra, Cady's Cas. at p. 460. By virtue of their managerial capacities, the board of directors, considered collectively, might be termed the principal executive officer of the corporation. Dillon v. Pan-Amer. Theat. Co., 96 

Misc. 501, 160 N. Y. Supp. 549. They are officers within the meaning of the term as used in statutes. Torbett v. 

Eaton, 49 Hun 209, 1 N. Y. Supp. 614. Brand v. Godwin, 29 N. Y. St. Rep. 143, 8 N. Y. Supp. 339. Thus a director has been held an officer within a statute providing for verification of pleadings by corporate officers. Eastham v. 

York State Tel. Co., 86 App. Div. 562, 83 N. Y. Supp. 1019.

In the management of the corporate property, directors act in the relation of trustees. The cestuis que trustent are the corporation, and, secondly, the stockholders. If they dispose of property, it must be for the equal benefit of all the stockholders; and if they divide, they must divide proportionately. G. C. L. 3 (6) specifies that the term "directors" shall include "trustees." Chase v. Vanderbilt, 62 

N. Y. 307. Hun v. Cary, 82 N. Y. 65, Cady's Cas. at p. 538. 

Natl. Drama Corp. v. Burns, 183 N. Y. Supp. 739, affd. (mem.) 194 App. Div. 959.

G. C. L. 27 provides that, "By laws duly adopted at a meeting of the members of the corporation shall control the ac-

tion of its directors except as therein otherwise provided." 

This section does not authorize the passage of bylaws inconsistent with the statutory power of the board to manage, conferred by G. C. L. 27. A stockholders bylaw requiring the unanimous vote of the board for a sale of corporate property is valid, and is not inconsistent with the provisions of G. C. L. 27 providing that "unless otherwise provided" the majority of a quorum at board meeting shall bind the corporation. Levin v. Mayer, 86 Misc. 116, 149 

N. Y. Supp. 112. In the absence of fraud or breach of trust, the judgment of the directors must govern. The stockholders bylaw is merely advisory insofar as it attempts to state what shall be done, but may be conclusive as to the method of doing it. Thompson, Corporations, 2d ed. §§ 

1184, 1197.

The powers of the board are original and undelegated. 

The stockholders do not confer these powers, and they can not revoke them. The powers are "derivative only in the sense of being received from the state in the act of incorporation," as a power that is necessarily implied. Manson v. Curtis, supra, at p. 322. Peabody v. I. R. T. Co., 121 Misc. 

647, 202 N. Y. Supp. 287. The court held in the Peabody case, that a provision in a lease of a railroad made by the Manhattan Railway Company to the Interborough pursuant to authority contained in the Railroad Law, to the effect that no reduction in rents should be made, except upon unanimous consent of the stockholders, was unenforceable and void, as an improper delegation of power by the directors. The statute then under consideration required the consent of two thirds the stockholders. The stockholders having consented, the directors made the lease containing the clause at issue. The directors, and not the stockholders, are the agents of the corporation, and the stockholders are not even parties to the lease. The directors may not thus delegate their authority to the stockholders. 

§ 176. Powers of the Board of Directors. 

The directors conclude the corporation and its stockholders by any act or contract authorized by the charter, statutes, or by the stockholders. In Beveridge v. N. Y. El.

R. Co., 112 N. Y. 1, 19 N. E. 489, the court said: "All powers directly conferred by statute, or impliedly granted, must be exercised by the directors who are constituted by law as the agency for the doing of corporate acts. The expression of the corporate will and the performance of corporate functions, in the management of a corporation, may originate with its directors, where the law or the bylaws have not expressly restricted their authority and made their action to rest for its validity upon the concurrence of the stockholders, by previous action or subsequent ratification.

Within the chartered authority, they have the fullest power to regulate the concerns of the corporation, according to their best judgment, and contracts, which the corporation could legitimately make, come within the scope of the ordinary powers of corporate management." See also, Cont. 

Sec. Co. v. Belmont, supra, Cady's Cas. p. 456. The directors decide the expediency of all propositions. Thus, directors have the power to bind the corporation by buying its stock, though the purchase price is paid indirectly out of capital through the giving of a corporate mortgage. 

Moses v. Soule, supra, Cady's Cas. p. 247. They may surrender a good mechanics lien belonging to the corporation, and take in its place an interest under a deed of trust, although the latter turns out to be unavailing. No stockholders votes are required for this act. In re North Babylon Est., Inc., 30 Fed. (2d) 372. At common law, the directors could make assignments for the benefit of creditors, but this power has been taken away by S. C. L. 15. Vanderpool v. Gorman, 140 N. Y. 163. Rogers v. Pell, 154

N. Y. 518. The board may borrow for the corporate business, and give the corporate note, but not if the borrowing is in bad faith, with a view to wrecking the corporation by binding it to pay greater interest than it reasonably can be expected to earn. Munson v. S. G. & C. R. Co., supra, Cady's 

Cas. p. 547. At common law, the board had power to mortgage the corporate property, but its powers are now limited by construction of law, to purchase money mortgages, and doubtless, it might bind the corporation by delivering to an assignee of the mortgage an estoppel certificate. Black v. 

Ellis, 129 App. Div. 140, 113 N. Y. Supp. 558, Cady's Cas. p.

ers. 

184. If the stockholders authorize an amendment of the charter, the board may accept the amended charter when granted, and the corporation is bound. Stockholders cannot revoke powers of directors. Manson v. Curtis, supra. The board may charge the losses against the capital stock, and so fix the book value of the stock of the stockholders. Peo. v. Bankers L. & T. Co., 13 Misc. 221, 34 N. Y. Supp. 235, 68 N. Y. St. R. 115, amended 42 N. E. 724. It may sell the real property of the corporation where it is organized to deal in real property, without the consent of the stockhold- 

Hangren v. Neeper, 213 S. W. 839 (Mo.). From the power to declare dividends, the board may fix surplus; but doubt arises, where, by the certificate of incorporation, extreme powers are granted. Thus, powers granted to the board of a certain Delaware corporation in the certificate of incorporation to "mortgage all property, real or personal, without first obtaining the consents of stockholders, and without limit as to amounts; sell all the property of the corporation without limit, and whether real or personal, without the consent of stockholders being first obtained; dispose of the corporate franchise and good will on such terms and conditions as in the sole judgment and discretion of the board shall seem meet and proper, without obtaining the consent of stockholders; prevent stockholders from inspecting books and records at will and without limit as to extent of time; repeal stockholders bylaws and pass others of their own; with a provision that these powers shall be in furtherance and not in limitation of the powers conferred by statute or herein contained," may well cause the directors to refrain from the exercise of any of the extraordinary provisions. The directors cannot bind the corporation by a resolution to dissolve it, since dissolution is governed by statute. Lake Ont. Nat. Bank v. Onon. Co.

Bank, 7 Hun 549. The board has no power to change the capitalization, change the nature or character of the business, wind up the corporation, or commit it to ultra vires or illegal acts. N. Y. & N. H. R. Co. v. Schuyler, 38 

Barb. 534, mod. 34 N. Y. 30, Cady's Cas. p. 473. Manhat tan El. Ry. Co. v. Metro. El. Ry. Co., 11 Daly 373, 14 Abb. 

N. C. 103. The amendment of S. C. L. 5 by c. 600 L. 1929

permits the certificate of incorporation to provide for "a class of preferred stock containing a fixed number of shares which may be subsequently issued in successive series, the respective designations, preferences and voting rights of which, within defined limitations, may be established, before issuance, by the directors, without further action of the stockholders. The decision to issue the stock will rest with the board.

This arrangement affords a corporation opportunity to issue preferred shares at a low dividend rate in times of easy money or at a higher rate when conditions are less favorable, without the delay and uncertainty attendant upon the calling of a stockholders' meeting every time it is desired to obtain additional working capital by the sale of stock. 

This issuance of stock in series is a comparatively new departure in the financing of corporations. The practice has been recently recognized by the statutes of some states, but was of doubtful legality in New York prior to this amendment." See article by Hon. Frank S. Sharp, deputy secretary of state in the New York State Bar Assn. Bulletin of 

June, 1929. Powers of the board upon dissolution of the corporation will be considered in chap. XIX, infra. See

G. C. L. 29. The whole G. C. L. was amended by the Fearon- 

Jenks bill, c. 650, L. 1929. 

§ 177. Liability of Directors and Officers. 

Directors and other officers are liable to the corporation, or to its stockholders injured, for losses resulting from acts in excess of power, or in fraud of the corporation, or for their negligence, malfeasance, misfeasance, or nonfeasance, whether occasioned by lack of oversight of corporate acts, or by failing to exercise the care, skill, diligence, or knowledge, or the ordinary means, methods, and prudent practices, of men of ordinary skill, similarly situated. Hun v. 

Cary, supra, Cady's Cas. p. 538. Where the directors took a lease of a railroad from one corporation which they owned, and then leased it to another of which they were directors at an exorbitant rental, they were guilty of fraud on the latter, since, as trustees, they owed it the duty of good faith. Sage v. Culver, 147 N. Y. 241. Directors who wasted the funds of the corporation by neglecting to prose-

cute a cause of action against their predecessors are liable for the loss, and ratification by the board will not exculpate. 

Harris v. Pearsall, 116 Misc. 366, 190 N. Y. Supp. 61.

Directors, who, owning practically all the stock, divide the property among themselves, without the formality of declaring a dividend, are responsible to the corporation for its value. Saranac & Lk. Placid R. R. Co. v. Arnold, 167 

N. Y. 368, 60 N. E. 647. Directors who fail to hold or attend meetings at the times provided by the bylaws, and to obtain from the treasurer the reports required by the bylaws, are liable to the corporation for his misappropria tions. Tri-Bullion Smelt. & Dev. Co. v. Corlies, 186 App. 

Div. 613, 174 N. Y. Supp. 830, affd. (mem.) 227 N. Y. 

581, 230 N. Y. 629. Only the directors who knew of, or should have known, or who, in the exercise of reasonable care, should have prevented the acts, are liable. Susquehanna Line v. Auditore, 223 App. Div. 585, 229 N. Y. 

Supp. 181.

Directors are not liable for mere mistakes of law or of fact, arising from errors of judgment, or from being overreached by superior business strategists, if they have used ordinary care and skill and ordinary methods of dealing and operating; and they are not liable for the acts of employees or agents if they have used ordinary care and skill in selecting, employing, and managing them. Thus, a director, who, through mistake of law paid debts instead of bonds, was held not liable to the bondholders. Seymour v. Spring 

Forest Co. Assn., 4 App. Div. 359, 38 N. Y. Supp. 726, affd. 

157 N. Y. 697, cf. Cady's Cas. p. 550. Thus, a director is liable to his corporation for losses occasioned by his failure to supervise the general manager of a subsidiary company who organized a rival corporation and used the funds of the subsidiary to finance it for a year, and eventually defaulted. Gen. Rubber Co. v. Benedict, 215 N. Y. 18, Cady's 

Cas. p. 531. In Sperlings Appeal, 10 Amer. Rep. 684 (Penn.), the court absolved the directors from liability to corporate creditors for an uninsured fire loss, by classifying their failure to insure as an honest mistake of judgment.

The directors act was on advice of counsel. The decision is criticised in Hun v. Cary, supra.

Officers who contract in behalf of the corporation and in its name warrant their agency and authority to bind the corporation and become liable to the other contracting party for damages suffered by acts in excess of the officers authority. Ratification by the corporation, performance, or estoppel of the other contracting party by his knowledge of the true situation, either actual or imputed, will be a complete defense to the officer. Weiss v. Baum, 218 App. 

Div. 83, 217 N. Y. Supp. 820. One who takes a check of a corporation in payment of the agents own debt is charged with knowledge of the agents lack of authority, and the corporation may recover the amount thereof. Huie v. Allen, 87 Hun 516, 34 N. Y. Supp. 577, affd. (mem.) 156 N. Y. 658.

The candidate for the directorate impliedly represents that he knows the business which he is to help manage. Lack of knowledge is a breach of trust. In the leading case of 

Hun v. Cary, supra, Cady's Cas. p. 540, it was said: “Like a mandatory to whom he has been likened, he is bound, not only to exercise proper care and diligence but ordinary skill and judgment. As he is bound to exercise ordinary skill and judgment, he can not set up that he did not possess them. When damage is caused by his want of judgment, he can not excuse himself by alleging his gross ignorance. One who voluntarily takes the position of director, and invites confidence in that relation undertakes, like a mandatory, with those whom he represents, or for whom he acts, that he possesses at least ordinarily knowledge and skill, and that he will bring them to bear in the discharge of his duties. Such is the rule applicable to public officers, to professional men, and to mechanics, and such is the rule which must be applicable to every person who undertakes to act for another, in a situation or employment requiring skill and knowledge; and it matters not that the service is to be rendered gratuitously." Richardson, Outl. of Bailments, sec. 91. He does not warrant that he knows the business like a skilled operative or an expert technician, but that he has the knowledge of the ordinary man, engaged in that business, of its proper and prudent ways and means, so that he may employ and manage operatives; as was said in 

Dovey v. Cory, H. of L. 1901, L. R. App. Cas. 477, where

directors were being sued to recover dividends paid and declared on the report of auditors which showed a surplus, and no director attended to any details unless brought to the attention of the board by the chairman or by a competent general manager whom they had employed, “I can not think that it can be expected of a director that he should be watching either the inferior officers of the bank or verifying the calculations of the audits himself. The business of life could not go on if people could not trust those who are put into a position of trust, for the express purpose of attending to details of management." See Hutchinson v. 

Stadler, 85 App. Div. 424, 83 N. Y. Supp. 509.

The director does not warrant that he has not a generous portion of human fallibility of judgment. Where lack of ordinary diligence, as distinguished from fraud, oppression or ultra vires acts, is the ground of the charge against the director, the case against him must unfortunately be tried from the view of hindsight, to ascertain whether he used the necessary foresight. The tangled skein of corporate affairs must be unravelled backwards at the trial, to the point where the tangle commenced with the first wrong step. The question at issue is whether the director was properly watchful at that time. As Lord Hardwick said in Charitable Corp. v. Sutton, 2 Atkins, 400 (1742): “In this respect they may be guilty of acts of commission or omission, of malfeasance or non-feasance......It is by no means just in a judge, after bad consequences have arisen from such executions of their power, to say that they foresaw at the time what must necessarily happen." Even if the wrongful methods were successful and profitable, they could have been enjoined by the corporation, or by a stockholder in a stockholders representative suit, brought on behalf of the corporation. Thus, a director who pays dividends out of capital may be held liable tho no injury has resulted to stockholders, and creditors rights are not involved. 

Hutchinson v. Stadler, supra. A board that employs a competent promoter to sell stock is not liable to purchasers who are deceived by the prospectus. Reno v. Bull, 226 N. Y. 

246, Cady's Cas. p. 529.

If the directors are merely extravagant or slightly im-

provident, or meet with superior business strategists, and merely misjudge in the performance of their duties, the only remedy of the stockholders is to attend the general meeting, and secure the election of other persons as directors in their places. Ramsey v. Erie Ry., 7 Abb. Pr. (N. S.) 156; Belmont v. Same, 52 Barb. 637. The directors can not act with blind devotion for the interests of the majority, or even for the interests of all the members, but must exercise their powers for the interest of all, including creditors. Chap. XVII, infra. See Ch. XVI for liability of directors and officers to third persons for torts and crimes. 

§ 178. Remedies against Directors and Officers. 

The remedies for breach of duty are an action at law, an accounting in equity, and injunction. G. C. L. 60. In the latter action, the court often holds directors responsible for constructive fraud in circumstances, where, because of inability on the part of the plaintiff to prove the necessary elements, no liability at law would be imposed. The stockholder may bring the stockholders representative suit against the directors for an accounting in equity, seeking a judgment for the benefit of the corporation; and since it is the directors themselves who are charged with the fraud, it is not necessary for the stockholder, as a preliminary for his suit, to demand that the directors, by virtue of their managerial position, should bring an action against themselves for the benefit and in the name of the corporation as plaintiff. Kavanaugh v. Commonwealth Trust Co., 181 N. Y. 121, Cady's Cas. p. 455. The accounting action proceeds on the basis of the fiduciary relation of the directors to the corporation, and their duty to act honestly, faithfully, and without negligence. Natl. Drama Corp. v. Burns, supra. G. C. L. 60, 61, permit the corporation, a judgment creditor of the corporation, a receiver or trustee in bankruptcy thereof, a director or officer, or the attorney general, to bring action against one or more directors or officers for an accounting, or to enjoin a threatened transfer of the corporate property, in breach of the directors duty, and to set aside a transfer where the transferee knew the unlawfulness; and to bring action to compel the direc-
