tors to pay to the corporation, or to the creditor, the value of corporate property or money, wrongfully acquired by the director for himself, wrongfully transferred to others, or wasted or lost through negligence, failure to perform, or other violation of duty. The "creditor" under this section must be one whose debt has become certain by being reduced to judgment, and one director may be sued on his several liability, without joining the others who are equally at fault. Buckley v. Stansfield, 155 App. Div. 735, 140 

N. Y. Supp. 953, affd. (mem.) 214 N. Y. 679. The section does not authorize a creditor to sue a director where the corporation has been wound up by a division of its assets without a formal dissolution, wherein the director was not guilty of fraud or bad faith, so that the creditor would not have been entitled to pursue the director if no dissolution had taken place. Curran v. Oppenheimer, 164 App. Div. 

746, 150 N. Y. Supp. 369. In Small v. Sullivan, 245 N. Y. 

343, it appeared that, in order to defeat the collection of a corporate mortgage, which was collateral to a bond issue, the defendant directors brought about a consolidation with another corporation of nominal assets, and, by means of the situation so resulting, declared and paid a dividend which so impaired the assets, that the bondholders, who later pursued the statutory liability of the new corporation (S. C. L. 

90), were unable to realize the amount of their bonds, and a deficiency judgment was entered. It was held that the complaint of the holder of the deficiency judgment suing as for a fraudulent diversion of assets, was good. Unwarranted increases in salaries paid directors who were also officers, may be recovered back. Kreitner v. Burgweger, 174 App. 

Div. 48, 160 N. Y. Supp. 256, Cady's Cas. p. 552.

Directors may be liable to stockholders for the depreciation of the value of their stock by reason of ultra vires acts, provided only, that the directors who are sued, participated in the acts; and the liability may exist for the benefit of the stockholder even though there is no liability to the corporation. Holmes v. Willard, 125 N. Y. 75, 25 N. E. 1083. 

Holmes v. Crane, 191 App. Div. 820, 182 N. Y. Supp. 270, affd. (mem.) 232 N. Y. 571. Chap. XV, infra.

§ 179. 

Committees of the Board.

As the board of directors is, in effect, but a committee of the whole body, so they may also, it was held at common law, for the sake of convenience, constitute, either for general or for special purposes, committees of their members, and transfer to such committees, though not to strangers, the requisite power and authority to act for the whole body. 

Corn Exch. Bank v. Cumberland Coal Co., 1 Bosw. 436.

Possibly the point of departure was the adoption of stockholders bylaws fixing a quorum of directors with power to transact business at a number less than a majority. Hoyt v. 

Thompson, 19 N. Y. 207. Olcott v. Tioga Ry. Co., 27 N. Y. 

546. Blatchford v. Ross, 54 Barb. 42. G. C. L. 27 and

S. C. L. 60 are affirmative of the common law insofar as they provide that (1) The board shall manage the business; (2) A majority of the board shall constitute a quorum when duly assembled; (3) The bylaws may fix a number, less than a majority, and not less than one-third the directors, as a quorum; and (4) The board may appoint officers and agents. The transfer of duties to the committee must not amount to a delegation or abandonment of powers by the board, unless it is specifically authorized by charter or bylaws to do so; but if the directors prescribe a proper regime of duties, without being chargeable with having closed their eyes, and are free from negligence or knowledge of improper procedure by the committee, those not on the committee are not liable for its acts. Hanna case, infra. 

Strangers, dealing with the executive committee of the board, are chargeable with knowledge of the limitations upon its powers, and in an action against the corporation, the plaintiff has the burden of proving the agency of the committee, and the delegation to it of authority to enter into the agreement at issue. Comr. Wood & Cem. Co. v. Northampton Port. Cem. Co., 190 N. Y. 1, 82 N. E. 730. The committee has no power to delegate the powers entrusted to it. Delegatus non potest deligare.

Committees must sit and act as a board, and can not bind the corporation ordinarily by acts of individual members. 

Young v. U. S. Mtg. & Tr. Co., supra. Acts, such as consolidation, in regard to which the statutes specify that ac-

tion shall be taken by the board, can not be delegated to committees. Blatchford v. Ross, 54 Barb. 42. In absence of a bylaw or charter provision a majority of a committee is requisite to constitute a quorum. Marshall v. Indus. Fed. of Am., 84 N. Y. Supp. 866. In Hanna v. Peo. Natl. Bank of Salem, 35 Misc. 517, 71 N. Y. Supp. 1076, a stockholder sued the directors for damages sustained by loss of his stock, which was forfeited by the directors for failure to pay an assessment. Plaintiff successfully asserted that the losses which were sought to be recouped by the assessment were occasioned by the fault of the directors. The facts shown were that the board had left the determination of "lines of credit" to a "discount committee" composed of directors, and that these had permitted one Long, a traveling organ peddler, to discount promissory notes of various persons, many of whom could never be found, without any preliminary investigation by the directors of the solvency of the makers. Long, having sold an organ for the purchasers promissory note, was enabled, by the practice permitted to exist, to discount it at the bank by merely presenting it to the cashier with Long's endorsement. At maturity a renewal note was ordinarily received. To make good the losses the assessment above referred to was voted by the board. It was held that the plaintiff should recover for the loss of his stock. It was not as though the cashier had made one large imprudent loan-the losses were only about $32,000-for there had been 200 or more such notes, and ordinary care would have put an end to such extraordinary banking. The bylaws provided that the directors on the committee should meet weekly-they met only twice a year. The cashier, by the bylaws, was required to report weekly to the board the condition of loans-he failed to do so. A director of a bank is presumed to know banking.

The Long notes "might well have made a bundle large enough to attract the dullest observation and excite the fears of the most phlegmatic financier." A recovery, therefore, was allowed against all the directors on the "finance committee." The complaint was dismissed as to a general director, who was not a member of either committee, and against whom no knowledge was proved. See also, Hanna v. Lyon, 179 N. Y. 107.

§ 180. Powers of Individual Directors. 

Directors, acting separately, and not collectively as a board, can not bind the corporation. G. C. L. 27, 28. The reasons influencing the rule are that there should be an opportunity for discussion and interchange of views between those who represent different interests on the board, and that the directors are given no power to act as agents for the corporation except at duly convened meetings at which the action is taken by a majority of a quorum. Thus, a deed executed in due form by a majority of the directors, pursuant to authority conferred upon them at a stockholders meeting purporting to convey corporate property and containing a recital of authority, carries no title to the grantee. Gashwiler v. Willis, 91 Am. Dec. 607 (Cal.). A promissory note executed in the corporate name by a majority of the directors, composed of the president and treasurer, and delivered by them to the payee, did not bind the corporation where the only authority to execute the note was a resolution duly adopted at stockholders' meeting. McCullough v. Moss, 5 Den. 567. Cf., Harrison v. Repetti, Inc., 177 

App. Div. 480, 160 N. Y. Supp. 1018, 164 N. Y. Supp. 257.

The board may ratify or disaffirm the acts of agents in excess of authority, but individual directors or officers may not ratify for the corporation, unless authorized by the board to do so. Story v. Furman, 25 N. Y. 214. In Rockford &c R. Co. v. Sage, 16 Am. Rep. 587 (Ill.), a promoter sued to recover for money paid for surveying before the company was incorporated. Before the company was formed, the board talked over the matter and agreed to pay each member, including plaintiff, $1,000 for services. The bylaws, duly adopted, made it the duty of the president to pay any bill against the company whenever certified correct by a majority of the executive committee of the board. Plaintiff procured the signatures of a majority of the committee to a clause formally approving his bill in writing, and on the president's refusal to pay, he brought suit. It was held that since the approval was not obtained at a meeting of the executive committee, there was no proof of compliance with the bylaws. Complaint dismissed.

Declarations of the individual members of their intent to

take certain action at a meeting is circumstantial evidence tending to prove what was done. Richardson on Evidence, sec. 335. Cf. Title G. & T. Co. v. Pam, 232 N. Y. at p. 448, 455. Action taken at a general meeting of officers including the directors will not bind the corporation, it not being either a regular or special meeting of the board. Cammeyer v. Unit. Germ. Luth. Churches, 2 Sandf. Ch. 186. 

See also, Catholic F. M. Soc. v. Cussani, 215 N. Y. 1, 109 

N. E. 80.

An exception exists where a contract has been signed by directors who own all the stock in a close corporation. Thus, in Gerard v. Emp. Sq. Rty. Co., 195 App. Div. 244, 187 

N. Y. Supp. 306, it was held that a contract of employment, executed outside of a board meeting by, first, three directors, and later by the other two, thereby being signed by all the stockholders, would be sufficient to support an action for unjust discharge, informality of method being a common characteristic of close corporations. Contrast, Barnes v. All Amer. Inv. Co., 206 App. Div. 631, 198 N. Y. 

Supp. 900, app. dism. 238 N. Y. 549.

The admissions of individual directors are not admissible in evidence against the corporation. There are two exceptions. If the director is, in addition, the authorized agent of the corporation, he has the powers appertaining to his agency. If the director testifies concerning a transaction of the corporation, being a stockholder or member at the time, and dies, his admissions on the stand may be proved against the corporation in a subsequent trial. C. P. A. 340, is as 

"The admission of a member of an aggregate corporation, who is not a party, shall not be received as evidence against the corporation unless it was made concerning and while engaged in a transaction in which he was the authorized agent of the corporation; or unless it was made while a member of such corporation and testifying as a witness concerning a transaction of the corporation, when the official record of such testimony shall be received." Cf. Richardson on Evi., chap. XVII, “Admission of Former Testimony." The acts of individual directors in excess of authority may be ratified. N. Y. 

Trust Co. v. Amer. Rty. Co., 244 N. Y. 209. 

§ 181. Meetings of the Directors. Quorum. Majority. 

Where the bylaws, charter, or statutes, contain no limitation of the manner in which the board shall exercise the

powers of the corporation, the provisions of G. C. L. 27 and 28 govern. The principles may be grouped as follows: -1. The certificate, the bylaws, or the resolutions of the board may provide for regular or stated meetings, e. g., the first Tuesday of each month at 6 P. M. at the board room. 

2. No call is required for a stated meeting, and, in the absence of bylaws fixing the number, a majority of the whole attending, is a quorum, which may act by major vote of those present. If a quorum is not present, the acts of the members present, intra vires the corporation, do not bind the corporation, unless ratified by the board or by the shareholders, or unless an estoppel has come in. 3. The bylaws may fix a number less than the majority as a quorum, but not less than one third of the total number of directors. 

G. C. L. 27. 4. If all the directors are present at a meeting that has not been called, or that is otherwise irregularly convened, a majority vote binds all. Due consultation is thereby secured. 5. At a meeting duly called, and duly assembled, the act of a majority of a quorum is binding upon the absentees and upon the corporation. 6. The unanimous consent of a majority, at a meeting that was not a regular meeting, or one not duly called and assembled, has no binding effect, even tho the separate assent of the absent directors is obtained. 7. When the act appears to be that of the board, it may be presumed to be regular and valid, until the contrary appears. Of a regular and stated meeting all, of course, have notice, so that notice need not be given. United 

Growers Co. v. Eisner, 22 App. Div. 1, 47 N. Y. Supp. 906.

The presence without objection of all those entitled to be present at any meeting is a waiver of the want or irregularity of notice, and they will be unable afterwards to repudiate the proceedings of the meeting. Kahn v. Colonial 

Fuel Corp., 198 N. Y. Supp. 596. Action taken at a mass meeting of directors and stockholders, in relation to a corporate matter that is legally determinable by the directors alone, will not bind the corporation, for there was no valid corporate act by the board as such. Cammeyer v. United 

Germ. Luth. Ch., 2 Sandf. Ch. 186.

At common law it was held that a bylaw, fixing 5 directors, counting the president as one, as a quorum of a board of 23 directors, was valid. Hoyt's Exctrs. v. Thompson, 19 

N. Y. 207. The bylaws may empower a number less than a quorum to adjourn a stated meeting; and no notice of the adjourned meeting is necessary to validate its acts, when later held. Smith v. Law, 21 N. Y. 296. If all members of the board are notified of a special meeting, those who stay away are bound by the acts of a majority of a quorum. 

Story v. Furman, 25 N. Y. 214. A director is disqualified by adverse interest from voting on a proposition to confer a benefit on himself at the expense of the corporation, and hence a meeting of 3 out of 4 directors, of whom one was the president and another the treasurer, can not bind the corporation by a vote of salaries to the president and treasurer. Sturndorf v. Samurai, 121 N. Y. Supp. 217. One director is not a majority, tho the other offices of directors are vacant. Mitchell v. Forest C. Pr. Co., 187 App. Div. 

743, 176 N. Y. Supp. 157. The fact that a director did not vote in the negative justifies the presiding officer in declaring that the vote was unanimous. Matter of Cathedral of 

St. John &c, 119 Misc. 610, 197 N. Y. Supp. 750. Herring- 

Curtiss Co. v. Curtiss, 223 App. Div. 101, 227 N. Y. Supp. 

489. Where 2 directors and the president were required to constitute a quorum of a committee, a meeting of the two without the president, and a resolution to hire a room, to which the president later agreed, did not bind the corporation, in a case where there was no ratification or estoppel. Corn Exch. Bank v. Cumberland Coal Co., 14 N. Y. 

Sup. (1 Bosw.) 436. Directors can not attend by proxy. 

Craig Medicine Co. v. Merchants Bank, 59 Hun 561, 14 N. Y. 

Supp. 16.

The shareholders may ratify all intra vires acts consummated at an irregularly convened meeting of the board, or at one at which a quorum was not present. First Nat. Bank v. Comr. Trav. Home Ass'n., 95 N. Y. Supp. 454, 108 App. 

Div. 78, affd. 185 N. Y. 575. Cont. Sec. Co. v. Belmont, supra. H. Remington & Son P. & P. Co. v. Caswell, 110 

N. Y. Supp. 556, 126 App. Div. 142.

The board may ratify any contract which it might have authorized an officer or agent to make, and, if the contract is one within the apparent power of the officer who made it, the one alleging its invalidity has the burden of proving that it was neither authorized nor ratified. Patterson v. 

Robinson, 116 N. Y. 193, 22 N. E. 372. 

§ 182. Minutes of Directors; of Board Committees, etc. 

It is not required that the board keep records. Records, if kept, are the best evidence of what occurred. Richardson on Evidence, sec. 209. Durbrow v. Hackensack Meadows 

United Growers Co. v. Eisner, 22 

Co., 71 Atl. 59 (N.J.). 

App. Div. 1, 47 N. Y. Supp. 906.

The ordinary business of the board may be transacted without even the formality of resolutions. Hall v. Herter 

Bros., 83 Hun 19, 31 N. Y. Supp. 692.

Where no records have been kept, the board having permitted the president to take such action as he saw fit on all matters after the general opinions of the members had been had at board meetings, the testimony of members present will be received in evidence to prove that the president's acts were within his authority. The relator, charged with despoiling an insurance corporation, of which he was president, by disbursing its funds by checks to his own order, and to others, including a large check for the purchase of a necklace with the agreement for repayment, was discharged from custody by means of a writ of habeas corpus, on proof by those present at the meeting that authority was ostensibly given him at board meetings. Peo. ex rel. Perkins v. Moss, 187 N. Y. 410, 80 N. E. 383. In 

Young v. U. S. Mtg. & Tr. Co., 214 N. Y. 279, 108 N. E. 418, it was held that, where formal action by the executive committee was proved, formal minutes to record the act were not necessary.

A resolution in the minutes providing for the employment of plaintiff for a year, and for his compensation, is satisfactory proof of his contract of employment. Fraker v. Hyde & Son, 127 App. Div. 620, 111 N. Y. Supp. 757. 

Failure to note a contract in the minutes does not vitiate it.

Farjeon v. Ind. Terr. Ill. Oil Co., 146 App. Div. 23, 130 

N. Y. Supp. 532. That the book produced and offered as the minutes is such, may be proved by anyone who knows the fact. It is not necessary to produce the secretary de jure of the meeting to prove the minutes. If the rule were otherwise, a paradoxical situation might well arise, in that, if the minutes could be proved only by the testimony of the secretary, and the election of the secretary could be proved only by the minutes, no proof could be made. Davis, Inc. v. Adler, 100 Misc. 92, 164 N. Y. Supp. 65. The fact that one minute book, offered as such, appears to be attested by the secretary's signature, does not prevent another book, unsigned, from being established by competent evidence as the true minutes, for there is no law or statute requiring the secretary to sign. Woodhaven Bank v. Brooklyn Hills 

Imp. Co., 69 App. Div. 489, 74 N. Y. Supp. 1023. Proof that the book offered is the official minute book, and that the signature to the minutes is that of the secretary, is sufficient proof to authorize the introduction into evidence of a resolution therein, as being, prima facie, the resolution of the board or committee. United Growers Co. v. Eisner, 22 App. Div. 1, 47 N. Y. Supp. 906, 908. Entries in the account books of the corporation are not admissible to impose a penalty on a director, in absence of proof connecting the director with the making of the entries. The mere fact that the board directed books to be kept did not make them evidence against the directors at common law; but the statute, as amended by c. 688, L. 1926, makes them competent evidence against corporation, officers, directors, or stockholders. Leonard v. Faber, 52 App. Div. 495, 65 N. Y. 

Supp. 391. S. C. L. 10. Thayer v. Schley, 137 App. Div. 

166, 121 N. Y. Supp. 1064. State Bank of Pike v. Brown, 165 N. Y. 216, Richardson's Cas. in Evi. p. 417. The original minutes are required to prove a directors' meeting, and the secretary's transcript is inadmissible, as hearsay, in a case where the corporation is not estopped from raising the objection. In re Mandelbaum, 80 Misc. 475, 141 N. Y. Supp. 

319, 320, affd. 159 App. Div. 909. See also, Abernethy v.

Church of the Puritans, 3 Daly 1. The books are not admissible in behalf of the corporation. Legrand v. Manh. Merc.

Assn., 44 N. Y. Sup. (12 J. & S.) 562, affd. 80 N. Y. 638.

See, generally, Poppenhusen v. Poppenhusen, 149 App. Div. 

307, 133 N. Y. Supp. 887. Rudd v. Robinson, 126 N. Y. 113, 26 N. E. 1046. Hubbell v. Meigs, 50 N. Y. 480. 1st Natl. 

Bank v. Tisdale, 84 N. Y. 655. 

§ 183. Interlocking Directors. 

A director should not act in a case where his personal interests are antagonistic to the corporation, not only on account of the rights of the corporation, and his duty towards it as a trustee and agent, but because every step he takes under such circumstances may be subjected to the most searching scrutiny at the instance of the corporation or in a stockholders' representative suit. Where two corporations deal, and there are overlapping directors, a serious conflict of duty may arise if there is an unfair provision in the contract, of which the director learned when sitting in the board of the corporation in whose favor the trap will operate, and the overlapping director perceives that the board of the other are going wrong, not perceiving the unfair contract provision. Being cognizant of his own breach of trust, if he remains silent, the contract is voidable at the suit of the injured corporation, and the director may be liable to it for damages resulting from his failure to disclose. Globe Woolen Co. v. Utica Gas & Elec. Co., 224 

N. Y. 483, Cady's Cas. p. 556. But it has not yet been held that it is his duty to make himself acquainted with what his codirectors are doing, and to take such steps as may be necessary to prevent them from doing an unwise or improvident act. Stone v. Cleveland, etc. Co., 202 N. Y. 352.

If there is no trap, the fact that there are common directors will not invalidate the transaction. Continental Ins. 

Co. v. N. Y. & H. R. R. Co., 187 N. Y. 225. The act may be ratified by the stockholders, acting with knowledge. Barr v. N. Y., L. E. & W. R. R. Co., 125 N. Y. 263. In said case, a lease made by one corporation to another through the efforts of interlocking directors, and containing a vice, was ratified by the stockholders and thus turned from a voidable contract into a valid one. See, generally, Cleve land-Cliffs Iron Co. v. Arctic Iron Co., 261 Fed. 15. Geddes

v. Anaconda Copper Co., 197 Fed. 860. The question frequently arises in connection with a merger of corporations having a common board, but different stockholders. Colby v. Equit. Tr. Co., 192 N. Y. 535, 84 N. E. 1111. Armstrong v. Hayden, 126 Misc. 786, 214 N. Y. Supp. 747.

An interesting case, involving a problem of interlocking directors, is Title G. & T. Co. v. Pam, 232 N. Y. 441, 134 

N. E. 525. The action was on two promissory notes, renewed several times for lengthy periods, made by the defendant to a building concern which was a depositor in plaintiff bank, in which it had a line of discount credit. By virtue of this credit the builders were entitled to discount the notes of any maker whatsoever up to an amount set forth in a resolution of the board of the plaintiff, without being subject to question. The various notes for the most part, discounted with the plaintiff, were given under protest by the maker to the builder, with a rather loose understanding that the amounts were to be adjusted if the bills of the builder for services were found to be erroneous in amounts. There were two defenses-fraud in procurement and use of the notes, and failure of consideration. 

The first defense failed, for letters written by the maker proved conclusively that the defendant, while protesting vehemently the amount claimed, had nevertheless delivered the notes to the builder for the express purpose of permitting the builder to discount them. There was proof of a partial failure of consideration. The court set forth the rule of burden of proof, to-wit, that if there was fraud in procuring or in negotiating the notes, the burden of proof would be on the plaintiff endorsee, in its rebuttal, to prove that it had no knowledge of the fraud when the proceeds of the discount were checked out by the builder; and the burden on the defendant to prove knowledge of the plaintiff bank of the lack or failure, partial or entire, of consideration. The plaintiff having sustained the burden of proof that was on it, the defendant proceeded to prove knowledge on the part of the bank. The defendant's proof lay in the interlocking directorate of the bank and the builder. "Notice," said the court, "must rest upon knowledge imparted to the officers of the (builder) and present in their

minds when acting as officers of the (bank) in the business of the discount." One of the interlocking directors was the vice-president of the bank, who passed on the discount when the notes were presented to the bank, without, however, examining them, but with an opportunity to examine. He was also a member of the finance committee and of the auditing committee of the builders. The president of the bank was chairman of the finance committee of the builders. The latter, however, had nothing to do with the discount. That all papers relating to building jobs, and finances, were on the table before the finance committee of the builders was admitted. The facts and circumstances proved for the purpose of fixing the date on which the interlocking directors first learned that a defense was claimed to the notes, and whether they learned it in the bank or in the meetings at the builders, were such as to permit the drawing of divers inferences. Under these circumstances, the duty of the finance committee to know the facts within their dutiable radius of activity, apparently carried great weight with the court, which struck off from the notes the whole expenditure for the builders payroll. 

There was no claim that the discount cashier, who was the sole agent of the plaintiff in the act of discount, had any intimation or suspicion of defects in the notes. 

The doctrine of estoppel was disregarded on the ground that the "fact" of a dispute of the amount due was known by plaintiff, by virtue of the interlocking directorate. The court cites Constant v. Univ. of Roch., 111 N. Y. 604, 19 

N. E. 631, in which it was held that, in order to charge a junior mortgagee with the knowledge gained by his attorney in closing the first mortgage, superior to the junior, the one claiming the benefit of the imputed knowledge has the burden of proving by a fair preponderance of evidence, that the facts were present in the attorney's mind at the time when he represented the junior mortgagee, that it was his duty to the junior mortgagee to disclose them, and that the disclosure would not constitute a violation of his duty to his former client, the holder of the first mortgage, not to disclose privileged communications. See also, Booth v. Robinson, 55 Md. 419.

$ 184. Removal of Directors and Officers. 

Directors, being the agents of the corporate entity, can be removed only by the will of their principal. Unless the charter provides otherwise, the will of the corporate entity can be exercised solely under the statute, which permits removal only by action brought by the attorney general. 

G. C. L. 136, 60 (3,4), 61. The directors can not remove other directors, for they have no implied authority to remove officers elected by the stockholders. Raub v. Gerken, 127 App. Div. 42, 111 N. Y. Supp. 319. The stockholders have no implied right of recall, and can not remove the corporate agent for misconduct or other cause, for he is not their agent. Peo. ex rel. Manice v. Powell, supra, Cady's 

Cas., p. 525. Cf. Shulman v. Star Suburban Rty. Co., 113 

App. Div. 759, 99 N. Y. Supp. 419.

A director takes office subject to existing recall or removal provisions contained in the charter or bylaws. In re 

Automotive Mnfgrs. Assn., Inc., 120 Misc. 405, 199 N. Y. 

Supp. 313, G. C. L. 13. Ewald v. Med. Soc., supra, Cady's

Cas. p. 331. The former sections 1781 and 1782 of the 

Code of Civil Procedure, which authorized a suit in equity, brought by other directors or creditors, for the removal of directors for misconduct, became G. C. L. 90, 91, which however do not authorize action by any person other than the attorney general. The former remedy is illustrated by 

Jacobus v. Amer. Min. Wat. Mach. Co., 38 Misc. 371, 77 

N. Y. Supp. 898. Peo. v. Lyon, 119 App. Div. 361, 104 N. 

Y. Supp. 319, affd. (mem.) 189 N. Y. 544. If the director is unable or unwilling to perform his duties, or threatens wilful mismanagement or financial disaster, the remedy is injunction, for which a stockholders' representative suit may be brought. Kavanaugh v. Commonwealth Tr. Co., supra, Cady's Cas. p. 455. A court of equity has no implied power to remove corporate officers appointed by the state, or to impose conditions for their conduct or tenure, in the absence of statute. Robertson v. Bullions, 11 N. Y. 243, applied to corporate officers in Belmont v. Erie Ry., 52 

Barb. 637.

S. C. L. 55 provides that if the number of directors be increased pursuant to the bylaws, or pursuant to an amend-

ed certificate filed under S. C. L. 35, the additional directors may be elected by a majority of directors in office at the time of the increase; or, if the bylaws so provide, they may be elected by vote of the stockholders; or, if the directors fail to elect, the places may be filled at the next annual meeting of the stockholders. If the election to the vacancies is cast to the stockholders, the same majority will then be represented by a majority on the board. This procedure will not be forestalled by the fact that the certificate sets forth a stated maximum number of directors. The effect is to overcome the voice of the dissenting directors, without removing them from office. S. C. L. 35. 

Sometimes the directors are divided into classes by the certificate of incorporation, the object being that there shall always be experienced directors on the board, by reason of diversified terms of office. The aforesaid additional directors must be classified proportionately. Ib. 

§ 185. Filling Vacancies in the Board. 

Bylaws may be adopted, prescribing the method for filling vacancies. S. C. L. 55. The bylaws may impose conditions as to quorum or qualifications, and the election of an ineligible candidate thereunder may be set aside. Peo. ex rel. Nicholl v. N. Y. Infant Asylum, 122 N. Y. 190, 25 N. E. 

241. The bylaws authorizing the remaining directors to fill vacancies are not satisfied by a vote cast by the sole remaining director. Mitchell v. Forest Ci. Pr. Co., 187 

App. Div. 743, 176 N. Y. Supp. 157. § 186.

Appointment, Powers, Term and Removal of Of ficers and Agents.

The directors at their first meeting ordinarily elect officers for such offices as they deem necessary for the conduct of the business of the company. The statute specifies president, vice-presidents, secretary, treasurer, and authorizes the appointment by the board of other officers and agents. S. C. L. 60. The offices may be designated by the bylaws. A stockholders' bylaw providing for the election of the treasurer by the stockholders is inconsistent with 

S. C. L. 60 and void. The power of appointment rests

with the directors only. Bechtold v. Stillwagon, 119 Misc. 

177, 195 N. Y. Supp. 66, Cady's Cas. p. 510. A contract between the stockholders that a designated stockholder shall be general manager and treasurer is invalid, and will not support an action for damages against the corporation. Harrison v. Repetti, Inc., 177 App. Div. 480, 164 

N. Y. Supp. 257.

S. C. L. 60 authorizes the directors to remove an officer, agent or employe at will. This removes the distinction which formerly existed between the removal of officers and the removal of agents. At common law it was held that an officer whose office was established by charter or bylaw for a definite term could not be removed by the board, while an agent could be dismissed at will and without cause, and that his only remedy would be an action for damages. 

Abbott v. Harberson Textile Co., 162 App. Div. 405, 147

N. Y. Supp. 1031. The basic principle of the decisions is that the agency, and the contract of hiring, are two entirely separate agreements. The principal may deprive his agent of authority to represent him, even in a case where this would violate the contract of hiring; but the principal can not rescind the contract of hiring unless the agent proves unfit to perform through a complete lack of the necessary qualifications and abilities, or wilfully violates his contract obligations. Certain breaches come under the Pen. L. See 

P. L. 664, 665, etc.

The term of office may be fixed by charter, statute, bylaw, or by resolution of the directors. The powers of an agent do not terminate with the expiration of the term of the directors who appointed him, for the directors, as managers of the corporation, have control of the policy of administration as well as the expediency of contracts, provided the contract is intra vires, and does not involve a fraud on the minority. Thus the employment of a manager of the corporation's stock farm for ten years, for a percentage of the profits and a 10 per cent annual "bonus," is valid, providing the bonus is not a mere gift or gratuity. Warner v. Morgan, 81 Misc. 685, 143 N. Y. Supp. 516. A resolution of the board "to engage Granger . . . at a salary of $5,000 per year" is a hiring at will, and not a hiring for

a year, or from year to year; for the period is indefinite, there being no agreement to render services for a year. 

Martin v. N. Y. Life Ins. Co., 148 N. Y. 117, 121, 42 N. E. 

416. Cf. Houghtaling v. Upper Kit. Brick Co., 92 Misc. 

228, 155 N. Y. Supp. 540. The prevention by a corporate agent of the performance of services would not be a breach of the agreement of indefinite hiring, but an election to terminate the contract. Granger v. Amer. Brew. Co., 25 

Misc. 701, 55 N. Y. Supp. 695. A contract of employment for life creates an issue as to whether the salary and employment are intended in part as a reward for past services and thus ultra vires. Beers v. N. Y. Life Ins. Co., 66 Hun 

75, 20 N. Y. Supp. 788. 

N. Y. 453, 57 N. E. 78. 

521, 119 N. E. 1076. 

Carney v. N. Y. Life Ins. Co., 162 

Schwartz v. Regensburg, 223 N. Y.

Officers of a corporation, elected or appointed for a certain time, hold over after the expiration of their term until their successors are elected or appointed. Vernon Society v. Hills, 6 Cow. 23, 16 Am. Dec. 429. Huguenot Nat. Bank of New Paltz v. Studwell, 6 Daly 13. Peo. v. Runkle, 9 Johns. 

147. One is still president of a corporation on a day on which he has submitted his resignation, to take effect at the pleasure of the board only, and not immediately, and which is not accepted till several days later, when another is elected as president. Boller v. Hunt Co., 198 App. Div. 

910, 188 N. Y. Supp. 911. An officer of a corporation may resign at any time and thereby cease to be an officer, subject to charter or agreement provisions. Van Amburgh v. 

Baker, 81 N. Y. 46. Bruce v. Platt, 80 N. Y. 379. Yorkville Bank v. Zeltner &c. Co., 80 App. Div. 578, 80 N. Y. 

Supp. 839. Pres. &c. v. Kaldenley, 165 N. Y. 1. A fraudulent resignation, for the purpose of enabling a receiver to be appointed, is ineffective for that result. Zeltner v. 

Zeltner Brew. Co., 174 N. Y. 247, 66 N. E. 810. 

If the directors remove an officer before the expiration of his fixed term, he may recover damages. Cuppy v. Stollwerck Bros., 216 N. Y. 591, 111 N. E. 249. The decision in 

Douglass v. Merch. Ins. Co., 118 N. Y. 484, 23 N. E. 806, is distinguishable by the fact that the employment, in that

case of a secretary, was not for a fixed term, but was "by the year."

The duly appointed officers of the corporation have all the authority to bind the corporation that is given them either expressly by the board, or raised by implication from the nature of their contract of employment and consequent duties. The chief questions arise under the general rule of agency that a principal who has created an appearance of power can not even expressly limit his liability arising out of the implied authority so arising, except as to persons who have notice, or who are put upon inquiry by being aware of facts or circumstances of such nature as to create some inference that the powers were less than the appearance of power. To all others the corporation will be liable, however much the agent or officer may have exceeded his instructions, provided only their acts are within the apparent scope of their authority. A corporate officer who exceeds his authority will be liable, like any agent, for damages suffered by those injured by the breach of the agent's implied warranty of authority. Considered from the viewpoint of the form of the contract, the agent must so contract as to bind his principal or else he binds himself. 

Sherman v. N. Y. C. R. R. Co., 22 Barb. 239. Pumpelly v. Phelps, 40 N. Y. 59.

An officer's or agent's authority will not be implied from any appearance of authority which his acts or declarations may create; but when his appointment as agent or officer is proved, he has, by implication of law, all the power that adheres to an agency of that kind. For the purpose of proving his appointment, the testimony of the officer or agent himself, as distinguished from his declarations, is competent evidence. He may identify by his testimony the writing by which he was appointed, or, if the appointment was by oral contract, he may testify to the conversation. Intra vires acts of the executive officers of the corporation within the apparent authority of their offices are binding upon the corporation as acts within their actual authority. Lyon v. West Side Transfer Co., 132 App. Div. 

777, 117 N. Y. Supp. 648. Limitations on the officers authority contained in the bylaws or in resolution do not affect

the validity or binding force of the act done or contract made by the officer within his apparent authority unless actually communicated to the non-member before the contract was consummated. Ib. The foregoing rule, however, does not overthrow the rule that one who deals with an agent does so at his peril, and has the burden, in an action against the principal on the contract, to prove facts sufficient to establish both the agency and its scope. For instance, plaintiff has taken either a negotiable instrument, or simply commercial paper, to which a corporation appears to be a party through being, say, an indorser by endorsement of the secretary, and has paid value therefor, before maturity, without notice of any defect. At the trial of the action, brought against the corporation, the plaintiff will have the burden of proof to establish the fact that the secretary was such, that as secretary he had received authority to endorse, and that the endorsement was by him. 

Karsch v. Pottier & Stymus Mfg. & Imp. Co., 82 App. Div. 

230, 81 N. Y. Supp. 782. N. I. L. 50, 91, 98. 

§ 187. The President. 

"A business corporation organized for the transaction of ordinary business must have some agent or representative who is authorized to transact such business. The president of the company, its principal executive officer, is impliedly vested with such authority; and, in the absence of express notice, a person dealing with such corporation is entitled to assume that in the ordinary transaction of its business the president is authorized to act for it, and the corporation is liable for contracts made in the conduct of its business." And so it was held, in Powers v. Schlicht 

Heat, Light & Power Co., 23 App. Div. 380, 48 N. Y. Supp. 

237, affd. 165 N. Y. 662, that, in defense of an action for services in preparing an advertising pamphlet for the corporation under employment for that purpose, the corporation was estopped, by the appearance of authority, from showing that the president was so limited by bylaws that he could not bind the corporation by the employment, unless it first showed that plaintiff had knowledge of the limitations. See Dubois v. Sheppard, 41 App. Div. 113, 58 N. Y. 

Supp. 563.

In the trial of an action to which the corporation is a party, it is presumed prima facie, until the contrary is proved, that the president, or any other executive officer, had authority to make any agreement shown to have been made, if it be one that the directors could have authorized or ratified. Hastings v. Brooklyn Life I. Co., 138 N. Y. 

473, 34 N. E. 289. Norman v. Loomis-Manning Filt. Co., 123 App. Div. 739, 108 N. Y. Supp. 261. Davies v. Hardy 

Steel Co., 6 App. Div. 166, 39 N. Y. Supp. 791. Reedy 

El. Co. v. Am. Groc. Co., 23 Misc. 520, 51 N. Y. Supp. 874.

The president has no power ex officio to bind the corporation or to control its property, outside of its ordinary business, and his authority must be sought in the charter, bylaws, or in the delegation of authority by the directors by bylaw, resolution, contract of hiring, or appointment, formally expressed, or implied from the course of dealing with the business of the corporation. Rockefeller v. Lamora, 96 App. Div. 91, 89 N. Y. Supp. 1. Stanley v. Franco- 

Amer. Ferment Co., 97 Misc. 401, 161 N. Y. Supp. 365.

Thompson v. Marseillaise F. Bak. Co., 85 Misc. 392, 147 

N. Y. Supp. 402.

The implied authority of the president depends on his actual functions, and the duties which he is in the habit of performing for the corporation, rather than on any theory based on the managerial nature of the office. If in fact the president in the particular corporation is the general managerial agent, from the circumstance that he has general charge of the business will arise presumptions of the possession of extensive powers not possessed by other officers. From proof of the fact that the president and cashier generally manage the affairs of a bank, and that compromises of claims are common occurrences there, the court will presume that the president and cashier may bind the corporation, without proof of formal authority conferred on them by directors' bylaw. Chem. Natl. Bank v. 

Kohner, 85 N. Y. 189. McComb v. Barcelona Apts., 134 

N. Y. 598. In Bright v. Can. Int. Stock Yd. & Abb. Co., 83 

Hun 482, 32 N. Y. Supp. 71, it was held that plaintiff, a broker, could not recover broker's commissions from the corporation for the sale of its property, tho he had intro-

duced to the president the persons to whom the corporation sold the property. The evidence in that case established that the corporation knew nothing about the employment of the plaintiff, and therefore did not ratify his employment, and that the president was without authority, either express or implied, to employ him. Western R. Co. v. Bayne, 11 Hun 

166. Bohm v. Loewers Brewery, 16 Daly 80. See St. John v. Fulton Market Rty. Corp., 248 N. Y. 636, 162 N. E. 555 (mem.). The president when authorized to sell stock or property of a company may employ a broker to sell the same. Sistare v. Best, 88 N. Y. 527. St. John v. Fulton 

M'kt. Realty Co., supra. A president of a corporation, has no power, merely by virtue of his office, to execute negotiable paper. Woolard v. Albany, 190 N. Y. Supp. 741. Col. 

Bank v. Gospel Taber. Church, 127 N. Y. 361, 28 N. E. 29.

People's Bank of N. Y. C. v. St. Anthony's Roman Cath. 

Church, 109 N. Y. 512, 17 N. E. 408. Nat'l Bank of Newport v. Snyder Mfg. Co., 107 App. Div. 95, 94 N. Y.

Supp. 982. Dabney v. Stevens, 40 How. Pr. 341. There may be express or apparent power given to the president, however, to sign negotiable paper. Fifth Nat. Bank of Prov. v. Nav. Phos. Co., 119 N. Y. 256, 23 N. E. 737. 

Maine Bank, City of N. Y. v. Clements, 31 N. Y. 33.

By reason of the administrative presumption of authority above referred to, the note is presumed prima facie valid. 

Westchester Mtg. Co. v. McIntyre, Inc., 161 N. Y. Supp. 390.

It has been held that the introduction into evidence of a note signed by the president in behalf of the corporation makes out a prima facie case without proving authority of the president to make the note, except in case of nonbusiness corporations. Ichelson v. Schein, 103 Misc. 673, 171 N. Y. Supp. 2. Authority to sign checks and drafts does not include or authorize indorsement of commercial paper. 

Notwithstanding the authority of the president or other officers to deal for the corporation, knowledge by the other party that the officer is acting adverse to the corporation will estop him from claiming that he relied in good faith upon the appearance of authority created by the officers' act. Thus, where the president had actual authority to draw checks on the corporate bank checking account to pay

corporate obligations, the bank might safely cash checks made payable to third persons, but, in absence of semblance of authority created by the corporation, the bank could not credit checks drawn by the president for deposit in his personal checking account. Moch Co. v. Security Bank, 176 

App. Div. 842, 163 N. Y. Supp. 277. The board might ratify the act, or authorize it, by a resolution expressly permitting the president to draw checks to his own order. 

Patterson v. Robinson, 116 N. Y. 193, 22 N. E. 372. Logan v. Fid.-Phenix F. Ins. Co. of N. Y., 161 App. Div. 404, 146

N. Y. Supp. 678. If the officer is induced by a bribe or gift to sell property or otherwise to contract with the briber, the latter can not hold the property as against the corpora tion. Public Shoe Stores, Inc. v. Goldstein, 225 App. Div. 

350, 233 N. Y. Supp. 73. 

Borrowing money, making gifts of corporate property, purchasing property, real or personal, for the site of the corporate business, mortgaging or pledging its property, and contracts for the sale of property not dealt in, have all been held to be beyond the implied power of the president, and to defeat the presumption. Olcott v. Tioga R. Co., 27 

N. Y. 546. Kraft v. Freeman, 87 N. Y. 628. Worthington v. Worthington, 100 App. Div. 332, 91 N. Y. Supp. 443. 

Tradesmen Natl. Bank v. Manh. Lumber Co., 64 Hun 635, 18 N. Y. Supp. 920. Nichols v. Scranton Steel Co., 137 

N. Y. 471, 33 N. E. 561. In re Utica Natl. Brew. Co., 154 

N. Y. 268, 48 N. E. 521. Express authority is requisite if the president is to settle or compromise suits by or against the corporation. Farmers L. & T. Co. v. Mann, 4 Robt. 356.

If the president acts beyond his powers in dealing with a person who is without knowledge of the limitations of his authority, the president's liability is not limited to the amount of the contract, but covers all injuries resulting from his lack of power. Moore v. Maddock, 251 N. Y. 420, 167 N. E. 572. 

§ 188. Powers of Vice-Presidents. 

In large corporations, it is frequently the case that each department of the business is presided over by a vice-president. This title is given him in order that he may have

apparent authority over the internal affairs of the department, with power to hire and discharge employes. His powers are limited by the scope of his prior and usual official acts. He, or any other person who knows the facts, may testify to the extent of the ordinary powers theretofore exercised. In this respect, the vice-president is held out by the corporation as possessing more powers than would be implied in the case of one whose title was general manager.

In the absence or illness of the president, the vice-president has substitutionary authority to act in the stead and with the same authority as the president. Aaronson v. 

David Meyer Brewing Co., 60 N. Y. Supp. 387, 29 Misc. 

289. He has no implied authority to exécute a guarantee binding on the corporation. Aaronson v. David Meyer 

Brewing Co., supra. Fuld v. Brewing Co., 18 N. Y. Supp. 

456. Where, however, a vice-president, who is also general manager, has full charge of the business of a brewing corporation, he has authority to enter into an agreement guaranteeing the debts incurred by a subsidiary corporation. 

C. F. Harms Co. v. Leonhard Michel Brew. Co., 228 N. Y. 

263, 126 N. E. 705. The president has no implied power to borrow money in the corporate name and pledge its responsibility, nor does the vice-president possess that power. 

Emmet v. North. Bank of N. Y., 173 App. Div. 840, 160

N. Y. Supp. 184. Life & Fire Ins. Co. v. Mech. Fire Ins. 

Co. of N. Y., 7 Wend. 31. In an action for services rendered, plaintiff, if employed by the vice-president, must prove that the vice-president had power to hire. Listemann v. Russian Symphony Soc., 125 N. Y. Supp. 1098. In 

Jacobus v. Jamestown Mantel Co., 134 N. Y. Supp. 418, 149 

App. Div. 356, affd. 211 N. Y. 154, Cady's Cas. p. 563, it was held that notice to the vice-president when acting within his scope, was notice to the corporation unless his interests were adverse to the corporation. He can not make admissions outside the scope of his agency, Davidge v. 

Guardian Tr. Co. of N. Y., 203 N. Y. 331, 96 N. E. 751; nor settle claims held by the corporation. Krauss Engineering Co. v. McKinnon, 66 Misc. 181, 121 N. Y. Supp. 396.

§ 189. Powers of Secretary and Assistant Secretary. 

There is no presumption of authority in the secretary excepting that he binds the corporation by a certified copy of the minutes, for he keeps the corporate records, minutes, and the seal. United Growers Co. v. Eisner, 22 App. Div. 

1, 5, 47 N. Y. Supp. 906, 908. Stovell v. Alert Gold Min. 

Co., 87 Pac. 1071 (Colo.). Where a secretary, who was also treasurer, employed all the help in connection with his work, the employment of a manager for his life time, was held without his power. Greaves v. Amer. Inst. &c., 116 

Misc. 413, 187 N. Y. Supp. 420. Cf. Schwartz v. Regensburg &c., 223 N. Y. 521, 119 N. E. 1076. The secretary has no implied authority to borrow money, sign contracts, purchase property, or execute and deliver a lease. The burden of proof is on the plaintiff suing the corporation to establish the authority. Stone v. U. S. Title Gty. & I. Co., 

159 App. Div. 679, 144 N. Y. Supp. 849, affd. 217 N. Y. 656. 

McCabe Hangar Mfg. Co. v. Bank, 167 N. Y. Supp. 581. 

Ward v. Jewish Leader Pub. Co., Inc., 95 Misc. 571, 159 

N. Y. Supp. 762. Klein v. Barnett Sons, 158 N. Y. Supp. 

627. Greene v. Iroquois Hotel & Apt. Co., 84 N. Y. Supp. 

591. Harvey v. West Side El. Ry. Co., 13 Hun 392. The secretary, like any agent, may be clothed with power to make corporate contracts and the corporation will be bound. 

Curnan v. Delaware & O. R. Co., 138 N. Y. 480, 34 N. E. 201. 

Ludington v. Thompson, 4 App. Div. 522, 73 N. Y. Supp 313. 

Arndt & Bros. v. N. Y. Fruit Water Co., 140 N. Y. Supp. 

471. Inference of authority of a secretary is to be drawn from things he is allowed to do. Barkin Const. Co. v. Goodman, 221 N. Y. 156, 116 N. E. 770. Beers v. Phoenix Glass 

Co., 14 Barb. 358. McCabe Hanger Mfg. Co. v. Chelsea Ex. 

Bank, supra. Karsch v. Pottier & Stymus Imp. Co., 82 

App. Div. 230, 81 N. Y. Supp. 782. Alexander v. Cauldwell, 83 N. Y. 480. An assistant-secretary has only such authority as is given him by bylaw or resolution of the board. 

First Nat. Bank &c. v. Levine, 136 Misc. 355, 239 N. Y. 

Supp. 655. The affixing of a corporate seal requires an express authorization which is presumed until the contrary appears. Hoyt v. Thompson, 5 N. Y. 320.

In an action in the municipal court of the city of New

York, the corporation is estopped by the signature of the corporation affixed by any apparent officer, unless the corporation files with the clerk a specific denial of genuineness of the signature within 8 days after joinder of issue. Ward v. Jewish Leader &c. Co., supra. Mun. court code, sec. 92. § 190. Powers of the Treasurer and Assistant Treasurer.

The treasurer has apparent authority to bind the corporation by receiving money. Molloy v. Conville, 138 N. Y. 

Supp. 1. He is responsible to the stockholders for the safekeeping of funds, but may not pay them out except as authorized. N. Y., Prov. & Boston R. Co. v. Dixon, 114 N. Y. 

80, 21 N. E. 110. He has no implied authority to make contracts or to dispose of assets. Alexander v. Cauldwell, 83 

N. Y. 480. Adams v. Mills, 60 N. Y. 533. Coney Is. Auto 

Race Co. v. Boyton, 87 App. Div. 251, 84 N. Y. Supp. 347.

Contrary to the current notion, the treasurer's office carries no implied power to execute and deliver negotiable instruments in the corporate name, or to endorse them. Hubbard v. Syenite Trap Rock Co., 178 App. Div. 531, 165 N. Y. 

Supp. 486. Hoberg v. Sofransky, 248 N. Y. 141, 161 N. E. 

449. Jacobus v. Jamestown Mantel Co., supra, Cady's Cas. p. 563. 1st Natl. Bank v. Water Works Co., 56 Hun 412, 9 N. Y. Supp. 859. There is no presumed authority of the treasurer to sign checks. A bona fide holder for value, bringing suit on a corporate check signed by the treasurer, must prove the signature of the treasurer, and also that he had authority to sign checks. The fact that checks given by the treasurer to others than the plaintiff were paid by the corporation will not be received unless known by the plaintiff before purchasing the check in suit. Marcus &c. v. 

Natl. Film Distrib. Co., 76 Misc. 429, 135 N. Y. Supp. 37. 

The issue must be raised by the corporation, or it is waived. 

Wright-Ogden Co. v. Strayer, 165 N. Y. Supp. 569. In 

Cardo Drug Co., Inc. v. Chatham & P. Natl. Bank, 215 App. 

Div. 318, 213 N. Y. Supp. 716, the plaintiff's board authorized the treasurer to cash checks drawn to the corporation, and to draw checks to his own order and cash them. A duly certified copy of the resolution was filed with the bank. 

The president having filed a "stop order" with the bank,

notifying them not to pay a check bearing a specified number, the treasurer endorsed the check in the name of the corporation and also personally, cashed it, and appropriated the proceeds. The corporation contended that the president's stop order to the bank constituted due notification that the treasurer's authority had been withdrawn. The next day after the check was paid the treasurer was ousted from his position, and two days later the bank was notified of that fact. The bank contended that the treasurer, who was also a general manager, by his act revoked the stop order, and in this contention it was ultimately sustained. 

The case was twice tried, and the issue of the bank's negligence was submitted to the jury, which, in each case, returned a verdict for plaintiff. At the final trial the appellate division reversed judgment for the plaintiff, and dismissed the complaint, on the ground that, in an entry in the corporate minutes, it was stated that the treasurer had "appropriated for his own use" the sum in issue, which the court construed as an admission that the moneys were paid to the corporation, which, if it received the money, was estopped from holding the bank liable. Where a corporate check is not paid because of insufficient funds, none of the officers who signed on behalf of the corporation are liable under Penal Law 1292A, making it larceny to make, draw, utter, or deliver any check without sufficient funds to meet it, provided money or property is obtained from another thereby, and making it a misdemeanor if the check was uttered "without intent to defraud" since it was the corporation and not the officers who made and delivered the check, the word, "deliver," not meaning the bare physical act of manual delivery but the formal act defined in N. I. L. 2. Peo. v. 

Fleischman, 232 N. Y. Supp. 187.

The treasurer may not, merely by virtue of his office, purchase goods, Alexander v. Cauldwell, supra; nor may he bind the corporation by an account stated, Harvey v. West 

Side El. Ry. Co., 13 Hun 392; nor may he sell, assign or pledge corporate funds or accounts, Maroney v. Cole, 52 

Misc. 451, 103 N. Y. Supp. 560. Clarkson Home v. Mo. etc. 

R. Co., 182 N. Y. 47, 74 N. E. 571.

§ 191. Manager and Assistant Manager. "The term 'general manager' is somewhat ambiguous, and of itself might indicate either an executive and important officer, or a person performing ordinary duties of an employe." Skouitchi v. Chic Cloak & S. Co., 230 N. Y. 296, 130 N. E. 299. Studebaker Bros Co. of N. Y. v. Rose Co., 65 Misc. 322, 119 N. Y. Supp. 970. In re St. Lawrence & 

A. R. Co., 133 N. Y. 270, 278, 31 N. E. 218. Willis v. James 

Rowland & Co., 117 App. Div. 122, 102 N. Y. Supp. 386.

A general manager or superintendent has ostensible powers to do all acts within his office relating to management except as restricted by the statute and certificate of incorporation. Sun Ptg. & Pub. Co. v. Moore, 183 U. S. 642.

The term "manager" ordinarily indicates a person employed indoors with charge over supplies, services, and implements. 

He has no apparent authority to employ salesmen, or to make conveyances. He has no more power to employ a broker than he would have to sell the corporate mills. Horowitz v. Slater & Sons, 164 N. E. 72 (Mass.). Trulock v. 

Kings Co. Iron Foundry, Inc., 216 App. Div. 439, 215 N. Y. 

Supp. 587. The manager of a branch office and factory has the ostensible authority of a superintendent; and where his duties included shipping in wholesale lots, it was held that he had authority to arrange for the construction of a spur track to supply the factory. Anglin v. Sears Roebuck 

Shoe Fact., Inc., 151 N. E. 313 (Mass.). See Cobb v. United 

Engineers, 191 N. Y. 475.

If the general manager is entrusted with the general management and control of the business, he has powers that are as coextensive as those of the president, acting under like authority. At all times he has the authority which the corporation has caused him to appear to have. Rathbun v. 

Snow, 123 N. Y. 343, 25 N. E. 379. Leonardi v. Times Sq. 

Anti. Co., 127 App. Div. 192, 111 N. Y. Supp. 523. It is generally implied that he may employ laborers, etc., appoint necessary agents, and agree upon their compensation within his department. Wilson v. Kings Cty. El. R. 

Co., 114 N. Y. 487, 21 N. E. 1015. Peck v. Dexter Sulphite 

Pulp & Paper Co., 164 N. Y. 127. Hooker v. Eaglebank of 

Rochester, 30 N. Y. 83, 86 Am. Dec. 351. Thomas v. Inter-

nat'l Silver Co., 48 Misc. 509, 96 N. Y. Supp. 218. The manager in charge of a branch of the corporate business may have implied power to renew a contract with a travelling salesman, where he has been accustomed to make original contracts in respect thereto. Thomas v. Internat❜l. 

Silver Co., supra. However, an advertising manager of a newspaper has no implied authority to employ an advertising solicitor for a year. Sloman v. Star Co., 149 App. 

Div. 500, 133 N. Y. Supp. 946. Norton v. Genesee Nat. 

Savings & Loan Assn., 57 App. Div. 520, 68 N. Y. Supp. 32.

If a general manager is put in complete control of the business he may borrow money to conduct the corporate business tho he has not been given express authority to do so. 

Huntington v. Attrill, 118 N. Y. 365, 146 U. S. 657. St.

James Co. v. Sec. Trust & Life Ins. Co., 82 App. Div. 242, 

81 N. Y. Supp. 739. Ordinarily, a general manager has no authority to bind the corporation by the execution of a promissory note, drawing and acceptance of bills or drafts, or indorsement of notes or bills, but the nature of the business and the scope of his employment may be such as to give him authority. Hascall v. Life Assn. of America, 66 N. Y. 

616. Rathbun v. Snow, supra. The purchasing agent of a railroad corporation authorized generally to "buy all materials and supplies in general use in every department of the service," and named in the bylaws as one of the officers authorized to conduct the company's business, may make yearly contracts for supplies. Levey v. N. Y. Cent. R. Co., 4 Misc. 415, 24 N. Y. Supp. 124. Studebaker Bros. v. Rose, 65 Misc. 322, 119 N. Y. Supp. 970. 

§ 192. Compensation of Directors and Other Officers. 

Directors, and officers who are at the same time officers and directors, are presumed to perform their duties for the sake of the dividends. It is well decided that they can not recover on a quantum meruit for services rendered within the scope of the duties of the office. Directors can not make themselves allowances, nor fix their own salaries as president, secretary, etc., nor vote themselves back pay. Sec. 

193, infra. Godley v. Crandall & Godley Co., 212 N. Y. 121, 105 N. E. 818. If the vote of the encumbent is counted to

make up the quorum, the compensation paid may be recovered back by the corporation, or at the suit of a single stockholder suing in a representative capacity to recover for the corporation. Butts v. Wood, 37 N. Y. 317. McNab v. McNab & Harlin Mfg. Co., 62 Hun 18, affd. 133 N. Y. 

687, Cady's Cas. p. 402. To entitle them to compensation, the bylaw, under which they claim, must have been passed before the services were rendered, for instance, at the organization meeting of the stockholders; for a subsequent vote of compensation is without the consideration which is requisite to the proof of a contract. Kelsey v. Sargent, 40 Hun 150. Butts v. Wood, 37 N. Y. 317. Mather v. 

Eureka Mower Co., 118 N. Y. 629, 23 N. E. 993. If the officer is not a stockholder the above considerations do not apply, and there is a presumption that beneficial services, dutifully performed, will entitle him to compensation. 

Smith v. L. I. Ry., 102 N. Y. 190, 6 N. E. 397. Gaul v. 

Kiel &c. Co., 199 N. Y. 472, 23 N. E. 993. Peo. Tr. Co. v. 

O'Meara, 204 App. Div. 268, 197 N. Y. Supp. 795, 22 F. (2d) 496.

Contracts may be made to pay for services performed outside the duties of the office, providing the salary was not voted or increased by the vote of the officer himself, or induced by his intriguing influence with the board. Jacobson v. Brooklyn Lumber Co., 184 N. Y. 152. Kreitner v. 

Bergweger, 174 App. Div. 48, 160 N. Y. Supp. 256, Cady's 

Cas. p. 552. Hirsch v. Jones, 115 App. Div. 156, 100 N. Y. 

Supp. 687. A director may lawfully be paid for services performed outside the ordinary duties of a director, but the burden of proof will rest with the director to prove that the services were outside the duties of his office, and that they were rendered with the expectation on both sides that they should be compensated for. James v. Alderdon Dock Yds., 225 App. Div. 675, 231 N. Y. Supp. 215, and 781. Fox v. 

Arctic Placer Mining & M. Co., 229 N. Y. 125, 128 N. E. 

154, Cady's Cas. p. 573. Bagley v. Carthage &c Co., 165 

N. Y. 179, 58 N. E. 895. Gaul v. Kiel & A. Co., supra. 

Zarriello v. U-Need Ice Co., 191 N. Y. Supp. 207.

Salaries improperly paid may be recovered by the corporation or on behalf of the corporation in a stockholders

representative suit. Stout v. Security Trust &c Co., 82 App. 

Div. 129, 81 N. Y. Supp. 708. Metzger v. Knox, 77 Misc. 

271, 136 N. Y. Supp. 681. Lewis v. Matthews, 161 App. 

Div. 107, 146 N. Y. Supp. 424. A president who consents to the sale of all the corporate property and to the merger of its property and business with that of another corporation, with the result that he thereafter performs no services worthy of compensation, is deemed to have consented to the cancellation of his employment. Long Island Ferry Co. v. 

Tarbell, 48 N. Y. 427.

Officers suing the corporation for salary have the burden of proof to establish their right to compensation. Farmers 

Loan Co. v. Housatonic R. Co., 152 N. Y. 251, 46 N. E. 504. 

Barrill v. Cal. Ins. Co., 50 Hun 257, 2 N. Y. Supp. 758. Outterson v. Fonda Lake Paper Co., 66 Hun 629, 20 N. Y. Supp. 

981, 49 N. Y. St. Rep. 556. Compensation is for services, and one who has merely held the office without performing services may not recover. Williams v. McClave, 168 App. 

Div. 192, 154 N. Y. Supp. 38. As was said by Elkus, J. in Fox v. Arctic Placer Mining & Milling Co., 229 N. Y. 

124, 128 N. E. 154, Cady's Cas. p. 573, in which the plaintiff, a mining engineer was an officer and director of a mining corporation, "there ordinarily would be no presumption that special compensation was intended or expected even if the services were rendered at the request of the corporation or of its officers, so far as the services do not differ from those required from anyone assuming the position, because it would be contrary to public policy to permit such a presumption, but, notwithstanding this, a promise to pay may be proven in the same manner as any other fact may be established. That is, an agreement may be inferred from other evidence, from a course of practice, or, where the services are outside of the usual duties of one holding the office which the plaintiff held." The court further said, quoting Bagley v. Carthage &c R. R. Co., 165 N. Y. 179, 182, "It is sufficient if, from the nature of the employment, the importance of the subject matter and the action of the directors of the corporation, the inference is authorized of the employment as alleged."

The disability of the director is complete whenever he is

entrusted to deal as an agent of the corporation in respect to its affairs. If the director is also a creditor of the corporation he is not disabled from protecting himself from loss by the same means open to other creditors, unless he is, at the same time, representing the corporation. A director whose duty it was to protect a corporation from mortgage foreclosure would obtain only voidable title by buying in at the mortgage foreclosure sale, tho his bid was, of course, the highest bid. But as holder of a mortgage against the corporation, representing a loan made by him to it, he would have the same right to foreclose as any creditor, and to protect his interest by buying in at the sale. South 

Baptist Church v. Clapp, 18 Barb. 35. Olcott v. Tioga R. R. 

Co., 27 N. Y. 546. Hoyle v. Plattsburgh &c R. R. Co., 54 

N. Y. 314, 328. The corporation undoubtedly might have rescinded the whole mortgage transaction by returning the consideration. 

§ 193. Dealings of Officers and Directors with the Cor poration.

The stockholder may deal with the corporation as freely as if they were strangers. The entity is distinct from the stockholder. It can give the stockholder its bond, secured by collateral mortgage on the corporate property, in order to secure a loan by it to him, and to secure the amount due him of the consideration for the repurchase by the corporation of his shares. Moses v. Soule, supra, Cady's Cas. p. 

247. Purchasings by a stockholder from even a close corporation on credit on the same terms as those of strangers are voidable, not void. Murray v. Smith, supra, Cady's

Cas. p. 200. A stockholder may buy in at a judicial sale of the corporate property, and gets good title, providing he is not an officer, or a majority stockholder oppressing or defrauding the minority. Where the facts present all the indicia of a fraudulent conveyance, a creditor may sue to set it aside. Littman v. Harris, 148 App. Div. 31, 131 

N. Y. Supp. 1006; 157 App. Div. 909, 142 N. Y. Supp. 341.

In the said case, it was shown that the stockholder, who was in substantial control, suddenly resigned his office, assigned all his stock to a relative, and purchased all the assets of the corporation at a time when suit was pending against it;

and it was held that, under such circumstances, he had the burden of proving that every step in the transaction was unobjectionable. Ib. A stockholder is not disqualified to take the acknowledgment of the corporation as notary, in any transaction in which he is not personally interested. 

In re Sparboe, 292 Fed. 782.

Directors, and all other officers of the corporation, are related to it as fiduciaries, mandatories, trustees or agents, and all contracts made by them with the corporation by which they derive any personal benefit are prima facie voidable at the suit of the corporation. Cumberland Coal & 

Iron Co. v. Sherman, 30 Barb. 553; Bosworth v. Allen, 168 

N. Y. 157; Hoyt v. Thompsons Exctrs., 19 N. Y. 207, 216; 

Seymour v. Spring Forest Cemetery Assn., 144 N. Y. 333, Cady's Cas. p. 550. Barnes v. Brown, 80 N. Y. 527, ib., p. 549. The directors are not absolutely precluded from making contracts with the corporation, or from being interested in contracts between the corporation and third persons; but all such contracts are voidable at the option of the corporation, or of creditors of the corporation. The reason is that the directors are fiduciaries, and therefore are not allowed to take a position adverse to the trust. They are not trustees prior to dissolution (G. C. L. 29), at least not in the technical meaning of persons having the legal title to property, the beneficial ownership of which belongs to another, for the property of the corporation is vested in the corporation itself. As fiduciaries, they manage this property as official agents, and therefore come under the rule that prevents a fiduciary from deriving, directly or indirectly, out of his position, any advantage hostile to the interests which he represents. G. C. L. 60 (2), 61. An agent appointed to buy cannot buy from himself and keep the profit; and an agent appointed to sell and selling to himself directly or mediately, holds the title in trust for his principal, who may retake on returning the consideration received. The director must not let his private interests compete with his duties to the corporation, but, if it is done openly, with the knowledge or concurrence of the corporation and its stockholders, and with a full disclosure of the

extent and nature of the directors interest, the arrangement may stand.

The rule is expressed as follows in Hoyle v. Plattsburgh &c R. R. Co., 54 N. Y. 314:-"Whether a director of a corporation is to be called a trustee or not, in a strict sense, there can be no doubt that his character is fiduciary, being intrusted by others with powers which are to be exercised for the common and general interests of the corporation, and not for his own private interests. He falls, therefore, within the just rule by which equity requires that confidence shall not be abused by the party in whom it is reposed, and which it enforces by imposing a disability, either partial or complete, upon the party intrusted, to deal, in his own behalf, in respect to any matter involved in such confidence. 

Nor is it possible to limit the duty of a director of a corporation, in this respect, to the time while he is acting as a director under any special delegation of power, or is in attendance at meetings of the board. He cannot, while director, divest himself of the knowledge which he has acquired in confidence of corporate affairs, or of the value of corporate property, nor be allowed to use it to his own advantage." The director in said case was also a plaintiff in a judgment against the corporation, and the court held he had a clear right to sell, upon execution on his judgment, the personal property of the corporation which was liable to sale on execution. It appears, however, from said case, that the fact that property of the corporation, purchased at foreclosure sale by a stranger, is soon after conveyed to a director for a nominal consideration, makes the title prima facie unmarketable. 

In New York Trust Co. v. Amer. Realty Co., 244 N. Y. 

209, 155 N. E. 102, action was brought by the plaintiff to recover on certain promissory notes given for part of the purchase price of land sold and conveyed to defendant by plaintiff as trustee under a deed of trust for one Underwood and more particularly, his wife, who had the larger interest. 

Underwood at the time of the sale was president and director of the defendant, and a director and member of the executive committee of the International Paper Co. which owned all the stock of American Realty Co. and which

guaranteed the notes. Before the sale of the land, Underwood disclosed to the two corporations his indirect interest in the sale by virtue of the trust deed, and abstained from voting as director of defendant for the purchase of the land. 

The defendant in its answer to the complaint counterclaimed for the profits of Underwood in the sale, without electing to rescind or offering to restore what had been received, and for the damages which it claimed it sustained through the alleged breach of trust of Underwood in acting as agent for the plaintiff, and indirectly, for the other beneficiaries under the trust deed, against the interest of the corporation, it being alleged in the counterclaims that Underwood had charge of such purchases for it, and exercised a dominant position with the defendant corporation in relation to the purchase. An order of special term granting judgment to plaintiff on the pleadings was reversed by the appellate division. The reversal was affirmed by the court of appeals, which distinguished between sales by a director to his corporation with a disclosed profit, and a sale wherein the director represents other interests than his own, saying, in part: "We assume that if the defendants, by reason of these circumstances, were induced to make a bargain which subsequently they discovered was not advantageous to them, they might rescind their contract of purchase. (Barr v. N. Y. &c R. R. Co., 125 N. Y. 

263; Munson v. Syracuse &c R. R. Co., 103 N. Y. 58; Wendt v. 

Fischer, 243 N. Y. 439.) The corporations have not chosen to rescind. Indeed they do not now urge that the contract of sale may not have been advantageous. They do say that the agreed consideration paid for the timberlands 'was greatly in excess of the fair value of the said lands, and also greatly in excess of the amount paid.

The amount of the said exorbitant profit was not disclosed to American Realty Company or International Paper

Company,' but it does not appear that the lands might not be of such use to the corporations in their business that the corporations would not be willing to pay even now more than the fair value of such land if such payment was required for its acquisition. Since the defendants retain the land to which they have no right or title except by virtue of the contract with the plaintiff they must pay the agreed purchase price." "Different question arises where the agent sells to his principal at a profit, property which the agent might have retained for himself or sold to a stranger. If the contract of purchase is rescinded the principal has no title to the property or right to retain it. If

the principal fails to return the property he may not claim that the contract was made without authority. A corporation may not repudiate the obligations of a contract made with a director and at the same time retain its benefits. If contract with the director was valid the corporation must pay the agreed price; if invalid the corporation must rescind or repudiate the contract in its entirety. A director who may sell or retain the property at his will may also determine the price which will induce him to sell to the corporation. Profit made is the fruit of his ownership, and not of his agency. (Burland v. Earle, 1902 A. C. 83; Matter of 

Lady Forrest [Murchison] Gold Mine, Ltd., 1901, 1 Ch. 582.)" "Undoubtedly it has frequently been held that a director or officer of a corporation must account to the corporation for profits received in disregard of duty owed to the corporation. (McClure v. 

Law, 161 N. Y. 78; Jackson v. Ludeling, 21 Wall. [U. S.] 616.)

The remedy has been granted at times even in cases where the corporation does not rescind the transaction through which such profits have been made by the delinquent trustee or agent. In such cases, however, affirmation of authority of director or agent to bind the corporation was not inconsistent with claim of wrong committed by him in the course of his representation of the corporation. Remedy there is granted for wrong committed by an unfaithful agent in accordance with general principles applicable to recognized agency." 

The following variations may be noted: 1. The transaction is valid unless avoided. The corporation can not escape liability while retaining the benefits. Where directors on the boards of two railroads fraudulently induced one to lease to the other, the lessee, having enjoyed the benefit of the lease for years, was held liable for rent when sued by the lessors stockholders. Barr v. N. Y. &c R. R. 

Co., 125 N. Y. 263, 26 N. E. 145. Skinner v. Smith, 134 

N. Y. 240, 31 N. E. 911. 

2. Collateral security or pledge, taken by the director for a debt, either present or precedent, justly due him by the corporation, may be enforced by him. In Duncomb v. New 

York, Housatonic &c R. R. Co., 84 N. Y. 190, the president received corporate bonds as security for past due salary.

The trustee of the mortgage collateral to the bonds foreclosed it, and it was held that the president might prove his bonds and receive his share of the assets like any other bond holder. The corporation could not pursue the grossly inequitable course of avoiding the contract unless it returned the consideration which it received. The director may loan

money to his corporation, and receive a corporate mortgage as security for the loan. Upon default, he may foreclose the mortgage. If a stranger forecloses a mortgage which he holds on corporate property, and a director of the corporation becomes the successful bidder at the sale, he gets only a voidable title, by reason of his fiduciary relationship, and the corporation may compel him to reconvey to it upon reimbursing him for the amount that he is out-of-pocket. But if the director has a mortgage which is subordinate to the one being foreclosed, he may become the highest bidder and buy the property at foreclosure sale in order to protect his subordinate interest. If the transaction is later attacked by the corporation, the director has to sustain the burden of proof of the bona fides. Preston v. Loughran, 58 Hun 210, 12 N. Y. Supp. 313. Tiffany v. Smith, 124 N. Y. Supp. 85.

The burden of proof is on the officer to show that a pledge of corporate property to him was fair. Kinsman v. Fish, 83 Hun 494, 31 N. Y. Supp. 1045. For a case where the director's purchase of the property, without notice of the rights of the corporation, from the successful bidder who was apparently a bona fide purchaser at the foreclosure sale, gave the director good title, see Rutgers Female Coll. &c v. 

Tallman, 82 Hun 20, 31 N. Y. Supp. 159, 63 N. Y. St. Rep. 

St. Rep. 481, affd. (mem.) 146 N. Y. 386. 

3. "If a profit is made in a transaction which is honest in itself, and is open and fully disclosed, and the transaction is consummated after an honest statement of the facts to the board of directors at a meeting, and to the stockholders at a stockholders meeting, there is no reason for criticism or for charging such director with any profits that he may make." Billings v. Shaw, 209 N. Y. 265, 103 N. E. 142. 

Welch v. Importers & Traders Nat. Bank, 127 N. Y. 177, 25 N. E. 269. Goldshear v. Barron, 42 Misc. 198, 85 N. Y. 

Supp. 395. Marbury v. Stone, 17 App. Div. 352, 45 N. Y. 

Supp. 184, affd. 160 N. Y. 701. Vounoh v. 67th St. Atelier 

Bldg., 55 Misc. 222, 105 N. Y. Supp. 155. 

4. If the director purchases unmatured claims against the corporation, at a time when he had no duties to the corporation to pay them or to do something else regarding them, he may enforce them at the full amount, and is not

limited to the amount which he invested. There is no con- 

Iflict with duty in such case. Seymour v. Spring Forest
