Cem. Assn., supra, Cady's Cas. p. 550. The director can not be compelled to account for corporate moneys paid him in extinguishment of valid claims for moneys advanced by him to the corporation. Stokes v. Stokes, 91 Hun 605, 36 

N. Y. Supp. 350. The director will not be permitted to obtain a preference through the making of advances to an insolvent corporation in return for its notes. Halpin v. 

Mut. Brew. Co., 20 App. Div. 583, 47 N. Y. Supp. 412. 

5. A director who engages in a competing business, either on his own behalf or as director of another corporation, can not be held to account for his profits therein as secret profits. 

N. Y. Auto. Co. v. Franklin, 49 Misc. 8, 97 N. Y. Supp. 781.

It is neither void nor voidable for the directors to rent property from an officer of the corporation. Metzger v. 

Knox, 77 Misc. 271, 136 N. Y. Supp. 681, affd. (mem.) 

153 App. Div. 911, 154 App. Div. 953. He must not imitate the name. Terminal Barber Shops, Inc. v. Zoberg ("Terminal Beauty Parlors"), 28 F. (2d) 807. 

6. When stock is for sale by the corporation, the director may compete with the stockholders in its purchase. 

Sec. 125 supra. 

7. The director may validly contract with the corporation for compensation for services. Sec. 192, supra. But while the board may fix the salaries of ministerial officers, they can not, in absence of charter, statute, or bylaw permitting it, vote salaries to each other as mere incidents of their office. Godley v. Crandall & Godley Co., 212 N. Y. 121, 105 

N. E. 18. If authorized by bylaw to vote themselves salaries, they must act in good faith, and excessive salaries may be recovered by minority stockholders for the benefit of the corporation in a stockholders representative suit. 

Carr v. Kimball, 153 App. Div. 825, 139 N. Y. Supp. 253, affd. 215 N. Y. 624, 714. Murray v. Smith, supra, Cady's 

Cas. p. 200. 

§ 194. Dealings Between Directors, Officers and Stock holders.

The fact that a director or officer, when dealing with a stockholder in a personal transaction wherein the director

or officer buys or sells corporate stock, withholds exclusive information acquired through his official position, will not support an action by the stockholder to rescind for constructive fraud, or for damages for fraud. The director, who deals with a stockholder on his own behalf, neither represents the corporation, nor does he bear a confidential relation to the stockholder. There is no trust relationship between them except in managerial acts. That the director made a large sum out of the transaction, or that an extraordinary dividend was declared soon after, are competent evidence, but are insufficient in themselves to support an action. In New York, Delaware, Idaho, Kentucky,

Minnesota and Utah, the courts have affirmed this principle. Carpenter v. Danforth, 52 Barb. 581. Stark v. 

Soule, 45 Hun 588, 9 N. Y. St. Rep. 555. Cahall v. Lofland, 118 Atl. 1 (Del.). Stout v. Cunningham, 196 Pac. 208 

(Idaho). Barth v. Fid. & Columbia Tr. Co., 224 S. W. 351 (Ky.). Seitz v. Frey, 188 N. W. 266 (Minn.). White v. Texas Co., 202 Pac. 826 (Utah). Cf. Berger v. Eichler, supra, Cady's Cas. p. 13. Kansas, Georgia and North

Carolina courts have held that under the special circumstances disclosed in the cases before them, it was the duty of the officer to disclose facts peculiarly within his knowledge. In each of the cases it appeared that at the time of the transaction the officer was made aware of the fact that the selling stockholder was ignorant of material facts, affecting value, which were known to the officer, and that the stockholder sold while laboring under a mistake as to the fundamental nature and character of his stock, believing it barren and unsound, whereas profit was near at hand. 

In each decision the general rule was announced, "that the ordinary relations between directors and stockholders in a business corporation are not of such a fiduciary nature as to make it the duty of a director to disclose to a shareholder the general knowledge which he may possess regarding the value of the shares of the company before he purchases any from a shareholder." In each case the court placed the burden upon the stockholder, suing to rescind, to prove that the officer knew that the stockholder was laboring under mistake, and that, to some degree, the officer's words or acts contributed to perpetuate it. Lyon v. Carey,

206 Pac. 1109 (Kan.). Oliver v. Oliver, 45 S. E. 232 (Ga.). 

Rucker v. Sanders, 109 S. E. 857 (N. C.). Similiter, Richardson's Outlines of Contracts, sec. 55, citing Sherwood v. 

Walker, 66 Mich. 568, 33 N. W. 919. In Strong v. Repide, 213 U. S. 419, 53 L. ed. 853, the stockholder was permitted to recover from the director the shares which he had purchased from her in a transaction with her agent. The director, owning about three fourths of the stock of a corporation formed to deal in the so-called "friars lands" in the Philippines, was appointed by the board the corporate agent, with managerial powers to go to the Philippines and negotiate for the sale of the lands to the United States government. Of all the negotiators he was the chief; and soon after the transfer of the stock in suit, the lands were sold to the government at a price which greatly enhanced the value of the stock. Returning with knowledge of the probability of the sale and of the probable price-knowledge which, by virtue of his agency, belonged to the companyhe set about secretly to obtain the other's shares, by craft and indirection. The director, concealing his identity under the guise of an undisclosed principal, negotiated for the stock through an agent ignorant of the facts, who took title in his own name and made payment with his own check. This concealment avoided disclosure of the information which the director alone had, and which, by inference, would have been inquired into had the director dealt in the open. By this “hiding” the director furnished strong evidence against himself, indicating guilty knowledge of the evasion of a duty that he had or thought he had. The attorney-in-fact of the plaintiff was completely deceived, and the plaintiff, who was away at the time, was also deceived. 

In Walsh v. Walsh, 226 S. W. 236 (Mo.), a confidential relation was held to exist, requiring disclosure, where the president of a bank, which was administrator of the decedent's estate, bought for himself shares belonging to the estate. The duty of disclosure, wherever a confidential relation exists, extends to making complete disclosure so that the sale may be the entirely free and voluntary act of the stockholders, under the most perfect understanding of their rights. In like manner, an exchange of stock by a director of a corporation, who was also a confidential agent of the

shareholder, a man of 90 years, was set aside, in re Parkers Estate, 179 N. W. 525 (Iowa); and similarly, where the vice-president obtained the stock of the president's widow through the confidential relationship combined with her ignorance and his false representations. Logan v. Arnold, 89 So. 551 (Fla.). In Von Au v. Magenheimer, 126 App. 

Div. 257, 110 N. Y. Supp. 629, affd. 196 N. Y. 510, 89 N. E. 

1114, the wife of a stockholder who was also his committee, succeeded in recovering damages against the directors for fraudulently inducing her to sell them her stock. After she was appointed committee, the directors approached her with a proposition to buy. In the ensuing conversation, she stated that if the dividends, theretofore from 9% to 15%, should shrink to 3%, she would be unable to support herself and children and care for her insane husband. Immediately, by means of a trick of bookkeeping alone, the company sustained "unusual losses"; salaries were largely increased temporarily without cause; a large surplus fund was put aside; and only a 3% dividend declared. The widow, having then become the executor of her husband's estate, was induced by these representations, and by further false statements that the stock was worth less than it was, that the company was less prosperous than before, and that it was doubtful whether it could ever be made to pay more, to sell for a depressed price. The purchasers were directors and were also president and treasurer, in sole control of corporate affairs.

If the officers fraudulently issue the corporation's stock to themselves they will be held to have received it for the benefit of the corporation. Brooklyn Crosstown R. Co. v. 

Strong, 75 N. Y. 591. Dunlay v. Ave. M Garage & Rep. Co., 253 N. Y. 274, 170 N. E. 917. Sec. 125, supra. The issuance of stock by the directors to themselves for an inadequate consideration is a fraud on corporation and stockholders which the majority can not authorize or ratify, and the concealment of the facts is some evidence of fraudulent intent. Pollitz v. Wabash R. Co., 207 N. Y. 113, 100 N. E. 

721, Cady's Cas. p. 465. The officers are liable to stockholders for the depreciation in the market value of stock brought about by fraudulent overissuance of stock, with the effect that the public mistakenly thought that the cor-

poration was liable for the whole issue. Mead v. Mali, 15 

How. Pr. 347, 25 Barb. 578. The issuance of stock to officers as compensation for services, in a case where the officer has already been generously paid for past services, and where he has not agreed to render services for any definite future period, may be ratified by a majority of the stockholders at the annual meeting, and thereafter may not be attacked by the minority. Wellington Bull etc. v. Morris, 132 Misc. 509, 230 N. Y. Supp. 122. A director or officer will not be permitted to receive and retain a commission or other secret profit or advantage in the case of a transaction in connection with the corporate business. Billings v. Shaw, 209 

N. Y. 265, 103 N. E. 142. Asphalt Const. Co. v. Bonker, 150 App. Div. 691, 135 N. Y. Supp. 714. Colonizer's Realty 

Co. of Brooklyn v. Shatzkin, 129 App. Div. 609, 114 N. Y. 

Supp. 71. Rickert v. White, 54 Misc. 114, 105 N. Y. Supp. 

653. Goldshear v. Barron, 42 Misc. 198, 85 N. Y. Supp. 

395. Ryan v. Grissinger, 136 N. Y. Supp. 134. Modlin v. 

Licht, 224 App. Div. 614, 231 N. Y. Supp. 265. 

§ 195. Qualifications of Directors and Officers. 

The statutory requirements are:-1. Of full age; 2. One a citizen of U. S. and a resident of New York; 3. A stockholder, unless otherwise provided in certificate of incorporation or in stockholders' bylaws; 4. Elected, except as to the directors for the first year, by a plurality of votes cast at a meeting of stockholders, duly called; 5. If elected at a general meeting, a quorum must have been present, and either the bylaws or the certificate of incorporation may fix the number of shares, not exceeding a majority, necessary to constitute a quorum for the meeting; 6. If elected at a special meeting, it must have been by a plurality of votes cast, and the bylaws or certificate can not make a different requirement; 7. If elected by cumulative voting, that kind of voting must have been permitted by provisions contained in the certificate of incorporation; 8. There must be at least three directors; 9. Directors for the first year must be named in the certificate of incorporation; 10. At least onefourth the directors of every stock corporation must be elected annually; 11. The place and time of the election should be set forth in the bylaws, adopter by either stock-

holders or directors; 12. The notice of the meeting must have been given as required by S. C. L. 45; 13. Vacancies shall be filled as provided in the bylaws; 14. If the number of directors be increased by amending the certificate under S. C. L. 35, the additional directors shall be elected by a majority of the directors of the board; 15. The certificate may fix a maximum or minimum number, and, if so, the bylaws should provide the method for determining the manner. S. C. L. 5, 55; G. C. L. 27.

Where stock was transferred prior to an election for the sole purpose of qualifying the transferees as directors, and the shares had been immediately assigned back to the true owners in blank, their election to the office was invalid. 

Matter of Ringler, supra, Cady's Cas. p. 516. An alleged purchase of stock by another person in the interest of, or as representative of the claimant to office, is insufficient. 

Matter of Hassam Pav. Co., 152 App. Div. 610, 137 N. 

Y. Supp. 453. If a director ceases to be a stockholder, his office becomes vacant ipso facto, this provision being self executing. Sturges v. Vanderbilt, 73 N. Y. 384. 

Sinclair v. Fuller, 158 N. Y. 607, 53 N. E. 510. People v. Albany & S. R. Co., 57 N. Y. 161. Peo. v. Powell, 201 N. Y. 194, 94 N. E. 634. Peo. v. N. Y. Infant 

Asylum, 122 N. Y. 190, 25 N. E. 241. The attorney general may bring proceedings to remove. Civil Practice Act, sec. 

1208. Merchants' Loan etc. Corp. v. Abramson, 214 App. 

Div. 252, 212 N. Y. Supp. 193. The directors for the first year become such by filing the certificate and their acceptance of the office. Directors for the first year need not be stockholders or subscribers for stock, since they are, in legal effect, appointed by the state. Davidson v. Westchester Gas Light Co., 99 N. Y. 558, 2 N. E. 892. Welch v. Importers' Nat. Bank, 122 N. Y. 177, 25 N. E. 269. Mc- 

Dowell v. Sheehan, 129 N. Y. 200, 29 N. E. 299. Ham. 

Trust Co. v. Clemens, 163 N. Y. 423, 57 N. E. 614. However, see Peo. v. McDonough, 28 Misc. 652, 60 N. Y. Supp. 45.

If they have once assumed the office, directors hold over until their successors are elected, or until they resign, or are removed, or until the corporation is dissolved or its charter forfeited. G. C. L. 21. Weil v. Defenbach, 208

Pac. 1025 (Idaho). Resignation may be implied. Halpin v. Mut. Brew. Co., 20 App. Div. 583, 47 N. Y. Supp. 412.

A resignation in good faith may be made at any time, even tho the corporation is on the verge of insolvency. No acceptance is necessary. Smith v. Danzig, 64 How. Pr. 320. 

Zeltner v. H. Zeltner Brew. Co., 174 N. Y. 247, 66 N. E. 810. 

§ 196. De Facto Officers and Directors. 

De factor officers and directors are such as serve as such under color of an invalid election or appointment, exercising the duties of office under such circumstances of publicity and acquiescence as would induce persons not cognizant of the situation to deal with them as bona fide officers. If, where three directors are authorized, the corporation, upon its organization, elects three additional, and permits a quorum of the six to sit and function as a board, the three additional directors are directors de facto, and officers appointed by them, who act under the appointment, are officers de facto. The acts of de facto directors bind the corporation in respect to their dealings with innocent third persons. Mtr. of Ringler & Co., supra, Cady's Cas. p. 516. The elements of proof of the authority of the de facto officer, in an action by a third person against the corporation, are two: possession of the office, and color of title. Carpenter v. Clark, 185 N. W. 868 (Mich.). There must also be a de jure office, and at least a de facto corporation. Cook v. Millers Indemnity Underwriters, 240 

S. W. 535 (Tex.). Herbst v. Held, 190 N. W. 153 (Iowa).

A person may become a director de facto by ceasing to be qualified, as where he has disposed of his stock, or by never having been eligible, as where he did not hold stock in his own name. Hygienic Health Food Co. v. Grant, 204 Pac. 

653, 204 Pac. 389 (Cal.). MacMahon v. Stepney Spare 

Wheel Ag., 140 App. Div. 554, 125 N. Y. Supp. 823. Re 

Manoca Temple Assn., 128 App. Div. 796, 118 N. Y. Supp. 172.

A de facto officer or director, acting within the scope of authority of the office, binds the corporation to the same extent as an officer de jure. The reason is based on public policy. Third persons can not always investigate. "If they see him publicly exercising its authority, if they ascertain

that this is generally acquiesced in, they are entitled to treat him as such officer." State v. Carroll, 32 Conn. 449. See 

Ham. Tr. Co. v. Clemes, 163 N. Y. 423, 57 N. E. 614, 15 

L. R. A. 418. 

A decision ousting de facto directors or officers does not become effective until the order is signed. Ringler case, supra. The validity of the de facto officers encumbency of his office can not be assailed collaterally, but only in a direct action brought to remove, or to seat his validly elected successor. Wallace & Sons v. Walsh, 125 N. Y. 26, 25 N. E. 

1076. Lovett v. Ger. Refd. Ch., 12 Barb. 67. Langan v. 

Francklyn, 29 Abb. N. C. 102, 20 N. Y. Supp. 404. 

§ 197. The Transfer Agent. 

Trust companies and banks are frequently employed to represent the corporation in the issuance and transfer of certificates of stock. The transfer agent has no implied authority to bind the corporation by making representations as to the ownership of stock. Henning v. N. Y. & 

N. H. R. Co., 52 N. Y. Sup. (20 J. & S.) 537. Persons, who have been deprived of their corporate stock on receipt and cancellation by the transfer agent of the original certificate under a forged endorsement or power of attorney, have a cause of action against the corporation to compel it to issue them a new certificate and account for the dividends or, if it has no stock which it can issue them, to pay them the value; but they have no cause of action against the transfer agent unless it has been guilty of negligence. Pollock v. Natl. 

Bank, 7 N. Y. 274. Jarvis v. Manh. B. Co., supra, Cady's

Cas. p. 480. The transfer agent is not liable to the stockholder for nonfeasance, for it is not the agent of the stockholder, but of the corporation. Thus, on refusal of the transfer agent to transfer promptly, resulting in losses through market changes, the stockholder has no action against the agent. Dunham v. City Tr. Co., 115 App. Div. 584, 101 N. 

Y. Supp. 87, affd. 193 N. Y. 642. Nicholson v. Morgan, supra, Cady's Cas. p. 497. A "security receipt" provision of c. 704,

L. 1926 as amended by c. 630, sec. 2, L. 1930 and composing secs. 260 and 261 P. P. L. declares what sorts of scrip and corporate bonds, including security receipts, and equipment trust certificates are negotiable, so that one who purchases

and received them before maturity, for present or antecedent value without notice of prior defenses, equities, or claims of ownership against the thief, finder, or other persons who delivers them, gets good title as against the true owner, as follows:-1. Bearer bonds, etc.; 2. Bonds, etc., made out to a named person, but containing apt words which state, in substance, that the instrument is negotiable, provided however that it is endorsed in blank, or to a specified person, and delivered to the said specified person; 

3. The transfer must have been made before maturity, the date fixed for performance or, if no date is fixed, after a reasonable time; 4. If not endorsed in blank by the aforesaid specified person, there is no presumption of title in the purchaser; 5. If the bond, etc., is to bearer, or, if to a specified person, and it has been properly endorsed, there is a prima facie presumption that the person in possession is the owner; 6. The presumption is overcome by proof that the title of some person in the chain was defective; and, if sair defect is proved, the burden is on the holder to prove by a fair preponderance of evidence that he or some person under whom he claims acquired title as a holder for value without notice. The defect in endorsement, aforesaid, is notice. The plaintiff, in an action based on the transfer, has the burden of showing that the title of some of the persons who negotiated the paper was defective; and the defendant in possession thereupon has the burden of establishing that he, or some person under whom he claims, acquired the title as a holder for value and without notice. The sections above referred to cover security receipts, equipment trust certificates, and corporate bonds. 

§ 198. Failure to make Corporate Reports. 

Of the various statutes, hitherto in effect, in New York imposing liabilities on the officers for the failure to make reports, none have survived except the statute requiring a financial statement to stockholders. S. C. L. 77. Sec. 

144a, supra. Under S. C. L. 61, the officers or directors signing a false certificate or report containing a material misrepresentation, become personally liable, jointly and severally, to any person who became stockholder or creditor on faith in the report, to the extent of the debt

contracted and not paid when due, or to the extent of the damage. A short statute of limitations of 2 years from making or giving the certificate, report, or public notice, is imposed, within which the action must be brought. As the statute now stands, the creditor must have relied upon the report. One who purchased an interim receipt, signed by the treasurer, entitling him to corporate notes "when, as and if issued," sued the treasurer under this statute. 

The notes were never issued by the corporation, and therefore it was held that, since the plaintiff's grievance was that he did not become a creditor, the statute did not apply. 

There was also a defect of proof to show that the notes had not been duly authorized by the corporation, and, if authorized, there was no material misrepresentation in the paper. Carpenter v. Witbeck, 212 App. Div. 181, 208 N. Y.

Supp. 545. The later tendency is to hold directors to a strict accountability for false reports. Van Slochem v. Villard, 154 App. Div. 161, 138 N. Y. Supp. 852. Ottinger v. Bennett, 144 App. Div. 525, 532, 129 N. Y. Supp. 819, 203 N. Y. 

554. Where the false report is issued by a foreign corporation, the liability may depend upon a foreign statute, which, if penal, another state may refuse to enforce. The question depends upon whether the purpose of the statute is to punish an offense against the public justice of the state, or to afford a private remedy to a person injured by the wrongful act. If the latter is the true construction, the statute may generally be enforced by the courts of another state, unless it involves a procedure contrary to the adjective law of the state in which the case is tried. Huntington v. Attrill, 146 U. S. 617, 36 L. ed. 1123.

§ 199. 

Powers of Majority.

The rule of the common law, permitting the majority to govern the operations and control the property of the firm, when acting bona fide and apart from restrictions in the agreement, was carried over, in essence, from the partnership to the newer form of association in the corporation, modified, however, to suit the artificial form. Re Overend, Gurney & Co., (Grissell's case), L. R. 1 Ch. 528. Welles v. March, 30 N. Y. 344. G. C. L. 27, 28. An opportunity is afforded the minority to express their objections to any proposed scheme at stockholders meetings. The majority are required to be true and faithful to the corporation, and not to change the enterprise by embarking in ultra vires enterprises; but where there has been no fraud, oppression, or unfairness, the majority may control all the ordinary affairs of the corporation and do all the acts permitted to the majority by the statutes and charter. Morse v. Equitable Life Assur. Soc., 124 App. Div. 235, 108 N. Y. 

Supp. 986. The majority may: 1. Control the corporate business through directors elected by them; 2. Prescribe the policy of the corporation, within charter provisions; 

3. Make themselves the officers and agents of the corporation; and 4. Take reasonable compensation for their services. For a majority of the corporation to say, "We do not care what the minority may think, we will do what we please, acting as arbitrarily and capriciously as we may, because we are the majority," is an attitude that the court would not sanction. What weight the majority will give 343

to the opinions of the minority is for the majority to determine; but it must not appear, from their words or conduct, that the opinion and judgment of the minority, and the effect of the proposed step on the minority as well as on the corporation, have been excluded from consideration. The corporation in theory is distinct from its members, but it can act only through the individual associates who compose it. Within the scope of the powers conferred by the charter, and in amending the charter powers, the majority are the corporation, providing they act within the law, and further providing that their acts are not done oppressively. 

Hart v. Ogdensburg & L. C. R. Co., 89 Hun 316, 35 N. Y. 

Supp. 566. If the majority have fulfilled these requirements, the will of the majority, in all internal matters, is supreme, and the court will not interfere, either to prevent the doing of acts, on the ground that the plan of the minority is better, or subsequently, to relieve from the effect accruing therefrom. Troy & R. R. Co. v. Kerr, 17 Barb. 581. Day v. 

Railroad Co., 107 N. Y. 129. See also, Thomas v. R. Co., 139 N. Y. 163, 34 N. E. 877. Rafferty v. Buff. City Gas 

Co., 37 App. Div. 618, 56 N. Y. Supp. 288. In Hawes v.

Oakland, 104 U. S. 450, 26 L. ed. 827, a stockholder of a waterworks company brought action on behalf of himself and such other stockholders as might come in, to restrain the corporation from supplying, without charge, water for watering the streets and for other municipal purposes, and the directors from giving away the said water belonging to the corporation. A contract existed between the corporation and the city, whereby, if the construction applied by the plaintiff was proper, the city was only entitled to water for fires and extraordinary purposes. The defendants demurred to the complaint, and contended that since, by the construction placed on the contract by the majority, the city was entitled to the water, the minority, represented by the plaintiff, had no standing in court to contest the decision of the majority, that being a matter of internal management with which was commingled the decision of the business policy to be pursued in dealing with the city. The demurrer was sustained. The court laid down the following tests, and held that a complaint which voiced the claim of the dissenting

minority, was fatally defective, unless it showed as a foundation of the suit- 

1. "Some action or threatened action of the managing board of directors or trustees of the corporation which is beyond the authority conferred on them by their charter or other source of organization; 

2. "Or such a fraudulent transaction completed or contemplated by the acting managers, in connection with some other party, or among themselves, or with other shareholders as will result in serious injury to the corporation, or to the interests of the other shareholders; 

3. "Or where the board of directors, or a majority of them, are acting for their own interest, in a manner destructive of the corporation itself, or of the rights of the other shareholders; 

4. "Or where the majority of shareholders themselves are oppressively and illegally pursuing a course in the name of the corporation, which is in violation of the rights of the other shareholders, and which can only be restrained by the aid of a court of equity." 

5. "Possibly other cases may arise in which, to prevent irremediable injury, or a total failure of justice, the court would be justified in exercising its powers, but the foregoing may be regarded as an outline of the principles which govern this class of cases."

Shares of its own stock, held by the corporation, can neither be voted, nor counted to make up a majority. Only stock actually issued to and owned by the stockholders can be considered. Greenpoint Sugar Co. v. Whitin, 69 N. Y. 

328; Atlantic Trust Co. v. Crystal Water Co., 72 App. Div. 

539, 76 N. Y. Supp. 647; Swan v. Stiles, 94 App. Div. 117, 87 N. Y. Supp. 1089. 

§ 200. Ultra Vires Acts of Majority. 

The minority stockholder may restrain threatened or partly executed or executed ultra vires acts, pursuant to the rules of the particular jurisdiction involved, as indicated on pp. 133 to 149 supra. Wormser v. Met. St. Ry. 

Co., 184 N. Y. 83. Schwab v. Potter Co., supra, Cady's

Cas. p. 542. The principle that the corporation is the best judge, and must be held to be the only judge, of what shall

be done to conserve its interests, applies only to a case where the majority are acting intra vires, in good faith, in the decision of disputes which the general body is legally competent to determine. 

§ 201. Fraudulent Transactions Completed or Contem plated.

In a stockholders representative suit, to which the corporation and the third persons, if any, implicated in the transactions complained of, are parties, the court may enjoin misapplications of capital or profits which might result in lessening the dividends of stockholders or the value of their shares. The majority can not condone such an act by ratification. Fraud and illegality can not be made binding by ratification any more than they could have been originally sanctioned by the majority. The votes of the guilty parties should not be counted in the majority. In Flynn v. Brooklyn City R. R. Co., 158 N. Y. 495, the situation disclosed was that all the stockholders, except the plaintiff, had voted to lease the lines of defendant, a 30 million dollar corporation, to the Brooklyn Heights Railroad, which only operated a half mile track on Montague Street, and two other small corporations with slender assets, in return for a rental equal to a 10% dividend on the stock, backed by a guarantee fund of 4 millions, together with the right to invest in $300 of the lessee's stock for every $100 of the lessors stock held, upon paying $15 additional per share. 

The directors, who were in the syndicate whose profits in the transaction were over 2 millions with a further prospective profit of half a million per year, were unanimously in favor of the scheme, and had recommended it to the stockholders before the meeting was held. The court said: "When a contract founded in fraud is executed by the directors with a third party upon the express approval of a required number of stockholders, with the intention on the part of all concerned to defraud the non-assenting stockholders, and the scheme will naturally result in serious injury to them and to the corporation, a court of equity will set aside the fraudulent transaction and compel the delinquent parties to account." Cf., Leslie v. Lorillard, 110 N. Y. 519, 535-6; Jacobus v. Amer. Min. Wat. Machine www

Co., 38 Misc. 371, 77 N. Y. Supp. 898; Loewenstein v. Diamond Soda Water Mfg. Co., 94 App. Div. 383, 88 N. Y. 

Supp. 313; Jacobus v. Same, 94 App. Div. 366, 88 N. Y.

Supp. 302. The fact that the majority is owned by a single stockholder whose nominees fill all the offices, with salaries fixed by him, will not support an action by the minority stockholder, in the absence of facts showing that the salaries are so excessive as to warrant the conclusion that the conduct of the parties was fraudulent. Swan v. Consol. Water 

Co. of Pomona, 28 F. (2d) 971 (Cal.). But if that conclusion is reached, the burden of proof is on the directors to show the value of their services. Godley v. Crandall & G. 

Co., 212 N. Y. 121, 105 N. E. 818. § 202. Acts of the Majority in Bad Faith, or for Their 

Own Interest. 

Where the majority, owning more than 2/3 the stock, organized another corporation in which they also owned a majority of the stock, and sold all the assets of the old corporation, valued at $250,000, to the new corporation for $66,000, against the protests of the minority, the transaction, at the suit of the minority, was set aside. Although the statute confers upon a 2/3 majority power to convey its property, rights, privileges and franchises, and the power is couched in clear and comprehensive language, without reservations or exceptions, the majority can not act under it unless they act in good faith. Hinds v. Fishkill and Matteawan Equit. Gas Co., 96 App. Div. 14, 88 

N. Y. Supp. 954. Although directors have the same legal right as others to purchase stock offered for sale by the corporation, it is inequitable conduct involving bad faith for the directors to issue unissued stock to themselves for the primary purpose of converting themselves from minority to majority stockholders. Dunlay v. Ave. M. Garage &c., 253 N. Y. 274, 170 N. E. 917. Altho under the statutes one corporation may acquire a controlling interest in the stock of a competitor, equity will prevent directors, elected by the majority, from leasing the latter's property to the first under such terms that interest on outstanding mortgage bonds theretofore issued could not be paid. Green v. Peoples 

Gaslight &c. Co., 118 Misc. 1, 192 N. Y. Supp. 232. Where

the overlapping directors of one of two roads made a lease from one to another at an exorbitant rental, and made large loans to other corporations of which they were stockholders, a stockholder who owned only a small part of the stock and bonds could bring the action and the defense of laches is one to be raised by the answer, and not by demurrer to the complaint. Sage v. Culver, 147 N. Y. 241. 

See, Nave-McCord Mercantile Co. v. Ranney, 29 F. (2d) 

383. Kreitner v. Burgweger, supra, Cady's Cas. p. 552. 

§ 203. Oppressive Acts of the Majority. 

The court will interfere at the suit of an individual stockholder if the proceedings of the majority purposely do injury to him individually. Thus the stockholder may force the corporation to observe his stock rights, Stokes v. 

Continental Tr. Co., supra, Cady's Cas. p. 436; to treat him like the rest of his class in the distribution of dividends; to call a special meeting for the election of directors, where those in power omit to do so, by accident or design, and so hold over. Peo. ex rel. Miller v. Cummings, 72 N. Y. 433. 

In Farmer's Loan & Tr. Co. v. N. Y. & N. Ry. Co., 150

N. Y. 410, the court collated the cases, and held, in a case where one railroad had bought a controlling interest in the stock and bonds of another, and was foreclosing the trust mortgage on default in payment of interest, that the minority stockholder should be permitted to prove that the majority had refused to accept traffic from other roads, which would have produced a sum sufficient to pay the interest in default, and had also diverted income of the road, which ought to have been employed to pay such interest. 

McLeary v. Erie Tel. & Tel. Co., 38 Misc. 3, 76 N. Y. 

Supp. 712. Jacobus v. Am. &c Mach. Co., 38 Misc. 371, 77 N. Y. Supp. 898. Witherbee v. Bowles, 142 App. Div. 

407, 126 N. Y. Supp. 954. Niles v. N. Y. C. & H. R. 

R. R. Co., 176 N. Y. 119. Male v. Atchison, T & S. F. R. 

Co., 179 App. Div. 87, 166 N. Y. Supp. 593.

The minority stockholder is bound by the act of the majority in good faith, tho the act is prejudicial to him, provided the act is neither ultra vires nor illegal, and not done for the purpose of damaging or injuring him. 

The mere fact that it is a hardship to have a call issued

at the particular time, with the danger of forfeiture, will not support an action to restrain. Leslie v. Lorillard, supra. 

Common instances of oppression are: the arbitrary depressing of the value of stock by refraining from declaring a fair dividend or one in accordance with the dividend policy of years of similar prosperity, capricious increases of salaries, increases of surplus without substantial reason, unfair bookkeeping entries, and the like, when pursued for the purpose of inducing the stockholder to sell his stock to the majority at a low price. Von Au v. Magenheimer, 126 

App. Div. 257, 110 N. Y. Supp. 629, affd. (mem.) 196 N. Y. 

510. The majority may not control where its acts are so unfair and oppressive and so clearly against the interest of the minority as to amount to a wanton and fraudulent destruction of the rights of such minority. Cutting v. 

Baltimore, etc., R. Co., 65 App. Div. 414, 73 N. Y. Supp. 

21. McManus v. Durant, 168 App. Div. 643, 154 N. Y. 

Supp. 580. But see Stone v. Cleveland &c., R. Co., 202 

N. Y. 352. A case must be clearly made out, however, to warrant the interposition of the courts. Gamble v. Queens 

Co. Water Co., 123 N. Y. 91. 

§ 204. Power to Wind Up and to Dissolve the Cor poration.

A majority of two thirds may wind up the business and dissolve an unprofitable corporation. S. C. L. 105. 

G. C. L. 100, 101. Skinner v. Smith, 134 N. Y. 240, 31 

N. E. 911. The resolution of the board of directors must be in good faith, as well as in accordance with the provisions of the statute. In Kavanaugh v. Kavanaugh Knitting 

Co., 226 N. Y. 185, a minority stockholder successfully brought a stockholders' representative suit to restrain the directors from dissolving the corporation. The court said that the directors should not consider "their personal wishes, comfort or advantage; their action must be based upon the belief that the interests and welfare of the corporation and the stockholders generally will be promoted by dissolution. The belief may be erroneous or ill-founded, but it must be formed in good faith."..."The law, as well as ordinary justice and sound business policy, requires that

the existence of the corporation should not be attacked, within the period fixed by its charter, by its board of directors acting in bad faith, fraudulently or through the intent to punish or oppress a stockholder because he defends himself in the courts or otherwise against their illegal or unfair acts relative to the corporation or because of any other reason." Dissolution will be enjoined where it is used to cover losses sustained through the directors' negligence. 

In re Great Northern Trading Co., 168 App. Div. 536, 153 

N. Y. Supp. 213. In re Rateau Sales Co., 121 N. Y. 420,

Cady's Cas. p. 601. The expense of dissolution proceedings must be paid by the corporation. Mtr. of French, 181 App. 

Div. 719, 168 N. Y. Supp. 988, affd. 224 N. Y. 555.

A corporation may sell all its property when the exigencies of its business require it to do so, without regard to whether minority stockholders consent or object. Holmes v. Holmes, 127 N. Y. 252. Hoag v. Edwards, 69 Misc. 237, 124 N. Y. Supp. 1035. On the other hand, the majority of a solvent prosperous corporation cannot, as against the dissent of the minority, direct the sale of the entire corporate property in bad faith where there is no exigency demanding such a course, since the contract between the stockholders is that their joint fund shall be employed for the purpose specified in their charter. Barclay v. Quicksilver Min. Co., 9 Abb. Pr. N. S. 283. Murrin v. Archbald 

Coal Co., 232 N. Y. 47, Cady's Cas. p. 182. Re Bickerton (N. Y. Theatre Co.), 232 N. Y. 1. Abbot v. Am. Hard 

Rubber Co., 33 Barb. 578. Sheldon Hat Blocking Co. v. Eickemeyer &c. Co., 90 N. Y. 607. Peo. v. Ballard, 134 N. Y. 269. Hinds v. Fishkill &c. Gas Co., 96 App. Div. 

14, 88 N. Y. Supp. 954. If good faith exists, the majority of the stockholders, may, against the objection of the minority, dispose of all the corporate property, where the corporation is conducted at a loss, and there is no prospect of its profitable operation. Weingreen v. Michelbacher, 149

N. Y. Supp. 110. It was held at common law that a corporation might not lease all its property where there was no power to lease given by the charter and some of the stockholders dissented. Copeland v. Cit. Gas-Light Co., 61 Barb. 

60. Hennessy v. Muhleman, 27 Misc. 232, 57 N. Y. Supp.

114. The New York statutes provide the necessary power. 

S. C. L. 16, 20. G. C. L. 50. 

§ 205. Defenses of the Majority. 

A minority stockholder may waive his right to question the acts of the officers or majority stockholders. Cont. Ins. 

Co. v. N. Y. &c. R. Co., 187 N. Y. 225. He may be estopped by participation, consent or acquiescence. Kent v. Quicksilver Min. Co., 78 N. Y. 159; Skinner v. Smith, 134 N. Y. 

240; Burden v. Burden, 159 N. Y. 287. A stockholder may estop himself to raise the question of the lack of power by delay, with knowledge, for such a time as would be equivalent to a ratification. Sheldon Hat Blocking Co. v. Eickemeyer &c. Mach. Co., 90 N. Y. 607; Parsons v. Hayes, 14 

Abb. N. C. 419. 

§ 206. Powers of Minority. 

The minority stockholders have the right to present their views at corporate meetings. Polhemus v. Polhemus, 43 

Misc. 141, 88 N. Y. Supp. 273. Courts generally decline to interfere with the internal management of a corporation at the instance of minority stockholders, unless the majority stockholders are acting ultra vires or a strong case of fraud or mismanagement is shown. In re Hinds, 172 App. 

Div. 140, 158 N. Y. Supp. 249. Union No. 1006 v. Brotherhood of Painters, 149 N. Y. Supp. 1025. The minority stockholder impliedly agrees at the time he acquires his stock that the will of the majority shall govern in all matters coming within the limits of the charter or the act of incorporation. Hoag v. Edwards, 69 Misc. 237, 124 N. Y. 

Supp. 1035. There can be no interference by minority stockholders with acts of directors or majority stockholders pursuant to law. Hinds v. Fishkill, etc., Gas Co., 96 App. 

Div. 14, 88 N. Y. Supp. 954. Livingston v. Lynch, 4 Johns. 

Ch. 573. 

§ 207. 

Rights in regard to Amendments of Charter. 

A majority has the power to make any alterations or changes in the constitution of the corporation which are authorized by its charter. Chicago City Ry. Co. v. Allerton, 18 Wall. 233. A bare majority has no power to make

a radical and fundamental change in the corporation as originally organized. Hartford, etc., R. Co. v. Croswell, 5 Hill 383. So, a majority of the stockholders of a railroad corporation cannot bind the minority by a charter amendment authorizing a consolidation where such consolidation has the effect of changing the objects of the corporation. 

Gardner v. Ham. Ins. Co., 33 N. Y. 421. Of course, the majority may alter a charter where it does not work radical change in corporate purpose. Hollender v. Roch. 

F. P. Corp., supra, Cady's Cas. p. 335. Schenectady &c. Pl. Rd. Co. v. Thatcher, 11 N. Y. 102. Buffalo, etc., R. 

Co. v. Dudley, 14 N. Y. 336. Union Hotel Co. v. Hersee, supra, Cady's Cas. p. 339. Hinckley v. Schwarzwald, 107 

App. Div. 470, 95 N. Y. Supp. 357 To change the corporate name or increase or reduce the capital stock it is not a fundamental change. Buffalo etc., R. Co. v. Dudley, 14 N. Y. 

336. Troy &c., R. Co. v. Kerr, 17 Barb. 581. Yonkers 

Gazette v. Taylor, Cady's Cas. p. 341.
