§ 208. Actions by the Stockholder in his Individual Right. 

The right of the stockholder to sue for damages or for the redress of individual wrongs, involving direct loss to him, has been discussed in the foregoing chapters. For damages for acts directly causing loss to the stockholder he may sue at law. His rights in equity to restrain acts that are ultra vires, fraudulent, illegal, or oppressive, and to enforce and protect his rights concerning stock, voting, transfers, dividends, elections, and, within the limits stated in the statutes, to dissolve the corporation, have been considered at length. G. C. L. 72. 14 C. J. 875 f. For injuries that concern him alone, he may sue alone. Filer v. Creole Syndicate, 230 App. Div. 509, 245 N. Y. Supp. 367.

But if the acts also concern other stockholders, he must sue for the behalf of all, or the others must be joined, because of the rule relating to multiplicity of suits. Godley's Outl. of Equity, secs. 147, 148. This is known as the stockholders representative action. § 209. Stockholder can not Interfere with Management. 

The stockholder has no right to interfere in the management, and therefore can not, as a general rule, sue to redress wrongs to the corporation, or bring trover, trespass or replevin to protect the corporate assets. He can not sue for specific performance of a contract made by the corporation with a stranger. VanCleave v. Demorest, 174 App. 

Div. 928, 160 N. Y. Supp. 923. In a case where plaintiff, being about to go to Palestine, put the management of the 353

1 corporation and the stock ownership in the hands of his wife's brother, the defendant, and found when he returned that the assets of the corporation had been secreted and a petition in bankruptcy filed by creditors against the corporation, it was held that plaintiff could not recover from his brother for the injury done to the corporation. Hirschberg v. Appel, 164 N. E. 915 (Mass.). Berger v. Burden, 173 App. Div. 680, 160 N. Y. Supp. 331; secs. 135, 145, supra. The corporation alone has the cause of action, and may sue its directors for mismanagement or gross negligence in the performance of their duties. Gen. Rubber Co. v. Benedict, supra, Cady's Cas. p. 531. The stockholder has no standing in court to enjoin the collection of a tax, wrongfully assessed by the state on the corporation, for "courts of equity have no jurisdiction over corporations, as such, at the suit of a stockholder for violations of charters, and none for the errors of judgment of those who manage their business ordinarily." Dodge v. Woolsey, 18 How. (U. S.) 

331. Altho the enforcement of unconstitutional legislation, involving a deprivation of liberty and property by forcing the corporation to make excessive expenditures for labor by shortening the hours of continuous employment, will curtail dividends, and altho the officers, impelled by fear of penalties, have refused to disobey the statute, the stockholder nevertheless has no standing to enjoin the enforcement of the statute by the public officials and can only secure relief through the corporation. Wathen v. Jackson Oil Co., 235 U. S. 635 (opinion of Mr. Justice Holmes). The only exception to these principles is the stockholders derivative action. 

§ 210. Stockholders Representative Actions. 

If the injury complained of was to the stockholders alone, and not to the corporation, any stockholder may bring a stockholders action, on behalf of himself and of all other stockholders of the corporation, who may be similarly situated, and who may come in and join in the complaint and contribute to the expenses of the action. Creditors of the corporation may bring the same form of action. Small v. 

Sullivan, 245 N. Y. 343. Lilienthal v. Betts, 185 N. Y. 153. 

Parish v. N. Y. Prod. Exch., 169 N. Y. 34. Actions brought

STOCKHOLDERS ACTIONS 

355 in this form avoid multiplicity of suits. C. P. A. 195. Recovery in the action is based upon an injury to the stockholders directly, and not upon an injury to the corporation. 

In Witherbee v. Bowles, 201 N. Y. 427, the plaintiffs, who were the majority owners of stock in the San Toy company, had contracted to buy the minority stock. As security for the deal, both sets of stockholders deposited their holdings with a trust company, to be sold in accordance with the plan. 

Through a subterfuge, the minority forestalled the majority, and caused a premature sale to themselves for property of slight value, and also, without proper notice, increased the stock. It was held that the plaintiffs should succeed in setting aside the entire transaction by a stockholders representative suit against all the conspirators. The corporation was necessarily made a party to the action, since the stock was to be cancelled by the judgment; but, on the doctrine of Waters v. Waters & Co., 201 N. Y. 184, Cady's Cas. p. 

445, no conceivable injury could have been sustained by it by reason of the issuance of its stock, and the whole injury was to the plaintiff stockholders, who, were alone entitled to the judgment. The action was held proper. In Waters v. 

Waters & Co., supra, one of the reasons for the dismissal of the complaint was that a derivative suit was brought where a representative action was the only appropriate remedy. 

See also Vogt v. Vogt, 119 App. Div. 518, 104 N. Y. Supp. 

164. The plaintiff must be a stockholder. If his membership is inchoate only, the complaint should be dismissed. Berger v. Burden, 173 App. Div. 680, 160 N. Y. Supp. 331. An action involving depreciation of stock values due to the fraud and negligence of the directors belongs to the corporation alone, even though, of course, the stockholder has necessarily suffered individually and personally by such directors acts. 

Cont. Ins. Co. v. N. Y. etc. R. Co., 187 N. Y. 225; Niles v. 

N. Y. etc. R. Co., 69 App. Div. 144, 74 N. Y. Supp. 617.

If the injury to the corporation is primary, and the injury to the stockholders secondary, the stockholders representative action is not the proper remedy. The corporation, having refused to bring an action for damages incurred through an injunction maliciously procured by the defendant, it was held that the owner of a majority of the stock could not

bring a stockholders representative suit to recover the damage suffered indirectly. Sigl, Inc. v. Bresnahan, 216 App. 

Div. 634, 215 N. Y. Supp. 735. 

§ 211. Estoppel of Plaintiff. 

The burden of proof is on the defendant corporation to plead and prove acts of plaintiff or of the preceding owner of the stock, constituting estoppel. Cont. Sec. Co. v. Belmont, supra, Cady's Cas. p. 456. If the acts of the defendants complained of are neither illegal per se nor immoral, plaintiff is bound by the assent of the former owner of his stock, and even by his acquiescence for a long time with full knowledge of the facts. Skinner v. Smith, supra; Murray v. 

Smith, supra, Cady's Cas. p. 200. Sedgwick v. Seward Dev. 

Co., 144 App. Div. 455, 129 N. Y. Supp. 209. There is no estoppel if the act is immoral-for instance, the use of the corporations money to prevent interference with violation of law. Roth v. Robertson, 64 Misc. 343, 118 N. Y. Supp. 

351. Laches in making complaint, coupled with the acceptance of benefits under the allegedly fraudulent contract, will estop. Norman v. Fed. Min. & S. Co., 180 App. Div. 

325, 167 N. Y. Supp. 794. In Jenkins v. Auburn City Ry. 

Co., 27 App. Div. 553, 50 N. Y. Supp. 582, a temporary injunction obtained by the minority stockholder, enjoining the company from leasing its property, was vacated on motion by the defendants, on proof being adduced to show that the plaintiff was acting in the interests of a rival railroad, to annoy and harass the defendants by a vicious and malicious attack. In Ramsey v. Gould, 7 Abb. Pr. (N. S.) 156, 8 Abb. 

Pr. (N. S.) 174, a case arising out of the Erie-Susquehanna railroad war, it was held that, in an action by one rival corporation against another, the fact that plaintiff was a volunteer would not suffice to dismiss the complaint in an action for a permanent injunction, unless it was also shown that either plaintiff had no meritorious cause of action, or that he was estopped. In Wormser v. Met. St. Ry. 

Co., 184 N. Y. 83, the action was brought to enjoin the directors from leasing the company's lines. The lease was consented to by all stockholders except the plaintiff. The complaint, among other charges, contained allegations of insufficiency of rental, inadequacy of security, and private inter-

STOCKHOLDERS ACTIONS 

357 ests of the directors which, if proved, would have made out a prima facie case. The plaintiff, after the action was commenced, availed himself of the privilege of stock rights under the very plan which he was attacking, and it was held that this act disposed of plaintiffs right to contest the power of the corporation to make the lease. It is not clear whether the ground of the decision is to be denominated estoppel, quasi-estoppel, acquiescence or election. The plaintiff can not both profit by a contract and deny its validity, providing it is neither prohibited by law nor evil in itself. See also, Jenkins v. Albany City Ry. Co., 27 App. Div. 553, 50 

N. Y. Supp. 852.

To prevent multiplicity of suits, it is held that a judgment on the merits dismissing the complaint concludes all stockholders, just as if they had been plaintiffs in the action, and the complaint in a subsequent suit based substantially, but not identically on the same facts, will be dismissed. 

Godley's Outl. Eq., secs. 147, 148; Grant v. Greene Consol. 

Copper Co., 169 App. Div. 206, 154 N. Y. Supp. 596, Cady's 

Cas. p. 469; Alexander v. Donohoe, 143 N. Y. 203, 38 

N. E. 263. 

§ 212. Stockholders Derivative Action. 

It is the province of the corporation to protect its own rights. If it is incapable of asserting its rights because it is in the control of the wrongdoers, or of those who are negligently lax or who otherwise act in breach of the obligations of the fiduciary relationship, the stockholder may, in a proper case, bring the stockholders derivative action in equity to redress or prevent acts, done or threatened, injurious to the corporation, and so, indirectly injurious to the plaintiffs, who must be non-consenting stockholders. 

Tho the act may have been accomplished in accord with the forms of law it may be in fact a fraudulent scheme, ingeniously devised in bad faith for the injury or oppression of the plaintiffs. Kavanaugh v. Kavanaugh Knitting 

Co., 226 N. Y. 185, 194. The unique features of the derivative action, as distinguished from the representative action, are that, while both are suits in equity, the derivative action demands judgment in favor of the defendant corporation, and is based on a precedent de-

mand made by the plaintiff stockholder upon the corporation to bring the suit, unless the complaint shows that a demand would be futile. Kavanaugh v. Commonwealth Tr. 

Co., 181 N. Y. 121, Cady's Cas. p. 455. In Greaves v. 

Gouge, 66 N. Y. 52, one of the earliest cases in the court of appeals in which the remedy was applied, the complaint was successfully demurred to. The complaint alleged that plaintiff was a stockholder of the defendant corporation; that the defendant A, who was its president, and the defendant B, who was one of its officers, had obtained by a conspiracy, through an act of the corporation, the surplus of the company, with the result that plaintiff's stock had become worthless; and demanded that plaintiff have judgment for the value of his stock. The insufficiency of the complaint lay in that the action was not brought by the plaintiff stockholder for the benefit of himself and for those similarly situated; that it did not allege that the corporation had refused to bring the action upon being applied to for that purpose; and, finally, that judgment was sought for the stockholder and not for the corporation. It it is self evident that a judgment in favor of the corporation would recoup not only the direct injuries to the corporation, but also the indirect injuries of the stockholder. The corporation must be made a party defendant, for it would be wrong, in case the stockholders were unsuccessful, to allow the corporation to renew the litigation in another suit, involving practically the same subject matter. Davenport v. Dows, 18 Wall. (U. S.) 626. 

Wells v. Jewett, 69 N. Y. 154. Corning v. Barrett, 22 Misc. 

241, 48 N. Y. Supp. 1013. Niles v. N. Y. C. &c. R.R., 176 

N. Y. 119, 68 N. E. 142. 

§ 213 Necessary Grounds of Action. 

The complaint in the stockholders derivative suit in equity must allege two sets of facts: 1. The facts necessary to a valid cause of action on which the corporation might have sued the other defendants, and that, as it has declined to sue, it is made a party defendant; 2. A good cause of action by the stockholder plaintiff against the corporation, in that the corporation, having a good cause of action against the other defendants, declined to sue them

STOCKHOLDERS ACTIONS 

359 upon due demand by plaintiff. The judgment prayed for must be one in favor of the corporation against the other defendants. If the facts alleged do not show a good cause of action by the corporation against the other defendants, the complaint must be dismissed. If the complaint shows no cause of action in favor of the plaintiff stockholder against the defendant corporation, or fails to allege the excuse for the action being brought by plaintiff, the complaint must be dismissed. Kavanaugh v. Commonwealth 

Tr. Co., supra, Cady's Cas. p. 455. Waters v. Horace 

Waters & Co., 201 N. Y. 184, Cady's Cas. p. 443. Flynn v. 

Brooklyn &c R. Co., supra. Grant v. Cobre Grande Copper Co., 126 App. Div. 750, 111 N. Y. Supp. 386. The stockholder stands in the shoes of the corporation. MacQuoid v. Queens Est., 143 App. Div. 134, 127 N. Y. Supp. 867. 

In Dusenberry v. Sagamore Dev. Co., 164 App. Div. 573, 150 

N. Y. Supp. 229, the corporate act complained of was a sale by the corporation of its stock to the officers and directors, giving them the control, after various turnings and twistings in the endeavor to get money by the sale of debentures to the stockholders. The complaint was dismissed, since it did not allege any injury or cause of action in the corporation. The entity is indifferent as to stock ownership, and there was no allegation that the defendants were conspirators, looters or wreckers, working, or contemplating harm to the corporation.

The complaint must show some harm resulting to the plaintiff. A bylaw, in Levin v. Mayer, 86 Misc. 116, 149 

N. Y. Supp. 112, required the unanimous consent of the directors to a sale of the business. The majority only of the directors sold. The stockholder brought a representative suit against the corporation and two of its three directors. The sale was for the fair value, and involved no adverse interest of the directors. The business had become unprofitable, and, while the directors had exceeded their powers in selling, the plaintiff had suffered no loss thereby. 

The complaint was dismissed. Ultra vires acts resulting in loss, waste, diversion to themselves, or misapplication of funds by the directors, and their negligence, fraud, and illegal acts, will support the action.

§ 214. 

Stockholders Derivative Actions Illustrated. 

The plaintiff corporation, and another stockholder named Venner, who bought stock in the Interborough Rapid Transit Company, four or five years after the transactions complained of, brought a derivative action against the syndicate head, one August Belmont, and others, to compel them to account for their profits in the formation of the Interborough. The subway contractor being unable to finance his contract, Belmont formed corporation A, which carried through the construction contract with the city, paying Belmont one fourth its profits for his services in financing. 

The Interborough company aforesaid was a reorganization of corporation A, the capital being increased from 6 to 25 million dollars. The Interborough was formed to obtain a franchise and operate the completed subway, $160 of its stock being exchanged for each $100 share of corporation A stock. In order to obtain a franchise, it was found necessary to buy up the stock of two railroads which possessed a franchise City Island, and the Pelham Park railroads― 95% of whose stock was obtained for $270,000 by Mr. 

Belmont. The Interborough's charter expressly permitted it to invest in the stock of other corporations. For acting as banker in this purchase and reorganization, Mr. Belmont, tho he was the salaried president of corporation A, and the other defendants, were allowed by the board of the Interborough to take 1½ million dollars of stock in the Interborough. It was held that the complaint in the derivative action was good (206 N. Y. 7), alleging, as it did, that the aforesaid payment to Belmont was extortionate, a fraud on the corporation and stockholders, and a misappropriation; that as salaried president of corporation A, Belmont should be allowed no profits for his services in the reorganization; and that due demand had been made on the corporation to bring the action. At the trial the complaint was dismissed on the merits on the rule laid down in Old 

Dominion Copper Co. v. Lewisohn, 210 U. S. 206, supra,

Cady's Cas. p. 128, and it was held that an allotment of 

15,000 shares by the associates in the scheme, where the whole arrangement was subject to scrutiny and avoidance at the time of the reorganization, was binding on the later

STOCKHOLDERS ACTIONS 

361 

stockholders. Cont. Sec. Co. v. Belmont, 168 App. Div. 483, 

154 N. Y. Supp. 54, affd. 222 N. Y. 673. A complaint was held good which alleged that plaintiff was suing on behalf of himself and other stockholders similarly situated who should come in, etc., to recover from a promoter for the corporation, which had refused to sue, damages for his failure to sell at par 500 shares of the stock, for which services and for his services in the promotion the board of directors had given him 1130 shares. Cummings v. Yates &c. 

Trad. Co., 122 App. Div. 505, 107 N. Y. Supp. 498.

Consolidation agreements may be attacked by stockholders in this form of action, if the change in capitalization or distribution is unfair to them. Colby v. Equit. Tr. Co., 124 App. Div. 262, 108 N. Y. Supp. 978. If the corporate property has been dissipated in violation of the theory that the capital stock of a stock corporation is a trust fund for the payment of creditors, the creditors, having first become judgment creditors of the corporation, may set aside the fraudulent conveyance and recover back the property for the satisfaction of their debts. The action in that case is the representative action, and not the derivative action; for if the latter were the remedy, the creditor would be bound by the fact that both parties to the transaction were in pari delicto. Hubbard v. United Wireless Tel. Co., 62 Misc. 538, 115 N. Y. Supp. 1016. The derivative action is properly brought to recover back for the corporation capital wrongly distributed in the form of dividends, or for excessive salaries paid to the defendant directors or officers, Godley v. Crandall & G. Co., 212 N. Y. 121, 105 N. E. 818; or, to compel a director to turn over to the corporation a lease secretly renewed in his own name instead of in the corporate name, since, if he could get the lease for himself, it is likely that he might have secured the renewal for the corporation. Thayer v. Leggett, 229 N. Y. 152, 128 N. E. 

133. See Stem v. Warren & W., 227 N. Y. 538, 125 N. E. 

811. Klaw v. Erlanger, 123 Misc. 332, 205 N. Y. Supp. 225, affd. 215 App. Div. 702. The action will lie to set aside a fraudulent bankruptcy, or other misapplication, misappropriation, or diversion of assets by a director to acquire for himself the assets. Drucklieb v. Harris, 158 App. Div. 

873, 142 N. Y. Supp. 912. Wangrow v. Wangrow, 211 App.

Div. 552, 207 N. Y. Supp. 132. Liability of the directors to the corporation for non-feasance and breach of duty may be remedied by a derivative action, tho the only remedy available to the corporation itself would be an action at law for damages. Moran v. Vreeland, 81 Misc. 664, 143 

N. Y. Supp. 522. 

§ 215. Demand and Refusal of Corporation to Sue. 

Since the cause of action belongs solely to the corporation, the complaint may be dismissed unless it alleges either a demand and refusal of the corporation to sue, or facts sufficient to show that the demand would be an idle ceremony, for the reason that the wrongdoers, or those confederated with them, compose the majority in control, and sit in the directors' seats. Flynn v. Bkln. City R. Co., 158 N. Y. 493, 53 N. E. 520; Godley v. Crandall & G. Co., supra; Dillon v. 

Pan. Am. Theat. Co., supra; Kavanaugh v. Com. Tr. Co., supra, Cady's Cas. p. 455; Hawes v. Oakland, supra; Bissell v. Taylor, 229 App. Div. 369, 241 N. Y. Supp. 717; Simon v. 

David, 241 N. Y. Supp. 188. 

Express refusal may be proved by resolutions, minutes, or admissions of agents within the scope of their agency. 

An unreasonable delay by the corporation after the request is an implied refusal, the question of what is an unreasonable time being a question of fact for the court, to be established to the courts satisfaction by proof of circumstances showing the importance of the decision, the amount of preliminary work or investigation necessary to be done before bringing the action, and the amount of time available to the officers for this purpose, and such other circumstances as may be relevant. Planten v. Nassau &c 

Bank, 174 App. Div. 254, 160 N. Y. Supp. 297, affd. 220 

N. Y. 677; Kavanaugh case, supra; Dillon case, supra; Security Tr. Co. v. Pritchard, 201 App. Div. 143, 190 N. Y. 

Supp. 871.

While the complaint must show that a demand was made on the board to bring suit, neither the complaint nor the proof need show that a demand was made on the stockholders to appeal to the board to bring suit. The bringing of the suit in equity is notice to all the stockholders, pursuant to the ancient doctrine of lis pendens. If the suit is

STOCKHOLDERS ACTIONS 

363 based on an act regarding which the stockholders had authority to act by virtue of special authority conferred on them by statute, no demand would be proper which was not addressed to the stockholders as well as to the board. Cont. 

Sec. Co. v. Belmont, supra, Cady's Cas. p. 460. The demand and refusal by those having authority to represent the corporation is sufficient. Planten v. National &c Bank, 174 App. 

Div. 254, 160 N. Y. Supp. 297, affd. 220 N. Y. 677.

The prayer for relief in the complaint should ask for direct restitution or payment to the corporation, and should not embody a scheme for distribution among the stockholders, or, much less, for direct payment of the injury suffered by plaintiff. Ebling v. Nekards, 148 App. Div. 193, 132 

N. Y. Supp. 309, affd. 210 N. Y. 566, 611. Miller v. Crown 

Perfumery Co., 125 App. Div. 881, 110 N. Y. Supp. 806.

Thus the prayer for relief will be consonant with the demand that was made on the board. § 216. Subsequent Transferee as Plaintiff—Derivative 

Action. 

Conflicting conclusions have been reached on the right of a stockholder who obtained his stock by transfer at a date subsequent to a fraudulent conveyance of the assets, or the fraudulent creation of obligations, to bring a stockholder's derivative action in behalf of the corporation. In

New York, it is held that such a transferee may bring the action, on the ground that the indivisible interest in the corporation, and in its rights, property and assets, which passes by the transfer of stock, includes the right to set aside voidable conveyances and obligations. Pollitz v. 

Gould, 202 N. Y. 11, 94 N. E. 1088. The New York rule is followed in Georgia, New Mexico, North Carolina, Iowa,

Nebraska, and several other states; but the federal courts, and those of Illinois, Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Montana, and some others, have held that the purchaser of stock takes it "as is," and that only the stockholder who owned the stock at the date of the fraudulent or oppressive transaction can assert the right to protect the value of his stock. 

The leading federal decision is Hawes v. Oakland, 104 U. S. 

450, 26 L. ed. 827, subsequent to which Federal Equity

Rule 94, now 27, infra, perpetuated the principle. The rea-

soning of the New York courts is that the outstanding wrong, suffered by the stockholder when the fraud was consummated, is inseparable from stock ownership. The right is not a personal right of election to disaffirm, and hence non-transferable because it is personal, for the power is not conferred on the stockholder by reason of his personal qualities but solely because of his character as stockholder -as one of the associates in the common enterprise. The successive stockholder therefore receives the right, with the stock, to protect the value of the stock. The transferee takes the stock, however, subject to all equities against it created by the acts of its prior owners. Thus where the prior owner had consented to the issuance of stock for nearly 100 times the value of the property received by the corporation, the stockholder who succeeded to his stockholdings was held bound, and his complaint in a stockholders' derivative action was dismissed. In re Seneca Oil Co., 153 App. Div. 594, 138 N. Y. Supp. 78, affd. 208 N. Y. 545. 

Federal equity rule 27 is as follows: "Every bill brought by one or more stockholders in a corporation against the corporation and other parties, founded on rights which may properly be asserted by the corporation, must be verified by oath, and must contain an allegation that the plaintiff was a shareholder at the time of the transaction of which he complains, or that his share had devolved on him since by operation of law, and that the suit is not a collusive one to confer on a court of the United States jurisdiction of a case of which it would not otherwise have cognizance. It must also set forth with particularity the efforts of the plaintiff to secure such action as he desires on the part of the managing directors or trustees, and if necessary, of the shareholders, and the causes of his failure to obtain such action or the reason for not making such effort." 

§ 217. Right of Non-consenting Stockholder to Appraisal. 

The non-consenting stockholder is empowered to require the corporation to buy his stock in the following instances:-1. The voluntary sale of franchises, or of property of the corporation, with or without the good will, and with or without negative covenants, S. C. L. 21; 2. Consolidation, S. C. L. 27; 3. The issuance of increased stock to employes, S. C. L. 14; 4. Dissolution without judicial proceedings, if the assets are to be sold to another domes-

STOCKHOLDERS ACTIONS 

365 tic corporation in exchange for its stock or bonds or both, S. C. L. 105 (9). The statutes relating to appraisals are remedial, and, therefore, are strictly construed in favor of the stockholder. In re Rowe, 107 Misc. 549, 176 N. Y. Supp. 

753. Consequently, he will be entitled to an appraisal altho his stock was not registered in his name at the time of the meeting. Ib. In a case that arose before the statute was enacted, it was shown that all the stockholders, excepting the plaintiff, had transferred their shares for stock in a new company. The plaintiff was held entitled to recover his share of the profits by means of an action in equity for an accounting, brought against the old company. Logan v. 

N. Y. Sug. Ref. Co., 176 App. Div. 660, 163 N. Y. Supp. 214, reargument denied, 177 App. Div. 926. There is no provision of law entitling the non-consenting stockholder to an appraisal, upon the corporation executing a mortgage, either on real estate or on chattels. The tendency of the decisions is to apply the remedy of appraisals to both sales and exchanges, so that, where the majority has put through an exchange of the assets of a corporation in a manner oppressive to the stockholder, he may obtain an order requiring the return of the assets by the purchasing corporation in order that he may be paid his aliquot part in the assets of the old corporation. Murrin v. Archbald Consol. Coal Co., 232 N. Y. 541, Cady's Cas. p. 183. In the case last cited, the exchange had been made in a way grossly oppressive of the plaintiff, for the purpose of maneuvering him out of his position as pledgee of the majority of the common stock of A corporation, into the position of pledgee of the minority stock of B corporation, organized with that end in view. Plaintiff sold an interest which he had in the coal mine to A corporation for certain cash and the promissory notes of N, and, as collateral security for the payment of the notes, N pledged with plaintiff more than two-thirds the stock of A corporation. N, as pledgor, still had power to vote the pledged stock, (S. C. L. 47), and, becoming insolvent, consented to the exchange of the property and stock of A corporation for the common stock of B corporation, which also had preferred voting stock at $1 par, equal in number to its shares of common stock. Plaintiff was given only 7 days' notice of the exchange, and was therefore

placed in a position, if the sale went through, where he would either have to invest in the preferred stock of B corporation, or else hold as pledgee, as security for the notes of N, a minority interest in B. It was held that plaintiff was entitled to an appraisal of the stock of A corporation, and to an injunction requiring the assets to be returned to 

A corporation for that purpose.

In order to appraise the value of the good will, the average annual net profits are to be multiplied by a proper number of years, dependent on the nature and character of the business. Von Au v. Magenheimer, 115 App. Div. 84, 100

N. Y. Supp. 659. The appraisers, appointed by the court to appraise the minority stock of two taxicab companies, which had voted to consolidate, divided the total net earnings by 212, the approximate number of months that the business had been running, multiplied the quotient by 12, to ascertain the average annual net profits, and multiplied the product thus obtained by 3 years. It was held that they had erred, and that they should have deducted from the average annual net profits, before they multiplied by 3 years, the interest for one year at 6% on the capital possessed by the corporation at the date when the stockholder objected. In the aforesaid capital on which interest was to be reckoned, there should not be included, of course, any allowance for good will, since the computation of the value of the good will is the problem in hand, A proper allowance should be made for depreciation and obsolescence. Seaich v. 

Mason-Seaman Transpt. Co., 170 App. Div. 686, 156 

N. Y. Supp. 579.

Though the statute does not expressly require a final order confirming the appraiser's report, it is construed to require such an order. Sec. 63, supra.

CHAPTER XVI. 

Sec. 218. 219. 

Capacity of a corporation to commit torts and crimes. 

Malicious crimes and torts. 

220. Ultra vires torts. Malfeasance, misfeasance, nonfeasance. 

221. Torts of charitable corporations. 

222. Liability of corporation for crimes and penalties. 

223. Personal liability of officers and agents for crimes and penalties. 

§ 218. Capacity of a Corporation to Commit Torts and 

Crimes. 

It is now completely established that a private corporation, tho it is but an ideal existence without soul, mind, hands, or body, may commit torts and most varieties of crimes, and consequently expose itself to actions ex delicto, and to the penalties of the criminal laws. Unsound reasoning would reject the idea that torts or crimes could be brought within the objects and purposes of the charter, which defines and limits the scope of corporate activities. 

G. C. L. 13. The fallacy consists in the assumption that the commission of torts and crimes must have been one of the objects of the corporation if it was to be held liable, and in overlooking the fact that in transacting its business a corporation may, through inadvertence, render itself guilty of a tort or crime. A corporation can not do any act, except through agents; and if the agents conduct themselves fraudulently, so that, if they were acting for private employers, the persons for whom they were acting would have been liable for their fraud, the same principles must prevail where they are acting for the corporation. "Corporations are liable for every wrong of which they are guilty." Merch. 

Bank v. State Bank, 10 Wall. 645. "A corporation...is... incapable of doing any act except through agents, to whom is given by its fundamental law, or in pursuance of it, every power of action it is capable of possessing or exercising. Hence the rule has been established, and may now be stated as an indisputable principle, that a corporation is responsible for the acts or negligence of its agents while engaged in the business of the agency, to the same extent 367

and under the same circumstances that a natural person is chargeable with the acts or negligence of his agent." 

N. Y. &c R. R. Co., v. Schuyler, supra, Cady's Cas. p. 473. 

A railroad which built its line adjoining plaintiff's house, pursuant to plans approved by the state, and wholly intra vires, was held guilty of maintaining a nuisance when smoke, cinders and soot from its engines made life unbearable in the house. The state's grant of a charter does not give immunity. Cogswell v. N. Y. &c Ry., 103 N. Y. 10.

Liability for a tort committed by a corporation before dissolution, survives such dissolution. Shayne v. Evening 

Post Pub. Co., 168 N. Y. 70; Marstaller v. Mills, 143 N. Y. 

398; Cunningham v. Glauber, 133 App. Div. 10, 117 N. Y.

Supp. 866. The earlier rule was that it did not. In re 

Yuengling Brewery Co., 24 App. Div. 223, 49 N. Y. Supp. 

12. If the corporation adopts the benefits it is usually liable for the tort. Tomson v. Sixpenny Sav. Bank, 18 N. Y. 

Sup. (5 Bosw.) 293. 

§ 219. For Malicious Torts and Crimes. 

Decisions holding that principals are not responsible for the wilful and malicious acts of agents, and that officers and agents of a corporation have no de facto powers outside the real powers of their office, have also been invoked to shield the corporation. The fallacy consists in disregarding the fact that the agents of the corporation compose its thinking and acting capacity. Thus, in fraud, the scienter of the agent is the scienter of the corporation, and the reports of the directors, tho based on representations made to the corporation, are representations made by the corporation fraudulently. Borschneider v. Knickerbocker Lf. Ins. Co., 76 N. Y. 216. The inaffluent typesetters are not the only ones to be liable if the corporation prints a libel in the course of its business, even if they act partly outside the scope of their employment. Kharas v. Collier, Inc., 171 

App. Div. 388, 157 N. Y. Supp. 410, Cady's Cas. p. 300.

In like fashion, the corporation has been held liable for slander, O'Brien v. Bates Corp., 211 App. Div. 743, 208 

N. Y. Supp. 110; (malicious prosecution) Morton v. Metropolitan Lf. Ins. Co., 34 Hun 366, affd. 103 N. Y. 645; 

Manasha v. Royal Ben. Soc., 20 Misc. 732, 46 N. Y. Supp.

1096, affd. 21 Misc. 474, 47 N. Y. Supp. 628; (false arrest) 

Schwartzing v. Van Wie N. Y. Groc. Co., 69 App. Div. 282, 74 N. Y. Supp. 747; (conspiracy) Buff. Lub. Oil Co. v. 

Standard Oil Co., 106 N. Y. 669.

Punitive damages are never given for compensation, but only for punishment of one who has participated in the offense, with wanton, oppressive or malicious intent. Consequently, they are never awarded as against a corporation unless the wrong is attributable to it and is not the mere delictum of its agents. Prior authorization or subsequent ratification of the tort, or the negligent employment or retention of improper agents or servants, must be proved in order to entitle the plaintiff to punitive damages. Caldwell v. N. J. Steamboat Co., 47 N. Y. 282; Cleghorn v. N. Y. C. & H. R. R. R. Co., 56 N. Y. 44; Macauley v. Starr, Inc., 194 

App. Div. 643, 186 N. Y. Supp. 197, affd. 233 N. Y. 601; 

Lake Shore Ry. Co. v. Prentice, 147 U. S. 101. 

§ 220. Ultra Vires Torts. Malfeasance, Misfeasance, Nonfeasance.

If an agent acts from a personal motive, and not in furtherance of his employment, the corporation is not liable for his ultra vires torts. Thus, where the plaintiff, a trespasser riding on the narrow platform on the front of the "blind baggage" car, next to the tender, was injured, while the train was in motion, by being struck by a lump of coal thrown at him by the fireman, the railroad corporation was not held liable. Polatty v. Charlestown & W. C. Ry., 45 

S. E. 492 S. C., 100 Am. St. Rep. 750. 5 Fletch. Enc. Corps. p. 5221 (85).

A corporation which commits a tort while engaged in an ultra vires transaction is liable to the one damaged, for it must be liable for the results of that which it has authorized. Bissell v. Mich. So. R. Co., 22 N. Y. 258, Cady's Cas. p. 289. Buffet v. Troy & B. Ry., 40 N. Y. 168. A tort ratified by the corporation is a corporate tort and the corporation is liable in damages. Nims v. Mt. Hermon School, 160 

Mass. 177, Cady's Cas. p. 163. Tortious acts committed in violation of instructions, but while engaged about the corporation's business within the scope of employment, bind the corporation. Palmeri v. Manh. R. Co., 133 N. Y. 261;

Kastner v. L. I. Ry. Co., 76 App. Div. 323, 78 N. Y. Supp. 

469. Torts committed by the agent or servant outside the scope of his authority or employment do not bind the corporation. Knox v. Eden Musee Amer. Co., 148 N. Y. 441; 

Man. Lf. Ins. Co. v. 42nd and Grand St. Ferry Co., 139 

N. Y. 146. 

Where officers who had no authority to employ, nevertheless employed a third person to do that which the corporation had no authority to do, it was held that the corporation was not liable to a person injured by the third person's negligence. Bathe v. Decatur Co. Agric. Soc., 34 

N. W. 484 (Iowa). 

Malfeasance is the doing of what one ought not to dothe commission of some act that is positively unlawful. Misfeasance is the improper doing of an act which a person might lawfully do the improper performance of a lawful act. Nonfeasance is the total omission to do an act which one promises to do. Burns v. Pethcal, 75 Hun 437, 27 N. Y. 

Supp. 499 at p. 503. A corporation is liable for its agents or servants torts of malfeasance or misfeasance, but not usually for their nonfeasance. The agent or servant is liable to the person injured by his malfeasance or misfeasance, and his principal is also liable. The agent or servant is not liable for nonfeasance, and the principal is not liable to the person injured, in the absence of a duty. 

5 Fletch. p. 3016. A municipal corporation was held liable for malfeasance committed by erecting, under statutory authority, a dam on the Croton River of insufficient strength to stand up against the freshets, altho a municipal corporation is not usually liable for the acts of its agents or servants unless it negligently selects improper ones. City of 

N. Y. v. Bailey, 2 Den. 433. Mechem on Agency, secs. 539575. The fact that it is illegal, and therefore malfeasance, for a private corporation to practice dentistry, will not relieve a department store corporation from liability for the negligence of dentists employed in rendering professional services to customers. Hannon v. Siegel-Cooper Co., 167 

N. Y. 244. A railroad, engaged in the carrying of passengers, and thus fixed with the duty to protect them, was held liable in compensatory damages to a passenger whom

the conductor arrested for purchasing another passenger's ticket. Lake Shore R. R. v. Prentice, 147 U. S. 101. 

§ 221. Torts of Charitable Corporations. 

Corporations formed for the purpose of public charity, and maintained by donations, are generally held exempt from liability for the tortious acts of their agents or servants. In many jurisdictions the ground of exemption is that the application of the funds donated to the charitable trust is limited to the specific charity, and that the fund therefore cannot be applied to compensate for injuries ex delicto, and thus frustrate the charitable purpose of the donor. Thus in Feoffees of Heriot's Hospital v. Ross, H. of 

L. 1846, 12 Cl. & F. 507, it was said, “Damages are to be paid from the pocket of the wrongdoer, not from a trust fund." One accepting the benefits of a charity at the time the injury was sustained can not deplete the trust fund. "The rights of those who are beneficiaries of the trust are limited by the will of the founder." This is known as the "trust fund theory." The federal and Massachusetts courts favor this rule.

Other states base the exemption on public policy in that the state is the one most interested in the maintenance of charitable corporations, which perform a public purpose without expense to the state, and that their funds, therefore, should not be dissipated for the recompense of private injuries. The reasoning is similar to that whereby a public officer is exempted from liability for acts performed in executing a statute. "If the thing done is within the statute, it is clear that no compensation can be afforded for any damages sustained hereby, except so far as the statute itself has provided it, and this is clear on the legal presumption that the act creating the damages, being within the statute, must be a lawful act." Duncan v. Findlater, 6 Cl. & F. 907 (1839). Others, notably New York, put the exemption of the corporation on the ground of implied assumption of risk by the patient or other beneficiary of the charity. 

Hamburger v. Cornell Univ., 240 N. Y. 328, Cady's Cas. p. 

307; Hondern v. Sal. Army, 199 N. Y. 233. In Schloendorf v. Soc. of New York Hospital, 211 N. Y. 125, Cardozo, J., said: "This exemption has been placed on two

grounds: first is that of implied waiver...the second is the relation existing between the hospital and the physician... which is not that of master and servant...but that the physician occupies the position so to speak, of an independent contractor...liable of course for his own wrongs to the patient...but involving the hospital in no liability if due care has been taken in his selection.” For a case where recovery was sustained see Gollob v. Congregation Ohel &c, 119 Misc. 346, 196 N. Y. Supp. 516. 

§ 222. Liability of Corporation for Crimes and Penalties. 

For reasons similar to those which were once held to exempt a corporation from liability for torts, it was "long the rule that corporations could not be indicted for a misdemeanor. ... The reason that no indictment could formerly be found against the corporation for a crime seems to have been founded... entirely upon the fact that, as a defendant could not then appear by attorney or agent the indicted corporation could not be brought into court". Rex v. Medley, 6 Car. P. 2992, quoted in Peo. v. Clark, 8 N. Y. Cr. 169, 14

N. Y. Supp. at p. 647. Today the corporation may be indicted and sentenced for all crimes except those which it is physically impossible for it to commit, such as crimes of personal violence, offenses against the person, and manslaughter. Peo. v. Roch. Ry. &c Co., 195 N. Y. 102, Cady's

Cas. p. 318. The corporation may be criminally liable for nonfeasance. It may be liable for malfeasance, for instance, for illegally advertising to practice medicine, Peo. v. Woodbury Dermatological Inst., 192 N. Y. 454. And it may be liable for misfeasance, for instance, for publishing a libel, Peo. v. Star Co., 135 App. Div. 517, 120 N. Y. Supp. 

498, or for maintaining a nuisance by erecting a building on the public highway and leaving it there. State v. Morris & E. R. Co., 23 N. J. Law 360.

The objection that a corporation has no mind and therefore is incapable of criminal intent is tenable in the case of crimes that require a real mind, such as perjury, treason, drunkenness, and drug addiction. The intent must, however, be the intent of the corporation, and not merely that of the agent; and, hence, the corporation is not liable for larceny, unless the acts constituting larceny were authorized

through action of its officers or were done with the acquiescence of its officers. Peo. v. Canadian Fur Trappers 

Corp., 248 N. Y. 159, 161 N. E. 455. Where the act is authorized, the intent of the agent is imputed to the corporation. N. Y. C. &c Ry. v. U. S., 212 U. S. 481, Cady's Cas. p. 31; U. S. v. N. Y. Herald Co., 159 Fed. 296, Cady's Cas. p. 33. "There is no more difficulty in imputing to a corporation a specific intent in criminal proceedings than in civil" Peo. v. Star Co., supra, quoting from Telegram News 

Co. v. Commonwealth, 52 N. E. 445 (Mass.). An ultra vires crime can not be adopted by ratification so as to impute an attributable intent. Peo. v. Hudson Valley 

Constr. Co., 217 N. Y. 172. Peo. v. Dunbar Contr. Co., 165 

App. Div. 59, 151 N. Y. Supp. 164. Sec. 666 of the Penal

Law provides that a corporation is criminally liable for the unlawful use of certain titles in connection with corporate name; such as the words "bank," "loan" etc. Sec. 671 of the Penal Law prohibits political contributions by corporations. Sec. 663 of the Penal Law subjects a corporation to criminal liability for acting in certain instances for a foreign corporation not authorized to do business in this state, and Sec. 663-a, subjects certain foreign corporations doing business in this state without authority to criminal liability. 

Secs. 390-394 of the Penal Law define and prohibit "bucket shops". Bergstrom v. Ridgway Co., 138 App. Div. 178, 123 

N. Y. Supp. 29. Sec. 1932 of the Penal Law provides that a corporation convicted of a felony for which a like act by a natural person would subject such person to imprisonment, will subject the corporation to a fine of not more than $5000. 

If a penalty prescribed by statute provides for imprisonment and fine, the inability to punish by imprisonment, does not prevent criminal prosecution. Overland Cotton Mill Co. v. Peo., 105 Am. St. Rep. 74 (Colo.). As to process of the court in a criminal prosecution against a corporation, see, Peo. v. Eq. Gas-Light Co., 6 N. Y. Cr. 189, 5 N. Y. Supp. 

19; Peo. v. Perfecto Chem. Co., 123 Misc. 443, 206 N. Y. 

Supp. 15.

§ 223. Personal Liability of Officers and Agents for Torts and Crimes.

One is personally liable for all torts of misfeasance committed by him, notwithstanding that he may have been acting as the agent or under the direction of another. This is true to the full extent as to torts committed by officers or agents of a corporation in the management of its affairs. 

The fact that the circumstances are such as to render the corporation liable is altogether immaterial. 

The person injured may hold either liable, and generally he may hold both as joint tort-feasors. Corporate officers are liable for their torts although committed officially. Chenango Bridge 

Co. v. Paige, 83 N. Y. 178; Morgan v. Skiddy, 62 N. Y. 319.

Officers are liable both for torts committed by them without the scope of the business, Roth v. Robertson, 64 Misc. 

343, 118 N. Y. Supp. 351; Seventeenth Ward Bank v. Smith, 51 App. Div. 259, 64 N. Y. Supp. 888; and for torts committed apparently wtihin the scope of the business, Mason v. Henry, 152 N. Y. 529; Bloom v. Nat'l. United Ben. Sav. & Loan Co., 152 N. Y. 114; Brinkerhoff v. Bostwick, 88

N. Y. 52. It has been held that a shareholder cannot sue the president personally for refusal to countersign a certificate of stock, on the theory that the refusal is an act of nonfeasance rather than misfeasance; but it seems there is no good authority for this holding. Cooley v. Curran, 54 Misc. 

572, 104 N. Y. Supp. 751. To hold an officer of a corporation liable in tort where the corporation is the wrong-doer and the officer sought to be held is not the main wrong-doer or did not participate therein, some knowledge and participation, whether actual or implied, must be brought home to him, in order to succeed. Fanning v. Osborne, 102 N. Y. 

441; Arthur v. Griswold, 52 N. Y. 409; Peo. v. Brainard, 192 App. Div. 816, Cady's Cas. p. 315. See also, Von Lengerke v. New York, 150 App. Div. 98, 134 N. Y. Supp. 832.

So an officer or agent of a corporation is liable for conversion of property belonging to a third party notwithstanding that in disposing of it or otherwise dealing with it he was acting for the corporation and under orders of a superior. Spraight v. Hawley, 39 N. Y. 441; Passaic Falls 

Throwing Co. v. Villeneuve-Pohl Corp., 169 App. Div. 727,

155 N. Y. Supp. 669; McCrea v. McClenahan, 131 App. Div. 

247, 115 N. Y. Supp. 720. A corporate officer is personally liable for fraud or deceit to the person injured thereby. 

O'Beirne v. Bullis, 158 N. Y. 466; Rives v. Bartlett, 156 

App. Div. 552, 141 N. Y. Supp. 561. So, depositors, induced to make deposits in a bank by fraudulent representations of officers, may hold them personally liable for damages suffered through the subsequent insolvency of the bank. Warner v. James, 88 App. Div. 567, 85 N. Y. Supp. 153. One director will not be liable for the fraud of others acting as an executive committee. Garrett Co. v. McComb, 58 App. 

Div. 419, 68 N. Y. Supp. 996; Ottman v. Blangas Co. of 

Cuba, 171 App. Div. 197, 157 N. Y. Supp. 413. See also: (libel) Keller v. American Bottlers' Pub. Co., 140 App. 

Div. 311, 125 N. Y. Supp. 212; (malicious prosecution) 

Murphy v. Eidlitz, 113 App. Div. 659, 99 N. Y. Supp. 950.

As respects negligence, corporate officers are not held liable for nonfeasance, Van Antwerp v. Linton, 89 Hun 417. 

Negligence in performing duties is misfeasance and not nonfeasance. An officer who refuses or neglects to make any report lawfully required is criminally liable. Penal Law, sec. 665, subd. 6. An officer or agent of a stock corporation who wilfully neglects or refuses to make any proper entry in a corporate book, or neglects or refuses to exhibit any such stock book to a person entitled to inspect it is liable to the person injured thereby. Sec. 10 S. C. L.; Peo. v. 

Consol. Natl. Bank, 105 App. Div. 409, 94 N. Y. Supp. 173; 

Peo. v. American Press Ass'n., 148 App. Div. 651, 133 

N. Y. Supp. 216.

CHAPTER XVII. 

Sec. 224.

CREDITORS 

Remedies of creditors against the corporation. 

225. Creditors' rights against stockholders. 

226. Creditors' rights against directors. 

227. Creditors' rights to interfere with the management. 

228. Classes of creditors and their rights. 

229. Marshalling. Offsets. 

§ 224. Remedies of Creditors Against the Corporation. 

1. A general creditor has no lien on corporate assets, and must first sue at law, obtain a judgment, and issue execution. In a proper case, he may have the auxiliary remedy of attachment. The franchise cannot be levied upon. Evan. Luth. &c House v. Buffalo Hyd. Assoc., 64

N. Y. 561. The property held by a public or quasi public corporation in trust for public uses can not be successfully levied upon. Leonard v. Reynolds, 71 N. Y. 498 (fire bell tower); Brinkerhoff v. Board of Education, 4 Abb. Pr. N. 

S. 428 (schoolhouse); Clarissy v. Met. Fire Dept., 7 Abb. 

Pr. N. S. 352 (fire house). 

2. The creditor may bring an action under the "trust fund theory" to enforce his rights, and those of creditors similarly situated, to the capital stock. If the corporation distributes its property to stockholders or to others who are not bona fide purchasers without notice, or if the corporation is dissolved, or becomes so disorganized that it cannot be made answerable to an action at law, a court of equity, acting either under equitable principles or under a statute adapted to enforce the rights of creditors, will lay hold of its effects and property, and apply them to the payment of creditors. S. C. L. 15. G. C. L. 70-75. The trust fund theory applies only when the distribution is made to stockholders or officers at a time when the corporation is insolvent, or when a transfer is made for the purpose of defrauding creditors. Wood v. Dummer, 3 

Mason 308; Bartlett v. Drew, 57 N. Y. 587; Cole v. Millerton Iron Co., 133 N. Y. 164; Hurd v. N. Y. &c. Steam Laundry Co., 167 N. Y. 89. See p. 260, supra. Statutory reme- 376

CREDITORS 

377 dies, unless expressly stated to be exclusive, do not deprive courts of equity jurisdiction from enforcing liability. The remedy is based upon two equitable doctrines, to wit, (1) following trust funds, and (2) holding directors acts to be those of quasi trustees or of trustees ex maleficio. Wood v. 

Dummer, 3 Mason 308. Three principal arguments advanced to support the proposition that the capital stock is a trust fund for creditors are: 1. The capital stock, as distinguished from the share stock, belongs to the corporation, apart from its members, and can, therefore, be disposed of only for corporate purposes. 2. The franchise substitutes capital stock for the personal liability of the stockholders. 

3. It has always been supposed that the requirement of capital stock was inserted in the charter for the protection of creditors. Ib.

The decision in Wood v. Dummer, supra, has been frequently limited in its scope. In Hospes v. N. W. Mfg. & Car 

Co., 50 N. W. 1117 (Minn.), 15 L. R. A. 470, it was held that, since the theory exists only for the benefit of creditors, the stockholders may divide up the assets without becoming liable to creditors whose debts were incurred subsequent to the division. There is no trust when there are no creditors. 

The decision pointed out that a trust implies two estatesthat of the trustee and the cestui que trust-which do not exist in any proper sense as between a corporation and its creditors, absolute control and power of disposition being inconsistent with the idea of a trust. See p. 260, supra.

In Sanger v. Upton, 91 U. S. 56, the court pointed out that a creditor could not follow the capital stock into the hands of a bona fide purchaser, for the latter's rights are superior, prima facie, to those of the creditor. The burden of proof, it was said, is on the purchaser to show that he bought in good faith. The inference arising from the recital of a nominal consideration in a conveyance of land by an insolvent corporation to a stockholder is that the conveyance was intended to hinder and delay creditors, lack of consideration being one of the "badges of fraud." Helms v. 

Green, 11 S. E. 470 (N. Car.); St. John Wood-Working Co. v. Smith, 178 N. Y. 629, 71 N. E. 1139. In Hollins v. Briarfield Coal & Iron Co., 150 U. S. 371, the court asserted that

the complete trust fund doctrine, announced in Wood v. 

Dummer, supra, was that transfers to stockholders and officers, for less than a fair consideration, could be avoided by a creditors suit, provided the transfers rendered the corporation insolvent, or were made when it was insolvent. 

The court further held that the plaintiff creditor in the representative suit must allege and prove that the property was that of the corporation; that he was a creditor; that it was transferred when the corporation was insolvent; and that the transfer was for the purpose of defeating plaintiff's claim. These decisions have been incorporated into the bankruptcy law and into the various state statutes. 

Bankruptcy Act § 60, b and c. S. C. L. 15, G. C. L. 60. Under the latter statute, the creditor must be a judgment creditor. 

Belknap v. N. A. Lf. Ins. Co., 11 Hun 282. Miller v. Barlow, 178 App. Div. 331, 164 N. Y. Supp. 210. Dissolution of the corporation, and the appointment of a receiver of its property, render it unnecessary for plaintiff to reduce his claim to judgment before bringing a creditors representative action. Lilienthal v. Betz, 108 App. Div. 222, 95 N. Y. 

Supp. 849.

A judgment creditor's third remedy is an action for sequestration. G. C. L. 70. The return of his execution, unsatisfied, establishes the insolvency of the corporation. 

Taylor v. Ellsworth Bldg. Corp., 183 N. Y. Supp. 394, affd. 198 App. Div. 1022. The truth of the sheriff's return cannot be inquired into collaterally, and no execution against real property need be issued as a prerequisite to bringing the action for sequestration. 11th Ward Bk. v. 

Heather, 22 Misc. 87, 48 N. Y. Supp. 449. There need be no preliminary examination in supplementary proceedings. 

G. C. L. 70. The property sought to be sequestered must be in New York state. Heyl v. Taylor, 137 App. Div. 641, 122 N. Y. Supp. 279. 

4. In a proper case, the creditor, on notice to the attorney-general, may bring an action to dissolve the corporation. In this proceeding, a receiver may be appointed, the property distributed, and the liability of stockholders, directors and officers enforced. G. C. L. 71-81. Cf. Investing 

Co. v. Gerkin, 200 App. Div. 503, 193 N. Y. Supp. 271. See

CREDITORS 

379 also, Dreyfus v. Seale & Co., 37 App. Div. 351, 55 N. Y.

Supp. 1111. 

§ 225. Creditors' Rights against Stockholders. 

Creditors representative actions, to collect the unpaid subscriptions of stockholders, may be brought by one or more creditors. Christensen v. Eno, 106 N. Y. 97, Cady's

Cas. p. 348. Creditors' rights are usually superior to those of stockholders, so that the latter, desiring to protect the corporation against the results of ultra vires acts, must forestall creditors. Sec. 98 (2), supra. Transferees, as well as original subscribers to par value stock, issued by domestic corporations, are liable by statute to creditors (S. C. L. 

69-73) to pay for stock issued as fully paid, if, in fact, the consideration for its issuance was inadequate. Sec. 129, p. 191, supra. If the said stock was issued by a corporation in a state not shown to have a statute similar to S. C. L. 69-73, the liability of the original subscriber is fixed by his contract with the corporation (p. 190, supra), and the creditor, under the trust fund theory, can only enforce whatever rights the corporation has. Against transferees of partly paid stock of corporations chartered in common law jurisdictions, creditors' rights rest, by the weight of authority, on the question of notice (p. 199 [2], supra.).

One who takes treasury stock from the corporation is under an implied obligation to pay for it at par (sec. 131, supra; 

Furlong v. Johnson, 239 N. Y. 141, Cady's Cas. p. 350).

A judgment creditor of the corporation may follow illegal dividends into the hands of the stockholders (p. 250, S. C. L. 

15). Stock, issued without consideration, may become fully paid by crediting proper dividends thereto, so as to release the stockholders from claims of creditors. All that is required by the statute is that the property that has, or that ought to be, put into the business pursuant to S. C. L. 69, 12, should be put in, and kept in. "A division of profits without declaring a dividend is the equivalent of declaring a dividend." Hartley v. Pioneer Iron Works, 181 N. Y. 73.

Consequently, where stockholders distribute assets under the guise of salaries, any part so distributed after the corporation becomes financially embarrassed or in danger of so becoming, may render the stockholder receiving it, and

directors whose dissent is not entered on the minutes, liable to creditors. S. C. L. 56. Caeser v. Bernard, 156 

App. Div. 724, 141 N. Y. Supp. 659, affd. 209 N. Y. 570.

Reasonable salaries may be paid to either stockholders or directors while the capital is impaired, and even excessive salaries if voted and paid in good faith. Shaw v. Ansaldi, 178 App. Div. 589, 165 N. Y. Supp. 872. The usual form of remedy to enforce the liability of stockholders of a private stock corporation on their stock, is a representative suit brought against all the stockholders, in behalf of all creditors who may come in and join in the complaint in the action. Bottlers Seal Co. v. Rainey, 243 N. Y. 333, 153 

N. E. 437; Natl. Bank of Auburn v. Dillingham, 147 N. Y. 

603; Moore v. Murchison, 226 Fed. 679. S. C. L. 73. See p. 188 (4), supra. The creditor who has advanced money to a stockholder on fictitious stock as collateral, may be able to hold the corporation if the corporation is estopped (secs. 

141, 142, supra).

The stockholder may be a creditor; but he may not offset debts owing to him from the corporation against his unpaid subscription for stock (sec. 151, supra). When he is a creditor, he has the rights possessed by any creditor to follow capital, erroneously distributed as dividends, or paid to the wrong person (sec. 164, supra).

If the corporate body by formal act releases stockholders from their obligation to pay for their stock, the release is ineffectual as against prior creditors (p. 192, supra, citing 

Randall v. Havemeyer, 49 N. Y. Supp. 520), but forefends against subsequent creditors (pp. 198, 210, supra; Richardson v. Green, 133 U. S. 30). If the subscriber was released by material amendment to the charter, he is not liable to creditors (p. 193); but if released by reduction of stock by amendment of charter, he remains liable to the whole extent of his original subscription to creditors whose debts were contracted antecedent to the amendment. Myers v. Sturges, 123 App. Div. 470, 108 N. Y. Supp. 528, affd. 197 N. Y. 

526. No rights, superior to those of the trustee and bondholders, arise to creditors by reason of the sale of collateral mortgage bonds for less than par (p. 202, supra). If the mortgage purports to cover after acquired property, a sub-

CREDITORS 

381 sequent creditor may have greater rights than the trustee or bondholders under certain conditions (p. 203, supra).

If a subscriber's stock was forfeited in good faith by the corporation, the delinquent stockholder is not liable to creditors, whether their claims arose before or after the forfeiture (p. 210, supra). Creditors may set aside the act of forfeiture if not done in good faith. The entry of the subscriber's name in the stockbook kept by the corporation, if idem sonans, is prima facie evidence of his stock ownership, and the burden of proof is on the stockholder of proving a valid transfer of the stock (p. 215). Transfer to irresponsible persons after the corporation has become in fact insolvent, or in contemplation of its insolvency, is prohibited. (sec. 138, supra). Judgment creditors may inspect the stock book (p. 229, supra; S. C. L. 113) and thus ascertain the names and addresses of stockholders and their respective holdings. 

§ 226. Creditors' Rights against Directors. 

Creditors gain no rights against directors by reason of the distribution in good faith by them of shares representing property accumulated by the corporation in excess of its capital stock. Equit. Life Assn. v. Union Pac. R. R. Co., 212 N. Y. 360, 373. Judgment creditors are limited by 

S. C. L. 58 to a`recovery against the directors of the "full amount of the loss sustained." For instance, if the dividend declared in good faith was $10,000, and the capital stock was thereby impaired by $5,000, the limit of recovery by the creditors against the directors would be $5,000. Shaw v. 

Alsaldi, 178 App. Div. 589, 165 N. Y. Supp. 872. Consequently, the fact that stock was paid for by dividends declared out of surplus does not render the director liable to creditors. Cullen v. Friedland, 152 App. Div. 124, 126 

N. Y. Supp. 659. The fact that assets were paid out without consideration with the consent and acquiescence of the defendant directors does not tend to prove liability of the directors, where it also appears that after the payment the corporation still had sufficient assets to cover its debts. Ib. 

The payment of dividends out of capital is an "offense against our laws." Cardozo, J., in German-Amer. Coffee 

Co. v. Diehl, 216 N. Y. 57. No matter what the motive of

the directors may have been, good faith is no defense. 

Osgood v. Laytin, 37 How. Pr. 63 (Ct. App.). The dissipation of assets can not be ratified. Cont. Sec. Co. v. Belmont, supra, Cady's Cas. p. 456.

Directors are not liable to creditors for the loss of corporate property, unless the loss was occasioned by the lack of ordinary care, skill, prudence, and knowledge (pp. 296-7).

It is now the settled rule that the creditors of a corporation have at all times an equitable lien on its capital stock, as distinguished from its assets in general. Bartlett v. 

Drew, 57 N. Y. 587; Hurd v. N. Y. &c Steam Laundry Co., 167 N. Y. 89; Darcy v. Brooklyn & N. Y. Ferry Co., 196 

N. Y. 99; Trotter v. Lisman, 209 N. Y. 174, 180; Small v. 

Sullivan, supra. See Christensen v. Eno, supra. It is the duty of the directors to conserve the assets of the corporation. If the assets should shrink below the capital, any distribution to the stockholders is a violation of their trust. 

Hutchinson v. Stadler, 85 App. Div. 424, 83 N. Y. Supp. 

509; Cottrell v. Albany Card & P. Co., 142 App. Div. 148, 151, 126 N. Y. Supp. 1070. A violation of this duty will sustain a creditors' representative (but not derivative) suit in equity brought on behalf of bondholders or other creditors of the corporation to compel the directors to account for their conduct in the management of the property and assets of the corporation. Ib. $ 227. ment.

Creditors' Rights to Interfere with the Manage- Creditors have no power to interfere with the management of the corporation to prevent it from making improvident contracts, or on any other ground, except where interference becomes indispensable. In the leading case of 

Hatch v. Dana, 101 U. S. 205, 25 L. ed. 885, the court approved a rule requiring the board to issue a call where the corporation abandoned all action under its charter. In 

Pond v. Framingham R. R. Co., 130 Mass. 194, the court refused to enjoin a corporation from leasing property to a single creditor, with a view to terminating an action brought by him against it. The lease was for 999 years at a rental insufficient to pay interest on its debts. In Reagal

CREDITORS 

383 

Cleaners & Dyers v. Merlis, 274 F. 915, where the directors could not decide whether to defend a proceeding in involuntary bankruptcy brought against the corporation, a creditor was not allowed to intervene and defend. In like manner, in Hilgers v. Gosselin, 179 N. Y. Supp. 703, 190

App. Div. 346, the court said, "In no case does a cause of action for wasting the funds of a corporation lie with the creditor." Fraudulent conveyances and breaches of trust may be set aside or remedied by appropriate action by creditors. G. C. L. 60, 61, 29. Littman v. Harris, 148 App. Div. 

31, 131 N. Y. Supp. 1006. The directors are under no fiduciary liability to bondholders, prior to default. The bondholders may sue to enjoin waste or damage to the mortgaged property, but in an ordinary case, they cannot assert any rights in the way of preserving the assets over and above the bond issue. Whitmore v. Inter. Fruit & Sugar Co., 102

N. E. 659 (Mass.). Hoyt v. Dupont De Nemours Powder 

Co., 102 Atl. 666 (N. J.). Carter v. Fortney, 170 Fed. 463, affd. 202 Fed. 454. In a reorganization, it is well established that the stockholders cannot obtain through a foreclosure, or otherwise, anything of value, present or prospective, except in subordination to the rights of prior creditors. North. Pac. R. R. Co. v. Boyd, 228 U. S. 482. Chi. 

R. I. &c R. Co., 7 Wall 392. Louisville Tr. Co. v. L. &c R. 

Co., 174 U. S. 674. Kansas Cy. &c R. Co. v. Cent. Union Tr. 

Co., 271 U. S. 445.

For the effect of transferring all the property to a new corporation, see the opinion of Cardozo, J., in Giles v. 

Klauder-Weldon Dyeing Machine Co., 233 N. Y. 470; Peo. ex rel. Giles v. Same, 180 App. Div. 149, 167 N. Y. Supp. 

429; and the dissenting opinion in 198 App. Div. 564, 190 

N. Y. Supp. 726. 

§ 228. Classes of Creditors. Their Rights. 

Creditors, for most purposes, may be classified as follows: 

1. Secured; 2. Unsecured, or general; 3. Long term or short term; and 4. Creditors whose rights arise prior, and those whose rights arose subsequent, to the act which is the crux of the litigation.

Secured creditors are those who have a lien on specific property. They are entitled, in most cases, to exercise their

security without regard to the losses of other classes. For instance, the pledgee may dispose of the pledge, and thereby pay his debt, and the trustee of the trust mortgage, collateral to a bond issue, may foreclose the mortgage, tho the aforesaid respective acts may wipe out all remaining assets of the corporation and leave the other creditors wholly unpaid. McNeil v. 10th Natl. Bk., 46 N. Y. 325, Cady's Cas. p. 394; Black v. Ellis, 197 N. Y. 402, ib. p. 184. When, however, the federal court under a creditors bill has taken into its custody, for instance thru a receiver, the property of a railroad, it assumes jurisdiction of all parties affected, and of all subsequent proceedings in rem which would in any way alienate property rights, including all subsequent defaults and foreclosures, regardless of the citizenship of the parties. Wabash Ry. v. Adelbert Col., 208 U. S. 33; 

Isaacs v. Hobbs Tie & Lumber Co., 281 U. S. 703, 51 Sup.

Ct. Repr. 332. A receiver displaces the directors, and thereby the internal affairs of the corporation are interfered with by the creditor or creditors who secure his appointment. While the receivership continues, neither the directors nor a liquidating committee can begin or pursue an action. Planten v. Natl. Nassau Bk., 174 App. Div. 254, 160 N. Y. Supp. 297, affd. 220 N. Y. 677. The federal court is unable, however, to avoid the rights of one who has anticipated the other creditors by obtaining and enforcing a judgment before the action was brought in the federal courts. Levy v. Equitable Tr. Co., 271 Fed. 49. In the case last mentioned, an unsecured creditor was enabled to obtain partial satisfaction of his claim thro having sued in the state courts and levied upon assets, aggregating millions, before actual default under a mortgage had been made. 

An unsecured, or general creditor, is, as the words indicate, one whose debt is not secured by a lien on specific property. Cf., Cady on Insurance, p. 27, citing Rohrbach v. Germania Fire Ins. Co., 62 N. Y. 47. The principal recourse of the general creditor, who has exhausted his remedies at law without obtaining payment in full, is the creditors representative action discussed in sec. 224, supra. 

Without a judgment and execution returned wholly or in part unsatisfied, he can not usually obtain a receiver in

CREDITORS 

385 the federal court, even though the statute, as in New York, gives him that remedy, unless the objection is waived. 

Waiver may be spelled out from failure to interpose the objection promptly. Hollins v. Briarfield Coal & Iron Co., 150 U. S. 371; Pusey &c v. Hansen, 261 U. S. 491. Diversity of citizenship between each plaintiff creditor and the corporation is a prerequisite for federal jurisdiction. The requirement of diversity of citizenship can not be waived. 

Devost v. Twin States Gas Co., 250 Fed. 349. No member of a creditor firm can be a citizen of the state of incorporation. Bankers Trust Co. v. Tex. & Pac. Ry., 241 U. S. 295; 

U. S. Code, sec. 42; Doctor v. Harrington, 196 U. S. 579, Cady's Cas. p. 84; Smith v. Lyon, 133 U. S. 315; Amer. 

Mills Co. v. Amer. Surety Co., 260 U. S. 360. Sec. 56 of the federal Judicial Code provides, in brief, that a federal receiver, upon giving bond, and filing and entering certified copies of the bill and order appointing him in the U. S. 

District Court of each district of the circuit within 10 days, becomes vested with title to all property in litigation, including, for instance, land situate in two states. In re 

Brown, 242 Fed. 452; Karatz v. Lion Bonding &c Co., 262 

U. S. 77. 

§ 229. Marshalling. Offsets. 

If it appear that the secured creditor has a claim on two sources of recoupment, whereas the general creditor has recourse to but one of them, the secured creditor may be required to enforce his claim against the fund to which his claim is paramount, in order that both may escape without loss as far as possible. But the creditor need not submit to marshalling the funds for the benefit of a subsequent encumbrancer so as to endanger in the least the security of the prior claim. Marshalling will not be enforced if to do so will delay the paramount creditor unduly, or be otherwise injurious to his rights. The necessity of marshalling frequently arises where security for the secured claim is a pledge or mortgage, and the holders of the bonds, to which the mortgage is collateral, have two sources of paymentthe property affected by the foreclosure of the mortgage, and the other assets of the corporation, which may be reached either by execution under the deficiency judgment,

or by action at law on the bonds. Cole v. Millerton Iron 

Co., 13 N. Y. Supp. 851, affd. 133 N. Y. 164, 30 N. E. 847;

Dorr v. Shaw, 4 Johns. Ch. 17; Bowery Sav. Bank v. Nosmo 

Rty. Corp., 218 App. Div. 160, 218 N. Y. Supp. 48; Farmers 

L. & T. Co. v. Kip, 192 N. Y. 266; Evertson v. Booth, 19 

Johns. 486; Herriman v. Skillman, 33 Barb. 378.

As between long and short term creditors, the former, in equity, may not accelerate for the purpose of preventing the receiver from paying such short term credits as the following:-taxes, deficits in operating income, repairs, betterments for the purpose of eliminating hazards, and interest on paramount mortgages and liens, where it appears to be for the interest of all. Wallace v. Loomis, 97 

U. S. 146; Am. B. S. & F. Co. v. P. M. Ry. Co., 205 

Fed. 14, certiorari denied, 229 U. S. 624.

A debtor of the corporation, when sued on his debt, or when suing the corporation on his claim, may set off his debt. Otis v. Shantz, 128 N. Y. 45, 27 N. E. 955; Van 

Schaick v. Mackin, 129 App. Div. 335, 113 N. Y. Supp. 408.

But a stockholder who is sued on behalf of the corporation on his stock liability cannot offset debts owing to him from the corporation, but must satisfy his statutory obligation or his subscription agreement first, and then he may enforce his claim as a creditor with other creditors of his class. Barnes v. Arnold, 45 App. Div. 314, 61 N. Y. Supp. 

85, affd. 169 N. Y. 611. In the case last mentioned, it was held that a stockholder of an insolvent bank could not offset his deposit against his statutory liability to creditors. If the action is brought, however, by a single creditor to enforce a several obligation, it has been held, apparently without a satisfactory reason, that the stockholder may offset a debt owing to him by the corporation. In re Empire Cy. 

Bank, 18 N. Y. 199; Garrison v. Howe, 17 N. Y. 458; Mathez v. Neidig, 72 N. Y. 100; Agate v. Sands, 73 N. Y. 620; 

Wheeler v. Millar, 90 N. Y. 353. A director, who purchased judgments against his corporation when insolvent, was allowed to offset only the amount that he paid for them, since, being a fiduciary, and the corporation insolvent, it was his duty to conserve its assets for creditors. Bulkley v. Whitcomb, 121 N. Y. 107, 24 N. E. 13.
