Sec. 230. Defined. Usual methods of reorganization.

231. Reorganization by agreement (novation). 

232. The court's part. 

233. The reorganization committee's part. 

234. Reorganization by reincorporation in another state. 

235. Merger and consolidation. 

Reorganization defined. Methods. 

Reorganization, as the term is used in this chapter, means the succession of a group, composed of stockholders and creditors, to the assets of the corporation. The term is also used to describe a reorganization within the corporation. 

Some states have statutes authorizing a court to confirm by its decree a reorganization plan. By the decree, the rights of all parties to the suit, whether creditors or stockholders, are finally and conclusively determined. Willins v. 

Mann, 98 N. W. 341, 367 (Minn.); Park v. Grant Loco. 

Works, 3 Atl. 162, affd. 19 Atl. 621 (N. J.); Linn v. Jos. 

Dixon Cruc. Co., 35 Atl. 2 (N. J.). This practice is similar to that under the English statute which empowers the court to examine into the reorganization plan and confirm it by a decree which the statute makes conclusive upon all those who have been made parties to the suit, including the dissenting stockholders and creditors, by a scaling down of debts by major vote of 34 in value of the claims of each class of creditors affected. 35 and 36 Victoria, chap. 41, § 7.

English Companies (Consolidation) Act of 1908, § 192; 

Halsbury's Laws of England, vol. 5, pp. 602, 604-609; 11 

Fletch. Cyc. Corps. sec. 4856.

Reorganizations may be divided into two great classes, consisting, first, of what might be termed "reorganizations without judicial proceedings" and second, "reorganizations brought about in litigation." The first class comprises such methods as reorganizing by the agreement of all, accompanied by the dissolution of the old corporation, and a novation by which the assumption by the succeeding corporation of all debts and liabilities of the old is consented to by all parties, or by sale (S. C. L. 20-22); or by dissolution 387

(chap. XIX, infra), which may be accomplished through the consent of a specified majority, or, if the statute so provides, by the acts of the board alone, or by merger or consolidation (S. C. L. 85-90). These, in contemplation of law, occasion no losses to creditor or stockholder. The second class includes reorganizations brought about in the course of litigation, by the use, frequently, of the means indicated in the first class, and the novation agreement, which is usually submitted to the court. The litigation usually assumes the form of bankruptcy proceedings, or a suit for the foreclosure of a mortgage made by the corporation, or other proceedings in which a receiver may be appointed (G. C. L. 

150, S. C. L. 98); suits or actions by bondholders or other creditors; sequestration proceedings (G. C. L. 70) ; involuntary dissolution (chap. XIX, infra); or assignments for the benefit of creditors, meaning thereby all creditors (Debtor and Creditor law, art. 2). The last is a proceeding of ancient origin, adapted to prevent a grasping, vindictive creditor from getting an advantage over the others by the use of judicial processes. The statutory sale of franchises and property contemplates a sale for the stock of a new corporation, tho it is a reorganization of the old corporation, and for that reason, the statute specifies that the sale shall be to a domestic corporation, thus perpetuating the jurisdiction of the New York courts. Wegman v. Levinson 

Shoe Mfg. Co., 195 N. Y. Supp. 535. 

§ 231. Reorganization by Agreement. 

When a corporation becomes distressed financially, the larger investors, motivated by a desire to save what they can of their investment or the debt, and to avoid the waste of a receivership or forced sale, are the only ones who can be induced to come to its aid. Sometimes the group incorporates to buy in the assets at a forced execution sale under a judgment held by some large creditor or lienor. 

S. C. L. 96-99. At other times, the group appoints a committee to salvage the wreck and to try to arrange for all creditors and stockholders to take stock in the new corporation, or reorganized corporation, scaling down their claims to a sum commensurate with the assembled assets and probabilities. Those who sign lose their remedy against

the old corporation, its officers and members, and are bound by novation, the elements of which are the agreement to discharge the former claim or right, and the agreement of the new corporation to assume the reduced claim. The old corporation is destroyed by some legal method (chap. XIX, infra), and such of its members and creditors as come into the novation are relieved and deprived-both individually and collectively-from and of all existing rights and liabilities, except such as have been expressly reserved to them by the agreement. Keeler v. Salisbury, 33 N. Y. 648. Richardson's "Outline of Contracts," secs. 329 and 418. Habirshaw Electric Cable Co. v. Habirshaw Electric Cable Co., 296 Fed. 875, 879. The dissentient stockholders and creditors can neither be deprived of such legal rights as they have, by the charter, to share in the assets in the old corporation, nor can they be compelled by judicial decree to enter into the new agreement, or to scale down their claims, or to omit any of their legal rights against the old corporation and its officers or members. Cole v. Millerton Iron Co., supra; Darcy v. Brooklyn &c Ferry Co., supra; Hurd v. 

N. Y. &c Steam Laundry, supra; Teague v. Ridgway, 145 

App. Div. 277, 130 N. Y. Supp. 84; Logan v. N. Y. Sugar 

Ref. Co., 176 App. Div. 660, 163 N. Y. Supp. 214, 177 App.

Div. 926. The whole novation agreement is one freely made and entered into as the result of negotiations with the committee, and it does not follow that each of the parties thereto signed for an equally proportionate consideration. In 

Canada, and other countries where the constitution does not forbid the enactment of laws impairing the obligation of contracts, the legislative power may pass valid statutory provisions, even retroactively, binding the minority creditors and stockholders in a reasonable way by the will of the majority; and where the power exists, its exercise in the foreign state is binding on stockholders and creditors residing in New York as well. Canada Southern Railroad 

Co. v. Gebhard, 109 U. S. 527. Without clear statutory power to do so, a corporation can not transfer its members to another, whether the latter be a reorganized corporation or not. But in no way can stockholders of the old corporation who come into the reorganized corporation be given preference over dissentient creditors of the old corporation,

as to the property and assets of the old corporation. Statutory provisions to that effect, whether retrospective or prospective, would violate the constitutional rights of creditors, by impairing the obligation of debts "contracted by...bodies corporate," and by depriving them of "property without due process of law." N. Y. Constitution, art. I, secs. 6 and 17.

U. S. Constitution, art. I, § 10; am. V, 1. The legislature has no power to take property from one individual and give it to another. The leading case in point is Northern 

Pacific Railway v. Boyd, 228 U. S. 508, 33 Sup. Ct. Rep. 562, 57 L. ed. 931. In the Boyd case, a mortgage was foreclosed against the Northern Pacific Railroad Company.

A reorganization committee, representing a number of bondholders and stockholders of the railroad, comprising the promoters of a reorganization, bid in the property at foreclosure sale for 61 million dollars, pursuant to a promotion plan of reorganization, to which the bondholders and stockholders had subscribed by a contract executed by such as decided to do so. The railroad company had outstanding in dollars, 157 millions of bonds, and 155 millions of stock,-circumstantial evidence tending to prove the inadequacy of the purchase price for which the stockholders of the old company bid in at foreclosure. The court order, which directed the sale of the property in the proceeding to foreclose the mortgage, directed that the property be sold free from the debts owing to subordinate lienors or creditors. So, by becoming the successful bidders at the foreclosure sale at public auction, the stockholders and creditors who were members of the reorganizing group, became, in appearance, possessed of the railroad's assets by a right which seemingly was superior to the corporate creditors who were cut off by the foreclosure, and who had not come into the agreement. The aforesaid subscribers incorporated under the name "Northern Pacific Railway Co." In pursuance of the aforesaid contract, made by the promoters, the railway company took care only of such of the bondholders of the railroad, and of the preferred and common stockholders of the railroad as had signed the novation agreement. With these alone, it exchanged the bonds of the railway company for the bonds of the railroad company, and, in similar fashion, the stock, upon the payment of

small assessments per share $10 preferred, $15 common. 

Boyd was one of the unsecured creditors, seemingly wiped out by the foreclosure decree, who did not sign the novation agreement. In fact, the reorganizers, after the promotion was under way, made no tender or offer of an opportunity to Boyd to come in on the same scale as the others, the reason being, it may be inferred, that Boyd had not taken the initial steps to align himself with those promoting the protective plan prior to the foreclosure sale, or to contribute to their expenses. After the railway company had taken title, Boyd brought his creditors suit to follow trust funds of the railroad company, and asked that a receiver be appointed for the railway company. The application for a receiver is always addressed to the grace of the court, and, in this case, it was held that the application would be granted, and Boyd be permitted to follow the property of the railroad into the railway, at least to the amount by which the stockholders of the railroad had profited thereby, determinable by an accounting. Equality is equity. Between equal equities the law will prevail, but the equitable right of the creditor to be paid out of the assets is superior to the legal title of stockholders derived from a foreclosure sale of the corporate assets. The stockholders, it is true, have the right to protect their interest in or about the property which is threatened by the foreclosure sale, but they will not be permitted to exercise this right to produce an inequitable result. Stockholders rights, by whatever device or semblance of title, under a decree consented to by the litigating parties, should not be held superior to those of corporate creditors. Central Imp. Co. v. Cambria Steel Co., 210 Fed. 696. The United States courts announced as a "fixed principle" that "no such proceedings can be rightly carried to consummation which recognize and preserve any interest in the stockholders without also recognizing and preserving the interests, not only of the mortgagee, but of every creditor of the corporation." Kansas City Ry. v. 

Cent. Union Tr. Co., 271 U. S. 445, 46 Sup. Ct. 549; Pierce v. U. S., 255 U. S. 398. See, generally, Kansas City Ry. v. 

Guardian Trust Co., 240 U. S. 166; Central Improvement 

Co. v. Cambria Steel Co., supra; Howard v. Maxwell Motor 

Co., 269 Fed. 292.

§ 232. The Court's Part in Reorganizing. 

The approval of the reorganization plan is discretionary with the court. In New Jersey, the court withheld its approval of an agreement which merely extended the time of payment where the corporation was hopelessly insolvent and no additional capital was pledged by the reorganization agreement. Fleming v. Fleming Hotel Co., 61 Atl. 739.

In the federal courts, in New York, and in other states where no statute similar to that in New Jersey has been passed, a contract, amounting to a novation, whereby all the bondholders and stockholders agree to readjust their rights and equities, will accomplish the same end, but is not binding on any stockholder or creditor who withholds his assent. Northern Pac. R. Co. v. Boyd, supra; Schwab v. Potter Co., supra; Logan v. N. Y. Sugar Ref. Co., 176 

App. Div. 660, 163 N. Y. Supp. 214, 177 App. Div. 926.

But the court may, nevertheless, approve the reorganization plan and the efforts of the reorganization committee as reasonable. The court may take the reorganization plan into consideration, if a creditor, who has been given opportunity to participate on a reasonable basis, rejects it. If such a creditor later seeks the grace of the court in an attempt to pursue the reorganized corporation by drastic equitable remedies, such as suits for an accounting, or injunction, or an application for the appointment of a receiver of the reorganized corporation-remedies that might put the reorganization out of business-the court, in its discretion, may refuse its favor and remit the creditor to his legal remedies. The creditor, so remitted to his legal remedies, will have, of course, the burden of proof of showing damages, including the difference in value between the assets of the old corporation and the amount paid for them by the new corporation. This burden is difficult to sustain. The 

Interstate Commerce Commission is vested with the right to pass upon the acquisition of properties pursuant to a reorganization plan of common carriers. 71 I. C. C. Rep. 653; 

79 I. C. C. Rep. 782; 99 I. C. C. Rep. 382; Sharfman, "The

Interstate Commerce Commission" in loc. So, too, the Federal Trade Commission, under authority of sec. 7 of the 

Clayton Act, has condemned mergers between competing

companies "where the effect may be to substantially lessen competition" between the companies. In New York state, the Public Service Commission is given express authority to pass upon the proposed merger and consolidation of all public utilities. See sec. 71, supra, dealing with combinations and prohibited pools. People ex rel. West. &c R. R. 

Co. v. P. S. C., 210 N. Y. 456.

Those contributing to the expense fund of the reorganization committee may provide that it shall not be paid out except by order of the court, and, in that event, the Interstate Commerce Commission can not reach it. U. S. v. 

Chi., Milwaukee, St. Paul & Pac. R. R. Co., 51 Sup. Ct. 

Rep. 159.

In the above instances, the reorganization of solvent companies whose assets exceeded their liabilities has been spoken of. If the company is insolvent, there are no trust funds to follow, and a creditor, who has been given an opportunity to come into the reorganized company on the same basis as the stockholder of the old company, will not be aided by the court if he brings an action to follow trust funds. The burden of proof will be placed on the plaintiff to show that there are trust funds to follow. The court also may grant an injunction restraining the creditor of the insolvent company from bringing an action to recover the earnings of the new company. Phipps v. Chi., R. I. & P. 

Ry., 284 Fed. 945. The measure of recovery by a dissentient creditor is based upon the value of the participation of the stockholders of the old company in the new company, so far as their interests were subject to the creditor. Okmulgee 

Window Glass Co. v. Frink, 260 Fed. 159. If their interest is valueless, he gets nothing. Howard v. Maxwell Motor 

Co., 269 Fed. 292, 305. If the said value is insufficient to pay all creditors in full, the plaintiff may recover only a proportion, calculated by determining the aggregate value of the interest given to said stockholders as a class, the value assigned to it being an aliquot share of the new corporation at the date of reorganization, considered as a going concern, and pro-rating that value among the unsecured creditors of the old, as a class. Southern Pacific Co. v. 

Bogart, 250 U. S. 483.

§ 233. The Reorganization Committee's Part. 

The committee's work is to ascertain the cause of trouble, for instance, whether it is too great boldness in the policy of expansion, or too little capital; to repair losses, which may include bringing stockholders representative or derivative actions; bring claimants into line, which may require the satisfying of importunate creditors, the holding off of those whose claims will be more economically settled by delay, and bringing as many as they can into the reorganization plan by a contract with the committee; to provide a new management by men whose names will inspire confidence; and generally to provide for readjustments. The club which the committee often brandishes to force all parties into line is that of a liquidation and dissolution with small dividends and large losses to all. The committee advertises for claims of creditors to be filed with it, and circularizes the stockholders. The agreement between the committee and those who join with them should be so drawn as to bind them, as by a contract. Sales will usually be delayed by a court where it is shown that a reorganization plan is under way, for a refusal of an adjournment is likely to prove disastrous. In the "maze of rights," compromises become necessary and the recalcitrant creditor must frequently be given a larger share. The latest expression of the court on this point is in Habirshaw Electric 

Cable &c Co. v. Habirshaw Electric Cable Co., Inc., 296 

Fed. 875 (1924, So. Dist. of New York). In that case, a receiver had been appointed. The bondholders deposited all their bonds with a committee under a deposit agreement and about 80% of the creditors were represented by a reorganization committee. Creditors claims for merchandise, etc., furnished the corporation, and bank claims and debenture bonds of $1,514,000 out of $1,894,500 issued, were deposited.

Their plan for reorganization necessitated a sale of the assets and contemplated raising 1½ millions of new money. 

Some of the creditors moved to be released from the reorganization agreement. The court restated the following propositions: 1. In a receivership the court may properly reorder a sale, irrespective of any plan of reorganization, and may, in some instances, divide the property pro rata

among creditors or stockholders, or confirm debts paid, or return it to the owners. The court has no power to decree what the reorganization plan shall be, but merely whether it is a properly liberalized plan. 3. The deposit and reorganization agreements are voluntary agreements over which the court has no summary jurisdiction and the "fact that parties intervene does not here transmit a summary proceeding into a suit in equity." 4. The court cannot compel anyone to deposit shares or bonds with the committee, nor can it relieve anyone from a deposit made, unless for proper cause it is established in an appropriate suit brought for appropriate relief. The procedure does not affect the res. How far reorganization managers can go towards rehabilitating the corporate affairs is shown in 

Nolte et al. v. Hudson Nav. Co., 47 Fed. (2d) 166, where it was held that it was neither against public policy nor against any other theory for the reorganization managers of bondholders to buy up large amounts of unsecured claims. 

§ 234. Reorganization by Reincorporation in another 

State.

Reincorporation in another state is usually held to create a new identity, exempt from the liabilities of the old. 

Okmulgee Window Glass Co. v. Frink, 260 Fed. 159; 

Quincy Ry. Br. Co. v. County of Adams, 88 Ill. 615; Goodwin v. N. Y. &c R. Co., 124 Fed. 358; Patch v. Wabash 

R. R. Co., 207 U. S. 277, 52 L. ed. 204, 28 Sup. Ct. 80.

Where there is an intent that the new corporation shall be a continuation of the old, it may be treated as a reorganization, subject to the liabilities of the old. In John H. Giles 

Dyeing Mach. Co. v. Klauder-Weldon Dyeing Mach. Co., 212 

App. Div. 771, 209 N. Y. Supp. 616, affd. 243 N. Y. 547, pursuant to the consent of the stockholders at a meeting duly called, the directors sold and conveyed, under the statute, the assets to a Pennsylvania corporation whose officers and stockholders were identical with those of the 

New York corporation. The Pennsylvania corporation assumed the debts of the New York corporation. The New 

York corporation was not dissolved. It was held that the directors of the New York corporation were not liable in an action brought by a dissenting stockholder to compel

them to account for the assets, and that the Pennsylvania corporation could be sued for the debts of the New York corporation. The court said: "It is generally true that a creditor of a corporation cannot be deprived of his equitable lien upon the assets of the corporation by an agreement between the corporation and the transferee of its property that the latter shall assume all the corporate debts without the consent of the creditor. Darcy v. Bklyn. & N. Y. F. 

Co., 196 N. Y. 99, 89 N. E. 461. But here there was statutory authority for the thing done, and there was no real change of the debtor; the debtor had simply changed its name and residence. Otherwise, all the circumstances of the two corporations were identical...It was but natural that after the transfer, the Pennsylvania corporation should avail itself of the unused check books of the New York corporation... These transactions did not occasion insolvency...in no respect has the plaintiff been prejudiced or suffered damage by these transactions." Complaint dismissed. See, also, Cardozo, J. in Giles Dyeing Mach. Co. v. 

Klauder-Weldon Dyeing Mach. Co., 233 N. Y. 470, 135 N. E. 

854, Cady's Cas. p. 567. Identity of purpose, name, stockholders, management, and assets, may be proved as evidence of intent. Racine Eng. & M. Co. v. Confectioners 

Mach. & Mfg. Co., 234 Fed. 876; Davis v. Hemingway, 127 

Atl. 514 (Conn.); 39 A. L. R. 133, 143. A mere change in name does not affect identity, but is a fact to be weighed with the other facts. First Soc. of M. E. Church v. 

Brownell, 5 Hun 464.

When a corporation succeeds to the property of another by purchase and transfer (S. C. L. 20, 21) in the absence of a statute imposing liability (as in merger and consolidation), it is not liable for the debts of the first. If there was an express agreement to pay or assume them, or if the transfer was a fraud on creditors of the old corporation, such as a transfer for a grossly inadequate price would evidence, the new corporation would be liable, at least to the value of the assets received, if pursued under the trust fund theory, in an action to set aside the transaction, or as a fraudulent conveyance. Cole v. Millerton Iron Co., supra. 

A reorganization under a statute does not operate to dis-

charge the former corporation from its debts, or transfer the members who do not consent to the change. Gardner v. Ham. Ins. Co., supra. 

§ 235. Merger or Consolidation as Methods of Reor ganizing.

While the statute, S. C. L. 86, permits consolidation of any stock corporations, the dissenting minority may interfere, and enjoin a proposed consolidation, where the resultant powers of the new corporation would not be, in all respects, intra vires the corporation of which he is a member, or where it will produce unfairness, fraud, or oppression. 

Colby v. Equit. Tr. Co., 124 App. Div. 262, 108 N. Y. Supp. 

978, affd., 192 N. Y. 535; Young v. Rondout & K. G. Co., 129 N. Y. 57, 29 N. E. 83; Morse v. Eq. Lf. &c Co., 124 

App. Div. 335, 108 N. Y. Supp. 986. In the absence of statute, an agreement between two or more corporations to effect a consolidation thereof is ultra vires and invalid unless the power to consolidate is expressly conferred by the corporate charters. In re MacDonald, 205 App. Div. 579, 199 N. Y. Supp. 873; Greenville &c Co. v. Planters &c Co., 70 S. W. 669 (Miss.); Peo. ex rel. Eikemeyer &c Co. v. Rice, 66 Hun 130, 21 N. Y. Supp. 48, affd. 138 N. Y. 614. While it is within the province of a legislature to determine the status of the reorganized corporation, it has no power to authorize the consolidation of a domestic corporation with a foreign corporation without first obtaining the consent of the legislature of the foreign state. Peo. v. N. Y., Chi. &c Ry. Co., 129 N. Y. 475.

The New York statute, S. C. L. 85, 86, provides that the possessor corporation in a merger, or the new corporation resulting from a consolidation shall, in either case, be liable for the debts and succeed to the property rights of the original and consolidated corporations. Barr v. Atcheson &c Co., 230 N. Y. 158, 130 N. E. 458; Irvine v. N. Y. Ed. 

Co., 207 N. Y. 425, 101 N. E. 358. Merger, however, does not extinguish the right of a creditor of the merged corporation to sue it on any debt, and to have execution against it, or to pursue its assets in equity. Ib. Royal Bak. Powd. 

Co. v. Hoagland, 180 N. Y. 35, 72 N. E. 674. See sec. 70,

supra. Guaranty Tr. Co. v. N. Y. & Q. Ry. Co., 253 N. Y. 

190, 170 N. E. 887, 254 N. Y. 126, 172 N. E. 264, affd. 51

U. S. Sup. Ct. 86. Merger is effectuated, under the statute, by the directors alone. If it is improvident, or if the directors were impelled by motives inconsistent with the welfare of the stockholders, a minority stockholder may enjoin the merger. Armstrong v. Hayden, 126 Misc. 786, 214 N. Y. 

Supp. 747. A covenant inserted in a mortgage of property belonging to a corporation, which is later merged by another, to the effect that the mortgage should cover property that might thereafter be acquired by it and its successors, can only be enforced against a merging corporation thru some other act sufficient to constitute an estoppel or kindred equity. Gty. Tr. Co. v. N. Y. & Q. R. R. Co., supra.

S. C. L. 86 was amended by c. 55, L. 1931, in effect July 

1, 1931. The object of the change is to furnish the secretary of state with the details of the shares to be issued so that there may be a basis for computing the tax under Tax Law 180. The amendment also provides that the secretary of state shall make and transmit to the county clerk a certified copy of the certificate of consolidation. This changes the practice, so that it will not be necessary for the corporation to file the certificate elsewhere than in the secretary of state's office. The statute also lays down a rule for the ascertainment of what part of the assets of the new corporation are required to be carried in capital account, and what part may be regarded as surplus, when the new company is to have shares without par value.

The statute dealing with consolidation is permissive merely, and though the required number of consents is obtained, a dissenting stockholder will be permitted a temporary injunction where he can show that the result of such consolidation will be injurious to the corporation and perhaps, even, an unconstitutional interference with vested rights of property. Young v. Rondout & Kingston &c Co., 15 N. Y. Supp. 443, appeal dismissed, 129 N. Y. 57, 29

N. E. 83. A dissenting stockholder may have an appraisal. 

S. C. L. 38.

Unless a stockholder shows that the proposed statutory consolidation and transfer of the assets to the new company

amounts to confiscation of its property, or to deprivation of its vested property rights, or to an illegal or unauthorized act of the majority, he can not obtain an injunction pendente lite enjoining the proposed consolidation under the statute. The proposed merger need not be such as would have been permitted under the charter, except for the statute. Colby v. Equitable Tr. Co., supra. In the case last mentioned, a stockholders suit to enjoin the proposed merger of the defendant bank with the Mercantile Trust Co., stressed the above points, and showed that while the two companies had equal capital, the Equitable stockholders were to turn in their shares for the new stock, and the Mercantile stockholders were to get %. The book value of the Equitable stock was about $870 a share, that of the new company $600 a share, and of the Mercantile $452 a share. The court held that there was no unfairness in this deal, and put greater emphasis on the earning capacity than on the book value. The Mercantile was earning unusual dividends of 51% on par value and the Equitable, 25%. The Equitable had suffered seriously from the depression of 1907, and had lost valuable connections, which would likely reduce its earning capacity to 4%. The estimated dividends on the new stock would be about 48% par.

In the 1930 proposed merger of Bethlehem Steel with the 

Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co., the Youngstown stockholders were to receive 1% shares of the new corporation for every share of Youngstown surrendered. The disparity in book value was not urged in the suit brought to restrain the merger, but only the earning power.

CHAPTER XIX. 

DISSOLUTION. 

Sec. 236. Dissolution defined. Methods. 

237. By expiration of time. 

238. By extinguishment. 

239. By surrender of charter. 

240. By proceedings against it by the state. Forfeiture for misuse of charter. 

241. By absorption. 242.

Directors and officers as trustees on dissolution. 

243. Suits and actions after dissolution. 

244. Dissolution of foreign corporations. § 236.

Definitions. Methods. 

By dissolution is meant the termination of the corporate franchise by means prescribed by law for putting an end to the corporation. Every corporate power is lost by dissolution, and the non-existence of the corporation may be pleaded to defeat claims arising from acts purporting to have been done pursuant to chartered rights in the corporate name, after dissolution. Matter of Brooklyn, Winfield & 

Newton Ry. Co., 72 N. Y. 245. Dissolution is, therefore, to be distinguished from a total cessation of business over a long period, James & Co. v. 2d Russian Ins. Co., 239 

N. Y. 248, 146 N. E. 369, Brock v. Poor, supra; from a liquidation, which merely means the winding up of the affairs of the company, Assets Realization Co. v. Howard, 70 

Misc. 651, 127 N. Y. Supp. 798, affd. 152 App. Div. 900, 211 N. Y. 430, 105 N. E. 680; and from a receivership, the effect of which is to leave the franchise intact, but denude the corporation of its assets, Peo. v. N. Y. C. Ry. Co., 57 

Misc. 114, 107 N. Y. Supp. 247.

A corporation may be put to an end in the following ways: 1. By act of Legislature repealing the charter, where the right to repeal has been reserved therein, or where the grant was unconstitutional. Long Sault Dev. 

Co. v. Kennedy, supra. See sec. 110, supra. 2. By expiration of the time limit stated in the charter. See sec. 35, supra. The fixed time may be specified to depend upon the performance of a condition, with or without action taken 1 400

DISSOLUTION 

401 by the state. Mtr. of Bklyn. W. & N. Ry. Co., supra. 3. By extinguishment, resulting from the death of all its members, or from the loss of some integral part of its property for the exploitation of which the corporation was formed. 

4. By the surrender of its charter, pursuant to some provision therein, or the acceptance of the surrender by the legislature. 5. By proceedings against it by the state, as a punishment for the misuse of its franchise. 6. By absorption into another corporation or by extinguishment as by consolidation, merger, or reorganization.

§ 237. Dissolution by expiration of time. 

If the charter provides that the corporation shall continue "until" a specified day, it expires at the end of the preceding day. § 35, supra. If the charter merely fixes a stated term of corporate existence, the corporation may

continue as a de facto corporation, providing there is a statute under which steps might be taken to extend the charter. If it so continues, nothing but quo warranto proceedings or voluntary dissolution will terminate it, § 35, supra. Peo. ex rel. Haberman v. James, 5 App. Div. 412, 39 N. Y. Supp. 313. The corporate existence can only be attacked by the state in a direct proceeding for that purpose. The issue can not be raised by the state or by anybody else collaterally to defeat actions brought by the corporation. Holmes Elec. Prot. Co. v. Williams, 181 App. 

Div. 687, 168 N. Y. Supp. 746, rev. 228 N. Y. 407. 

§ 238. Dissolution by Extinguishment. 

Dissolution by demise of all the members, or of those necessary to constitute a quorum, disrupted corporate life at common law, at a time when there were only ecclesiastical, eleemosynary, municipal, and nonstock corporations. 

Philips v. Wickham, 1 Pai. 590. The rules of law derived from this principle can have no application to modern stock corporations wherein the stock, upon the death of a member, passes to others by inheritance or through bequests. Even a membership corporation is not dissolved by the death of all its members. M. C. L. 55, 56. The want of proper officers does not dissolve the corporation, for others may supply their place. Peo. v. Twaddell, supra. Foss v. Harbottle, supra. Statutes permit the court to dissolve a corporation where there are not enough to carry on. G. C. L. 

170. If the legislature has reserved power to amend the charter, a means of exercising the powers granted might be provided by special act of the legislature, although the remaining members were too few to constitute a quorum for the election of officers; or, the legislature itself, it seems, might designate officers, and so overcome the "torpidity" of the body, without thereby creating a new corporation. § 110, supra; New York Constitution Art. III, § 18; Art. VIII, § 1. 

G. C. L., 5.

Nonperformance of the act of incorporation is ground for an action by the state to forfeit the charter, but such default does not, of itself, work a forfeiture. In re Kings 

County El. R. R. Co., 105 N. Y. 97, 13 N. E. 8; Day v.

DISSOLUTION 

403 

Ogdensburg & Lk. Champlain R. R. Co., supra. A statute may make a ground of forfeiture self executing. Bklyn. 

Steam Transit Co. v. Bklyn., 78 N. Y. 524. Cf. G. C. L. 30.

Such construction of the statute is not favored, and requires strong and unmistakable language. N. Y. & L. I. 

Bridge Co. v. Smith, 148 N. Y. 540. Peo. v. Buffalo Stone & 

Cement Co., 131 N. Y. 140. Some decisions holding the statutes there under consideration self-executing, and working an ipso facto dissolution are: Re Brooklyn Winfield & 

Newtown R. R. Co., supra; Ib., 72 N. Y. 245; Sturges v. 

Vanderbilt, supra; Peo. v. Stillwell, supra. The words, "shall be deemed dissolved," were held not to be self-executing in Peo. v. Hillsdale & Chatham Turnpike Road, 23 

Wend. 254.

By the New Jersey statutes, the dissolved corporation is a necessary party to a stockholders representative action, and if there are no members remaining of the board of directors, the plaintiff stockholder bringing said action must appeal to the stockholders to elect a board as a condition precedent to his action. In default of an election in accordance with the aforesaid demand, the plaintiff stockholder must move for the appointment of a receiver as a substitute for liquidating trustees. Watts v. Vanderbilt, 45 Fed. (2d) 968. 

§ 239. Dissolution by Surrender of Charter. 

At common law a corporation was dissolved by the voluntary surrender of its charter with the acceptance of the state. Acceptance might be evidenced by special act of the legislature. Slee v. Bloom, 19 Johns. 456, 5 Johns. Ch. 366. 

There are today two methods of voluntary dissolution.

Voluntary dissolution of a domestic corporation without judicial proceedings is accomplished by filing the papers required by S. C. L. 105. Either unanimous consent of the stockholders is requisite, or, if no stock has been issued, the consent of all the corporators and subscribers to stock, or, in the alternative, the consent of a two thirds majority at a meeting duly called. For other details, the statute should be consulted. Creditors are not made parties to the proceeding, and receive notice only through the publication of the notice of dissolution, and its filing with the county

clerk. No consent of creditors is required, and their rights and actions are not affected. S. C. L. 105. 

While the stockholders under S. C. L. 105 have the ultimate determination as to dissolution, the majority must exercise the corporate power in good faith. Kavanaugh v. 

Kavanaugh Knitting Co., 226 N. Y. 185; Major v. American 

Malt &c Co., 110 Misc. 132, 181 N. Y. Supp. 152. The court is not bound by the action of the stockholders, and must exercise its own discretion if the minority oppose and endeavor to enjoin the dissolution, but the decision by the majority to dissolve will not be lightly overruled. In re 

American Tel. & Cable Co., 139 Misc. 625, 248 N. Y. Supp. 

98. If the stockholders reject the proposition for voluntary dissolution, and the board purposes to give the assets to the majority, a continuing director, in order to avoid complicity in the bad faith of the management, should bring proceedings for a judicial dissolution under G. C. L. 101. Kroger v. 

Jaburg, 231 App. Div. 641, 248 N. Y. Supp. 387. After the dissolution is completed under the statute, the directors wind up the business. Dissenting stockholders are entitled to an appraisal, if they take the necessary steps to require it. 

S. C. L. 105 (9). Creditors, learning of the proceeding, may apply for a receiver. S. C. L. 106.

The assets of the corporation will be protected by the court to prevent any person from obtaining an undue advantage. About the only advantage which an unpaid judgment creditor of the corporation has over a simple creditor is the ease of proving his claim, owing to the fact that the amount thereof has been liquidated and established. The assets of a dissolved corporation are protected in equity as a trust fund for creditors and stockholders, and persons receiving them with notice of their character, particularly when such persons are officers or stockholders of the corporation, take them subject to the trust and to the decrees of a court of equity with respect thereto. Failure to obey such decrees may be punishable as contempt of court. 7 

Ruling Case Law p. 740; Wheeler v. Pullman Iron & Steel 

Co., 143 Ill. 197, 32 N. E. 420, 17 L. R. A. 818; Clokey, admx. v. International &c Co., 28 Misc. 326, 59 N. Y. Supp. 

878. Where the dissolution is brought about by voluntary

DISSOLUTION 

405 judicial proceedings, it is usual for the decree dissolving the corporation to provide for the winding up of the company, the payment of its debts, and for the continuance of suits and actions in the names of the directors as trustees. All provisions of such a decree are to be construed together, and hence it has been said that "the corporation is not absolutely extinguished for all purposes, but, on the contrary, is expressly kept alive, so far as its existence may be necessary, to collect and apply its assets to the payment of debts." S. C. L. 105 (8). Commercial Loan & Trust Co. v. 

Mallers, 242 Ill. 50, 89 N. E. 661. § 240. 

Dissolution by Proceedings taken against the Corporation by the State.

The amendment of the corporate charter in invitum by the state does not dissolve the corporation. The non-acceptance of the amended charter, by the corporation, merely entails the discontinuance of business. Secs. 110, 111, supra.

The taking of all the corporate property under eminent domain proceedings does not terminate the corporation, unless the franchise is also taken. Sec. 114, supra. Even though the right to appeal and amend the charter has not been reserved by the state, the state, nevertheless, may proceed to dissolve the corporation by an action brought against it. Peo. v. North R. Sug. Ref. Co., supra. The essential feature of the complaint by the attorney general in said action is the performance of ultra vires acts. From earliest times, it has been held that a corporation which turns its privileges towards improper purposes is liable to suffer forfeiture. Peo. v. Manhattan Co., supra. The common law had two forms of proceedings applicable to the situation. One was quo warranto by which it was sought to suspend the corporate franchises. The other was scire facias which was brought to terminate an existing body. 

Quo warranto was the only proceeding that could be brought against a corporation de facto. Matter of New York and 

Long Island Bridge Co. v. Smith, 148 N. Y. 540; Peo. v. 

Utica Ins. Co., 15 Johns. 358. Though scire facias be brought, the court has discretion to determine whether there shall be a forfeiture. Peo. v. Ulster & Del. Ry. Co., 128 

N. Y. 240. G. C. L. 71 authorizes an action by the attorney

general. If he shall fail to bring such action for 60 days after a creditor or stockholder has submitted to him a verified statement of facts showing grounds for the action, the statute provides that a creditor or stockholder may apply on notice to the attorney general for an order from the supreme court for leave to bring such action. The grounds of the action may be that: 1. The corporation has remained insolvent for at least one year. 2. It has neglected or refused, for at least one year, to pay and discharge its notes or other evidences of debt. 3. It has suspended its ordinary and lawful business for at least one year. Under 

G. C. L. 91, the attorney general, upon leave being granted by the court, may bring an action to procure a judgment vacating the charter or annulling the existence of the corporation, upon the ground that it has, either 1. Offended against any provision of an act, by or under which it was created, altered or renewed, or an act amending the same; or, 2. Violated any provision of law whereby it has forfeited its charter, or by the abuse of its powers has become liable to be dissolved; or, 3. Forfeited its privileges or franchises, by a failure to exercise its powers; or 4.

Done or omitted any act, which amounts to a surrender of its corporate rights, privileges, and franchises; or, 5. Exercised a privilege or franchise, not conferred upon it by law. The granting of the order permitting the stockholder to bring the action rests in the sound discretion of the court. 

Atty. Gen. v. Cons. Gas Co., 124 App. Div. 401, 108 N. Y. 

Supp. 823.

The action under G. C. L. 71 does not require a preliminary application for permission or leave of court to bring the action. Under G. C. L. 91, an application to the court is required, but the parties are entitled to a jury trial. 

Herring v. N. Y., Lake Erie & Western R. R. Co., 105 

N. Y. 340, 389. Corporations have been dissolved for entering into partnership, Peo. v. North R. Sug. Ref. 

Co., supra; for acts in express violation of statute, for example, banking, Peo. v. Utica Ins. Co., supra; for the increase of capital stock without charter authorization, Peo. v. Parker Behn, 10 How. Pr. 1023; for unlawful restraint of trade, Peo. v. Exchange, 145 N. Y. 267; or for a failure

DISSOLUTION 

407 to make an annual report, Peo. v. Buffalo Stone & Cem. Co., 131 N. Y. 140. The state may bring in as parties defendant lessees or other persons interested. Peo. v. Albany &c Co., 77 N. Y. 232. § 241. Dissolution by Absorption, as by Merger or Consolidation.

Merger and consolidation have been discussed in secs. 70 and 227, supra. Upon filing the certificate of merger with the secretary of state, the possessed corporation ceases to exist. The possessor corporation takes its property subject to the liabilities and obligations of the possessed corporation and the rights of all creditors thereof. S. C. L. 85. 

In addition, the possessor corporation becomes liable for the said liabilities and obligations. Ib. If, after the certificate has been filed, the possessor corporation continues to conduct business in the name of the possessed corporation, it may be enjoined by the attorney general under C. P. A. 

1217 and 1218 (pp. 286, 287, supra) and the costs of the proceeding may be collected by execution against any of the persons who claim to be members of the corporation. 

C. P. A. 1220. The injunction action is triable by a jury and the witnesses called by the attorney general are entitled to immunity. C. P. A. 1219 and 1221. A similar action may be brought against those who use the name of the corporation that was absorbed by consolidation. Cf., Pen. 

L. 440.

At common law, even tho the right to sell all assets to another corporation was included in the charter, as is the case today with all New York stock corporations (S. C. L. 

20), it was nevertheless held that unless the member consented, or unless, by virtue of a voluntary novation, by the stockholder, the new corporation succeeded to the rights and liabilities of the old under its contracts with the stockholders, he was entitled to his share of the property of the old corporation. Gardner v. Hamilton Mut. Ins. Co., 33 N. Y. 

421. The mere receipt of benefits from the new corporation has never been held to constitute per se a novation, and the statute requisite to making such act a novation was passed, first in England (Re Family Endowment Soc., L. R. 5 Ch.

118), and later in New York. S. C. L. 105, (9). The exact position of the dissentient stockholder or creditor under this provision seems to be as follows:-1. He may assent to the particular reorganization, and accept the proposed substitution of the new corporation, by a contract with or without particular modifications adapted to his case, and consented to by the corporation. This, by novation, binds both. Investment Reg. v. Chi. &c Ry., 212 Fed. 594. 2. The stockholder may dissent, and have his stock appraised, provided he gives notice within the time specified. Creditors who are pledgees of stock, also have the right of appraisal. 

Murrin v. Archbald Con. Coal Co., supra. 3. If he dissents, and his stock is appraised and purchased, he still remains liable to such creditors of the old corporations as have not consented to the reorganization plan by a valid and binding novation, providing he would have been liable to them by virtue of his stock not having been paid for, or for other related reason (S. C. L. 69-74). And if the corporation is insolvent, he may, under proper conditions, become liable for the corporate assets received by him. 

§ 242. Directors and Officers as Trustees. 

G. C. L. 29 provides that upon the dissolution of any corporation, its directors shall be the trustees for the creditors, stockholders, or members, and may sue and be sued in the corporate name. However, if other persons are designated by law, or by a court of competent jurisdiction, the power of the trustees fails.

A court of equity has power to appoint a receiver to carry out contracts, corresponding to the statutory provisions by which, upon dissolution, the directors are made trustees, vested with legal title to the corporate property, to administer the same for the benefit of all concerned. G. C. L. 29, 96. There is a distinction between a receiver of the property of the corporation, and a receiver of the corporation. 

The power of the court to appoint the former is inherent in the supreme court, Hegewisch v. Silver, 140 N. Y. 414, 35 N. E. 658; whereas the power to appoint the latter is entirely lacking unless conferred by statute. Mtr. of Atlas 

Iron Const. Co., 38 N. Y. Supp. 172, 72 N. Y. St. 801.

DISSOLUTION 

409 The situation is aptly illustrated in People v. O'Brien, 111 N. Y. 1. The company was incorporated in 1884 as a street railway corporation, and, within its powers, laid tracks and ran cars from Broadway to 15th street. Its license from the city to use its streets obligated it to make an annual payment to the city. After it had mortgaged its property and franchises, floated a bond issue, and made contracts with other companies for the use of their tracks to run its cars to distant parts of the city, the legislature repealed its charter. Thereafter the attorney general brought this suit to wind up its affairs and dissolve the corporation, perform its contracts, pay its debts, and to restrain the use of the defunct corporation's property by its lessees. It was held that the act of the legislature dissolving the corporation could not constitutionally destroy its vested property rights. The affairs of the company were being administered by the court through its receiver, and it was held that the attorney general was without power to bring an action on behalf of the people to regulate the procedure of this officer of the court. The franchises of the corporation derived from the municipality to lay its cars and to operate were vested property rights and were not destroyed. 

A receiver should not be appointed under G. C. L. 191 if the corporation is solvent, unless waste is either being committed or is being threatened. In re Seneca Oil Co., 153 

App. Div. 594, 138 N. Y. Supp. 78. If no diversion of funds is shown, the courts will not appoint a receiver. Miller v. 

Albertina Rty. Co., 198 App. Div. 340, 190 N. Y. Supp. 407.

On appointment, the receiver must marshal the assets of the corporation and the court has control of the declaration of dividends therefrom. If, however, it is for the best interests of all concerned, the receiver may be empowered by the court to continue the business. In re Union Bank of Brooklyn, 96 Misc. 299, 161 N. Y. Supp. 29. 

§ 243. Rights, Suits and Actions after Dissolution. 

Since a creditor has in general no right to interfere in the management, sec. 227, supra, he can not prevent the dissolution of the corporation before his debt is paid. 

Mumma v. Potomac Company, 8 Pet. 281. Neither will a court forfeit the charter on the application of creditors, tho

they show grounds on which forfeiture might be granted at the suit of the state. Cole v. Knickerbocker Life Ins. Co., 23 Hun 255, affd. 91 N. Y. 641. It is held, however, that a creditor, in an existing suit, may be granted an injunction to restrain the corporation from dissolving after the suit is brought. Fisk v. Union Pacific R. R. Co., 10 Blatch. 518.

If the state repeals the charter of the corporation, or if the corporation is dissolved under a general act of the legislature, creditors lose all rights to bring new actions or proceedings against the corporation, since there remains no existing corporate person who may be served with process. 

Thornton v. Marginal Freight Ry. Co., 123 Mass. 32. The corporation, after dissolution, is not liable for its debts. 

Discussing the constitutionality of a statute that repealed a charter, Justice Story, in the Mumma Case, supra, said: "We are of opinion, that the dissolution of the corporation under the acts of Virginia and Maryland...can not, in any just_sense, be considered, within the clause of the Constitution of the United States on this subject, an impairing of the obligations of the contracts of the company by those States, any more than the death of a private person can be said to impair the obligation of his contracts. The obligation of those contracts survives; and the creditors may enforce their claims against any property belonging to the corporation, which has not passed into the hands of bona fide purchasers; but is still held in trust for the company, or for the stockholders thereof, at the time of its dissolution, in any mode permitted by the local laws...A corporation, by the very terms and nature of its political existence, is subject to dissolution, by a surrender of its corporate franchises, and by a forfeiture of them for wilful misuser and nonuser. Every creditor must be presumed to understand the nature and incidents of such a body politic, and to contract with reference to them. And it would be a doctrine new to the law, that the existence of a private contract of the corporation should force upon it a perpetuity of existence contrary to public policy, and the nature and objects of its charter.” 

In the absence of statutory provision to the contrary, a corporation, after it is dissolved, can neither sue nor be sued. Sturgis v. Drew, 11 Hun 136. If, after it is dissolved, a complaint is served and the corporation answers, it is estopped to set up its dissolution. Fred S. James & 

Co. v. 2d Russian Ins. Co., supra. So, too, where the corporation is dissolved subsequent to the time when a suit was brought, the action will abate unless an order of continuance, continuing the action against the receiver or trustees, is entered, authorizing the continuance of the action. Mc- 

Cullock v. Norwood, 58 N. Y. 562. In many states, includ-

DISSOLUTION 

411 ing New York, the statute provides for a continuance by special term order of all suits that have been commenced against domestic corporations prior to their dissolution, the directors as trustees being substituted for the corporation as a defendant. G. C. L. 29. S. C. L. 105 (8) covers new actions, commenced by service of the summons after dissolution and permits the corporation to sue or be sued in its corporate name. City of New York v. N. Y. & So. 

Bklyn. Fy. & Steam Trans. Co., 231 N. Y. 18. The statute, as it now stands, applies to actions to enforce "existing liabilities and obligations." The amendment substituted this language for "debts and obligations" in order to meet the decision in the case last mentioned. For any debt, a creditor, if a judgment creditor, may sue the trustees. 

Bristol Mfg. Co. v. Elk Textile Co., 209 App. Div. 95, 204 

N. Y. Supp. 427. The stockholders may validly contract among themselves as to how losses from liquidation and obligations to creditors are to be shared among them. 

Mautner v. Eitingon, 197 App. Div. 754, 189 N. Y. Supp. 

565; Natl. Union Bk. of Watertown v. Landon, 45 N. Y. 

410. A creditor, even tho he is not a judgment creditor, and tho his debt does not become due till after dissolution, may enjoin waste by the directors after the dissolution, since he has an interest in the surplus assets. City Inv. 

Co. v. Gerkin, 200 App. Div. 503, 193 N. Y. S. 271.

The following principles have been laid down as to contracts not wholly performed at the date of dissolution:- (1) If the contract at the date of dissolution is wholly executory, and no breach has occurred to create a cause of action apart from the contract, the contract fails for impossibility of performance. The contracting party loses the goodness of his bargain because the chance of dissolution working this result must be conceived to be an implied condition of the contract. Illustration:-Where a general agent of a life insurance company, who had a contract with it to render services over a stipulated time at a specified salary, was prevented from rendering any services by reason of the fact that it was restrained by court order from prosecuting its business, it was held that he could not re cover. People v. Globe Mutual Life Ins. Co., 91 N. Y. 174.

(2). If the contract calls for personal services to be rendered to the corporation, its dissolution terminates the right to serve further. Ib. (3). If the corporation is dissolved when the contract is partly performed by the other party, the burden of proof is on the defendant, or its receiver, to plead and prove that the dissolution was necessary; and whether the dissolution relieved the corporation of its contracts is a question of fact to be determined at the trial. Ib. Mason v. Standard Distilling & Distributing 

Co., 85 App. Div. 520, 83 N. Y. S. 343. Stannard v. Robt. 

H. Reid & Co., 114 App. Div. 135, 99 N. Y. Supp. 567.

The rule of the common law as to the abatement of the cause of action against a corporation is unlike that concerning an individual. Under the common law, the maxim, "Actio personalis moritur cum persona," was interpreted to mean that actions for libel, slander, and assault and battery, and the like (Gen. Const. Law sec. 37a) did not survive the defendant's death, unless a different result was prescribed by a statute such as Dec. Est. Law, 130-134.

Actions ex delicto abated on the death of either party. 

Clough v. Gardner, 111 Misc. 244, 169 N. Y. S. 421. Civil death of either party was held insufficient to abate the action. Dissolution of a corporation does not so nearly simulate the death of an individual and the devolution of his property, as to relieve the corporate assets from the legal burden. The trustees of the corporation, after its dissolution, may be sued for a libel published by the corporation before it dissolved. Shayne v. Eve. Post Pub. Co., 168 N. Y. 

70. The receiver of a corporation is liable for instalments of rent accruing under a lease to the corporation, altho the receiver vacated the premises. These instalments might have been assigned by the landlord prior to dissolution, and thereby would not abate by the death of the tenant. Peo. v. Natl. Tr. Co., 82 N. Y. 283; C. P. A. 82. 

§ 244. Dissolution of Foreign Corporations. 

If a foreign corporation is dissolved in its domiciliary state, all actions pending against it in other states abate. 

To have this effect, the statute under which it is dissolved must not be penal. Huntington v. Attrill, supra. The foreign statute, providing for dissolution, is part of its charter

DISSOLUTION 

413 and it ceases to exist elsewhere for any purpose. Even actions that were pending against it in this state at the date of the foreign dissolution fail for want of a party defendant. 

Sturges v. Vanderbilt, 73 N. Y. 384; Mtr. of Stewart, 39 

Misc. 275, 79 N. Y. Supp. 525, affd. 86 App. Div. 627, 177 

N. Y. 558.

The receiver appointed for a foreign corporation in the foreign jurisdiction usually takes precedence of an ancillary receiver appointed in New York. Creditors residing in 

New York are entitled to the protection of the laws of New York as to property found in this state, at least to the extent necessary to prevent the expense and inconvenience of requiring them to prove their claims in the foreign state. 

Drury v. Doherty, 131 Misc. 642, 227 N. Y. Supp. 593.

In a proceeding under G. C. L. 101 brought by a majority of the directors, the corporation may be dissolved and all claims of creditors disposed of, tho the majority of the stockholders oppose the proceeding. By the procedure indicated in G. C. L. 101, creditors may be restrained from beginning any actions against the corporation, and further proceedings in pending actions may be stayed. If the petitioning group holds one half the common stock, they have an absolute right to bring the proceeding. Re Willat Studios & Laboratories, Inc., 201 App. Div. 136, 194 N. Y. S. 243.
